It is also called the "voice of great exposition" because it expounds the profound meanings of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great clarification" because it clarifies the obscure points of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great illumination" because it illuminates the darkness of ignorance. It is also called the "voice of great rain" because it rains down the Dharma-rain upon all sentient beings. It is also called the "voice of great wind" because it sweeps away the dust of afflictions. It is also called the "voice of great fire" because it burns away the fuel of karma and afflictions. It is also called the "voice of great water" because it washes away the stains of defilement. It is also called the "voice of great earth" because it supports all sentient beings. It is also called the "voice of great space" because it pervades all places without obstruction. It is also called the "voice of great time" because it is eternal and unchanging. It is also called the "voice of great direction" because it reaches all directions without limit. It is also called the "voice of great realm" because it pervades all Buddha-realms. It is also called the "voice of great assembly" because it is heard by all assemblies of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. It is also called the "voice of great vehicle" because it carries all sentient beings to the Great Vehicle. It is also called the "voice of great emptiness" because it realizes the emptiness of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great signlessness" because it transcends all signs. It is also called the "voice of great wishlessness" because it is free from all desires. It is also called the "voice of great non-arising" because it realizes the non-arising of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-ceasing" because it realizes the non-ceasing of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-self" because it realizes the non-self of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-purity" because it realizes the impurity of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-impurity" because it realizes the purity of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-duality" because it realizes the non-duality of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-distinction" because it realizes the lack of distinction between all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great equality" because it realizes the equality of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great suchness" because it realizes the suchness of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great reality-limit" because it realizes the reality-limit of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great dharma-realm" because it realizes the dharma-realm of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-obstruction" because it is unobstructed in all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-hindrance" because it is unhindered in all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-grasping" because it does not grasp at any dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-abandoning" because it does not abandon any dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-increase" because it does not increase any dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-decrease" because it does not decrease any dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-birth" because it does not give birth to any dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-death" because it does not die in any dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-suffering" because it is free from the suffering of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-joy" because it transcends the joy of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-grief" because it is free from the grief of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-desire" because it is free from the desire of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-love" because it is free from the love of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-hatred" because it is free from the hatred of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-delusion" because it is free from the delusion of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-view" because it is free from the views of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-conceptualization" because it is free from the conceptualizations of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-discrimination" because it is free from the discriminations of all dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-manifestation" because it does not manifest any dharmas. It is also called the "voice of great non-appearance" because no dharmas appear therein. It is also called the "voice of great non-existence" because no dharmas exist therein. It is also called the "voice of great non-non-existence" because it is not a mere non-existence.

[The Buddha speaks] for three reasons: first, to fulfill their wishes; second, to sever their doubts; and third, in accordance with those to be converted, he may speak using unchanging forms or by transforming his forms.
One school asserts that it is impossible for a single sound to cause all to understand; this is the tenet of the Sarvāstivāda and other such sects.
However, the statement in the *Gāthā* that [the Buddha] is able to cause them to understand does not necessarily require such an interpretation, nor is it contradictory.
Because it is the Tripiṭaka and because it transcends reality, as the Vibhajyavādins say: "The Blessed One’s mind is always in meditative concentration," and so forth.
Furthermore, one reconciles the meaning of the "single sound" (*ekasvara*) through three points: first, because it is foremost in every respect, it is called "one";
second, because its swiftness is like being one, it is called "one"; third, because its benefit is the same, it is called "one. Now, based on this...
The Mahāyāna is able to teach with a single voice; thus, the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* states: "One is able to respond universally to all voices with a single sound.
Furthermore, the *Great Sūtra of the Inconceivable* states: "In a single utterance of the Tathāgata’s teaching, he expounds an ocean of boundless sūtras.
And the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "When the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings each [hear it] according to their own kind."
This is understood. Furthermore, the sixth fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) manifests transformed vocal actions according to the differences in the inclinations and dispositions of sentient beings, expounding various meanings and severing all doubts; that is to say, it emits a single sound."
This represents all meanings and ensures that all sentient beings obtain benefit according to their respective types. As the Sūtra says:

"The Buddha expounds all dharmas with a single voice; sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind—some feel fear, some feel joy, some develop weary detachment, and others sever their doubts.
This is the inconceivable array set forth by the Tathāgata’s original vows.
The transformative speech produced by the power of deliberation can sever all the doubts of the multitude with a single sound. Such explanations as these cannot be recounted in full.
However, this "single sound" refers to the one Brahma-voice; thus, the *Anantamukha-nirhāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra* says: "I bow my head and take refuge in the Brahma-voice.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 86, states: "Desiring to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings..."
He understands the languages and sounds of all sentient beings and preaches the Dharma using the Brahma-voice. Question:
Is that which is spoken by this single voice of the Tathāgata the primary substance (*bhāva*) or a reflection (*pratibimba*)?

If it is the primary substance, how do you reconcile this with the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, which states that [phenomena] lack intrinsic nature? If it is a reflection, it would become manifold according to each listener.

How can it be said that they are one? The explanation is as follows: According to the school of Dharmapāla and others, based on the definitive, primary teaching, [the *ālayavijñāna*] is only the original and not the reflection;

yet when both the primary and the derivative are discussed together, it encompasses both the original and the reflection. As for saying they are "one," this refers to their sharing the same Sanskrit sound (*brahmasvara*), which makes it difficult to distinguish them based on the phonetic sound alone.
It may be that the same sound is perceived as either agreeable or disagreeable; or, if one were to distinguish blue and yellow based on form (*rūpa*), then blue and yellow would have to become one.

To this, the explanation says: there is no fault even if this is granted. As stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, when the eye-faculty is impaired by the disease of jaundice (*kāmalā*), one perceives blue as yellow.
This case is also like that: through the Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*), various different perceptions arise regarding a single object such as form; therefore, the Buddha...

The sixth fascicle of the *Dilun* states: "As for the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), when it manifests as a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it also causes sentient beings to perceive a single substance in different ways, thereby accomplishing the task of benefiting and bringing joy.
Question: It may be possible that through mastery of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vaśitā*), a single substance is perceived differently;

however, how can it be that through mastery of supernormal powers, different substances are perceived identically? Explanation: In the Mahāyāna, all four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) are established.
First, different perceptions of the same substance: as with a single emanation body, sentient beings each perceive it differently. Second, identical perceptions of different substances:
as with a single emanation body manifested by many Buddhas together; although in reality there are many, they are perceived as one.
Therefore, the *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only), Volume Ten, states:

"The bodies of enjoyment for others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) and the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) are either common or uncommon according to the sentient beings to be converted by the Tathāgatas.

Regarding those who are common objects of conversion, at the same place and at the same time, the various Buddhas each transform themselves into bodies and lands; their forms are similar, they do not obstruct one another, and they interpenetrate."
It acts as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). That which is produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is the manifestation of one's own consciousness (*sva-vijñāna-pariṇāma*).

That is to say, within a single realm there is a single Buddha-body, which manifests supernormal powers and preaches the Dharma for the benefit of others. Regarding those who are not common [to all], it is transformed by a single Buddha alone.

This is because, from beginningless time, the lineage (*gotra*) of sentient beings is established by the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), such that they are mutually interconnected—either many belonging to one, or...

One [Buddha] belongs to many; therefore, among those beings to be converted, there are both common and uncommon [objects]. Otherwise, if many Buddhas were to remain in the world for a long time, each would labor in vain, as it would truly be of no benefit.
Since one Buddha is able to benefit all sentient beings, [the first case applies]. (3) Those with identical substance and identical views;
(4) those with different substance and different views—these are accepted by all schools, and their meaning is clear upon examination. Question: [This is] distinguished according to form (*rūpa*).
Blue and yellow are established as blue and yellow; this can be distinguished by the mind, yet the eight consciousnesses should likewise be one. The explanation says:
material form and sound are coarse phenomena that appear differently despite having the same substance; mental phenomena are subtle and difficult to know, so they should not be said to be one.
Furthermore, "one sound" and so forth refer to the secrets of body and speech among the Three Mysteries of the Tathāgata. Regarding the secret of the body:

As stated in the first fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: When the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma, the Bodhisattva Saṃdhāra came from another direction, desiring to measure the Buddha’s body.
He ascended through empty space across immeasurable Buddha-fields until he reached the world-system called Puṣpapradāna;
there he saw the Buddha’s body as it had been before, and spoke verses in praise. Furthermore, the *Guhyakapada-sūtra* states that the Buddha possesses three secrets (*triguhya*).
Regarding the secrecy of body, speech, and mind, all devas and humans neither understand nor know them.
Among the sentient beings gathered in one assembly, some see the Buddha’s body as golden in color, others as the color of white silver, and others as the colors of various miscellaneous jewels;
some see the Buddha’s body as one zhang and six chi in height, while others see it as one li, ten li, a hundred thousand, ten million, or even infinitely large.
Throughout the immeasurable reaches of empty space—such as these are called the secrecy of the body (*kāyaguhyaka*). As for the secrecy of speech (*vāgguhyaka*):

there are those who hear the Buddha’s voice at a distance of one *li*, and there are those who hear it at ten *li*, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, or even at immeasurable, limitless, and infinite reaches of empty space.
Within a single assembly, some may hear him speak of giving (*dāna*), while others may hear him speak of ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), or diligence (*vīrya*).

second, the section on the incomparable realm, referring to the next four chapters; third, the section on incomparable practice, referring to the next two chapters; fourth, the incomparable... [text truncated]

The section on the fruit of equality refers to the final category. The section on following the teaching with reverence refers to the phrase at the end of the sutra, "Rejoicing and putting it into practice.

The introduction, the main body, and the dissemination. "Introduction" refers to the prologue, which establishes the causal conditions for the commencement of the formal teaching. "Main body" refers to the orthodox doctrine, the primary meaning being elucidated.
"Dissemination" refers to the propagation [of the teaching] for the benefit of future generations.

When it is said here that "the causes and conditions for the arising of the instruction," etc., the Bhagavān is designated as the "cause" because he is the original author of the sūtra; this serves to clarify what has been heard and so forth.
Because it is not the formal exposition itself, it is termed the "Pratyaya" (Condition); thus, the introductory section is called the "Nidāna" (Causes and Conditions) division.
Because it correctly reveals the categories of the Dharma-gate that is to be explained, the seven chapters are called the "Ārya-deśita" (Taught by the Noble Ones) division.

Because the assembly, having heard the teaching, rejoices and accepts it with faith, this is called the "Pratipatti" (Practice) division. Regarding the Nidāna division, there are two meanings: first, the "Śraddhā-prasāda" (Faith and Confidence).
There are two parts: the introduction (*nidāna*) and the prologue (*upodghāta*). Regarding the distinction between these two parts, there are briefly three points. First, the difference in name:

namely, the "Introduction of Testimony" (*samyakpratyaya-nidāna*) and the "Prologue. These are also called the "General Introduction" (*sāmānya-nidāna*) and the "Specific Introduction" (*viśeṣa-nidāna*).

Stating "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) and so forth, which causes beings to produce faith, is called the "Introduction of Testimony. Because it is common to all sūtras, it is called the "General Introduction. By... [text continues]

Second, there is the distinction of time: that which is initiated by the Tathāgata is called the "Preamble to the Sūtra" (*pūrva-nidāna*), and that which is requested by Ānanda is called the "Postscript to the Sūtra" (*paścāt-nidāna*), because these two preambles are distinguished by their respective times. Third, there is the distinction of persons: first, the preamble of the Tathāgata, regarding all...
In the sūtras, there are two types of introductions (*nidāna*) initiated by the Tathāgata. Because Ānanda requested that these introductions be spoken, they exist;

however, in the present sūtra text and the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and others, there is only the "testimony of faith" (*saddharma-śraddhā*), while the "initiation" (*pravartana*) is absent. Within this testimony of faith:
Explaining this in terms of its meaning, there is no contradiction with reason. Within the context of the faith of realization, there are three points:

5. "Buddha, the World-Honored One" identifies the teacher who expounded it. 6. "The dwelling place" reveals the location where it was spoken.
There is a source [for this]. The "seven great bhikṣus" indicates that it was not heard by [the Buddha] alone; however, these seven items collectively comprise only four meanings:
first, "thus" (evam) clarifies the Dharma that was heard; second, "I have heard" (śrutam mayā) distinguishes the person who heard it;

the next two items corroborate the Dharma heard; and the final two items corroborate the person who heard it. This is explained in detail in Paramārtha’s *Commentary on the Seven Items*. Second, based on the Dragon...

In the introductory section (*nidāna*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is divided into six meanings: first, faith; second, hearing; third, time; fourth, the teacher; fifth, the location; and sixth, the assembly.
In Vasubandhu Bodhisattva’s *Pradīpa-ṭīkā*, it is likewise said that there are six meanings. Thus, the verse therein states: "The first three clarify the disciples;

the latter two establish the teacher's discourse. This applies to all sūtras. Its meaning is as follows: [the first three] clarify the disciples who hear the teaching, while the latter two establish the teacher who expounds the teaching. All sūtras...
All matters are thus. Third, according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* by Bandhuprabha, many [elements] are subsumed under five categories:
first, the general indication that it has been heard; second, the time when the sutra was spoken; third, the speaker; fourth, the place where it was spoken; and fifth, the audience who heard it.
Regarding the purpose of stating the introduction (*nidāna*): Question—By what causes and conditions are all sutras preceded by the statement "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) and so forth?
The *Record of the Seven Matters* by Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha states: "Because he severed the three doubts. It further says:

"Moreover, the *Sūkṣma-vinaya* clarifies that when Ānanda ascended the high seat to bring forth the Dharma-piṭaka, his body immediately became like that of a Buddha, endowed with all the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*)."
When he descended from his high seat, he returned to his original form. When the assembly beheld this auspicious omen, three kinds of doubt arose:
first, the doubt that the Great Master Śākyamuni, out of compassion, has arisen from nirvāṇa to further proclaim the profound Dharma;
second, the doubt that other World-Honored Ones have come from other directions; and third, the doubt that the Bhikṣu Ānanda, being the Buddha’s younger brother, is capable of representing him.
The Elder Brother has already turned his body into Buddhahood. Now, wishing to dispel three doubts, he states the seven matters beginning with "Thus have I heard.

This clarifies that [the teaching] was personally heard by me from the Buddha; it is not something arising out of compassion from within Nirvana, nor did it come from another Buddha in a different direction, nor is it a sutra spoken by myself after I had already turned my body into Buddhahood. (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*)

It says: "When teaching regarding time, place, and persons, it is because he wishes to cause sentient beings to give rise to faith in their minds. Furthermore, the second fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"At the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the land of Kuśinagara, between the śāla trees, he lay down with his head to the north."

As he was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, Ānanda, because his personal affection had not yet been eliminated and he had not yet abandoned desire, was submerged in grief and regret, unable to emerge from it on his own.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa said to Ānanda: "You are the guardian of the treasury of the Buddha's Dharma;
you should not, like an ordinary person, sink into grief and regret. All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)..."
"This is impermanent; why do you grieve and worry? Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, entrusted the Dharma to you with his own hand.
Now that you are distressed and despondent, you have lost what was to be accomplished. You should ask the Buddha: after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how should one practice? Who shall act as teacher?
How should one dwell together with the ill-spoken Ānanda? (The *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 4, states: "How should one dwell together with the bhikṣu Cunda? [The Buddha said to] all...
At the beginning of the sutra, what words were spoken? Ānanda immediately asked the Buddha about these words. The Buddha told Ānanda: "Practice the four foundations of mindfulness;
let the precept-sūtra be your teacher. The bhikṣu Canda is to be governed by the Brahma-punishment.
The fourth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama* and the thirty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottara Āgama* both state that "being governed by the Brahma-punishment" means precisely this.

This is spoken in common. A detailed explanation is as found in that [text]. Regarding the opening of the various Buddha-sūtras, they all begin with the words "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) and so forth.
According to the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* (Latter Part), this is largely the same as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*; fearing prolixity, I shall not describe it further.
The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states that Upāli instructed Ānanda to inquire [about this]. As for why the sūtras and śāstras differ in their explanations:
The two masters together taught, each relying on a particular interpretation, yet they did not contradict one another.

Furthermore, following the scriptural text, they provided distinct explanations according to specific matters. Regarding the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), it refers to three of the seven topics:
that which is heard, the hearer, and the personal reception of the teacher’s voice and intent. Among the six meanings [of the word *evam*], it corresponds to the two matters of faith and hearing.
Among the five [aspects], the first generally indicates what has been heard. Although there are three ways of explaining it, we shall here rely on the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*.
"Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) has three interpretations: first, a general explanation of "thus have I heard"; second, a specific explanation of "thus have I heard."
Third, to express the intent of the combined explanation. Regarding the "general explanation," this refers to the transmission of the Buddha’s teachings;

Mañjuśrī, Ānanda, and others all made these statements, such as: "Regarding what has been taught as profound and so forth, I have heard it thus in the past" (the *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra* states that among the three types of Ānandas, it is the Mahāyāna Ānanda who transmits the Great Teaching). Regarding the "specific explanation," one first distinguishes the term "thus" (*evam*).

Next, regarding the explanation of "I have heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), the term "thus" (*evam*) is explained differently by various teachers. (In this regard, the masters of this land have briefly eight explanations; the meaning is as commonly taught. As for these eight explanations: first, the explanation based on faith and compliance. To say "thus" is a word of faith and compliance.

For when there is faith, the principle of what is spoken is compliant; when there is compliance, the way of teacher and disciple is established. Whether a sutra is extensive or concise, it is not transmitted without faith. Therefore, the words "thus" are stated at the beginning.

This is the explanation of Master Sengzhao in his commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. Second, the explanation based on the meaning of the text. Taking the text as "thus" (*evam*) and the principle as "is" (*mayā*). The skillful expression of the text is "thus"; the principle, being free from error, is "is. This is the interpretation of the Wise One [Zhiyi] in his *Chan*...)

The Master [Seng]wei’s *Vimalakīrti Commentary* contains this interpretation. Third, the interpretation based on the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (saṃvṛti): the ultimate does not contradict the conventional, hence it is called "thus" (yathā); the conventional accords with the ultimate, hence it is called "correct" (iti).

This is the traditional explanation. Fourth, the interpretation based on the disciples: that which Ānanda speaks is "thus" because it accords with the Buddha's words; thus it is named "thus. To distinguish it from a mere semblance of suchness, it is further termed "correct. Fifth, the interpretation based solely on the Buddha:

Ānanda said that the Dharma spoken by the Buddha is "thus" because it is no different from what was spoken by past Buddhas; thus it is named "thus. Because it is as the Buddhas have spoken—right and not wrong—it is further called "correct. The above two interpretations were taught by Master Daoyuan. Sixth, the interpretation based on both the Buddha and his disciples: to say "thus" (evam) refers to the resonance between the response and the stimulus.

This is an auspicious omen. If one receives the name according to the capacity of the faculties (*indriya*), then there is nothing that does not establish a designation. Sentient beings evoke [the response] through "thusness" (*tathatā*), while the Tathāgata responds by conforming to their faculties. Those who transmit the sūtras maintain that the teaching of names arises from this interaction of stimulus and response;

therefore, they say "Thus" (*evam*). This is the interpretation found in the commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Seventh, Master Guangzhai said: "As for saying 'Thus,' it is intended to transmit what has been heard. By first citing the title of the entire work, it means: 'Such a sūtra as this, I have personally heard from the Buddha.'"

This is what I have heard. Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty said: "The phrase 'Thus' (evam) means that such words as these were spoken by the Buddha; therefore, one says 'Thus [and so forth],' though it cannot be described in full detail.
The masters of the Western Regions hold three different explanations. First, the *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra* by Bodhiruci states: "If one distinguishes according to the world..."
There are many paths; to speak briefly, there are generally four kinds: first, generating the mind in this manner;
second, instructing others; third, through analogies; and fourth, through determination. Regarding "generating the mind in this manner":
it is when one thinks to oneself, "I shall thus generate the bodhicitta and cultivate virtuous practices. Regarding "instructing others": it is when one teaches those before them, saying:
"You should thus resolve upon bodhicitta and cultivate virtuous practices and so forth. As for the analogy "such as this":
that person’s majestic power is blazingly intense like the light of the sun; their wisdom is deep and vast like the great ocean;
their countenance is upright and handsome like the full moon—and so on, as explained at length. "It is certainly thus" means: I see it in this way.
"Having heard," and so forth—this is called "determined to be thus. Now, regarding the phrase "thus": it refers specifically to the fourth determination, "to be thus.
It clarifies that what I have heard from the Buddha as the taught principle and instruction, and what I now speak, is neither more nor less, neither erroneous nor mistaken;
it is determined to be thus, without the fault of misrepresentation. Therefore, it is called "thus" (yathā).

This is so. (The commentary explains that the underlying intent is largely the same as that of Bandhuprabha. The Tripiṭaka Master Dīrghaśrotra provides three interpretations: First, with respect to the Buddha:

the teachings spoken by all Buddhas of the three periods of time are without difference; therefore, they are called "Thus" (*tathā*). Because they are taught identically, they are designated as "So" (*iti*). Second, with respect to the Dharma:
because it is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, it is called "Thus. Because it is taught in accordance with that reality, it is called "So."
Third, regarding the Sangha: because what Ānanda transmitted does not differ from the Buddha’s own teaching, it is called "Thus" (*tathā*);

because it is eternally free from error and fault, it is termed "So" (*tatha*). This is the explanation by the Tripitaka Master Sanzhendi. Regarding the term "thus" (*evam*), it has the sense of certainty and is of two kinds:

first, the letter (*vyañjana*); second, the principle (*artha*). The letter is that which expresses, while the principle is that which is expressed. A detailed explanation is as found in those [texts]. In summary:
The commentary explains: That which was transmitted by Ānanda is definitive in both principle and expression, just as the Buddha taught; therefore, it is called "evam" (thus).
Regarding the explanations found in various treatises, there are also three types. First, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle one: "The meaning of 'evam' is faith (*śraddhā*).
In the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma, faith is that by which one enters, and wisdom (*jñāna*) is that by which one crosses over."
Those who have faith and compliance say, "This matter is thus. Those who lack faith say, "This matter is not thus," as explained extensively in that [text].
Second, according to the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it says:

"Thus have I heard" indicates that this was expounded by the World-Honored One based on his direct realization, and was not his own composition. Third, according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, there are four [meanings].

[The meaning is as follows. Therefore, the first [section] states: "Thus, this general statement proceeds according to four meanings. First, it proceeds based on a simile; that is, regarding the text to be explained:
'Thus have I heard in the past' (this uses the past to illustrate the present). Second, it proceeds based on instruction; that is, addressing the assembly:
'In this way, you should listen to what I have heard in the past. Third, it proceeds based on question and answer; that is, when someone asks: 'You..."

Regarding what is to be spoken: "Have you heard this in the past? Therefore, he answers, "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*). This is the permission granted by the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*);
that is to say, at the time of the compilation, the assembly of bodhisattvas all together requested, saying, "Just as you have heard it, so should you speak.
The Bodhisattva who transmits the Dharma granted their request, saying, "In this way it shall be spoken, just as I have heard it. Regarding these four...

Regarding the meaning [of "I have heard"], there are three masters' explanations. One says that among the four [meanings], it relies solely on the fourth. Another says that herein it relies solely on the latter two.
Yet another says that among the four, it is explained by relying on all four meanings in total. These are fully detailed therein. To explain "I have heard" specifically:

the Dharma-transmitting Bodhisattvas, Ānanda, and others, conventionally designate the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) as the "self. As for the "ear": [The remainder of the text continues with the explanation of the ear.]
The sense faculty gives rise to consciousness, through which one hears what is spoken; therefore, it is said, "I heard. Thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"I" refers to the conventional, provisional entity consisting of the aggregates (*skandhas*). "Hearing" refers to the ear-faculty giving rise to consciousness to listen and receive. Setting aside the particulars for the sake of the whole, it is thus said, "I heard.
Question: Within the Buddha-dharma, there is no person and no self. How is it that all sūtras state, "I heard"? How is this to be explained?
It is said: Regarding this meaning, various explanations differ. According to the school of Nāgārjuna, "I have heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*) is explained by means of the four *siddhāntas*.

(The Sanskrit term *siddhānta* is itself subject to various interpretations: some say it should not be translated because it contains many meanings; others translate it as *zongcheng* (宗成), *mo* (墨), *yin* (印), or *ding* (定); or they translate it according to its ultimate sense.

Such diverse translations make it difficult to establish a definitive standard. Master Nanyue said: "It is like the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, where both the foreign and Chinese names are used together. *Xi* is a sound from the Sui period, while *tan* is a foreign word. *Xi* means 'pervasive' (*vyāpta*), and *tan* is translated as 'giving' (*dāna*)."

The Buddha bestows four dharmas universally upon all sentient beings; therefore, they are called *siddhānta*. The Master Zhi (Zhi Daolin) states in his commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: "If one relies on the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, there are four kinds. The commentary on the second fascicle explains:

"*Siddhānta* means either 'tenet' (*zong*), 'accomplishment' (*cheng*), or 'principle' (*li*). Regarding the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*, as explained in the first fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
1. **Lokasaṃvṛti-siddhānta** (Worldly *siddhānta*): For example, the aggregates (*skandha*) constitute a person; "Thus have I heard" exists because of the world. (These are the four *siddhāntas*.)

First, from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no [self]. Second, from the perspective of the *puruṣapudgalasiddhānta* (the standpoint established for each individual), one observes the mental conduct of people and teaches the Dharma accordingly;
within a single matter, one may either permit or prohibit [certain views]: to sever the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), one speaks of the continuity of rebirth;

to counteract the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*), one speaks of the non-existence of a person (*pudgala*). Third, from the perspective of the therapeutic standpoint (*pratipakṣasiddhānta*), it is like the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) as an antidote to greed.
Regarding anger, however, there is none. There are four *paramārtha-siddhāntas*, which refer to the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena:
it is beyond the path of language and the sphere where mental activity ceases. Thus, a verse is spoken:
All is real, all is unreal, And all is both real and unreal;
All is neither unreal nor not-unreal: This is called the true mark of all phenomena.

(An extensive explanation of this verse is found in the third chapter of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*. Furthermore, that same treatise states: "Moreover, there are three kinds of worldly discourse: first, the false..."

Second is pride. Third is the name; because it relies on the third [the conventional], it is called "self. This corresponds to what is termed the "provisional designation of self" (*prajñapti-ātman*) in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Question: In the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, within the inquiry into the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), it states that there is neither self nor non-self.
How is it then that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* speaks of "non-self"? Answer: There is no contradiction. According to the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint), it is indeed spoken of as such.

In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), I am said to be "non-self" (*anātman*). For the sake of various individuals, one may speak of either "self" or "non-self" in order to simultaneously dispel the two types of grasping.
Thus, it can also be said that there is neither self nor non-non-self. Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"The Buddhas sometimes speak of a self, and sometimes they speak of non-self; within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there is neither self nor non-self. If [one were to] be partial...
Regarding "self," it is taught that "non-self" is the true nature (*dharmatā*). If one simultaneously dispels both attachments, then "neither self nor non-self" is taken as the true nature.
Since each is based on a specific meaning, they do not contradict one another. If one relies on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, then "true self" is taught as the true nature;
this should be understood according to the principle. According to the system of Maitreya, [the self is taught] in relation to the aggregates (*skandha*) by way of four meanings.
It is conventionally designated as a "self" by way of a provisional designation. Thus, the sixth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The Blessed One said:
'O Bhikṣus, you should know that for four reasons, sentient beings are provisionally designated: first, because it is easy for worldly discourse;
second, because one wishes to conform to the ways of the world; third, in order to eliminate the fear of those who are certain that there is no self.'"
The fourth [purpose] is to proclaim the gains and losses for oneself and others, so as to cause them to attain a mind of resolute faith and understanding.

This is stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; it accords with the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* (Chapter 9) and the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra* (Chapter 13). Regarding the term "hearer" (*śrotṛ*), various schools differ in their explanations.

According to the Sarvāstivāda school, hearing is performed by the ear and not by consciousness. The master Dharmatrāta maintains that hearing is performed by consciousness and not by the ear, as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Regarding the thirteen [points] and so forth: according to the Sautrāntika school, consciousness hears and not the ear, as in the sixth chapter of the *Tattvasiddhi*.

According to the Dārṣṭāntika masters, the conjunction [of conditions] is able to hear, as in the thirteenth fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*. Now, according to the Mahāyāna, Master Nāgārjuna himself provides two explanations:
first, that just as the divine eye sees form, one may infer by analogy that the ear hears; second, that the conjunction [of conditions] is able to hear.
Regarding the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Volume One, and so forth, although there are two interpretations, their synthesis constitutes the correct view.

This is because, within the correct explanation of "hearing," it is stated that hearing is a synthesis. According to the school of Maitreya, there are three specific positions: first, some say that hearing by the ear is not consciousness (*vijñāna*).
As stated in the first fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*: “What is the characteristic of the ear-element (*śrotra-dhātu*)? It is that which is capable of hearing sound.
Furthermore, the third fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: “Because it repeatedly reaches for and hears this sound, it is called the ear.

One interpretation holds that it is consciousness (*vijñāna*) that hears, not the ear; as the first fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-bhāṣya* states: “Hearing (*śravaṇa*) refers to listening. That is to say—

This is because the ear faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) gives rise to the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), which hears verbal teachings. Furthermore, the first fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Hearing" refers to the ear faculty giving rise to consciousness to listen and receive. Alternatively, it may be that in both treatises, it is the ear that hears rather than the consciousness;

one [view] says that the combination [of the three factors] is what can hear. As the second fascicle of the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-bhāṣya* asks: "Does the eye see form, or is it the consciousness and so forth?"
Question: Is it not the case that the eye does not see forms? Answer: It is shown that it is not consciousness and so forth, because all phenomena are devoid of functional activity (*nirvyāpāra*).
It is designated as "seeing" only by virtue of their conjunction. The same applies to the ear and the other [senses], as explained at length in those [treatises].

The reason why these various treatises differ is to clarify that the ear is the most excellent basis for hearing sounds; thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* and others state that the ear is [the faculty of hearing].

Regarding the term "hearing" (*śruta*): from the perspective of analyzing its meaning, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts state that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is hearing, in order to demonstrate that all phenomena lack real functional activity.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā*, however, maintain that the conjunction [of conditions] constitutes hearing.

Each is based on a single specific sense, and thus they do not contradict one another. (Question: If there is no real functional activity, one cannot admit that the ear hears; if there is no real functional activity, wisdom (*jñāna*) should not take [an object] as its condition. Herein, a response should be provided according to the principle of Consciousness-Only. This is the reasoning of Vijñaptimātra.
Regarding those who hear through discernment, as stated in the first fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, there are two masters' interpretations. Thus, that treatise says:

"There is an interpretation [which holds] that by the power of the Tathāgata’s compassion and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) of his original vows, the aspects of words and meanings arise within the consciousness of the listener.
Although these aspects of words and meanings arise directly based on the power of one's own roots of goodness, they are designated [as such] according to their powerful condition."
It is said to be "spoken by the Buddha" because it is manifested within one's own mind through the power of the auditory faculty; thus, it is called "I have heard.

According to another interpretation, it is due to the dominant condition of the listener’s roots of goodness and original vows that the aspects of word and meaning arise upon the consciousness of the Tathāgata.

These aspects of word and meaning are produced by the Buddha’s roots of goodness for the benefit of others, and are therefore termed "spoken by the Buddha. Although these aspects do not [actually enter] the listener’s consciousness-mind...
It is acquired; however, because it appears clearly as if it were that [object], it is called "I heard. The commentary states:
regarding the explanations of the two masters of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, the former is Nāgasena, who does not admit that the fruit of Buddhahood possesses form, sound, and so forth;
the doctrine of the second master admits that the fruit of Buddhahood is endowed with form, sound, and so forth. The Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang, Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, employs both.
This will be explained later, as it was discussed previously in the section concerning the existence or non-existence of the original and the reflection. Question:

"Ānanda, twenty years passed from the day the Tathāgata attained enlightenment before you became his attendant. Since the sūtras spoken prior to that time were not heard directly from him, why do all those sūtras state, 'Thus have I heard'?
The *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra* by Bodhiruci and Vajraṣeṇa states: "In the past, when the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa..."
Subsequently, there were three occasions for the compilation of the Dharma-piṭaka.
First, in the Indrasailaguha cave at Rājagṛha, five hundred bhikṣus compiled the Dharma-piṭaka. Śāriputra and other arhat bhikṣus each declared:
"The *sūtra* named so-and-so; thus have I heard: the Buddha spoke it in such-and-such a place. Later, due to evil...
The king destroyed the Buddha-dharma. After this, seven hundred bhikṣus again compiled the Dharma-piṭaka;
they all stated, "This such-and-such sūtra I heard from such-and-such a bhikṣu," rather than saying, "I heard it from the Buddha.
This second compilation was performed entirely by those of the Hīnayāna who compiled the Dharma-piṭaka. Furthermore, as...
They came from outside the Iron Ring Mountains and did not go to other worlds.

In the space between the two realms, immeasurable Buddhas gathered together there and finished reciting the *Buddhaghoṣa-sūtra*. Desiring to compile the Mahāyāna Dharma-piṭaka, they again summoned their followers:
there were eight billion nayutas of arhats, and an immeasurable, boundless assembly of bodhisattvas.
Inconceivable as the sands of the Ganges, they all gathered there. At that time, the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas all said: "Thus have I heard:
at such-and-such a place, the Tathāgata preached such-and-such a sūtra. Regarding this, the *Seven Matters Record* by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha states:
"To have heard directly is called 'Thus have I heard' (*evam mayā śrutam*); to have heard through tradition is called 'I have heard thus' (*mayā evaṃ śrutam*). Furthermore...

The *Buzhi ji* (Record of Sectarian Tenets) states: "To have heard directly is called 'I have heard' (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*); to have received it through transmission is called 'that which was heard'. The commentary explains:
"Such explanations contradict the teachings of the *Bao'en jing* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness). According to the *Bao'en jing*, there are three meanings for this [term]: first, hearsay."
Second, [the Buddha] knew Ānanda’s mundane mind (*saṃvṛti-citta*). Third, the Buddha spoke again for his sake. Therefore, the sixth [chapter] says:
"The Buddha preached the Dharma for twenty years, yet Ānanda did not hear it. How can you say 'I have heard'? Answer: The devas told Ānanda;
furthermore, it is said he heard it from the side of the bhikṣus; and furthermore, it is said the Buddha entered his mundane mind and caused Ānanda [to hear].
[He] knows. Furthermore, it is said that Ānanda requested a boon from the Buddha, saying: "Whatever Dharma the Buddha has taught during twenty years, please explain it all to me.
The Buddha is skillful; within a single dharma and a single phrase, he can expound immeasurable dharmas, and by means of immeasurable dharmas...
This constitutes a single point of meaning. The Buddha briefly indicated its outline, and Ānanda was able to fully comprehend it due to his swiftness, sharpness, and power of retention.
Furthermore, the *Vajrapuṣpa Sūtra* states that the bhikṣu Ānanda attained the Samādhi of the Sovereign King of Awakening to the Nature of Dharmas;
by the power of this samādhi, he was able to remember and maintain all the sūtras previously spoken, as if he had heard them directly.
There is no difference. It is just as one with the supernormal power of recollecting past lives sees past events without anything being unclear;
likewise, because Kātyāyana had attained the power of wisdom through his vows, he was able to remember and uphold all the sūtras spoken by the Buddha. Ānanda was also like this. Question:
Since Ānanda was a śrāvaka, how could he uphold Mahāyāna sūtras? Answer: It is as described in the *Mahāyāna-saṃgraha-dharmaparyāya*.
The Sūtras state that there are three types of Ānanda: first, Ānanda the Joyful (Ānandita), who upholds the Dharma of the Śrāvakas;
second, Ānanda the Worthy (Ānanda-bhadra), who upholds the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas; and third, Ānanda the Ocean (Ānanda-sāgara), who upholds the Mahāyāna Dharma.

The *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra* likewise records this regarding the compilation of the Dharma. Furthermore, Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha’s commentary on the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* cites the *Rājākṣema-kṣamāpanā-sūtra*.
The *Āyuṣparyanta-sūtra* mentions three types of Ānanda. Among these three, it is the third Ānanda who upholds this sūtra;
therefore, there is no contradiction. To explain the intention behind the collective statement of the third type, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* says:
"One should know that the purpose of stating 'Thus have I heard' is to avoid the faults of addition, subtraction, and heterogeneity. That is to say, regarding such a Dharma, I..."
"Having heard from the Buddha, not through successive transmission from others," this demonstrates that the hearer possesses the requisite capacity.
Whatever has been heard is entirely free from the faults of exaggeration, underestimation, or deviation; it is explained exactly as it is.

"At one time. The commentary explains: among the five [aspects], this is the second, the temporal period when the teaching arises. Regarding this "one time," the masters of this school offer four interpretations:

first, that it refers to the fifty-year period of the Tathāgata’s entire career of preaching; second, that it refers to the time of preaching a specific sūtra; third, that it refers to the time when the spiritual capacities of the assembly have matured; and fourth, that it refers to the time when the speaker and the listeners meet in harmony. (This is from Master Jizang’s *Fahua shu*).
The masters of the Western regions hold three different explanations. First, Bodhiruci states that "at one time" has many meanings:
it may refer to a single moment, a day and night, a hundred years, all time, or the seasons of spring, autumn, winter, and summer.
What is meant here by "at one time" is none of these; it refers precisely to the time when the Tathāgata spoke this [sūtra].
Regarding the passage of time: although it is said to be "at one time," because a specific month, year, or day is not mentioned, the exact date remains unknown.

For instance, the "Pure Eye" chapter (*Vimalanetra-parivarta*) of the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra* was spoken on the day the Tathāgata attained enlightenment; the "Ten Stages" chapter (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*) was spoken during the second week [after his enlightenment].
As for the *Śatasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*, there is a textual record stating it was spoken five years after the Tathāgata’s enlightenment. Other cases follow this pattern.
Regarding the seven sections of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, they merely state that they were taught "at one time," and none know in what year they were spoken.

Furthermore, it is said therein: "According to tradition, from the time the Tathāgata attained enlightenment until his parinirvāṇa, he constantly preached the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* without interruption.
(The commentary states: Based on this, even the Western Tripiṭaka masters cannot definitively determine the dates of the various sūtras. Second, the Long-Eared One. Third...
The *Zangyun* states: "At that time there were two kinds [of teaching]. First, the time of the 'half-sound,' which did not reach all objects of perception;

second, the time of the 'perfect sound,' which reached all objects of perception universally. From the initial attainment of the Way until the final end at the Twin Śāla Trees, these two sounds proceeded together, and both the partial and the complete teachings were expounded."
The "partial manifestation" (*kṣaṇa*) refers to the time of a half-syllable; the "complete manifestation" (*lava*) refers to the time of a full syllable.

Furthermore, there are three ways of explaining time: first, the time of sequential transition (*prabandha-vṛtti*); second, the time of inconceivable transformation (*acintya-pariṇāma*); and third, the time of conventional designation (*prajñapti*).
The former two are precisely the times of the two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). As for the time of conventional designation, it is the *kalpa* in the Sanskrit language.
The *pāṭha* has three meanings: first, the *kāla* period; second, the *samaya* period; and third, the period of worldly dissemination (*loka-pracāra*).

As for the *kāla* period, this is translated as "the time of specific characteristics. Regarding the Tathāgata’s precepts: one hears the major precepts at their [specific] time, but does not hear them at the time of the minor precepts;
one hears them when one is ordained, but does not hear them when one is a layperson; and a king may hear them, whereas other people do not.
"At the time of *samaya*. This translates as "the time for destroying wrong views.

It means that within the fivefold Āgamas and the ninefold Dharma, one may hear everything without distinction between the black and the white. (Regarding the "ninefold," as stated in the first volume of Paramārtha’s *Samayabhedoparacanacakra-ṭīkā*:

"The True Teaching of the Tathāgata consists of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma. The Sūtras are the five Āgamas, namely: the Long, the Increase, the Middle, the Numerical, and the Miscellaneous Collections (*Ekottara*). The Vinaya does not exceed three divisions: first, the Vinaya of One Hundred and Fifty Precepts; second, the *Kṣudraka-vinaya*; and third, the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya.")

The Abhidharma consists of nine divisions: first, the analysis of the precepts; second, the analysis of the world; third, the analysis of causes and conditions; fourth, the analysis of the elements (*dhātu*); fifth, the analysis of simultaneous attainment; sixth, the analysis of names, phrases, and syllables;

seventh, the analysis of the cultivation of meditative concentration; eighth, the analysis of the accumulation of karma; ninth, the analysis of the aggregates (*skandha*). Each division contains six thousand verses; six times nine is fifty-four, totaling fifty-four thousand verses. Regarding the two aforementioned periods, they are largely the same as described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
As for what is currently circulated in the world, it is as when it is said: "At one time, the Buddha was staying..."
On the banks of the Ganges, at one time, [the Buddha] was in the Śiṃśapā Forest. Regarding the phrase "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*), it shall here be based on the latter two [meanings].

The *Record of Seven Matters* by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha states that there are ten meanings for "one time": first, the time when a Buddha appears in the world; second, the time when the True Dharma is preached;
third, the time when the True Dharma is heard; fourth, the time when the True Dharma is upheld; fifth, the time when the True Dharma is contemplated; sixth...

1. The time of correcting the Dharma; 2. The time of the seven lower wholesome seeds (namely, the bodhicitta); 3. The time of accomplishing the roots of goodness (namely, being born in a central land).

Practicing the four foundations of mindfulness (*catur-smṛtyupasthāna*) occurs at the time of the roots of goodness of the nine liberations (*navavimokṣa-kuśalamūla*). (That is to say, by means of these five conditions—hearing the Dharma, preaching the Dharma, upholding the Dharma, calming the mind, and practicing cultivation—one attains entry into liberation;

therefore, it is called the time of the roots of goodness of liberation. It occurs at the tenth stage, the time of the equanimity of impartial relinquishment (*upekṣā-citta*). If the mind is prone to excessive withdrawal, it is called a "lowly mind" (*hīna-citta*), and one does not enter into hearing the Dharma. If the mind is agitated and exultant, it is called a "proud mind" (*unnata-citta*), and one does not enter into hearing the Dharma.

If one forms a mind that rejects the True Dharma, this is a mind of ignorance and inequality, and one likewise does not enter into hearing it. If one can pull out what is submerged and subdue what is floating, balancing them to attain the middle, and through mindfulness and knowledge attain the equanimity of relinquishment, one attains entry into the True Dharma.

Therefore, it is said that at the time of the mind of equanimity, these ten meanings are complete; hence, it is called "at one time. (The detailed explanation is as found in that [text]). Now, according to various treatises, there are three explanations. First, the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* by Guṇaprabha states:
"At one time" means at the time this sūtra was spoken, for at other times immeasurable sūtras were also spoken.
Second, according to the school of Nāgārjuna, there are two kinds of time: the first is named *kāla*, which is general and conventional.
Furthermore, [the term] *samaya* is used both literally and metaphorically. While it is real in its internal and external applications, when referring to time, it is merely conventional and not real.
It is based on this that our own school speaks of "time" (*samaya*) in a single sense. Thus, the first fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Question: In India, there are two kinds of terms for time: first, *kāla*, and second, *samaya*. Why does the Buddha not speak of the temporal divisions as *kāla*, but..."
[The opponent] says: "One should speak only of *samaya*. (This is the outsider questioning Nāgārjuna’s school. [Nāgārjuna] replies: "Even with *kāla*, there is doubt" (Nāgārjuna answers briefly:
even if one speaks of *kāla*, this same objection remains; therefore, it should not be answered). [The opponent] asks:

"In this context, one should speak of *kāla*, because those two syllables can be easily modified in speech, whereas one should not speak of *samaya*, because those three syllables are difficult due to their heavy prosodic weight."

Therefore, [others challenge Nāgārjuna]: "Why do you not rely on the light [concept] but instead rely on the heavy? He replies: "In this context, because we are eliminating false views, we speak of *samaya* (conventional time) and not *kāla* (absolute time).
The full explanation is as follows" (as extensively explained by Nāgārjuna): "If one were to speak of *kāla*, the non-Buddhist outsiders who cling to the existence of time would say:

'Time can produce all phenomena; the World-Honored One admits that time is substantially existent (*dravya-sat*). Thirdly, according to Yaśomitra, there are four kinds of time: first, the completion of the speaker and the listener in general...
This is called "at one time. Thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The phrase 'at one time' refers to the time of speaking and listening.

This, in terms of a continuous succession of moments without interruption until the completion of the speaking and listening, is collectively termed 'one time. (This is a general statement that the teaching and listening within a single assembly were completed.)"

[The term] "simultaneously" (ekakṣaṇam) is used as a collective designation. If it were not so, since the letters, names, and phrases would be heard and spoken at different times, how could one say they are "one"?

(This is an explanation by way of reductio ad absurdum: if "simultaneously" did not refer to the completion of both speaking and hearing, then—just as a letter is spoken first and a name or phrase follows later, and so on up to verses, chapters, sections, and volumes—the times of speaking and hearing would all be different;

how then could one say they are "one"? Second, because one is able to retain, speak, comprehend, and receive [the teaching] within a single moment (ekakṣaṇa), it is called "simultaneous. Therefore, that...
The treatise states: "Alternatively, the speaker may have attained *dhāraṇī*, such that within a single syllable and in a single *kṣaṇa*, they are able to uphold and expound all dharma-gates.
(The commentary explains: Because Bodhisattvas on the stages have attained *dhāraṇī*, in a single *kṣaṇa* they can uphold and expound all dharma-gates.
"Alternatively, the listener may have attained the pure faculty of hearing, such that when hearing one syllable in a single *kṣaṇa*, regarding the remaining [syllables]..."

All [of these] are without obstruction and can all be received; therefore, it is called "at one time" (*ekasamaya*). (The commentary explains: Bodhisattvas on the stages obtain *dhāraṇī*, whereby they can receive [the teaching] all at once; hence it is called "at one time.
Third, the mutual encounter [of teacher and listener] is called "at one time. Thus that treatise says:

"Alternatively, because there is no distinction in the temporal period of their mutual encounter, it is called 'at one time'; that is, the speaker and the listener mutually encounter one another together."

Regarding the meaning of "one time" (*ekakāla*): [The commentary] says that when [beings] invoke the sages and respond to their capacities, such that they meet one another, it is called "one time. Alternatively, it may be divided into four; for when the time of opening [the teaching] and the time of listening are taken as two times, there are four.
Question: What is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of "one" and "time"? Answer: "One" is a number, and "time" refers to a temporal division (*kāla-bhāga*). There are various differing explanations.

According to the Sarvāstivāda school and the Sautrāntika masters, these take the five conditioned aggregates (*saṃskṛta-skandha*) as their nature. Within the categories of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), they are likewise [treated in this manner].

It takes the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) as its nature. (This challenges the Sarvāstivāda school, which distinguishes between identity and difference based on form (*rūpa*); according to them, there exists identity and difference apart from form, or alternatively, one might distinguish number and time based on form, yet these too would have to possess separate substantial entities.
Now, following the Mahāyāna, there are two interpretations. First, the school of Nāgārjuna: number, time, and so forth, all lack any substantial entity.
Because they are not subsumed within the three categories of aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle one, states:
"Dharmas such as number and time do not truly exist; they are not subsumed within the aggregates, bases, or elements. That same treatise further states:

"Ordinary people become attached to names such as time, direction, separation, conjunction, identity, difference, long, and short, asserting them to be substantially existent. The details are as explained therein.
According to the system of Maitreya, number and time are provisionally established as temporal states (*avasthā*) upon conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*);

that is, they are among the twenty-four dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), namely number and time. Within the framework of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), they are subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Within the frameworks of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), they are included because they are the objects of the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) within the base of phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*) and the element of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*).
According to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, they may also be temporal states upon the mind itself.
The image is non-associated; this is stated according to the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). Question:

Why do the two schools differ regarding existence and non-existence? Answer: In the school of Nāgārjuna, because it seeks to refute the externalist [notions] of substance, number, time, and so forth, there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
According to the school of Maitreya, these are established separately in order to manifest the principles of the Mahāyāna dharma-lakṣaṇa;
therefore, there is no contradiction. Alternatively, they may be subsumed under the five hundred *viprayukta-saṃskāras*, which would not contradict reason.

Although the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* establishes seven hundred *viprayukta-saṃskāras*, such a principle exists even if it has not yet been seen in a formal textual record. Question: Why is the beginning of the day not specifically explained?

From the time of departure until midnight, this sūtra was preached. Just as specific locations and so forth are distinguished in other cases, yet in this sūtra it simply says "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*).
The answer is that, according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, the divisions of day and night are not fixed across all directions and cannot be specified individually (the commentary explains:
for example, when it is noon in Jambudvīpa, the sun is rising in the west, it is midnight in the north, and the sun is setting in the east).
"Bhagavān. The commentary explains:
among the five [categories], the third specifically clarifies the Teacher. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are five types of persons who preach the Dharma;
thus, the second fascicle states: "There are five ways of preaching the Dharma: first, the Buddha speaks himself; second, his disciples..."

It is said that there are five types of speakers: first, the Buddhas; second, the Śrāvakas; third, the three classes of ṛṣis; fourth, the devas; and fifth, emanated persons (*nirmāṇa-puruṣa*). Now, to exclude the other four, the term *Bhagavān* is specified. Question:
At the beginning of this sūtra, the Bodhisattva explains the profound meaning and secret intent (*sandhyābhāṣya*), stating that all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-dual.
Why, then, is it said here simply that the Bhagavān speaks? Answer: There are three reasons. First, [the title is given] by following the majority from the minority...
First, because it is frequently mentioned; second, because it is stated in terms of what is preeminent; third, because of the Buddha’s empowerment (as seen in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and others).

However, at the beginning of various sūtras, the titles are designated differently, resulting in four types. There are some sūtras where only the name of the Buddha is placed at the outset, such as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
In some sūtras, at the very beginning, there is only the term *bhagavat*, as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others.

In some sūtras, both titles are presented together at the outset, such as the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra* (*Buddhabhagavatprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*). In other cases, neither of the two appears in the text, as in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*.
As for why these various versions differ in this way, [the reason is found in] the *Saṃdhinirmocana*...

The *Mukta* (Detachment) consists of the final two chapters within a single section; therefore, its name is not specifically designated. The *Bahu-citta-prajñāpāramitā* (Many-Minded Prajñāpāramitā) is none other than the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*;
it should be understood as a separate record compiled by Bodhisattvas for circulation, and thus its name is likewise not designated.
Regarding the remaining three phrases, the masters of the Western regions have three distinct interpretations. First, in the *Record of Seven Matters* by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha:
There are two intentions [for this]. First, according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, the Buddha possesses ten meanings;
therefore, among the ten titles at the beginning of various sūtras, the title "Buddha" alone is established. Thus, the *Ji qishi* (Record of the Seven Matters) states:

"In the sūtras concerning the Great Master’s ten titles, why is he not distinguished by the other nine, but called only 'Buddha'? There are ten reasons for this explanation: first, awakening surpasses the celestial drum; second, not..."
1. Awakening through others; 2. Freedom from the two types of ignorance (ignorance regarding the obstacles to liberation and ignorance regarding the obstacles to omniscience);

3. Having transcended sleep; 4. Being like a lotus flower; 5. Being inherently undefiled; 6. Possessing three meanings (the three meanings being: first, the Buddha of designation, which refers to the six supernormal powers;

second, the Buddha of cessation, because afflictions do not arise; third, the Buddha of reality, which is suchness); 7. Endowed with the three virtues (the virtues of dharmakāya, prajñā, and liberation).

Ninth, possessing the nature of the Three Jewels; tenth, knowing for oneself and causing others to know. Altogether there are four pages; fearing that it would be too much, I shall not describe them further.
Paramārtha himself stated: "These ten meanings are derived from the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*. Second, Paramārtha himself set forth the principles through a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Thus, at the beginning of every sutra, two titles are jointly presented. Therefore, it is said in the *Saptavastuka*: [text continues].
Regarding the term "Buddha-Bhagavān," there are four permutations: 1. One who is a Buddha but not a Bhagavān refers to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the two vehicles.
Having contemplated the Four Noble Truths and realized Nirvana without remainder, they are designated as "Buddhas" within their own respective stages;
however, because they do not cultivate meritorious deeds, they are not Bhagavāns. 2. One who is a Bhagavān but not a Buddha refers to the Bodhisattvas.
One whose meritorious conduct is fulfilled is called Bhagavān. As long as one remains in the causal stage and wisdom is not yet fulfilled, one cannot be called a Buddha.
Third, those who are neither Buddhas nor Bhagavāns are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*);

because they do not cultivate wisdom, they are not called Buddhas, and because they do not cultivate merit, they are not Bhagavāns. Fourth, those who are both Buddhas and Bhagavāns are indeed the Buddhas.

"World-Honored One, because your wisdom is perfected, you are called Buddha. Because you are endowed with all merits, you are Bhagavat. (The extensive explanation of *Bhagavat* occupies three or four pages;
fearing it would be too prolix, it is not related here. It continues until he says: "If one were to speak only of 'Buddha,' there is the fear of confusing [the title] with those of the Two Vehicles.
If one uses only 'Bhagavat,' it would be confused with Great Bodhisattvas and Wheel-Turning Kings. Therefore, one should know that speaking of them together is precisely the Tathāgata."
Therefore, both the *Anuttaraśrayasūtra* and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* employ this expression, "Buddha Bhagavān.
The *Samayabhedoparacanacakra-śāstra* likewise agrees on these seven matters.
Second, regarding Bodhiruci’s *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra*, which follows the authentic Western (Indian) manuscripts, all sūtras begin with "Bhagavān. As for the various sūtras of this land (China)...
Whether it is "Buddha," "Bhagavān," or the dual expression "Buddha-Bhagavān," these vary according to the translator's intent.
According to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* by the Bodhisattva Asvabhāva, this is consistent with Vajrabodhi; thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states that the Buddha possesses ten kinds of meritorious titles.
For what reason, then, do the transmitters of the Tathāgata’s teachings place [these titles] at the beginning of all sūtras?
Setting aside such names as "Bhagavān," this single name is universally respected by all; thus, even non-Buddhist practitioners refer to their own founders as "Bhagavān.
Furthermore, this single name encompasses all virtues in a way that other names do not.
For these reasons, this name is placed at the beginning of every sutra. The intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is the same as that of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*; therefore, the first...
Second, it is said: Question: Is "Bhagavān" his only name, or does he have other names as well? Answer:
