This demonstrates the Bhagavat’s supreme merit of being able to correctly sustain his own undefiled body.

That is to say, the bodies of all Buddhas do not arise from false conceptualization, because they are free from the defilements of afflictions, karma, and birth. Thus, the Tathāgata’s body is not a part of the defiled realm.

Because it arises separately, it is "indiscernible" (avikalpa). (In general, because the manifested body does not arise from false conceptual discrimination, it is called "indiscernible. Alternatively, because the manifested body is not produced by false discrimination, others cannot discern it.
This later explanation by Bandhuprabha is largely the same as that of Asvabhāva; thus, his treatise states:
"That is to say, although the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is without conceptual discrimination, like a mani-jewel, it [manifests] through the sovereign power (*adhipatibala*) of all Tathāgatas."
Furthermore, by the power of one’s own resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one perceives the body of the Tathāgata as being like the color of gold.

Yet, the Tathāgatas are without conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and without discursive conceptualization (*parikalpa*). This is explained as being "like that" [in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*]. (Regarding "without conceptualization": it means there is no conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*). Regarding "without discursive conceptualization":

it means there is no conceptualization of differentiation. Moreover, Bandhuprabha states: "Alternatively, they are of the same category as those [beings], and thus cannot be conceptually distinguished. (The commentary explains: "This means they are identical to the lack of intrinsic nature.")

Because the manifestation of false and other such modes of conduct cannot be known, they are "indistinguishable" (*avibhāga*). Alternatively, it may mean that while he can manifest bodies within the six realms of existence, these are indistinguishable from those of the six realms in that they possess no distinct characteristics;

thus they are called "indistinguishable. According to the *Liang* commentary, the number, appearance, time, and location of the manifested transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) are all indistinguishable.
As for the various explanations above, there are four interpretations in total. The first states: whatever body is manifested does not arise through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).

Because it arises spontaneously, it is called "indiscernible. Alternatively, it is called "indiscernible" because, among sentient beings, its manifestations such as wrong conduct and so forth cannot be known.
"The wisdom that is the true object of pursuit for all bodhisattvas.
The commentary states: This is the fifteenth virtue. Vasubandhu says it is the merit of the application (*prayoga*) of the immeasurable basis for the discipline of sentient beings;
that is to say, it is the immeasurable basis for bodhisattvas, capable of performing the work of disciplining all sentient beings.
This is not because the Buddhas, having already attained equality between self and others, further seek this wisdom.

Rather, it is because the Buddhas have already performed such supreme acts of subduing (*vinaya*). (The general explanation of the meaning is as follows: the Buddha’s wisdom of subduing is that upon which immeasurable bodhisattvas rely;

it is realized through the gradual application of the bodhisattvas’ practices and is not something sought by the Buddhas, because the Buddhas have already realized the most excellent subduing. Other explanations of the distinctions are as cited later. As for the commentary by Asvabhāva, he says: "That is to say, by means of the immeasurable..."

The basis of the bodhisattvas, for the purpose of taming all sentient beings, they initiate application through the sovereign power of the Buddha, preceded by hearing the Dharma, and thereby obtain sublime wisdom.

Bodhisattvas of various classes receive it, entrust it, and pass it on in succession, revolving without interruption. By means of this, they realize the wisdom sought by all bodhisattvas alike. (In this regard...)

In this commentary, first the merits are explained, and subsequently the scriptural phrases are explained. Regarding the phrase "the support of immeasurable bodhisattvas," this explains the aforementioned "immeasurable support. This immeasurable support is none other than the Buddha-wisdom (*buddhajñāna*). Some say it is the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*) of the bodhisattvas;

because they wish to subdue the minds of sentient beings that cling to grasping, they initiate the wisdom of application (*prayogajñāna*) to seek Buddha-wisdom. Alternatively, one may seek the wisdom of the bodhisattvas. Although there are these two interpretations, seeking Buddha-wisdom is superior. Below, the scriptural phrases are explained.

Through the sovereign power of the Buddha, there are bodhisattvas who, preceded by hearing the Dharma, attain the non-conceptual sublime wisdom of the first bhūmi, or may even attain the Buddha’s all-encompassing sublime wisdom. It is like a single lamp transmitting its flame to a thousand lamps.

Bodhisattvas of diverse types prior to the bhūmis, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas of indeterminate lineage, are personally taken into the care of the Buddha. At the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he entrusts them to other Buddhas and great bodhisattvas, and to all virtuous people, so that they may successively cause others to hear, contemplate, and cultivate wisdom.

By means of this, all bodhisattvas and others alike realize the fruit of Buddhahood, which is the wisdom sought by all. In Vasubandhu’s *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, "skillfully protecting and mindful" refers to bodhisattvas whose faculties are mature, while "skillfully entrusting" refers to bodhisattvas whose faculties are not yet mature.
Wuxing further states: "In order to categorize and sustain śrāvakas and bodhisattvas of indeterminate lineage, the Mahāyāna is praised.
To manifest this matter, it is next stated that 'it is the wisdom sought by all bodhisattvas and others. (The commentary explains:

In order to list the śrāvakas of indeterminate lineage and cause them to advance, and to sustain the bodhisattvas of indeterminate lineage so they do not regress, the wisdom of the Mahāyāna is taught. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: 'Throughout the buddha-fields of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle; there is no second, nor..."*
"There are none [who possess it], except for the Buddha’s skillful means" (as stated in the *Tri-svabhāva-nirdeśa*). Bandhuprabha’s commentary explains:

"This reveals the supreme merit of the Blessed One’s skillful means in ensuring that the lineage of the Buddhas (*buddhavamsa*) remains uninterrupted. That is to say, it is the Bodhisattvas who diligently cultivate the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) in order to prevent the lineage of the Buddhas from being severed, and not the Śrāvakas and others.
Therefore, the wisdom of the Buddha is that which only Bodhisattvas should rightly seek. (Based on this).

The Buddha-wisdom is that which is sought; it is not the bodhisattva-wisdom that is sought. The subsequent commentary by Bandhuprabha is also the same as that of Asvabhāva, as in the various explanations above.
There are two explanations in total: first, the virtue of benefiting others; second, the non-interruption of the Buddha-lineage, which is the virtue of self-benefit.
One attains the supreme other shore of the Buddha’s non-dual dwelling.
The commentary states: Regarding the sixteenth virtue, Vasubandhu’s explanation says it is the merit of the fulfillment of the *pāramitā* of the equal *dharmakāya*.
That is to say, the non-dual *dharmakāya* is called the "equal *dharmakāya*.

It is within this very non-dual *dharmakāya* that one attains the perfectly pure *pāramitā*. (Explanation: According to the Liang translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, this refers to the fulfillment of the *dharmakāya* and the four virtues.)

The *pāramitās* constitute the essence of merit. Thus, the *Liang* commentary states: "The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is said to abide in the four virtues; when these are perfected, they are called *pāramitās*. (The full explanation is as stated therein. Vasubandhu’s commentary (*Vasubandhu-vyākhyā*) says: "Because it is non-dual, it is called 'equality' (*samatā*).
It is based on this Dharma-body of equality that the fruit-stage of the *pāramitās* is brought to fulfillment.

(The explanation [of the sub-commentary] says: "The Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas are non-dual; therefore, they are called 'equal'."). Vasubandhu further states: "In the fruit-stage, the six perfections neither increase nor decrease."

Therefore, it is called "equality. The details are explained as therein. Bandhuprabha’s commentary states: This reveals the supreme qualities of the Blessed One’s own essential body (*svābhāvika-kāya*).
That is to say, the non-differentiated aspect of the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* is termed "non-duality" (*advaya*).
The Buddha’s abiding in non-duality has the *tathatā* of the *dharmakāya* as its essence; it is a non-differentiated aspect regarding all dualistic aspects of division.
All other [mental states] do not manifest; because one relies on the supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and constantly abides within it, it is called "abiding" (*vihāra*).

This very non-dual abiding is named the "Supreme Other Shore" (*paramapāramitā*). Since the Buddha has fully reached its limit, it is said that he has "attained" (*prāpta*) it. (The commentary explains: These three different explanations by Bandhuprabha are distinguished as follows:

first, citing the meditative concentration in which one abides to reveal the objective realm—the *dharmakāya* of equality; second, although citing the objective realm in which one abides, the intent is to take up the meditative concentration itself; third, taking both the objective realm and the meditative concentration together to establish the name of the attainment. Furthermore, Bandhuprabha...
The text says: "It means that in the Buddha-ground, the non-dual Dharma-body and all the *pāramitās*, such as giving, are equally perfected.

(The commentary explains: Because the Dharma-body is one, it is called "non-dual"; because all six perfections are fulfilled, they are called "equal. As in the various treatises mentioned above, there are generally two interpretations.

One interpretation states that it is called "non-dual" because the Dharma-body is one. Another interpretation states that it is called "non-dual" because within the Dharma-body there are no various dualities.
It is not interspersed with anything else; it is the ultimate, wondrous wisdom of the Tathāgata’s liberation.
The seventeenth virtue. Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "It refers to the ultimate perfection of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) within the unmixed wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Herein, 'resolute conviction' is termed 'liberation' (*vimokṣa*"; that is, the merit of manifesting various distinct Buddha-fields according to that resolute conviction.

[Commentary: The intent of Vasubandhu’s treatise can be understood by relying on Asvabhāva’s explanation. Regarding the term 'unmixed' (*asaṃbhinnam*): the Buddha-fields manifested through the Tathāgata’s resolute conviction are not intermingled."

Regarding the phrase "intermingled," it means that what is called the liberation of the Tathāgata is precisely the Tathāgata’s superior resolve (*adhimukti*) in manifesting his land. Within that which is manifested, there is nothing he does not fully know; therefore, it is called the ultimate consummation of wondrous wisdom (*jñāna*). Wuxing’s commentary states:

This refers to observing the differences in the resolute convictions (*adhimukti*) of sentient beings and manifesting various Buddha-fields of gold, silver, and so forth, without them being intermingled.
When the World-Honored One’s own resolute conviction manifests before him, he reveals everything according to what beings enjoy, with nothing that is not fully known.
Furthermore, Wu-xing said: "Upon hearing the statement that all Buddhas have attained equality, one immediately thinks that [all] should..."
Regarding identity (*ekatva*): in order to dispel this doubt, it is stated next that "the Tathāgata’s wondrous wisdom of liberation is ultimate.

Prajñākaragupta’s commentary explains: "This demonstrates the excellence of the Blessed One’s enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) division; [it is so called] because it establishes the name 'excellence of merit.
That is to say, the enjoyment-bodies are not intermingled, for the enjoyment-bodies of all Tathāgatas are each distinct."
(Explanation of the non-intermixture of the self-enjoyment body: The sublime wisdom of the Tathāgata is able to bring liberation to all sentient beings;
therefore, it is called the "Tathāgata’s sublime wisdom of liberation. The Buddha has attained the ultimate perfection in this wisdom.

Thus, it is said that the Tathāgata’s sublime wisdom is non-intermixed. (This explains the non-intermixture of the sublime wisdom: In the pure buddha-fields, he manifests the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

Nor are they intermingled. (This explains that the bodies of enjoyment for others are not interspersed. Within the great assemblies, he manifests various bodies to bestow the dharma-bliss upon the bodhisattvas;
these too are not intermingled. (This explains that the enjoyment of dharma-bliss is not interspersed.

The Tathāgata’s manifestation of bodies through this wisdom also reaches ultimate perfection. (This is a re-explanation of "ultimate perfection. The later interpretation by Sthiramati is identical to the initial interpretation by Asvabhāva.
(The five preceding explanations of the text are clear enough to understand).
"Realizing the equality of the Buddha-ground, which is without middle or extremes.
The commentary states: This is the eighteenth quality. Vasubandhu’s commentary says: It refers to the three bodies of the Buddha (*trikāya*) being without spatial limitation.
The merit of being beyond limitation refers to the Buddha’s Dharma-body, which cannot be limited to such-and-such a spatial location;

likewise, its Enjoyment-body and Transformation-bodies cannot be said to occupy such-and-such worlds. (The meaning of the text is clear and may be understood accordingly. The *Liang* commentary explains:

Among the Tathāgata’s three bodies, the Dharma-body cannot be measured in terms of its location; the same applies reciprocally to the two bodies of the Response and the Transformation. It cannot [be so measured].

It is said that while this world exists, that world does not; yet there is not a single dharma that exists outside the Dharmakāya, nor is there any realm of sentient beings that exists outside the two bodies of the Nirmāṇakāya and the Saṃbhogakāya.
Regarding the two explanations of "non-existence," the first of these further contains four types.
The intent is the same as that of Vasubandhu; thus, his treatise states: "Just as the world has neither middle nor end, so it is with the Buddha-ground."
It is likewise. The spatial dimensions of merit have no limits; or rather, the spatial dimensions of the world are infinite.
Within these, the three bodies of the Buddhas pervade everywhere equally, corresponding to the measure of the world, by means of the Dharma-body and the others.
It abides precisely within these various worlds and not in any other place. Alternatively, the *dharmakāya* and so forth pervade the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*) equally and universally;
it has no center and no periphery, and is without limitation.

This *dharmakāya* and so forth pervade all locations, manifesting transformations for the benefit of all sentient beings; however, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is neither centerless nor boundless. (Exegesis:)

"Neither middle nor extreme" has four aspects: first, explaining "neither middle nor extreme" by means of analogies and dharmas; second, explaining "neither middle nor extreme" by means of the supported and the support, as in the passage beginning "Alternatively, regarding the world"; third, explaining "neither middle nor extreme" solely in reference to the Buddha-stage, where there is no limitation, as in the passage beginning "Alternatively, regarding the Dharmakāya, etc.";

and fourth, clarifying that while the manifestation of the body for the sake of sentient beings has no limitation—as in the passage beginning "This Dharmakāya, etc."—it is not that the body's own nature lacks middle or extreme.
Furthermore, [Wu]xing said: "It is neither one nor different. To answer the question of what its characteristics are, it is stated next: "Realizing the non-..."

The Middle Way and the Buddha-ground are equal and do not intermingle; therefore, it is said they are "not one. Following the previous point that attaining Buddhahood is non-dual, it is said they are "not different.
Regarding these characteristics of being neither one nor different, how should they be understood? (Answer: Within these qualities, first the question is posed, and then the answer follows.)

Because the preceding section was intended as an answer to this question, it is next stated that the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*) is equal in being free from center and periphery (*anantapāra*). Although these [qualities] are not one, each is all-pervasive; and since they are non-dual, they are also omnipresent.
Thus, there is no center or periphery. Vinitadeva states: "This reveals the preeminent merit of the Blessed One’s realization of the characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness).

That is to say, the characteristic of *tathatā* is without center or periphery, because it is far removed from all characteristics of center and periphery pertaining to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and because it is far removed from spatial [limitations]."
Because it characterizes the middle and the extremes, such *tathatā* (thusness) is the equal *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*).
By realizing this equality of the Buddha-ground, one thoroughly knows all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena and remains unstained therein.

(Commentary: "Because it is far removed from all characteristics of the conditioned and the unconditioned, as well as the extremes" means that, for example, to cling to the conditioned as definitely existing is the extreme of permanence; to cling to it as definitely non-existent is the extreme of annihilation; that which is neither existent nor non-existent is the Middle Way.)

The meaning of the Middle Way is established in dependence upon the extremes; since the nature of the extremes is itself devoid [of self-nature], what is there for the Middle to be the middle of? Therefore, the Buddha realized equality, being free from both middle and extremes. As it is with the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), so it is with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

If one speaks according to worldly convention regarding regions and locations, there may be a "middle" and "extremes"—for example, the Central Kingdom (*madhyadeśa*) is the middle and other countries are called the extremes. Yet the Buddha realized equality because he has no fixed region or location; thus he is far removed from the characteristics of middle and extremes regarding direction and place.

Alternatively, the conditioned and the unconditioned may constitute the two extremes, while that which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned is the middle. Since the extremes do not exist, what is there for the middle to be the middle of? The middle and extremes regarding direction and place should be explained accordingly. (The later explanation by Bandhuprabha is identical to that of Vasubandhu.)
"Extending to the limit of the dharma-realm. The commentary states:
The nineteenth virtue. Vasubandhu’s commentary says: That which is the utterly pure dharma-realm is called "extreme."

Within the *dharmadhātu*, it is that which reaches the limit of the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), constantly manifesting the merit of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
(This may be understood according to Asvabhāva’s commentary. Asvabhāva’s commentary states:

"Because this *dharmadhātu* is supremely pure, it can give rise to the *sūtras* and other teachings that are its natural outflow (*niṣyanda*). Reaching the ultimate extent of this *dharmadhātu*, for all sentient beings in future ages..."
That which is appropriate, it is always able to manifest for the sake of benefit and peace. (The commentary explains: From the most pure *dharmadhātu* flows forth correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*).

Because of correct wisdom, subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) flows forth. Because of subsequent wisdom, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) flows forth. Because of great compassion, the twelve divisions of the scriptures, such as the *Sūtras*, flow forth. Because this *dharmadhātu* is eternally abiding, it is always able to manifest benefit in future worlds. Master Bandhuprabha’s commentary states:
This reveals the supreme merit of the World-Honored One’s realization of the fruit, namely, that he has attained the ultimate...

The utterly pure dharma-realm (*suviśuddhadharmadhātu*). Thus, regarding the fruit of the path cultivated within this dharma-realm, the later commentary by Bandhuprabha (Cintāmaṇi) agrees with Asvabhāva:
it is coextensive with the nature of empty space.
The commentary states: Regarding the twentieth virtue, Vasubandhu’s explanation says it is "inexhaustible merit," meaning that the Buddha's wisdom is inexhaustible because it is like space.

Asvabhāva’s explanation says: Like that space, it is boundless and limitless, inexhaustible and undiminished, without arising or ceasing, and without change; at all times, it manifests and accommodates all things.

All things that possess material obstruction are likewise the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Its characteristic is to constantly manifest before [beings] to bring about the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
It exhausts all realms, universally performing various acts of benefit for sentient beings without ceasing. As explained at length therein:
[it is like space].
"Extending to the limit of the future.
The commentary states: This is the twenty-first virtue. Vasubandhu’s explanation says that this refers to ultimate merit (*niṣṭhā-guṇa*).
The word "etcetera" implies that this Buddha-wisdom is ultimately coextensive with the limit of the future, being without interruption; therefore, it is called "supreme."
Regarding "pure awakening," Wu-xing’s commentary states: "The term 'etcetera' includes ultimate merit;

that is to say, these merits continue without interruption until the end of the future, reaching the very limit of the boundless future, thereby manifesting that the Buddha's merits are eternally inexhaustible because the sentient beings to be converted are eternally inexhaustible. According to Bandhuprabha, the latter two...

Combined Explanation: Therefore, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states: "The two subsequent kinds of preeminent qualities demonstrate that the Tathāgata’s qualities are inexhaustible, pervading the nature of space and reaching the limits of the future.
This demonstrates that the Tathāgata’s two virtues—those for his own benefit and those for the benefit of others—are inexhaustible.
That is to say, like space, they remain eternally inexhaustible throughout the kalpas of cosmic formation and destruction. Thus, the Tathāgata...
All true merits are likewise thus: they are eternally uninterrupted and inexhaustible, having no end as long as the limits of the future.
The merits for benefiting others are also thus: they reach to the end of the future, because they constantly perform deeds for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
Master Bandhuprabha’s subsequent commentary states: "This demonstrates that the World-Honored One is inexhaustible."
The ultimate, supreme merit is like space: it is eternally inexhaustible. The merits arising from the *dharmadhātu* of all Buddhas are likewise so;
because they are inexhaustible, they have no end as long as the future limit (*anāgata-koṭi*) endures.

Because the application (*prayoga*) for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings is without rest. (The commentary explains: Regarding the two explanations by Bandhuprabha, there is a distinction.

In the former explanation, the names of the qualities are established as being entirely inexhaustible. In the latter "furthermore" explanation, he follows Vasubandhu and others, including questions and answers; the full details are as presented therein. The above constitutes the explanation of the Tathāgata’s qualities.
I have fully set forth the various treatises. Those who lecture upon them may expand or abbreviate according to their own inclination.
If one employs only one [commentary], one should take Vasubandhu’s explanation or the initial exposition by Bandhuprabha. If one employs both, one should combine the two schools.
"Together with a great assembly of immeasurable śrāvakas.

The commentary states: From this point downward is the fifth section, the teaching for those of capacity (the sixth of the six [sections], namely the accomplishment of the assembly). Within this, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the śrāvakas;
second, the explanation of the bodhisattvas—referring specifically to these two assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas. Furthermore, regarding these two assemblies, there are four gates.
[This section] first provides a general analysis and subsequently explains the text. Regarding the "four gates," they are: first, distinguishing between existence and non-existence;

second, explaining the sequence of before and after; third, clarifying the provisional and the real; and fourth, revealing the existence or non-existence of other assemblies. Regarding the distinction between existence and non-existence, there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

First, there are scriptural passages that belong exclusively to the Lesser Vehicle and not the Great Vehicle, such as the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Āgamas*. Second, [there are those that] belong exclusively to the Great Vehicle and not...

1. Small [vehicle] alone, such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Tattvārtha-śāstra*. 2. Both small and great [vehicles] listed together, such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. 3.

Neither small nor great [vehicle] listed together, such as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*. Question: If there are these four categories, [how are they to be understood]?
How should one interpret the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*? It states: "In the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, only the śrāvakas are listed;
in the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, both the assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas are fully listed. Regarding this, there are two explanations.

One says that while it is according to reality as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is because the intentions of those who compiled the sūtras in the fourfold manner differ. Another says that it is according to reality...

This involves four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). However, because the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dazhidu lun) seeks to clarify the distinctions between the superiority and inferiority of the two Piṭakas, it fully explains only two propositions.

It has been traditionally transmitted since ancient times that this is because [the two groups] respectively possess or lack the reality [of the teaching], or because of the expansion and abbreviation [of the text]. As the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha states in his *Commentary on the Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*: "Three reasons are established for not having the same audience hear [the teaching]:

first, the assembly at Gṛdhrakūṭa heard only the latter portion of the formal exposition, but did not hear the causes and effects clarified in the former portion of the formal exposition; the assembly at Rājagṛha heard the causes and effects of the former portion, but did not hear the conditions of the latter portion."

Regarding the purpose of [the term] "equal assembly" (*sabhāga-śravaṇa*): at that time, there were those among the assembly who heard [the teaching] and those who did not; for this reason, the term "equal hearing" was not established. As for the second meaning: it is taught that the fruit of the four virtues is the Four Buddhas, while the cause of the three bodies is Śākyamuni.

It is not only that the assembly listening differs, but also that the Lord of the Dharma is distinct; therefore, "equal hearing" is not established. As for the third meaning: the hearing of the repentance was a personal dream-vision experienced by the monk Xinxiang alone; it could not be shared with a multitude of equal hearers. For these three reasons, "equal hearing" is not established. Regarding the distinction between "before" and "after": this is not fixed.
There are scriptural passages where the Great [Vehicle] comes first and the Small [Vehicle] follows, such as in the *Five Turbidities*.
Sūtra: There are indeed sūtras that present the Small Vehicle first and the Great Vehicle later, such as this very sūtra and others. Question:
If this is so, why do the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* both state that the Śrāvakas come first?

Answer: As stated in the fourth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are two kinds of Buddha-dharma: first, the secret; second, the manifest. Within the gate of manifestation, [the Śrāvakas] come first.
Regarding the mention of *śrāvakas*, it is because their afflictions (*kleśa*) have been extinguished without remainder.

Within the secret gate (*guhyamukha*), the Bodhisattvas are mentioned first, as they attain the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*) and thereby sever the afflictions. The commentary explains:

"Therefore, the two sūtras each rely on one specific meaning and do not contradict one another. However, the reason *śrāvakas* are mentioned first is according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, for there are eight [reasons]."
The second [purpose] says: First, for those who harbor doubts regarding the Mahāyāna, it is to eliminate those doubts.

Those who doubt that the Mahāyāna teachings were spoken by the Buddha hear them directly from the Buddha and thus believe they are the Buddha’s word. Second, for those of indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*), it is to cause them to develop firm conviction.
As for those of indeterminate nature who desire to attain the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle, they are sent near the Buddha [to turn them toward the Great Vehicle].

They attain great fruit. Third, because the various great śrāvakas have already purified themselves by relinquishing pride regarding their own nobility, and so forth, as explained at length (meaning that they were personally transformed and instructed by the World-Honored One; this is the ultimate gateway of abandoning high arrogance).
Fourth, furthermore, because the śrāvakas constantly follow the Buddha, whereas bodhisattvas who transform sentient beings do not constantly follow the Buddha, the śrāvakas are listed first.

Fifth, because his physical appearance is identical to that of the Buddha (having shaved his hair and donned dyed robes, his form is identical to the Buddha’s; since Bodhisattvas are not fixed [in this regard], this is mentioned later).

Sixth, because he is an inner retainer (one who has left the household life and stays close to the Buddha is called an inner retainer). Seventh, furthermore, it causes Bodhisattvas to give rise to reverence, and so forth, as explained at length (because he personally attends upon the Buddha).
The Bodhisattva’s reverence is like that of an attendant toward a king, whereas others’ respect is [merely] for the sake of [the Bodhisattva’s] status.

Eighth, by means of this, he praises the virtues of the Śrāvakas so as to cause other sentient beings who are Śrāvakas to develop pure faith; thus he further explains the Bodhisattva’s intention for revering the Śrāvakas.

If even a Bodhisattva shows such reverence, how much more so should the rest of the assembly? According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are two successive explanations. It says: Question: If...
If counting from above, the Bodhisattvas should come first; if counting from below, the Upāsikās should come first.

Why, then, are the four assemblies of Śrāvakas mentioned first, followed by the Bodhisattvas? The answer is: although the wisdom of Bodhisattvas is vast, they should be spoken of immediately after the Buddha because their delusions are not yet exhausted;
for this reason, they are mentioned later. Although the wisdom of the Arhats is slight, their delusions [are exhausted].

[The afflictions] have already been exhausted; therefore, this was explained first. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva, through the power of skillful means (*upāya*), manifests entry into the five realms of existence (*pañca-gati*) and undergoes the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*) in order to guide sentient beings.
If he were to appear above the level of an Arhat, gods and worldly people would give rise to suspicion and wonder;
for this reason, it was explained later. The detailed explanation is as in that [text]. As for the terms "expedient" (*prajñapti*) and "reality" (*bhūta-tathatā*): this entire sutra is like...
Regarding the meaning as it truly is, as previously stated, there are two locations where this is taught: first, the Pure Land; second, the Impure Land.
Now, in explaining this sūtra: if within the Pure Land, the bodhisattvas are real while the followers of the Two Vehicles are provisional, then the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 79, states:
Question: Which sentient beings are not born in the Pure Land? Answer: Ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the Two Vehicles.
Because [the *bodhisattvas*] are those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), one knows that the two vehicles are transformations and not real.

If, within a defiled land (*saṃkliṣṭa-kṣetra*), the two vehicles were real and the *bodhisattvas* were provisional, then because they undergo the transformation of death (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) which is invisible, and because from the seventh stage onward they may still undergo the death of the physical body (*prādeśika-maraṇa*), they would possess a real body;
thus, there would be no error in this meaning. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "From the seventh stage onward, [they have not yet...]"

Regarding the statement that there are other assemblies, whether existent or non-existent, among those who have cast off their insect-like or physical bodies: if one relies on the defiled lands (*saṃkliṣṭa-bhūmi*), there are actual beings such as nāgas and so forth.
Therefore, the second fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* states: "Within this assembly, there are also other beings.
Those who compiled the Dharma briefly describe two assemblies because of their preeminence, as the sutra later says: 'The world with its devas, humans, and asuras...'"
Luo and the rest of the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it.
If [these beings] are in a Pure Land, there are transformed dragons and the like; thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* says:

"There is no fault in transformation, as it serves to adorn the assembly for the preaching of the Dharma. Whether manifested by the Buddha or manifested by a Bodhisattva—[as stated in] Vasubandhu’s and Asvabhāva’s [commentaries].

Regarding the assembly of śrāvakas, there are three distinct sections: first, the enumeration and classification of their types; second, the detailed explanation of their various virtues beginning with "All... (*sarva...*) and so forth;

Discriminating the categories: this refers to distinguishing the bodhisattvas from within the two assemblies; therefore, they are called *śrāvakas*. The text consists of five sections:

first, discriminating those who accompany [the Buddha]; second, explaining "immeasurable"; third, interpreting its "greatness"; fourth, clarifying the term *śrāvaka*; and fifth, manifesting the assembly.

Regarding the term "together with" (*sārdham*): it refers to the Buddha being in the presence of the assembly; because his person is joined with theirs, it is designated as "together. Furthermore, "together" implies "in common.

Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that one is "together with the Great Saṃgha," and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains that being in the same place, at the same time, with the same mind, the same precepts, the same views, the same path, and the same liberation is what is meant by "commonality. The "together with" in this sutra refers precisely to that.
Regarding the term "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*), Bandhuprabha’s commentary states that their number is so vast as to be difficult to calculate;
hence they are called immeasurable. As for the term "great" (*mahat*), according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it has three meanings: first, greatness; second, abundance.
It is "Great" because it is supreme among the assemblies, because all obstacles have been severed, and because it is revered by kings and others.
It is called "Many" because its number is exceedingly vast. It is called "Victorious" because it triumphs over the treatises of the ninety-six non-Buddhist schools.
According to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, there are four interpretations: first, śrāvakas of the lineage characterized by the various pāramitās who possess sharp faculties;

second, because they have attained the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); third, those of indeterminate lineage who, according to the meaning of reality, turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle.
Therefore, it is called "Great. Fourth, it is called "Great" because of its multiplicity, as in the case of a "great assembly" today.

(Paramārtha’s commentary states: There are three meanings of "Great": first, greatness of number, as when one speaks of a "great army"; it is called great because the number is many. Second, greatness of magnitude, as when one speaks of a "great mountain"; it is not called great because the number is many, but rather because its physical dimensions are high and vast. Third, greatness of excellence, as when one speaks of a "great king";

this has nothing to do with the number being many or the dimensions being high and vast, but is so named solely because of the excellence of his virtue. It is the same for the Śrāvakas; because their number is not one, they are thus [called a great assembly].)

"Numerous" means great in number. "Seeking the fruit of Buddhahood by turning back [from the Lesser Vehicle], practicing the Bodhisattva path, and reaching the ultimate unsurpassed state" refers to being great in excellence (*viśeṣa-mahat*). "Vast, bottomless, and immeasurable" refers to being great in magnitude (*pramāṇa-mahat*). As for the term "Śrāvaka":

"Because one enters the noble path by hearing the Buddha’s vocal sounds, one is called a Śrāvaka. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 82, states:
"Because one hears the vocal sounds of the sublime Dharma from others, and can also cause others to hear the sound of the sublime Dharma, one is called a Śrāvaka. (10)
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "Because one attains penetration by hearing sounds from others, one understands the meaning through hearing sounds; thus, the Śrāvaka-yāna is established.

To explain the intent of that sūtra, refer to the fourth fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. A "harmonious assembly" (saṃgha) refers to the union of both principle and phenomena; thus it is called an "assembly. This is explained in detail in the third fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

"All are sons of the Buddha.
The commentary states: This is the second virtue, that of perpetuating the lineage of the Buddhas. Furthermore, these "sons of the Buddha" have three meanings.
First, there is the interpretation of "son of the Buddha" applying exclusively to the śrāvakas, as in this very *Sūtra* and the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*. As Sthiramati explains:
Because the Noble Path arises through the power of the Buddha, one is called a "Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*). As it is said: "All are born from the mouth of the World-Honored One;

they are born from the True Dharma. According to another interpretation, all are "Sons of the Buddha" because they are Great Śrāvakas who proceed toward [Nirvāṇa] and are able to succeed the lineage of the Buddha, ensuring that it is not severed.
A second view explains "Son of the Buddha" by referring exclusively to Bodhisattvas, as in the *Liang* translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
The eighth fascicle states: "The Son of the Buddha possesses five meanings: first, aspiring to the Unsurpassed Vehicle as the seed;
second, taking Prajñā as the mother; third, taking Samādhi as the womb; fourth, taking Great Compassion as the wet nurse;

and fifth, taking all Buddhas as the father. Paramārtha’s commentary explains: "To form the body of a sentient being, one must necessarily possess five things: first, the father; second, [the mother...]"
First, the seed; second, the mother; third, the womb; fourth, the wet nurse. The father is the fundamental source from which the child is produced;
therefore, the father is explained first. Since the father’s physical remains serve as the seed of the body, the seed is explained second.
Although there is a seed, if there is no mother to conceive it, the body cannot be formed; therefore, the mother is explained third. Although the mother conceives...
If there were no womb, the body likewise could not be formed; since the womb is the place where the body is established, the fourth [section] clarifies the womb.
After birth, if there were no wet nurse to suckle and nourish one, the body would still not be formed; therefore, the fifth [section] clarifies the wet nurse.
It is the same for the Son of the Buddha, who possesses five superior conditions: first, the superiority of the father—the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
1. Superiority of the father: because the bodhicitta serves as the seed. 2. Superiority of the seed: because the bodhicitta serves as the seed. 3. Superiority of the birth-mother:
because prajñā serves as the birth-mother. 4. Superiority of the womb: because the sustenance of merit and wisdom serves as the womb. 5. Superiority of the wet-nurse:
because great compassion serves as the wet-nurse who nurtures and raises [the child]. (These three points summarize the analogies.)
Regarding "Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas as Sons of the Buddha," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle 72, states:

"There are five kinds of sons of the Buddha, all born from the mouth and born of the Dharma; namely, the Srotāpanna up to the Arhat, as well as the Bodhisattva who has entered the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and the Pratyekabuddha.
Although they have planted the causal conditions within the Buddha-Dharma, they are able to attain [their respective fruits] by themselves when there is no Buddha."

Regarding the Way, one cannot say that it is "born from the Buddha’s mouth," because the causal conditions are remote (as explained in *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* 84, *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* 2, *Vyākhyāyukti* 1, *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* 6, *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* 13, and *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* 41, all of which comment on the term "Son of the Buddha"; fearing prolixity, they are not cited here).
"His mind is well-liberated and his wisdom is well-liberated. The commentary states:
This refers to the third quality, the liberation of mind and wisdom. As stated in the Sūtra: "Because he has attained freedom from craving, his mind is liberated;
because he is free from ignorance, his wisdom attains liberation. For this reason, various masters offer differing interpretations of the Sūtra. [They] divide...

The proponents of a separate doctrine (*pṛthagvādin*) state as follows: "The nature of the mind is originally pure; because it is defiled by adventitious afflictions (*āgantukakleśa*), it is said to be impure.
However, according to its actual fundamental nature, the mind attains liberation and wisdom is well-liberated.

According to the Sarvāstivāda school, regarding the "well-liberated mind," when the mind is separated from greed, there is the resolve (*adhimokṣa*) associated with that mind. This is the [liberation].
Because it is liberated from craving, it is called "liberated mind through resolute conviction" (*adhimukti*). As for "liberated wisdom through resolute conviction":
when wisdom is separated from ignorance, the resolute conviction associated with that wisdom is liberated from ignorance; therefore, it is called "wisdom liberated through resolute conviction.
This does not refer to liberation as unconditioned *nirvāṇa*. For a detailed analysis, see the *Mahā-* [Vibhāṣā].
The *Vibhāṣā* states this in its twenty-seventh, twenty-eighth, and seventy-second fascicles. Now, following the Mahāyāna as explained in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*:
"One becomes liberated in mind by being free from craving for the three realms. As the sūtra says: "Because one is already free from craving, the mind attains liberation.
And as the sūtra says: "By being free from ignorance, wisdom attains liberation. The commentary explains:
The intent of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* is that, by means of mental wisdom (*citta-prajñā*), one realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) attained through the departure from craving and ignorance;

this constitutes the essence of liberation, and there is no contradiction with principle, as the treatise does not make such a distinction. However, according to the third fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it further states:
"Moreover, the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) belong to craving and belong to views. The afflictions belonging to craving obscure the mind, while those belonging to views..."

Affliction obscures wisdom. Thus, because of detachment from craving (*tṛṣṇā*), one is also detached from the fetters and underlying tendencies associated with craving, and attains liberation of mind (*ceto-vimukti*).

Because of detachment from ignorance (*avidyā*), one is also detached from the fetters and underlying tendencies associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*), and attains liberation by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*). Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Chapter 25) states:
"Because the minds of greed, hatred, and delusion are forever severed and extinguished, the mind is well-liberated; regarding all phenomena, one knows [them as they truly are]."
There is no obstruction; wisdom is well-liberated. According to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, the third fascicle, "good" (*praṇīta*) is used as a synonym for "excellent" (*śobhana*).
However, "excellent liberation" itself carries three meanings: first, it distinguishes [this liberation] from that of non-Buddhist practitioners who have abandoned desire;

although they attain liberation of mind through a certain place or a certain path, it is not attained in all respects, and thus it is not called "excellent. Second, it distinguishes [this liberation] from that of those within our own school who are still learners (*śaikṣa*); although...
They have attained liberation; however, because residual fetters and proclivities remain, it is not a "good" liberation.

This excludes the Arhats of the *parihāṇadharman* (subject to falling away) among those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), who attain "timely liberation" (*sāmayikī vimukti*) rather than a good liberation. Therefore, "good liberation" is spoken of only in reference to Arhats of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*).
"Precepts are virtuously pure.

The commentary states: Regarding the fourth virtue, the virtuous purity of precepts, Bodhisattva Bandhuprabha explains it through three meanings: first, explaining the virtuous purity of precepts by way of the six branches;
second, explaining the virtuous purity of precepts by way of the untainted (*anāsrava*); and third, explaining it by way of the Mahāyāna.
"Precepts are virtuously pure. Thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "As it is said in the sūtras, being endowed with six factors is called 'virtuous purity of precepts':

(1) abiding in pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), meaning that one does not transgress the three types of action regarding the training rules one has undertaken; (2) skillfully guarding oneself through the prātimokṣa vows."

(That is, being able to guard the seven most excellent restraints. Third, being complete in the three rules of conduct (*īryāpatha*). (This refers to being accomplished in proper conduct regarding the four postures—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down;

or regarding activities such as dressing and attending to bodily needs; or regarding the application to wholesome qualities, such as reciting scriptures and practicing meditation. It means acting in accordance with the world and not transgressing worldly norms, and acting in accordance with the Vinaya and not transgressing the Vinaya.

Fourth, all that one undertakes is entirely complete. (This refers to the five places where a bhikṣu should not go: namely, the houses of singers, prostitutes, taverns, kings, and *caṇḍālas*. These are the five types of households, as well as...)

1. Regarding the places prescribed by the Tathāgata, one practices according to the remaining rules based on the appropriate time; this is called "perfection of conduct. 2. One perceives great dread in even minor transgressions.

Following the training rules for small matters, one never intentionally commits an offense even when faced with life-threatening circumstances, and so forth, as explained at length. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Even regarding a minor offense, one maintains great fear.

3. One undertakes the training rules (*śikṣāpada*). This means personally vowing: "I shall fully train in all the rules of training," and so forth, as explained at length. If analyzed in detail, this is as found in the twenty-second fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the seventh fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavāca-śāstra*.

2) Regarding the explanation of "wholesome precepts" (*śīla-kuśala*) in terms of the untainted (*anāsrava*): because one may also attain untainted precepts in all respects, they are called "wholesomely pure.
3) According to the meaning as it truly is: abiding in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), one dedicates oneself to the Mahāyāna;
because one purifies one's own [Hīnayāna] precepts and cultivates the bodhisattva precepts, it is called "wholesomely pure."
"Seeking the joy of the Dharma.

The commentary explains: This is the fifth quality, the seeking of the joy of the Dharma. Vinitadeva provides three interpretations: (1) When seeking the true Dharma, one seeks the joy of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) and does not seek any other joy;
(2) Alternatively, when seeking the Dharma, it is for the sake of bringing joy to others, and there is no fault in seeking [it].
Furthermore, he is free from improper conduct. Regarding these three points of reality, this great śrāvaka seeks exclusively the joy of the Dharma, not seeking fame, gain, or honor.
"Extensive learning, retaining what has been heard, and the accumulation of that which has been heard.
The commentary states: This is the sixth quality, the accumulation of hearing and retention (*śrutadhara-saṃbhāra*).

These three types of wisdom (*prajñā*)—distinguished according to their initial, middle, and final stages—are explained as being threefold solely in terms of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). As Bandhuprabha stated: "In immeasurable sūtras, [the Buddha spoke of] the beginning, middle, and end..."

Because one is able to hear and receive all [teachings] divided [into parts], it is called "hearing" (*śruta*). Because one is able to remember and maintain the meanings as they were heard, ensuring they are not forgotten, it is called "retaining what has been heard" (*śrutadhara*).
Because one repeatedly practices the words and their meanings so that they remain firmly established, it is therefore called the "accumulation of what has been heard."
"One thinks what is well-thought, speaks what is well-spoken, and acts what is well-acted.
The commentary explains: "The seventh is the virtue of the three types of action conforming to wisdom (*jñāna-anuvartana*). As Yaśomitra explains:
'Worldly fools think what is ill-thought, speak what is ill-spoken, and act what is ill-acted; the supramundane noble ones (*ārya*) transcend those qualities and [possess the opposite]."
The opposite of that is called "well-considered in what is considered, well-spoken in what is spoken, and well-done in what is done.
Thus, the three types of action are pure, and one acts in accordance with wisdom. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 70, states:

"Whatever is currently manifested as bodily, verbal, or mental action—whether it be ill-considered in what is considered, ill-spoken in what is spoken, or ill-done in what is done—all such [actions] do not..."
Pure. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 25, states: "What are the characteristics by which one recognizes a wise person?
It is said that through the characteristic of their actions, one recognizes a fool; and through the characteristic of their actions, one recognizes a wise person. What is this matter like?

It is that fools think what should not be thought, speak what should not be spoken, and do what should not be done. [The wise, however, are the opposite...]"* *(Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the wise. The full passage typically continues to describe how the wise think well, speak well, and act well.)*
The wise person is one who reflects well upon what is to be reflected upon, speaks well what is to be spoken, and performs well what is to be performed;
this is called the mark of one accomplished in wisdom.
It is swift wisdom, rapid wisdom, sharp wisdom, emergent wisdom, superior discerning wisdom, great wisdom, vast wisdom, and incomparable wisdom.
"The accomplishment of the treasure of wisdom.
The commentary states: This is the eighth [topic], the qualities of the various distinctions of wisdom. Regarding the explanation of these various forms of wisdom, there are differing opinions.

One says that this sutra explains eight types of wisdom in general, with their names as listed in the sutra; the subsequent phrase "accomplishment of the treasure of wisdom" then subsumes the aforementioned [eight].

The eight [kinds of] wisdom constitute the treasure of wisdom; it is not that wisdom is established as a separate category. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks only of the "treasure of wisdom" (*prajñā-ratna*) and does not speak of "wisdom-treasure" (*ratna-prajñā*).
One school asserts there are nine kinds of wisdom; thus, both the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (the *Dazhidu lun*) refer to it as "precious wisdom" (*ratna-prajñā*).

Thus we know there is a distinct wisdom. One interpretation states that this sutra refers to the ten wisdoms of the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, adding "profound and subtle wisdom" (*gambhīra-sūkṣma-prajñā*).
Therefore, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* says: "There is a version which further speaks of profound and subtle wisdom, because others cannot fathom its depths."
For now, we shall rely on nine [types of wisdom] to distinguish the various forms of prajñā. Thus, Bandhuprabha states:

because one swiftly enters into the meaning of the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Buddha, it is called *tīkṣṇaprajñā* (swift wisdom). Because one enters deeply into the meaning within that very [teaching], it is called *javanaprajñā* (rapid wisdom);
for one who can traverse much is said to possess rapid wisdom. Because one penetrates subtle meanings, it is called *niścitaprajñā* (sharp wisdom).

Because one attains the sublime wisdom capable of transcending birth and death, it is called "wisdom of transcendence" (*niḥsaraṇaprajñā*). This wisdom serves as the cause of realization for *nirvāṇa*;
therefore, it is termed "supreme discerning wisdom" (*viśeṣaviniścayaprajñā*). It is called "supreme discernment" because it is supreme discernment, which is itself *nirvāṇa*.
Since this wisdom serves as the cause of realization for that [nirvāṇa], it is designated by that name. (The above explains "wisdom of transcendence"; now follows the question and answer.)
Because its discernment is inexhaustible, it is called "Great Wisdom" (*mahāmati*). Because it is profoundly vast, perfect, and thoroughly penetrating, it is called "Extensive Wisdom" (*vipulamatī*).
Because this wisdom is superior even among the assembly of Śrāvakas with dull faculties and the like, it is called "Incomparable Wisdom" (*asamamatī*).

Because this wisdom can bring about the supreme goal (*paramārtha*), it is called the "jewel of wisdom" (*prajñāratna*). All *śrāvakas* possess this jewel of wisdom; therefore, they are said to be "accomplished in the jewel of wisdom.
(The commentary explains that the "supreme goal" is *nirvāṇa*). According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there is a slight difference from that [definition].

The eighty-third fascicle states: "It is called 'swift wisdom' (*javanaprajñā*) because it understands with rapidity, and it is called 'unimpeded wisdom' (*asaṅgaprajñā*) because it is free from obstruction."
It is called "swift wisdom" because it is able to thoroughly understand things as they are and in their full extent.
It is called "sharp wisdom" because it thoroughly understands the phenomena of renunciation and the world-transcending freedom from desire.

It is called "wisdom of emergence" because it can thoroughly understand all worldly phenomena that lead to freedom from desire. It is called "supreme wisdom of discernment" because this very wisdom, over a long period of time...
Through repeated cultivation, it is called "Great Wisdom" (*mahāmati*). Because this very wisdom has immeasurable and boundless spheres of activity, it is called "Vast Wisdom" (*vipulamati*).
Because no other wisdoms are equal to it, it is called "Incomparable Wisdom" (*asamamatī*). Among all the faculties...
Because wisdom is supreme, it is like a mani jewel that causes the lapis lazuli treasure of a wheel-turning monarch to manifest, making its light pure;
by being associated with that [wisdom], all the treasures of wisdom are fully accomplished.

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, there are eleven types of wisdom, as extensively explained in sequence in the eighty-third fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Fearing prolixity, they are not detailed here.
[The text] does not elaborate.
[He is] "endowed with the three types of clear knowledge" (*tisro vidyāḥ*).

The commentary states: The ninth [quality] is the virtue of being endowed with the three types of clear knowledge. As stated in the Sūtra, there are three kinds of clear knowledge: first, [the knowledge of past lives]...

The supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) of the realization of the knowledge of recollection (*anusmṛti-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā-vidyā*), second, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapāda-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā-vidyā*), and third, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna-sākṘātkriyā-vidyā*).
Regarding these three knowledges, according to the Sarvāstivāda school and the intent of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, they are analyzed through four gates.
First, the essential nature (*svabhāva*): they take wisdom (*prajñā*) as their intrinsic nature. In their respective order, they correspond to the fifth among the six supernormal knowledges.

The first is the knowledge of past lives; the second is the divine eye; and the sixth is the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). These three supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) constitute their essential nature.

The intention behind establishing these three is that they respectively counteract the three types of delusion regarding the prior limit, the subsequent limit, and the intermediate limit. Third is the distinction between the provisional and the ultimate.

The "clear knowledge of the destruction of the outflows" (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna-vidyā*) encompasses both the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*), because it penetrates the untainted (*anāsrava*). The other two [knowledges] are conventionally designated as such because they are exclusively tainted (*sāsrava*).

(Both tainted and untainted knowledges are termed "destruction of the outflows," because both arise within a body that has exhausted the outflows. The ultimate is named untainted, while the conventional is named tainted; these are designated as conventional or ultimate by comparing their superior and inferior qualities.

Fourth, the distinction between those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*): this [knowledge] exists only in those beyond training, because those in training still possess darkness. Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* [states]: [One]... (The provided text ends here).
The one hundred and second fascicle says: Question: Among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), why are only three designated as "clear knowledges" (*vidyā*)? Answer:

The supernormal power of the realization of knowledge regarding the basis of psychic power (*ṛddhividhi-jñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*) functions like the spheres of craftsmanship (*śilpasthāna*). The supernormal power of the realization of knowledge regarding the divine ear (*divyaśrotra-jñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*) can only apprehend sound.

The supernormal power of the realization of knowledge regarding the minds of others (*paracitta-jñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*) only apprehends specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Because they lack superior utility, they are not established as "clear knowledges. As for the latter three supernormal powers...
All possess superior efficacy; therefore, they are established as "clairvoyances" (*vidyā*). As for this superior efficacy:
it means that all are able to accord with the renunciation of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), all are able to bring forth sublime qualities (*guṇa*), and all are able to lead toward sublime *nirvāṇa*.

Question: How is it that the latter three all possess superior efficacy? Answer: The fourth, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*), sees the former...

[He] deeply generates weary detachment regarding phenomena of the posterior limit (*aparānta*). Fifth is the supernormal knowledge of realization through the wisdom of birth and death (*cyutyupapādajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*); seeing phenomena of the posterior limit, he deeply generates weary detachment.

Sixth is the supernormal knowledge of realization through the wisdom of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*). Having already generated weary detachment, he takes delight in *nirvāṇa*.

As explained extensively therein, now according to the Mahāyāna, the commentary of Bandhuprabha states that these three supernormal knowledges are obtained by those of sharp faculties who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), excluding...

Because of the delusions regarding the three time periods—defiled, undefiled, and both—the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) are taught. According to one interpretation, "clear knowledge" has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its intrinsic nature;

since wisdom can eliminate darkness, it is called "clear knowledge. Others say that its intrinsic nature is the wholesome root of non-delusion (*amoha*), as it is the opposite of ignorance (*avidyā*).

It is stated that in the Mahāyāna, these are all permeated by the untainted (*anāsrava*); this does not contradict reason, provided one accepts that subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is untainted.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 69, states: "Among the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the first three are supernormal powers but not clear knowledges (*vidyā*);

the latter three are both supernormal powers and clear knowledges, because they serve as antidotes to ignorance regarding the three periods of time. Furthermore, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 2:
"Recollection of past lives, the divine eye, and the exhaustion of outflows are called the three clear knowledges. Question: Regarding supernormal powers and...
Question: What is the difference between them? Answer: To simply know the events of past lives is called *abhijñā* (supernormal knowledge).

To know the causes, conditions, and karmic actions of the past is called *vidyā* (clear vision). To simply know that one dies here and is born there is called the *divyacakṣur-abhijñā* (clairvoyance).
To know and practice such that the convergence of causes and conditions is never lost is called *vidyā* (clear knowledge).

To directly know the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*)—knowing neither further rebirth nor non-rebirth—is the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*). If one knows the destruction of the outflows and that they will not arise again, this is called *vidyā*.
These are the three *vidyās*, attained by Great Arhats and Great Pratyekabuddhas. A detailed explanation of these three *vidyās* is as found in the *Dharmasaṃgīti*.
The third [section] of the *Sūtra-piṭaka*; the forty-third of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*; the fifty-first of the *Madhyama Āgama*; the sixth of the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*;
the twenty-seventh of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*; the seventy-sixth of the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*; and the eighty-first and one hundred-second [sections] of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
"Attaining all dwellings in happiness in the present life.

The commentary states: This is the tenth quality, dwelling in happiness in the present life. Regarding this dwelling in happiness, according to the Sarvāstivāda school, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 81, says:
"Question: For what reason did the Blessed One state that the four dhyānas are dwellings in happiness?"

Question: Yes. Answer: Only within the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) do both types of bliss exist; therefore, they are called "abodes of bliss" (*sukhavihāra*). The first type is the bliss of sensation (*vedanāsukha*); the second is the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhisukha*).

The first three meditative absorptions possess both types of bliss. In the fourth meditative absorption, there is no bliss of sensation, yet the power and function of the bliss of pliancy are so vast that it surpasses the former two types of bliss.
Although the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) possess pliancy, [they lack the other bliss].

Because it is not extensive, it is not called "bliss. Furthermore, when the fundamental dhyānas manifest, they nourish the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), causing them to arise throughout the entire body and bringing about full satisfaction; therefore, they are called "abiding in bliss.

When the access concentrations (*sāmantaka*) and so forth manifest, they nourish the primary elements, but these arise only at the periphery of the mind and do not bring extreme satisfaction; therefore, they are not "abiding in bliss."
As explained extensively in that treatise, there are nine successive stages;

furthermore, they appear in the *Nyāyānusāra* (79), the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (28), the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra* (8), the *Tattvasiddhi* (20), and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (19). Bandhuprabha’s commentary states:

"Because one has realized and attained the non-retrogressive, supreme meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). Moreover, the eleventh fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Furthermore, these various meditative absorptions..."
Regarding the distinction of its names: it is called "higher mind" (*adhicitta*), because one correctly and thoroughly examines through the predominant power of mental purity;
or it is called "abiding in bliss," because within this state one experiences supreme bliss. Why is this so?
Because the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) involve the experience of joy and bliss, the bliss of tranquility, and the bliss of equanimity and physical and mental well-being;

and because one who has attained concentration repeatedly enters and emerges from these meditative absorptions to experience a state of abiding in bliss in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Thus, while experiencing this abiding in bliss in the present life within concentration, and having arisen therefrom, one speaks as follows: "I have already..."
One experiences such a pleasant abiding; however, in the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), such a feeling does not exist.
Therefore, they are not described as "pleasant abidings. The full explanation is as stated there.
"The Great Pure Field of Merit. The commentary states:
This is the eleventh virtue of the supreme pure field of merit. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle two, "Chapter on the Field of Merit," says:
Question: For what reason are these noble ones called the "field of merit"? Answer: Because they have severed greed.

Because wisdom and other afflictions have been exhausted, they are called "fields of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*). As it is said: "If tares and weeds are not removed, they will harm the sprouts of the good grain.
Therefore, by giving to those who are free from desire, one obtains a great reward and benefit; thus they are called fields of merit. The detailed explanation is as stated therein.
Bandhuprabha’s commentary states: Being eternally free from afflictions, they are like a fertile field in this world, capable of swiftly producing vast and expansive fruits;
their majestic deportment is tranquil and entirely perfect.

The commentary states: Regarding the twelfth virtue, the tranquility of deportment (*īryāpatha-praśāntatā*), Bandhuprabha explains that it consists in dwelling with clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 71, states: "Tranquility of deportment means that the sense faculties (*indriya*) are tranquil and free from agitation."
Furthermore, he does not lift his body high, nor does he move his limbs, yet he speaks; this is called tranquility of deportment.
Because his deportment is without deficiency, it is called "perfect."
"Great patience and gentleness are accomplished without diminution.
The commentary states: "The thirteenth virtue is that of patience and gentleness. Vinitadeva explains: it is the endurance of suffering because one is easy to dwell with.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 92, says: "As for what is called patience, it means that toward the enmity of others, one never..."
Regarding the response: "Gentle" means that the mind is free from resentment and does not afflict others; this is explained in detail as in the twenty-fifth [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Thus, one has properly practiced the holy teachings of the Tathāgata.
The commentary states: "The thirteenth [verse] reveals that [the teaching] has been duly practiced. Bandhuprabha explains:

"Because all that was to be done has been brought to completion, these śrāvakas, having attained the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), have all emerged from saṃsāra; therefore, they have well-practiced the holy teachings of the Tathāgata."
Furthermore, there was an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had gathered from various buddha-fields.

The commentary states: From this point downward is the second section, the explanation of the assembly of bodhisattvas. This contains three parts; first, the enumeration and classification of their types.
Next, following "all abide in the Mahāyāna," their various merits are praised; subsequently, under their respective names, they are listed according to their excellence.

This constitutes the first section, which indicates the number and distinguishes the categories. Specifically, within the two assemblies, the *śrāvakas* have already been explained; therefore, the categories of the *bodhisattva* assembly are now explained separately.
Furthermore, there are three sections: first, the explanation of "immeasurable"; second, "the bodhisattvas, etc."; and third, the analysis of their arrival.
Regarding the term "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*), it indicates that the number is immeasurable because there is no limit.
As for the term "bodhisattva-mahāsattva," if expressed in its full Sanskrit form, one should say *bodhisattva-mahāsattva*.
However, for the sake of brevity, it is simply called "bodhisattva. "Bodhi" means awakening; "sattva" is translated in this land [of China] as "sentient being" (*sattva*).
Alternatively, it has the meaning of "diligence. For this reason, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* by Bandhuprabha explains that there are three meanings. Thus, the second [section] states:
"That which is called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva refers to those bodhisattvas who seek enlightenment (*bodhi*). This term applies generally to all three vehicles;
however, in order to specifically select the Great Vehicle, the word 'mahāsattva' must be further stated. Furthermore, regarding the bodhisattva...

Because they take *sattva* as their object, they are called *bodhisattvas*. They are so named because they fulfill the great vows for their own benefit and the benefit of others, seeking great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Furthermore, *sattva* carries the meaning of "courageous. Because they seek great enlightenment with diligent courage, they are called *bodhisattvas*.
This term applies to all stages; however, here we are referring specifically to the great bodhisattvas on the grounds (*bhūmi*). Therefore...
Furthermore, regarding the term *mahāsattva*, the Bodhisattva Asaṅga, relying on the latter two meanings, states in the first fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*:
"One is called a bodhisattva because 'bodhi' (enlightenment) and 'sattva' (being) serve as the objective referents;
thus, one is named after these objects, just as in the case of the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and so forth. Alternatively, it refers to that very mind which seeks enlightenment."
Because his resolve possesses capability, he is called a Bodhisattva. Furthermore, Bandhuprabha states that within this context, a Bodhisattva is called a Mahāsattva due to three great matters:
first, greatness of number, meaning "immeasurable" and so forth; second, greatness of virtue, meaning abiding in the Great Vehicle;

and third, greatness of activity, meaning the pacification of calamities and misfortunes. According to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are likewise three meanings; thus, [the term] "Great" refers to...
One explanation states that they are called *mahāsattva* because there are three kinds of greatness: first, greatness of aspiration; second, greatness of practice;
and third, greatness of benefiting sentient beings. (For a detailed analysis of the meaning of *bodhisattva-mahāsattva*, see the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicles 37, 71, 411, 486, and 538–556;
as well as the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicle 6; and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicles 4, 5, 34, 5, and 45. From...
Regarding those who have gathered from various buddha-fields: this is the third [point], which clarifies their place of origin.

They have come from the ten directions for the sake of hearing the Dharma. Question: Is it not the case that Maitreya resides in this very region? Why, then, do you say they have come from other directions? Answer:
As stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, it is because one wishes to counteract indolence, arrogance, and the failure to attend.
Because they have gathered here seeking to hear the Dharma, I shall speak briefly of those from other lands.

A full explanation of the reasons why Bodhisattvas come from other lands may be found, for instance, in the first fascicle of the *Jiejing shu* (Commentary on the Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra), the first fascicle of the *Ratnakūṭa-śāstra*, and the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
"All abide in the Mahāyāna.
The commentary states: From here below is the second section, praising all the virtues. Regarding the classification of this sūtra, Bodhisattva Bandhuprabha provides four successive expositions:
first, explaining the ten phrases of the sūtra by way of the ten great themes; second, explaining the ten phrases of the sūtra based on the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Third, the ten-phrase sūtra is explained by way of the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*). Fourth, the ten-phrase sūtra is explained by way of the ten vows;
this is the first [of those]. The text of the ten phrases is divided into ten sections. This is the first explanation of the greatness of diligence (*vīrya*). Bandhuprabha’s commentary states:
"By the power of diligence, one abides securely in the Mahāyāna, rescues beings from existence, and causes them to transcend birth and death. And...

Spontaneously setting out for unsurpassed enlightenment (the commentary explains: "Mahāyāna" refers to those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) and those who seek enlightenment; some say that the *dharmatā* or *tathatā* constitutes Mahāyāna;
here, however, it is explained according to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, where the "vast mind" and so forth constitute abiding in Mahāyāna).
"Roaming the Mahāyāna Dharma. The commentary explains:
the second [verse] praises its greatness as a cause. *Sthiramati*’s commentary states: "Within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one roams progressively by means of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

(The sub-commentary explains: "The 'ten stages, etc. includes the stage of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) by way of inclusive abbreviation. This is the Mahāyāna, and it is also the place where one roams. [It consists of] hearing, reflection, and cultivation, etc.")

These are the three types of mundane wisdom (*prajñā*). The word "etc. includes the untainted wisdom of cultivation (*anāsrava-bhāvanā-prajñā*). This clarifies that these three wisdoms arise in succession regarding the objects of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and are able to produce the stage of Buddhahood; therefore, it is called the "greatness of the cause" (*hetu-mahattva*). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the Mahāyāna is entirely the *dharmatā-tathatā* (the suchness of the nature of phenomena).

Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, by means of the three wisdoms and their associated mental factors, gradually come to realize the realm of suchness and are able to produce the fruit of Buddhahood; therefore, it is called the "greatness of the cause."
"His mind is impartial toward all sentient beings. The commentary explains:
this is the third explanation of the greatness of the object (*ālambana-mahattva*). *Sthiramati*’s commentary states:

"That is, regarding all sentient beings, one attains equality between self and others, by means of the equalizing expedient of great compassion and so forth" (the sub-commentary explains: this virtue has great compassion and so forth as its essence; all sentient beings...).

It takes as its objective referent (*ālambana*) that which is called the "greatness of the object.
