While the former virtue takes *tathatā* (suchness) as its object because it has wisdom as its essence, this [compassion] takes sentient beings as its object because it lacks an intrinsic nature such as [the specific qualities of] loving-kindness and so forth.
This is precisely what is meant in the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* by the term "equal skillful means" (*samatopāya*), due to the identity of essence in great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
"Free from all conceptualization (*vikalpa*), non-conceptualization, and various kinds of conceptualization.
The commentary explains: "The fourth [verse] clarifies the greatness of time (*kāla*). Vinitadeva’s commentary states:
"At all times, it proceeds with equality, as if it were a single moment (*ekakṣaṇa*). An eon (*kalpa*) is called 'conceptualization,' because within all eons and non-eons..."
Because it is a distinct abandonment. Since one does not differentiate between kalpas and non-kalpas, one is able to practice for a long duration without weariness.

The commentary explains: the Sanskrit term is *kalpa*, which is translated here as "differentiation. Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are subsumed within temporal kalpas and are characterized by successive distinctions;
unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are not subsumed within temporal kalpas and possess no such [distinctions].
The differentiation of time and eons is called "non-differentiation. These two are the objects of perception (*ālambana*).

"Various conceptualizations" refers to the conceptualizing mind that takes the aforementioned differentiated and non-differentiated objects as its conditions; thus it is called "various conceptualizations.
The intended meaning here is that if there were conceptualization, one would perceive: "This is time and eons," or "This is not time and eons."
At that time, the kalpas are long, and there may be weariness in practice. Therefore, the bodhisattvas and others distinguish between all kalpas and non-kalpas.
Why? Because by not distinguishing between kalpas and non-kalpas, they are able to practice for a long duration without weariness;
even throughout three incalculable kalpas, all such long durations proceed with equanimity, as if they were but a single thought-moment.
It is like a person who, while not sleeping, discriminates between day and night and thus perceives the night as long;
yet when one is asleep, one does not discriminate the night, and so even though a long night passes, one does not perceive its length. It is the same with passing through incalculable kalpas.
Therefore, the sixth volume of the *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* states: "Only after passing through immeasurable kalpas does one attain the fruit of Buddhahood."
Since the duration of time is so long, how can it be called "swift"? This argument is not tenable, because kalpas of vast duration are merely conceptual constructions.
As a verse says: "In a dream one may think a year has passed, yet upon waking it is but a moment.

Thus, although the time is immeasurable, it is subsumed within a single kṣaṇa. Furthermore, because the Buddha’s diligence is so intensely blazing, even though much time has elapsed, [it appears as if it were brief].
This refers to a short duration. As a verse says: "Though the fool practices for but a short time, his lazy mind feels as if it has been long;
the Buddha, through immeasurable eons, regards them as but a moment. This is also like that; therefore, this statement was made:
at all times, it is as if it were but a single thought-moment.
"Subduing all Māras, enemies, and adversaries. The commentary explains:

The fifth [greatness] reveals the greatness of being untainted (*asaṃkliṣṭa*). Bandhuprabha’s commentary states: "This means that those who subdue the Māras and enemies do so because they have relinquished everything that is grasped.

They are able to subdue the Māras and enemies [because they have relinquished the grasping for the objects of the five kinds of sensory pleasures (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*); thus they are able to subdue the Māra of the afflictions (*kleśamāra*). Alternatively..."
Based on this as the foundation, one is inherently free from the four māras. Furthermore, Bandhuprabha states:
"As it is said, if a bodhisattva regards all things that are grasped as being insubstantial and does not crave them with the mind, they are then able to subdue all māras and enemies.

(The commentary explains: Bandhuprabha cites a sūtra to establish this proof. As the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra* says: 'All dharmas are not solid; always remain established in mindfulness. For one who understands and perceives emptiness, there is nothing at all in terms of mindfulness. This principle of subduing the māras reaches its ultimate limit here. Relying upon...

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* establishes eight kinds of māras: namely, the four inversions regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), with the addition of the four inversions regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

These are collectively termed "māras. This does not constitute a fault within the Hīnayāna school, nor is it a contradiction within the Mahāyāna, as they are subsumed under the "māra of afflictions" (*kleśamāra*).
Therefore, they are omitted in various teachings. A detailed explanation of the four māras is as previously presented in the section on the eighteen perfections (*paripūrṇa*).
The *Madhyāntavibhāga* states:
"It is far removed from all mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

The commentary explains: "The sixth [topic] distinguishes the greatness of mental orientation (*manasikāra-mahattva*). Vinītadeva’s commentary states: "It is far removed from the conceptual mental orientations of the two vehicles."
[The commentary on] the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* by Vasubandhu and Asvabhāva, in the sixth fascicle, is also the same as that of Bandhuprabha.
The seventh fascicle of the Liang translation of the *Saṃgraha* states: "Because one abandons the mental orientations (*vitarka*) of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

The mental orientations of the two vehicles consist of repeatedly contemplating the suffering and impermanence of saṃsāra in the past, and repeatedly contemplating the merit of the tranquility of nirvāṇa. These contemplations merely involve attachment."
"Abandoning one's own benefit for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, and being sustained by the joy and bliss of the vast flavor of the Dharma.
The commentary explains: "The seventh is the sustaining greatness. Jin-guang (Sthiramati) explains that this refers precisely to the joy and bliss of the flavor of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Regarding food, the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) states: "The twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna sūtras are called the Great Dharma;

True Suchness, liberation, and so forth constitute its flavor. By partaking of this flavor of the Dharma, various joys and pleasures arise, nourishing the Bodhisattva’s fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*).
This passage precisely clarifies the maintenance of perfect purity. Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "The food of the joy of Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna... and so on.
"Free from the notion of further food;
transcending the five fears.
The commentary states: "The eighth is the purity of greatness. Jin-guang (Bandhuprabha) explains: "This means transcending the five fears, which refers to the three types of action (*trikarma*)."
It is pure. It emerges from all fears, as there is no longer any violation of the precepts or other such causes for fear of the various evil destinies.
Regarding the five fears: first, the fear of not being able to make a living; second, the fear of faulty recitation; third, the fear of death;

fourth, the fear of the evil destinies; and fifth, the fear of being intimidated by an assembly. When one realizes the stage of pure intention (*śuddhāśayabhūmi*), these five fears are all completely abandoned.

(An extensive explanation of the five fears is found in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* 2, the *Śīla-sūtra* 8, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* 2, the *Tathāgatagarbha-śāstra* 3, the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra* [blank], the *Vibhāṣā* 75,
the *Nyāyānusāra* 49, and so forth.)
"Unwaveringly entering the stage of non-retrogression.
The commentary explains: "The ninth is the attainment of greatness. Bandhuprabha’s commentary states: "Unwaveringly entering the stage of non-retrogression."

At the moment one receives the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), one never again regresses. Within the first seven stages (*bhūmi*), there is still movement through applied effort (*prayoga-vyāyāma*);
the non-regressive path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*) has not yet been attained.

In the remaining stages, one proceeds without applied effort, moving directly toward the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*). (According to the present Dharmapāla school, within the three gates of knowledge, [this pertains to] applied effort...)

Wisdom is exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*). It does not function at all from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward. Furthermore, from the eighth stage upward, no afflictions (*kleśa*) manifest; this is called the "stage of non-retrogression" (*avaivartika-bhūmi*), which will be analyzed later.

Moreover, the tenth fascicle of the *Vyavahāra-śāstra* (The Treatise on Ornamentation) states that there are three types of non-retrogressive bodhisattvas: first, those who have not yet achieved non-retrogression.
The first is the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryā-bhūmi*). The second is that which has already attained non-retrogression, referring to the stages from the first to the seventh.

The third is that which has fully attained non-retrogression, referring to the eighth stage and above. The *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*, the *Bodhicaryāvatāra-ṭīkā* (or *Bodhisambhāra-śāstra*), and the sixth chapter of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* all state that the eighth stage and above are called the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*). Fearing prolixity, I shall not elaborate further.
"The ground that pacifies all calamities and misfortunes of all sentient beings manifests before one.
The commentary explains: this refers to the tenth [ground], which clarifies its greatness of activity (*karmamahattva*). Bandhuprabha’s commentary states:

"It means that all Bodhisattvas are able to pacify the internal and external suffering and afflictions that oppress all sentient beings; the stage of this ground manifests before them. Within this ground..."
Great compassion and great kindness: by means of these two, one is able to pacify all internal sufferings such as illness, as well as the external afflictions such as greed with which one is beset.
Since these two predominantly bring about the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, one who attains them is said to possess "greatness of karma.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Calamities and misfortunes are the karma produced by the afflictions of the path and the fruits thereof. (Liang Dynasty)

The *Chao lun* states: "The Truth of Suffering within the three realms is termed 'all calamities and misfortunes. The preceding section has concluded the explanation of the ten phrases of the sūtra by means of the nine virtues and karma.
Second, in the next sequence, the ten phrases of the sūtra are correlated with the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)."
Therefore, Bandhuprabha says: "Furthermore, 'all dwelling in the Great Vehicle' refers to dwelling in the first stage (*bhūmi*).
When one realizes the all-pervading true *dharmadhātu*, one attains for the first time the true Dharma of the Great Vehicle; hence, it is called 'dwelling in the Great Vehicle.

'Wandering in the Dharma of the Great Vehicle' refers to the second stage, because one practices the three clusters of bodhisattva precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*); these are the practices of the Great Vehicle."

Regarding the three clusters of precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*): "having a mind of equality toward all sentient beings" refers to attaining the various supreme concentrations (*samādhi*) and giving rise to the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*) in the third stage (*bhūmi*), thereby benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings with impartiality. "Being free from all conceptual discriminations," and so forth.

This refers to the fourth stage (*bhūmi*). One attains the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and becomes free from all conceptualization (*vikalpa*), non-conceptualization, and various forms of conceptual differentiation.
As for "conceptualization," this refers to the conceptualization of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) which is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*);

this has already been abandoned in the first stage. As for "non-conceptualization," this refers to the innate view of self (*sahaja-ātmadṛṣṭi*) which is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*); it is in this stage that one becomes free from it.

These two types of associated dharmas are called "various discriminations" because their modes of activity and understanding differ. Although they are separated sequentially, they are collectively described in terms of their ultimate cessation.
This is like the Fourth Dhyāna being said to be free from the faculty of suffering, or like the Third Fruit (Sakṛdāgāmin) being said to be free from the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
According to one interpretation, in this stage, all innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) within the seventh consciousness are completely abandoned.
Regarding this meaning: in this stage, within the sixth consciousness, all innate views of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) are completely abandoned; this does not refer to the seventh consciousness.

This is because from the seventh stage onward, subtle afflictions (*kleśa*) still manifest. If the seventh consciousness did not exist, there would be no basis for defilement (*kliṣṭāśraya*), and it would not resemble the [other] five [consciousnesses].
If the subtle delusions of the seventh consciousness were already abandoned, then in the fifth, sixth, and seventh stages, the six consciousnesses...
Coarse afflictions would then fail to manifest, which contradicts the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*’s explanation in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.

Furthermore, it would contradict the fact that during the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) of the two vehicles, the seventh consciousness—whether functioning simultaneously with it—or the most subtle afflictions among the six consciousnesses, are all severed at once.
Why is it that, in this context, one first abandons the subtle afflictions of the seventh [consciousness] and subsequently abandons the coarse afflictions of the six consciousnesses?

Therefore, upon attaining the wisdom of selflessness in the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), one extinguishes the innate view of self within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), yet has not yet abandoned the subtle afflictions of the seventh [consciousness] nor the remaining afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation within the six consciousnesses. This statement is intended to suppress such objections; it is not [the final position].

This is their permanent cessation. It is at the time of the tenth stage, the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*), that the seeds to be abandoned through cultivation are suddenly and completely extinguished.

Regarding "subduing all demonic adversaries and enemies": this refers to the fifth stage, wherein one contemplates the four noble truths as being entirely equal in nature, thereby subduing the demonic adversaries who cling to the distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, and remaining far removed from all śrāvakas.

The mental attention (*manasikāra*) of the pratyekabuddhas refers to the sixth stage, wherein one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)—both in their defiled and purified aspects—as being entirely of the nature of equality (*samatā*), thereby remaining far removed from the conceptualization of mindfulness that involves the two vehicles’ aversion to defilement and longing for purity.
Being sustained by the joy and bliss of the vast flavor of the Dharma (*dharmarasa*) refers to the seventh stage, wherein one realizes the principle of signlessness (*animitta*). Regarding...
The wisdom of emptiness possesses superior practice and experiences the great joy of the Dharma. It transcends the causes of the five fears; thus it is called "transcending the five fears.
The results of these five fears have already been abandoned from the first bhūmi onward. That which exclusively enters the stage of non-retrogression refers to the ninth bhūmi.
That which definitely enters the stage of non-retrogression where the various practices of the tenth bodhisattva bhūmi are perfected refers to the cessation of all... [text ends].

"Sentient beings who are equal" refers to the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*). Having attained the Great Dharma-body (*mahā-dharmakāya*), one gives rise to the clouds of great compassion (*mahā-karuṇā*) and rains down the great rain of Dharma, extinguishing all matters of suffering and affliction that oppress sentient beings.

The third [set of] ten perfections (*pāramitā*) and the fourth [set of] ten vows (*praṇidhāna*) are to be correlated with the ten phrases of the sūtra and explained accordingly. The ten perfections and ten vows are as described in the fourth fascicle of the sūtra.
The commentary explains that their names were as follows: the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gambhīrārthasāmdhyābhijña, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Yathārthaparipṛcchaka,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suviśuddhamati, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Pṛthu...
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas Prajñā, Guṇamati, Paramārtharāja, Avalokiteśvara, Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, and others were the leaders.

The commentary states: Regarding the third section, names are listed according to their preeminence. Briefly, three points are explained: first, the explanation of the names; second, the reasons for enumerating ten;
and third, the analysis through questions and answers concerning those in the stage of "one birth remaining" (*ekajātipratibaddha*). As for the explanation of the names, there are two meanings.
I. General [Explanations]. II. Specific [Explanations]. Regarding the general names, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 46:

"All Bodhisattvas have sixteen kinds of provisional names according to their virtues. These are: the name 'Bodhisattva,' 'Mahāsattva,' and so on up to the sixteenth, which is the name 'Dharma-preacher' (*dharma-bhāṇaka*).
The eighth fascicle of the *Xiǎnyáng shèngjiào lǜlùn* is the same as the *Yogācārabhūmi*. The *Zhuāng*... [text continues]
The *Yán* (莊嚴) [Sūtra] consists of twelve fascicles; although the names differ slightly, their essential meaning is largely the same. Furthermore, the *Zhuāngyán* states:
"These sixteen names are all established according to their respective meanings, and all Bodhisattvas collectively possess these names.
If a person hears these names, they should know that this refers to a Bodhisattva. The commentary explains: "What is now called 'Bodhisattva-mahāsattva' is a general name."
[This is] the middle [section]. The first two are titles. Their explanations are as before. (Sixteen names: 1. Bodhisattva;

2. Mahāsattva; 3. Accomplished Awakened Wisdom; 4. Supreme Illumination; 5. Most Excellent True Son, also called Most Excellent Child; 6. Supreme Sustainer, also called Supreme Basis; 7. Universally Able to Subdue, also called Supreme Servant;
8. Supreme Sprout; 9. Valiant, also called Fierce and Valiant; 10. Supreme Sage, also called Superior Preceptor; 11. Caravan Leader; 12. Possessor of Great Fame.)

Thirteenth, he is named Compassionate; he is also named Accomplished in Loving-Kindness and Compassion. Fourteenth, he is named Great Merit. Fifteenth, he is named Sovereign; he is also named Sovereign in Wealth. Sixteenth, he is named Dharma Master. Regarding these alternative names:
This will be explained extensively below. The term "etc. (*ādi*) includes the other immeasurable bodhisattvas. Regarding their being "foremost" (*agrya*):
this refers to the ten bodhisattvas who are called "foremost" because they are the most preeminent within this assembly.
Thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states: "Because the Bodhisattva Sudhana is the most preeminent within this assembly, he is called 'foremost'."
Regarding the explanation of the ten intentions, there are three reasons. First, it is because the first bodhisattva explains the profoundly deep meaning.

Second, it is because the next three bodhisattvas each inquire about one aspect of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Third, it is because the final six bodhisattvas each inquire about the distinct meanings of a single category.
Therefore, only ten are listed. Furthermore, it is explained that they are stated as ten merely for the sake of conciseness. As...
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 2, states: "Because this sūtra is concise, it lists only one name;
as for the remaining members of the assembly, it merely cites their numbers. This is because the intention of those who compiled the Dharma was to be brief.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 7, asks: "Question: Since bodhisattvas are exceedingly numerous, why are only the names of twenty-two types of bodhisattvas mentioned?"
The answer is: Bodhisattvas are immeasurable; they cannot be fully described. If one were to describe them all, it would be difficult for words to contain them.

Furthermore, bodhisattvas do not exceed two types: namely, those who are householders and those who have left the home life. There are also those of this world and those of other worlds. Householders refer to figures such as Bhadrapāla;
those who have left the home life refer to figures such as Mañjuśrī. Those of this world refer to figures such as Maitreya; those of other worlds...
This refers to Avalokiteśvara and others. If these two are mentioned, it should be understood that all such beings are fully included. Question:
The *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states that Maitreya, Avalokiteśvara, and Mañjuśrī are all bodhisattvas in their "last birth before Buddhahood" (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

What is the difference between being in one's "last birth before Buddhahood" and being in one's "final body" (*caramabhavika*)? Answer: According to the Sarvāstivāda school, it is as in the case of Maitreya.
...and so forth. A body in Tuṣita Heaven is called "one-life-bound" (ekajātipratibaddha). A body that attains Buddhahood after being born among humans is called the "final body" (caramabhavika).
Therefore, the Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya, fascicle 11, states:
"Bodhisattvas bound by one birth in Tuṣita Heaven and those in their final body certainly do not suffer premature death. The Nyāyānusāra-śāstra, fascicle 31, is likewise.

The *Abhidharmakośa* [asks]: "According to principle, it should be that [the Bodhisattva] has undergone immeasurable births in Tuṣita; why then is he said to have only 'one birth' remaining? If one were to say that because the Bodhisattva has attained mastery, there is only one birth, how would this be reconciled with the *Mahāvibhāṣā* and other texts?

This point is difficult and requires further reflection. Now, according to the Mahāyāna, the various teachings differ. There is indeed a sacred teaching that asserts only the celestial body [in Tuṣita] is called "one birth.
As the seventh fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "One bound by a single birth in Tuṣita..."
Regarding the Bodhisattva in Tuṣita Heaven, there is its own sacred teaching which states that only the celestial body is called the "final" [birth].
As the fifth fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* says: "The Bodhisattva in his final body in Tuṣita Heaven teaches and transforms therein;
according to its own sacred teaching, only the celestial body is designated as 'one more birth' (*ekajāti*) and 'the final birth' (*paścima-janman*)," as in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra-pañjikā*.
The first fascicle states: "A Bodhisattva bound by one birth enters Tuṣita; a Bodhisattva in his final birth dwells in Tuṣita.
There is an authoritative teaching which explains that only a human body is termed "one birth," as seen in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* and other texts.
Regarding Avalokiteśvara and Mañjuśrī being called "one-birth-remaining" (*ekajātipratibaddha*), there is an authoritative teaching which explains that this refers only to the human body.
This is called the "final birth. As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 48:
"Regarding the final birth, it is that in this life all bodhisattvas are able to manifest the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The details are as explained therein.
Within our own sacred teachings (*āgama*), it is taught exclusively that the human body is designated as the "one-life" and "final" birth, as in the case of Jñānaketu.
The *Dapilun* (Treatise on the Stages of Practice), fascicle 40, states: "Regarding those in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), they may be known through signs.
For example, the seer Asita observed the marks of his body and knew he would attain Buddhahood in this lifetime; seeing him consume the milk gruel, he knew he would attain Buddhahood that very day.
A Bodhisattva in his final body, by the power of skillful means, undergoes the retribution of evil karma and manifests such things as demonic afflictions."
Within the sacred teachings, it is said that for devas this is called "one more birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*), while for humans it is called "the final existence" (*paścima-bhava*).

As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 40, and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, fascicle 8: "One bound by one birth" refers to one who will realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment immediately after this life.
"The final existence" refers to one who, while remaining in this very life, is able to realize [enlightenment].
Regarding the supreme perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), it is largely the same as the Sarvāstivāda school.
However, concerning the statement that gods and others are called "one-birth" (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*), there have been three traditional interpretations handed down from antiquity.

First, it is said that the celestial body itself is called "one-birth," because human birth is subsumed within the final existence. Second, it is said that the human body is called "one-birth," meaning that one will receive human birth once more.

Because he was about to attain Buddhahood. One interpretation states that humans and devas are combined and referred to as "one birth," just as it is said of the *saptakṛtvaḥ-parama* (seven-birth) *srotāpanna* and so forth;
here, two births are combined and spoken of as one. Question: If the celestial body is called "one birth," how should one reconcile this with the statement in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*?
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 38, says: "Three births..."
"Bodhisattvas are born only in Tuṣita. To explain this: according to the actual reality, there are three births—namely, birth as a human, birth as a deva, and the final birth.
However, it is said that the celestial body constitutes "three births" because it is one of the three;
furthermore, since the human body has already been received and the final body will achieve Buddhahood, the human birth and the subsequent birth are not separately designated as "three births."
Question: Maitreya Bodhisattva may be called a "Successor" (kṣetra-parigraha), but why are the others also referred to as "Successors"?
Answer: As the seventh fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains:

"With the exception of Maitreya, although the other bodhisattvas are not in this world occupying the position of a Buddha's successor, they all occupy the position of a Buddha's successor in the lands of the ten directions; therefore, they are called 'Successors. Question: Maitreya... [text fragment ends]
Question: According to the principle that a Bodhisattva should undergo many births, why is it said that he takes birth only once as a deva?

Answer: In reality, he does take many births; however, because they are all within the same category of devas, they are termed "one birth. Question: If this were so, it would contradict the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Thus, the fourth fascicle states: "The lifespan of the lower heavens is short; since their lives have already ended before the Buddha appeared, [the Bodhisattva did not appear there]. The lifespan of the upper heavens is long."
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, because his life span has come to an end, the Tuṣita Heaven is neither long nor short;

for when a Buddha appears in the world, the conditions coincide perfectly, and the Bodhisattva who is to succeed him is always born therein. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 178, is also the same as the *Jñānaprasthāna* (as recorded in the *Sī*).
Question: With reference to what body is "one more birth" (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*) spoken? Is it in terms of a person of actual practice (*satya-caryā*), or a manifested being (*nirmāṇakāya*)?
Question: Is it so? Answer: Among the three bodies, the *dharmakāya* does not possess the meaning of "filling the place" (*pūrvasthāna*), because it has neither beginning nor end.
As for the *saṃbhogakāya*, there are two types. First, the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*):

although it lacks the meaning of entering *parinirvāṇa*, it possesses the meaning of assisting in the initial attainment of Buddhahood. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 46, states: "Ultimate..."
Bodhisattvas are of two kinds: first, those bound by only one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*); second, those dwelling in their final body (*caramabhavika*).
According to this actual practice, there is no contradiction in principle. Why is this so? To speak according to reality, as for the bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment:

In the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), although there is no discrimination regarding the transformation of birth and death (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*) such that one maturation perishes and another arises separately, it nonetheless involves the separate exhaustion of one maturation and the separate arising of another due to the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
Because of this, there is also the distinction between having entered the state of equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and not yet having entered it; thus, it is divided into two kinds. This...

The Chinese masters explain that the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāma-vaśika-janma-maraṇa*) occurs through the power of the seeds of the two obstacles, whereby there is repeated arising and ceasing.
Thus, the *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) states: "When the previous maturation has already exhausted, another maturation arises again.

This is unlike the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), who, because they lack the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), do not allow for the exhaustion of a previous maturation to be followed by the arising of another maturation; rather, it is said that [for them] only the life-span is extended.

They undergo transformation and change; this is explained in detail as in that [sūtra]. Both the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) and the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) possess the meaning of being "one birth away from Buddhahood" (*ekajātipratibaddha*). This is like the meaning of Amitābha Buddha having parents and entering *nirvāṇa*.
Because of this, Avalokiteśvara is praised as filling the Buddha’s place and is thus called an "Ekajātipratibaddha Bodhisattva. However, that Amitābha himself...
There are two kinds. First, that manifested for Bodhisattvas on the stages (bhūmi), which is the Body of Enjoyment for Others (parasaṃbhogakāya).

Second, that subsumed under the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) for ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles who have not yet reached the stages. Question: If this is so, then those of gradual enlightenment (anupūrva-abhisambodhi) should consist of only a single lifetime, as there would be no distinct exhaustion of separate lifetimes.
Answer: It is explained that, for example, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva is said to be "one lifetime" [in his final birth], and this is consistent with reason.
This contradicts [the principle] that the final body constitutes a single lifetime.
*Commentary on the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, Scroll One;
*Commentary on the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, Scroll Two.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuance of Ximing Monastery.
Commentary on the Second Chapter, "The Characteristics of Ultimate Truth" (Paramārtha-satya-lakṣaṇa).

There are briefly two meanings to the explanation of this chapter’s text: first, the explanation of the chapter title; second, the formal explanation of the text. Regarding the term "ultimate truth" (paramārtha):
The Chapter on the Characteristics of the Truths (*Satyalakṣaṇavarga*) concerns the supreme designation among the truths. There are two kinds of truths: first, the conventional (*saṃvṛti*);

second, the ultimate (*paramārtha*). Regarding the conventional: "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*) has the sense of concealment (*saṃvṛti*), while "conventional" (*loka*) has the sense of being coarse and manifest.

This refers to things such as jars and garments—coarse and manifest objects of the world that conceal the ultimate; therefore, they are called "conventional. Regarding the term "ultimate": "supreme" (*para*) means...

"Ultimate" (*paramārtha*) refers to "supreme knowledge" (*paramajñāna*). "Object" (*artha*) here has the sense of "domain. That is to say, the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) is the domain of supreme knowledge; therefore, it is called "ultimate object" (*paramārtha*).
This is the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound among the six types of grammatical analysis. Alternatively, "object" (*artha*) means "benefit" (*artha*), referring to the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
Since this is the supreme benefit, it is called "ultimate" (*parama*). This is the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound among the six types of grammatical analysis. Or...
Furthermore, the Noble Path has "supremacy" as its primary meaning; thus it is called the "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compound.

Now, within this context, we shall provisionally rely on the first meaning. There are two meanings of "truth" (*satya*), as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 55: first, the sense of not deviating from the characteristics as they have been described;
second, the sense of reaching the ultimate through contemplation of these [characteristics]. Therefore, they are called "truths. Regarding their characteristics:

This refers to the essential nature (*svabhāva*) or, alternatively, the formal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). This is because all five aspects, such as being beyond words, constitute the essential nature and characteristics of *tathatā* itself;
or, alternatively, because the single *tathatā* possesses these five formal characteristics, such as being beyond words.
Within this chapter, the meaning of the five aspects of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is elucidated; therefore, it is titled "Chapter Two: The Characteristics of Ultimate Truth."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Yathārtha-paripṛcchaka, in the presence of the Buddha,
addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gambhīrārthasamdhinirmocana, saying:

The commentary states: This second section provides the formal explanation of the sūtra text. The preceding portion has already concluded the "Section on the Causes and Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching.
From here begins the second part, the "Section on the Formal Exposition of the Holy Teaching," which consists of seven chapters organized into three segments.

The first segment comprises four chapters that clarify the objects of observation (*ālambana-viṣaya*): [Chapter 1] "The Characteristics of Ultimate Truth" (*Paramārtha-lakṣaṇa-pariccheda*), [Chapter 2] "The Characteristics of Mind, Thought, and Consciousness" (*Citta-manovijñāna-lakṣaṇa-pariccheda*), [Chapter 3] "The Characteristics of All Phenomena" (*Sarvadharma-lakṣaṇa-pariccheda*), and [Chapter 4] "The Characteristics of the Absence of Self-Nature" (*Niḥsvabhāva-lakṣaṇa-pariccheda*).
Next follow two chapters that distinguish the practice of contemplation (*yogācāra*) (the "Chapter on the Analysis of Yoga" and the "Chapter on the Grounds and Perfections").

Finally, there is one chapter that reveals the fruit attained (the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Accomplished State"). The reason for explaining these in three parts is as follows: regarding the practitioner of contemplation...

One must rely upon superior objects; based on these objects, one initiates practice; and through practice, one attains the fruit. Therefore, in the *Abhidharma Mahāyāna Sūtra*, the Blessed One taught ten kinds of superiority:
the first two are the objects (*ālambana*)—namely, the basis of the knowable (*jñeyāśraya*) and the characteristics of the knowable (*jñeyalakṣaṇa*);

the next six are the practices (*pratipatti*)—namely, entering the knowable, entering cause and fruit, the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*), the training in meditative concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*), and the training in wisdom consisting of the distinctions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prabheda-prajñā-śikṣā*); and the final two are the fruits (*phala*)—namely, the abandonment that is the fruit (*prahāṇaphala*) and the wisdom that is the fruit (*jñānaphala*). By means of...
This is the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* by Asaṅga, which explains ten types of excellence based on the three equalities.
Maitreya Bodhisattva also expounded the seventeen stages (*bhūmi*), likewise distinguishing three categories. The first nine are the objects:

(1) the stage associated with the five consciousnesses, (2) the mental stage, (3) the stage with vitarka and vicāra, (4) the stage without vicāra, (5) the stage with vitarka and without vicāra, (6) the stage without vitarka and without vicāra, (7) the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*), (8) the stage not in meditative equipoise, (9) the stage with mind, and (10) the stage without mind). The next six are the practices: (1) that which is heard... [text continues]

The *Bhūmi* of Realization (*abhisamayabhūmi*), the *Bhūmi* of Thought-Realization (*cintāmayībhūmi*), the *Bhūmi* of Cultivation-Realization (*bhāvanāmayībhūmi*), the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*, the *Pratyekabuddha-bhūmi*, and the *Bodhisattva-bhūmi*. The latter two are the fruits (*sopadhiśeṣa-bhūmi* and *nirupadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*).
This sutra explains three peerless [qualities] as three divisions. Regarding the objects of observation, it is further divided into two:

the first two chapters clarify the objects of the ultimate and the conventional (the "Chapter on the Characteristics of Ultimate Truth" clarifies its ultimate truth, while the "Chapter on the Characteristics of Mind, Intellect, and Consciousness" clarifies conventional truth); the latter two chapters...

This clarifies the objects characterized by the nature of existence and non-existence (i.e., the first chapter clarifies the objects of the three natures, while the subsequent chapter clarifies the objects of the three absences of nature).

Within the context of the two truths, according to the sequence of fundamental and derivative, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is presented first and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) follows; thus, the ultimate truth is explained here.

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, this chapter is determined to discern five types of characteristics; therefore, the *Śāstra* (Treatise), volume 75, states: "Furthermore, the ultimate truth has five characteristics."
1. The characteristic of being free from names and expressions; 2. The characteristic of non-duality; 3. The characteristic of transcending the sphere of discursive thought; 4.

The characteristic of transcending the nature of identity and difference among all phenomena; 5. The characteristic of the single flavor pervading all things. Now, based on this sūtra, these are subsumed into four sections:
first, clarifying the characteristics of being beyond words and non-dual; second, from the passage "At that time, Dharmodgata... onwards, clarifying the transcendence...

1. Transcending the characteristics that are the objects of discursive investigation; 2. At that time, "O Suvibhaktaprajña," the following explains the characteristic of being neither one nor different; 3.
At that time, "The World-Honored One," the following explains the characteristic of the single flavor pervading all things; 4.

The phrase "beyond words" (*anabhilāpya*) should apply throughout these four sections, as all four characteristics possess the characteristic of being beyond words; yet it is explained together with "non-duality" in one place, according to the principle.
Because it can be understood, the remaining three sections are omitted and not explained. Regarding the first two characteristics, the text is divided into two parts:
first, an extensive explanation in prose; second, a brief exposition in verse. Within the former, there are six sections: 1. Inquiry; 2. Brief answer; 3.

Interrogation; 4. Extensive explanation; 5. Repeated interrogation; 6. Explanation by analogy. (According to Paramārtha’s classification, four sections are the same as before; regarding the first, they are divided into five.)

1. A brief explanation of the ineffable non-duality; 2. An extensive explanation; 3. Illustration by analogy; 4. A summary conclusion; 5. Verses in praise. This constitutes the first section: the Bodhisattva’s inquiry.
Within this, there are two parts: first, the introduction consisting of the initial inquiry; second, the inquiry based upon the teaching. This is the first part. The text contains four sections: 1.
"At that time" refers to the time of the inquiry. (The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "When the Buddha Bhagavān was surrounded by a great assembly and preaching the profound Dharma.
This is an error of the translators. 2. "The Bodhisattva Who Inquires According to Principle" identifies the questioner as one who poses inquiries in accordance with the principle.

Therefore, he is called the Bodhisattva Who Questions According to Principle (*yoniśaḥ-paripṛcchaka*). (The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* says "one who asks correctly according to principle," while the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* [or *Saṃdhinirmocana* variant] says "the Bodhisattva Who Asks Well.
Third, "in the presence of the Buddha" refers to the location from which the question is posed. This is as stated in Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*:

"The Bodhisattva who has skillfully entered into the presence of the Bhagavat" indicates that there is an object of veneration and an absence of discordant speech. Furthermore, Asvabhāva states that it indicates...
The Buddha granted permission for its wide circulation because there was no contradiction with what he had personally taught to the World-Honored One.
Regarding the phrase "the Bodhisattva who understands the profound meaning and secret intent": this identifies the person who poses the question.

This Bodhisattva is so named because he is able to explain the profound principles and secret intents through the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). This is as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle three.
Seventeenth, the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Exposition). The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra* (*Jiejing*) states: "The Bodhisattva who can explain the knots of the profound meaning.
Paramārtha’s commentary explains: "To 'explain' (*vyākhyā*) means to interpret; 'knots' (*grantha*) has the sense of firm entanglements.

Because he interprets the knots of the firm entanglements of the profound meaning, he is named the Bodhisattva who Explains the Knots of the Profound Meaning. He is also called Ratnacūḍa (Jewel-Crest). The original [name] of Ratnacūḍa..."
This is the name of the Buddha. This present bodhisattva is a disciple of that Buddha; he received his title from his teacher.
A detailed explanation is as found in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (where it says "Bodhisattva Saṃdhinirmocana").
The Son of the Victorious One says that all phenomena are non-dual. Regarding the statement that "all phenomena are non-dual," what are all phenomena?
And what constitutes non-duality? The commentary states:
this is the second section, consisting of questions raised based on the teaching. The text contains two parts; first is the statement by the Son of the Victorious One.
"All phenomena are non-dual" raises the teaching that was questioned; subsequently, "all phenomena are non-dual, etc. poses a question based upon that teaching.

Now, regarding the term "Sons of the Most Victorious" (*jinazizun*, *jina-putra*), they are all sons of the Buddha. The *Zhendi ji* (Record of Paramārtha) states that there are five meanings of "Son of the Buddha":
first, the meaning of seed, which means that those who believe in and delight in the Mahāyāna can serve as the seeds for attaining Buddhahood.
2. The sense of "mother": This means that the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) can give birth to the Buddha-dharmas; therefore, it is called "mother. 3. The sense of "womb":
This means that the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) of a bodhisattva is the place of abiding; therefore, it is called the "womb. 4. The sense of "nurse":

This means that it can nourish and sustain the bodhisattva, enabling them to attain enlightenment; therefore, compassion (*karuṇā*) is said to be the nurse. 5. The sense of being "like a father": This refers to [the role of] from...
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the Buddha-stage, the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) resembles that of a Buddha;

therefore, it is said to be "like a father. Thus, the Bodhisattva *Vimuktimati* is addressed as a "son of the Buddha. This is explained in detail as previously stated. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "The Bodhisattva is the true son of the Buddha;
therefore, the Bodhisattva is named a 'Son of the Buddha' (*jinaputra*). Now, according to the Tang edition, he is named the "Most Victorious Son" (*jyeṣṭhaputra*). From here on...
There are two explanations. One says that "Most Excellent" (*jyeṣṭha*) is a name for the Bodhisattva;

because he is the most distinguished among the children of the Three Vehicles and is able to succeed the lineage of the Buddhas, he is called a "child. This is an *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. Another says that "Most Excellent" is a title for the World-Honored One (*bhagavat*).
Thus, the *Asvabhāva-ṭīkā* states: "Most Excellent indicates that the Buddha is superior to the Two Vehicles. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says:

The Buddha is the most supreme (*parama-jina*), because he is able to triumph over all externalists, afflictions, and other māras; and because his lineage, clan, and so forth outshine those of all others.
According to this interpretation, one who is the son of the Most Supreme is called a "Son of the Most Supreme" (*jina-putra*).

Thus, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "A bodhisattva is also called a Son of the Most Supreme. For this reason, they are referred to elsewhere as "Sons of the Buddha" (*buddha-putra*). It is said:
This refers to verbal instruction; that is, the teaching that all phenomena are non-dual. This also has two interpretations: first, it is the instruction of a bodhisattva;
second, it is the word of the Buddha, as in the *Śataśāstra* (Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas), where the World-Honored One says, "All phenomena are without self."
Furthermore, the subsequent verse states: "The Buddha taught that words are transcended and that there is no duality;
all phenomena (dharma) are non-dual. This cites two sections from the sutra: first, "all phenomena," and second, "non-duality. Regarding "all phenomena are non-dual":
what are all phenomena? What constitutes non-duality? This is the second part, which poses questions based upon the teaching; the text contains two [sections].
Section. Initially, when about to pose the questions, both chapters are cited together; subsequently, by examining them according to their respective chapters, two questions are formed:
first, the question regarding what constitutes "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*); second, the question regarding how they are "non-dual.

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are generally five types of inquiry: first, inquiry due to lack of understanding; second, inquiry due to doubt; third, inquiry for the sake of... [text truncated]
One asks for the sake of benefit and happiness; one asks for the sake of verifying the four admonitions; and one asks because of being slighted or offended.
Now, this bodhisattva relies on the third type of inquiry, desiring to benefit all sentient beings; alternatively, it may apply to all three.
Furthermore, it is not based on the latter two types, as there is no lack of understanding or doubt regarding the meaning, and the Unsurpassed Dharma King is not to be slighted or offended.

And because it serves as a warning and a verification. (The *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-sūtra* states: "All dharmas are non-dual; all dharmas are non-dual. What is the meaning of this? The *Jinzhendi-ji* says: This scripture is cited to pose a question.

The phrase "all dharmas are non-dual" is repeated for five reasons: first, because it is taught in various sūtras; second, because conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas are non-dual; third, because the six internal sense bases (*ādhyātmika-āyatana*) and the six external objects (*bāhya-āyatana*) are non-dual;

fourth, because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and sages (*ārya*) are non-dual; fifth, because cause and effect are non-dual. Now, regarding the textual meaning of what is being said here: this Bodhisattva answers by means of "that which is done" and "that which is not done").
The Bodhisattva Who Understands the Profound Meaning and Secret Intent addressed the Bodhisattva Who Questions According to Principle, saying:

[The commentary states: From here on is the second section, which provides a brief answer based on the question. This section contains two parts; first, the presentation of the questioner and the respondent.
The following is the formal response to the question; this is the first [section].
"Good son, all phenomena (dharmas) are briefly of two kinds: namely, the conditioned (saṃskṛta) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)."
The commentary states: The second part consists of the formal response to the question, which has two sections. First, "Good son" (*kulaputra*) praises the questioner;

second, from "all phenomena" (*sarvadharmāḥ*) onwards, is the formal response based on the question. This is the first section. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle 35:
the term "son" (*puruṣa*) excludes those who are not sons and others who are unfit for instruction. "Good" (*kuśala*) refers to that which is wholesome.
Characteristics: This refers to being endowed with compassion; having no faults in the three karmas of body, speech, and mind; delighting in virtuous people;
not manifesting one's own virtues; conforming to the multitude; not speaking of the faults of others; not seeking worldly fame or similar pleasures, but delighting only in the Way and its virtue;
having pure actions in one’s own affairs; cherishing the true mark (dharmatā) in the mind while disparaging worldly matters. There are such immeasurable wholesome dharmas as these.
These characteristics are mostly found within the bodies of men; therefore, they are praised as "good sons" (*kulaputra*). Question:
Why are only two kinds of phenomena—conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—expounded? Answer: As stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, there are two intended meanings.

He said: "In order to refute the notion of a *pudgala* (person) and to demonstrate the excellence of wisdom, these two kinds of phenomena—the conditioned and the unconditioned—are taught. Regarding the refutation of the *pudgala*:"
This means it is shown that there are only conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, and that a truly existent person (*pudgala*) absolutely does not exist;
furthermore, it is to demonstrate the excellence of wisdom—that is, those who possess intelligence and excellent wisdom [rely] upon these two types of phenomena.
"Thoroughly penetrating all phenomena. Because these two encompass all phenomena, regarding "all phenomena" and so forth, there is a formal response to the question, which contains two parts:
first, the answer concerning all [phenomena], and second, the explanation of non-duality. This is the answer concerning all [phenomena].
The text consists of two sections. First, "All phenomena briefly comprise two kinds" indicates the topic and enumerates the number.
Second, "conditioned and unconditioned" lists the names according to that number. Generally speaking, there are three ways to discuss all phenomena:
first, the brief exposition which holds that there are only two kinds, namely the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); second, neither extensive nor brief, which has...
There are five categories: first, mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*); second, mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*); third, material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*);
fourth, formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-dharma*); and fifth, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* merely list these five categories without providing detailed explanations. The third [category], the extensive exposition, fully elucidates the one hundred dharmas; here, we shall briefly summarize that extensive treatment.
Therefore, it is said that this is a brief explanation. Regarding the terms "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) and "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*), various teachings differ. The *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"Because they are produced by the collective gathering of various conditions, they are called 'conditioned. That which is contrary to this should be understood as 'unconditioned'. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"If a phenomenon depends upon and is subject to the functional activity of causes, conditions, and their combination, it is called 'conditioned. If a phenomenon..."
That which does not depend upon the functioning of causes, conditions, or the synthesis of combinations is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The *Tattvasaṃgraha* (Pal-zhen-lun) states:

"Because it is produced through the combination of various conditions and involves volitional activity, it is called conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); because it is not conditioned, it is termed unconditioned.
Thus, being the opposite of the conditioned is the meaning of the unconditioned. The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* by Bodhisattva Asaṅga states: "The unconditioned is..."

The meaning of "non-conceptual" (nirvikalpa) implies, by extension, that the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is conceptual (*savikalpa*). Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "That which possesses arising, abiding, change, and cessation is called conditioned;
that which lacks arising, abiding, change, and cessation is called unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 100, says:
"'Conditioned' refers to that which has arising and cessation and is bound to causes and conditions; one should know that what is contrary to this is [unconditioned]."

Regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that that which has something to be attained is called conditioned, while that which has nothing to be attained is called unconditioned.
The *Guṇaprabha-śāstra* likewise explains it in this way. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 93, says:
"Grasping at signs is conditioned; not grasping at signs is unconditioned. If one were to provide a detailed analysis, it would be as found in a separate chapter. However—

Regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) now being discussed, there are three different interpretations. First, it is said that what is described here refers to the conditioned and unconditioned as they are conceptually constructed (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
thus, the subsequent scripture states: "One firmly clings to the conditioned and unconditioned as truly existent, and accordingly gives rise to verbal expressions.
Second, it is said that this refers exclusively to the conditioned nature of the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) arising from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

It is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, the subsequent scripture states: "There is definitely no truly existent conditioned or unconditioned. Nevertheless, there are formations (*saṃskāra*) arising from conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*).
One view holds that the conditioned is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), while the unconditioned is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Although there are these three explanations, the latter is correct. Why is this? Because the intention here is to state that the conditioned is the dependent nature, and the perfected...
It accomplishes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Above these two dharmas, there is no nature of grasping regarding the conditioned or the unconditioned; therefore, it is said to be non-dual.
This shall be analyzed later:
herein, the conditioned is neither conditioned nor unconditioned, and the unconditioned is likewise neither unconditioned nor non-unconditioned.

The commentary states: The second [section] explains the characteristic of non-duality. This refers to the "ineffable characteristic" and the "characteristic of non-duality" among the five [characteristics].

Why is this so? Because it cannot be said to be either conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), nor does it possess the dual characteristics of being both conditioned and unconditioned.
However, regarding the interpretation of this passage, various explanations differ. The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (or *Jiejie jing*) states: "That which is produced..."
This is neither that which is produced nor that which is not produced. That which is produced is also neither that which is not produced nor that which is produced.

The *Tattvārthā* commentary states: "The two subsequent phrases exclude conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), while the [preceding] two phrases exclude unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
'That which is produced' refers to conditioned phenomena; conditioned phenomena are produced by the gathering of causes and conditions."

That which is called "produced" refers to conditioned phenomena; that which is not produced refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Unconditioned phenomena are primordially existent and eternal;
they are not produced by the aggregation of causes and conditions, and are thus termed "non-produced. This first dispels [the notion of] the conditioned by means of three meanings.
First, because of the conceptualization of a distracted consciousness, there is that which is produced; yet what is produced is actually non-existent, being merely conceptualization.

Furthermore, because there is an object of apprehension (*grāhya*), there is an apprehending subject (*grāhaka*). Since the object of apprehension is non-existent, the apprehending subject is also non-existent;

therefore, it is not something produced. Second, because the root is fundamentally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): the root of all phenomena is fundamentally due to improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).

Improper mental attention gives rise to the various afflictions; the various afflictions give rise to various karmas; and karma gives rise to retributive fruits. Improper mental attention arises from grasping.
Since objects do not truly exist, one erroneously grasps them as existing. Because objects are non-existent, improper mental attention is also non-existent.
Since improper mental attention is non-existent, the various afflictions are also non-existent. Because the various afflictions are non-existent, various karmas are also non-existent.
Since all karmas do not exist, their retributions also do not exist. Because their fundamental basis is unreal, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are likewise unreal.
Third, by virtue of non-arising: these produced phenomena do not depart from the two natures—imagined (*parikalpita*) and dependent (*paratantra*).
Since these two natures are fundamentally without characteristics and without arising, what meaning can there be for "production"? Therefore, they are not produced.

When existence is contrasted with non-existence, since existence itself is absent, by principle, non-existence itself is also absent. Second, because the root is non-existent, that which is produced [is likewise non-existent].

This serves as the fundamental basis. If there were truly something produced, one could speak of it being called "non-produced," just as when one previously had an illness and later says the illness has been cured.

Free from existence and free from non-existence, it is fundamentally not something produced, nor is it not something produced.
"Not something produced" refers to the following two phrases, which eliminate unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). The first phrase clarifies the unconditioned by means of three meanings;

The meaning is not different from what was stated previously; whether one advances or retreats, one ultimately does not depart from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Therefore, there is no distinction from the previous analysis. This is precisely to reveal the sense of being ineffable and non-dual. The reason for providing this brief answer is as follows:

(Examination) They are formless, shapeless, and of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*).

The Buddha speaks of them by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), not by way of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The full explanation is as stated there. The commentary says: this ultimate truth functions as suchness (*tathatā*).

This is the essence. As for the statement that they "do not exist," the word "non-existent" is spoken in order to negate what is grasped; in reality, they are not non-existent. Therefore, the sutra below states: "All phenomena lack intrinsic nature.

By the power of great compassion, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are provisionally designated. This is because they are expressed through terminology gathered by pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) within the Tathāgata’s subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*);

He establishes the doctrine of five dharma-treasuries, namely: the three time periods, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the ineffable dharma-treasury.

Because its essence cannot be described as existing [in a conventional sense], that ineffable essence is precisely the true reality (*tattvārtha*). It is simply because there are four reasons why it cannot be described:

It clarifies that "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) is a mere conventional designation. Next, it addresses how one clings to this designation as being substantially real based on the Buddha’s teaching.

Finally, it demonstrates that it is not real, thereby concluding that it is not truly unconditioned. This is the first [section]. Within it, there are two interpretations; these should be understood according to what has been stated above.
If these are the provisional designations established by the Teacher, they are merely verbal expressions collected through conceptual construction (*parikalpita*).
The commentary states: this refers to the second [type of] reliance on the Buddha’s provisional designations, which one clings to as being substantially existent.

If it is that which is gathered through pervasive conceptualization and expressed by verbal designations, then it is ultimately nothing more than various things expressed by pervasive conceptual verbal designations;
because it is not established as real, it is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The commentary states: The third [point] distinguishes that it is not substantially existent and concludes that it is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
"Good son, that which is called 'conditioned' (*saṃskṛta*) also falls within the realm of verbal expression.
The commentary states: The second [point] negates the characteristics of the conditioned; this should be understood according to what was stated above.
Even if one were to set aside the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), whatever little might be said, its characteristic would likewise be so.
The commentary states: the third [point] excludes that which is neither unconditioned nor conditioned as being a characteristic.
"However, it is not that there is nothing to be said. The commentary states:
The second explanation resolves an anticipated objection and demonstrates the correct principle. This consists of three parts:
first, stating the thesis and answering in general; second, a counter-interrogation; and third, the formal exposition. This is the first part.
"What is the objective basis?
The commentary states: This is the second counter-question.
It refers to the fact that the noble ones, by means of noble wisdom and noble vision, having transcended names and expressions, have realized perfect enlightenment regarding suchness. That is to say:

This is the ineffable nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Because one wishes to cause others to realize perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*) regarding it, one provisionally establishes names and concepts, calling it "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).
The commentary states: This is the third correct explanation by the Bodhisattva. The text consists of two sections; the first clarifies that all noble ones are free from... [text continues].

Because it is designated by names and conventions, one attains perfect enlightenment. Subsequently, for the sake of others, one provisionally establishes names and concepts based on that very [enlightenment].
If one were to provide a detailed analysis, it may be understood by analogy with what has been stated above.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Yathārtha-paripṛcchaka again addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gambhīrārthasamdhinirmocana, saying: [The commentary states:
From here below is the fifth section, the repeated inquiry regarding provisional designations (*prajñapti*). This section contains two parts; first, the introductory inquiry.
Later, when the formal inquiry was made, this was the first point of the dialectical interrogation, serving as the introduction:
"O Son of the Victor, how is it that those noble ones, by means of noble wisdom and noble vision, are free from verbal expression?"
Having manifested perfect enlightenment, for the sake of causing others to likewise manifest perfect enlightenment regarding this ineffable nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
one provisionally establishes names and concepts, referring to it as either "conditioned" (saṃskṛta) or "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta).
The commentary states: This is the second formal inquiry. Although it has already been explained at length, it has not yet been fully understood.
What is the analogy? The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* omits this inquiry; this is an error on the part of the translators, or perhaps it was intentionally omitted for the sake of brevity.
The Bodhisattva Who Understands the Profound Meaning and Secret Intent addressed the Bodhisattva Who Questions According to Principle, saying:

[The commentary states: From this point downward is the sixth section, which reiterates the teaching by means of analogies. This section contains two parts: first, clarifying the occasion for the teaching;
second, providing a detailed explanation in response to the inquiry. This is the first part.
"Good son, it is like a skilled illusionist or his disciple who, standing at a crossroads,
gathers grass, leaves, tiles, pebbles, and the like, and manifests various illusory feats."

The commentary states: From here below is the second section, which provides an extensive explanation based on the inquiry. This section contains three parts: first, an analogy is presented and explained again; second, from "In this way, if...
onwards, the dharmas are presented as being analogous to the analogy; third, from "In this way, O son of good family... onwards, the conclusion addresses external objections.
Within the first part, there are three sub-sections: first, the analogy of a magician’s illusions; second, from "If among the masses of beings... onwards, the deluded...
The former refers to the analogy of the real illusionist; the latter, "if there are sentient beings below," refers to the analogy of the awakened one realizing the illusory nature.

This constitutes the first analogy of the illusionist’s magical feats. Within this, there are two parts: first, a general explanation of the magical feats; second, that which follows the phrase "namely" (*yaduta*).
The illusion is explained separately. In the preceding section, there are four parts: first, explaining the illusionist; second, revealing the place of the illusion;
third, identifying the basis of the illusion; and fourth, a general explanation of the illusory phenomena. However, the intended meaning of this metaphorical passage is difficult to comprehend;

therefore, I shall first set forth the explanation of Master Paramārtha, and subsequently interpret this scriptural text in reliance upon various teachings. The *Paramārtha-ṭīkā* states: "The purpose of teaching the metaphor..."

This is an analogy for sentient beings who, due to deluded inversion and various forms of conceptual discrimination, have long remained in birth and death, undergoing all manner of karmic retributions.
They do not know the illusion’s basis—the ineffable, non-dual *tathatā* (suchness)—and instead grasp it as being truly existent.

The Noble Ones clearly understand that this is not real; yet ordinary beings do not realize that they themselves are the illusion and that the basis of the illusion exists. This is because they possess ignorance and have not yet attained [realization].
Because of noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*). Noble ones realize that illusion is fundamentally non-dual and ineffable in essence;
by severing ignorance and attaining the noble path, they do so. The illusionist is likened to the intelligent ordinary person, who is none other than the non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*).

The illusionist’s apprentice is likened to the deluded ordinary person, who is none other than the icchantika. Furthermore, the illusionist is a metaphor for afflictions (*kleśa*), and the apprentice is a metaphor for karma (*karman*).
Because karma arises from afflictions (*kleśa*), the illusionist serves as the analogy for the cause, while the disciple serves as the analogy for the effect.

"At the crossroads" is an analogy for the four kinds of birth and death within the three realms and the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), or alternatively, it is an analogy for the fourfold sphere of objects consisting of the sense faculties, their objects, the self, and consciousness.
According to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra-ṭīkā*, the illusionist is the *ālayavijñāna*.

From the very beginning, that which is able to produce false illusions is likened to the "disciples," which refers to the seven consciousnesses. Subtle delusive phenomena are produced by the ālayavijñāna;

those of intermediate degree are produced by the *manas* (the defiled mind); and coarse phenomena are produced by the six consciousnesses. Furthermore, the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) act as the teacher.

Attachment and delusion are the disciples; furthermore, the mental afflictions (*kleśa*) are the teacher. Skin and flesh represent the disciples, while the crossroads serve as a metaphor for the principle of the four perversions (*catur-viparyāsa*).
Now, regarding the interpretation of this sutra according to various teachings, there are four explanations for the term "illusionist" (*māyākāra*):
first, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* takes karma as the teacher; second, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 60, [takes] the afflictions and karma...
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (translated during the Tang dynasty) and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* take the Three Baskets as their teacher. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* takes the Bodhisattva as its teacher.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (in eighty-four fascicles) takes the eight consciousnesses as its teacher. Regarding the phrase "the four crossroads," there are three interpretations.
1. The *Ekottarika Āgama* and the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, volume 15, state that the Four Noble Truths constitute the four crossroads. 2.

The *Saṃyukta Āgama*, chapter 20 and others, explain that the four foundations of mindfulness constitute the four crossroads. 3. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 84, takes the four stations of consciousness (*catasra vijñānasthitayaḥ*) as the four crossroads.
Regarding the phrase "accumulating grass, leaves, wood, tiles, and pebbles": [it refers to the accumulation of defilements].

The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) distinguishes the basis upon which the illusion depends; that is to say, it serves as a metaphor for the accumulation of all seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Alternatively, it may signify that the three types of perfuming (*vāsanā*) reside within the *ālayavijñāna*. The grass and leaves, being fine and soft, are likened to wholesome seeds;

the wood, stone, and other such materials, being coarse and rigid, are used as metaphors for unwholesome seeds. The phrase "manifesting various illusory transformations and activities" refers to the totality [of these processes].
This clarifies illusory phenomena. Just as various illusory objects arise from blades of grass and leaves, so too do various fruits arise from seeds that are wholesome or unwholesome.

These include the bodies of elephants, chariots, horses, and infantry; as well as bodies consisting of mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, and various kinds of wealth, treasures, and storehouses.

The commentary states: The second section specifically clarifies the matter of illusions. This refers to the previous general indication that various illusory activities are manifested, which was not explained in detail;

therefore, it is now explained specifically. The *Tattvārthā* commentary states: "The fourfold army is a metaphor for causes and conditions, while the pearls and so forth are metaphors for the results.
Because of the fourfold army, [the pearls] can exist as such. Alternatively, the fourfold army may be a metaphor for the classes of sentient beings.

The "jewels" and so forth serve as metaphors for insentient categories. The general explanation of the meaning is as follows: the *ālayavijñāna* acts as a magician, with the seven consciousnesses as its disciples;

dwelling within the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), it accumulates various seeds of names and phrases (*nāma-pada*) to produce the manifold fruits of the three realms, five destinies, and four modes of birth, including both sentient and insentient beings.
Those who are deluded prior to the stages [of the bodhisattva path] cling to these as being truly existent.
Regarding the various conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, those who have attained realization on the stages perceive all phenomena as being like illusions and devoid of reality.
Within the various teachings, karma is described as the illusionist and the Four Noble Truths and so forth as the crossroads. Generally speaking, there are three types of illusionists:
first, that which is called an "illusionist" because it is capable of creating illusions—namely, afflictions, karma, and the like.
Second, because they are like illusions, they are called "illusionists"; this refers to the Bodhisattvas. Third, because they are the creators of illusions, they are called "illusionists";
this refers to the eight consciousnesses (*vijñānas*). Here, we follow the third [meaning]. Alternatively, one may also include afflictions and karma;
or, one may speak of all three types generally, as there is no error in such an interpretation. Regarding the "four-way intersection," there are also three meanings. First, the removal of...
The four paths of delusion are the Four Noble Truths. Second, the path observed by beginners is the Four Foundations of Mindfulness.

Third, the path where the illusory master dwells is the Four Bases of Consciousness (*catasraḥ vijñāna-sthitayaḥ*). Here, we rely on the third; alternatively, one may take all [four] collectively, as there is no loss of meaning in doing so.
"If there are sentient beings who are foolish, dull-witted, of a nature characterized by evil wisdom, and lacking any understanding.
The commentary states: This is the third section, the analogy for the attachment to reality by the ignorant. It contains five parts: first, clarifying the person who clings;
second, revealing the object to which they cling; third, correctly analyzing the arising of their clinging; fourth, explaining based on that clinging; and fifth, exhorting them.
Contemplating again: this refers first to the clarification of the person who grasps, namely, the provisional being consisting of the five aggregates as perceived by all deluded worldlings.
The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* (True Dharma Record) states: "Deluded ordinary beings" refers to infantile ordinary beings, that is, icchantikas;
"those of the class of evil wisdom" refers to intelligent ordinary beings, that is, non-Buddhists capable of giving rise to views. Herein, "deluded" is explained as follows:
"Emerging from the essence of ignorance" refers to the dullness and rigidity [of ignorance], which manifests its function of delusion; this is the very basis for the arising of grasping.
"Destructive wisdom" (pāpīyā prajñā) refers to the essential nature of grasping, which consists of the various views (dṛṣṭi). "Lacking any understanding" is the function of destructive wisdom;
this clarifies that, due to delusion, one grasps at the conditioned and the unconditioned as being truly existent.

Regarding the phrase "various illusory manifestations upon grass, leaves, wood, tiles, rubble, and so forth," the commentary explains that this second section distinguishes the objects of grasping. That is to say, the grass, leaves, and so forth are metaphors for wholesome and unwholesome karma;
the various illusory manifestations are metaphors for the things produced by karma, or the various phenomena transformed by consciousness.
Having seen and heard this, they form this thought: "What has been seen here truly exists as the body of an elephant; it truly exists as the body of a horse, a chariot, or an infantryman;
and it truly exists as various treasures such as mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystal, coral, as well as bodies of wealth, grain, and storehouses."

The commentary states: The third section clearly explains the arising of grasping. This means that through ignorance, one gives rise to conceptual views and grasps at elephants and so forth as being truly existent.
