That which is stored within the apprehension of consciousness and that which is grasped by consciousness is called "appropriated" (*sopādāna*). Although this is said, it does not contradict [the definition].

Briefly stated, there are two types of appropriated phenomena (*dharmas*): first, those associated with craving and the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which are grasped as "mine" and thus termed appropriated;
these are immediately severed when pure wisdom (*viśuddhajñāna*) arises. Second, those that serve as causes [for future existence]...

"Arising as suffering and pleasure, until parinirvāṇa, it continues to function without being abandoned. This means that the Sūtras and Śāstras each rely on a single perspective. The explanation is as follows:

the Sūtras define "appropriated" (*upātta*) based on the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) accompanied by craving, which grasps [the body] as its own. Regarding the Śāstra, there are three interpretations.

The intention of the first master is that it is grasped as a basis (*āśraya*). The intention of the second master is that it is capable of producing suffering and pleasure. The [intention of the] third master...

The intended meaning is that grasping [the body] as one's own essence accords with the root treatise; that which is comprised within one's own person is termed "appropriated" (*sopādāna*), which carries the sense of being the cause for the arising of pleasure and pain.
However, according to the second master, it is only the arising of pleasure and pain [that constitutes appropriation], whereas the first and last masters [hold the aforementioned view].
Incorporating other meanings as well, the sūtras and śāstras present a total of four explanations, which are fully detailed therein.
If one relies on the *Vibhāṣā*, chapter 148, the section on "Appropriation" (*upādāna*) presents six different teachings; fearing prolixity, they are not described here.
Now, according to the Mahāyāna, there are three different explanations. Some maintain that it is called [feeling] solely because it produces pleasure and pain.
Regarding "appropriated" (*upātta*): the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that the five material elements (*dhātu*) in their entirety and one portion of four [other] elements are called "appropriated.
Since it does not mention sound therein, we know that they are termed "appropriated" solely in reference to their capacity to produce suffering and pleasure.
Alternatively, some define "appropriated" simply as being grasped as one's own body, as stated in the fifty-first fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and elsewhere: "If there were no..."
The eighth [point] is because the appropriation of the basis (*āśraya*) cannot be apprehended. Furthermore, the fifty-sixth [fascicle] states again: "Five are appropriated;
the rest are exclusively non-appropriated. Based on such passages, it is clear that appropriation is explained solely in terms of taking something as one's own body (*svabhāva*).
Alternatively, there are cases where appropriation is explained by encompassing both meanings, as the fifty-third [fascicle] says:
Regarding "consciousness grasps" and "does not grasp": if consciousness relies upon and grasps something, it is called "appropriated matter" (*upātta-rūpa*). What does this mean?

It refers to that which consciousness relies upon, sharing the same state of security and peril, and which grows together with it in harmony. Furthermore, because this serves as a basis, it can give rise to various sensations (*vedanā*).
That which is contrary to this is not included within the category of the appropriated. Moreover, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 100, states: "As for the phenomena that are appropriated..."
This means that material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are grasped and maintained by the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

Because they rely upon those [mental states], the mind and mental factors proceed with a commonality of security and peril. Regarding this commonality of security and peril: by the power of the maintenance and support of the mind and mental factors, that matter remains uninterrupted, undestroyed, and uncorrupted.
It is precisely through such appropriated matter that there occurs either its relinquishment and impairment, or its occasional benefit and nourishment.
The mind and mental factors likewise undergo benefit and harm accordingly. That which is contrary to this is termed "non-appropriated" (*anupātta*).
In this present sutra, when "appropriated" is mentioned, it is based on two meanings: first, the ālayavijñāna appropriates the sense organs and their bases as its own support;
second, it appropriates and maintains the seeds as what is gathered by itself. This is fully detailed in the various treatises.
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), both types of appropriation (*upādāna*) are present; in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the two types are not present.
The commentary states: this is the third [section], which analyzes according to the realms.

Based on this text, according to the Mahāyāna school, within the formless realm there are no ten types of material elements such as the eyes and ears, unlike what is asserted by the Mahāsāṃghika school.

It possesses the ten material elements and the five groups of sensory consciousness. Furthermore, in the *Mūlakarma-sūtra*, it is stated that "the gods of the formless realm come into the assembly," and in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there is the passage concerning the "fragrance of the Peak of Existence" (*bhavāgra*).
Such textual passages all describe matter as it is subsumed within its respective bases (*dharmāyatana*).
"O Viśālamati, this consciousness is also called the *ādāna-vijñāna*. Why is this? Because this consciousness follows and sustains the body.
Commentary: This is the second explanation of the *ādāna-vijñāna*. In Sanskrit it is called *ādāna*, which is translated here as [the appropriating consciousness].
"Appropriation" (ādāna) means that by means of this consciousness, it follows after the body and appropriates the material sense-faculties (rūpīndriya), ensuring they do not perish;
therefore, this consciousness is called "appropriation. According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, there are two meanings for the explanation of *ādāna*.
First, because it maintains the appropriated sense organs so that they do not perish; second, because it maintains the personal existence and takes up rebirth therein.
As in the first [category], there is extensive analysis. According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it possesses these three meanings; therefore, the third [category] says:
Because it can maintain the seeds of all phenomena (*dharmas*), can grasp the basis of the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*),
and can also take up the continuity of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*), this consciousness is called *ādāna*. This corresponds to the "grasping" (*upādāna*) described in the two treatises.

It is also called the *ālayavijñāna*. Why? Because this consciousness, in relation to the body, performs the functions of grasping (*parigraha*), storing (*ālaya*), and being concealed (*gupti*), sharing a common fate of security and peril.
The commentary states: This is the third explanation of the *ālaya*. In Sanskrit it is called *ālaya*, which is translated here as "storehouse" (*zàng*).

The term "storehouse" (ālaya) has three meanings: first, the storehouse as agent; second, the storehouse as object; and third, the storehouse as that which is clung to. Thus, the second volume of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Because this consciousness possesses the meanings of being the storehouse as agent, the storehouse as object, and the storehouse as that which is clung to;
because it serves as a mutual condition for the defiled phenomena; and because sentient beings cling to it as their internal self. The first volume of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* likewise [states]:...
To distinguish these three meanings, that treatise states: "Furthermore, for what reason is this consciousness also called the *ālaya*?
Because all born phenomena belonging to the category of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) are stored within it as their fruit-nature;
and because this very consciousness is stored within them as its own nature; or because sentient beings store this consciousness [within themselves] as a self."
Therefore, it is called the *ālayavijñāna*. To explain: the three distinct meanings of "storehouse" (*ālaya*) are as follows. First, the "storing agent" (*nibandhana*);
this refers to the resultant phenomena, which are stored within the cause. That is to say, the seeds within consciousness produce the seven manifest, defiled consciousnesses;

because these resultant phenomena do not exist apart from their productive cause, they are said to be stored therein. Second, the "object of storage" (*ālīya*); this refers to the causal seeds, which are stored within the result. That is to say, the object...

Because the perfumed seeds are stored within the seven manifest perfuming consciousnesses as causal natures, this constitutes the third sense of being "appropriated and stored" by self-love (*ātmasneha*);
that is, the object is stored within the appropriating subject. Now, based on this sūtra, it differs from the various treatises.
This means that by means of this consciousness, it is able to appropriate the body with its sense organs and serve as their support;
because it is hidden within them and shares their same security and peril with the supporting body, it is called the "store" (*ālaya*).

Since it resides within the support of the store-consciousness, it is named the "store. Because it represents one aspect of the meaning of being "stored," the *Saṃdhinirmocana* states: "It dwells within that body."
Because it is of a single essence and is associated [with them]. As for its abiding, it is precisely this gathering together and concealment;

being of a single essence and associated [with them], sharing the same security and peril, it is also called "mind" (*citta*). Why? Because by means of this consciousness, form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and so forth are accumulated and nourished.
Therefore, the commentary states: this is the fourth explanation of the meaning of "citta. In the Sanskrit language, *citta* is translated here as "mind" (*xin*).

It possesses many meanings: first, it is called "accumulation and origination" (*jìqǐ*), because it accumulates the seeds of all phenomena and gives rise to all phenomena, as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
The fifth fascicle states: "The second is called 'accumulation' (saṃcita). It has two meanings:

first, because it is the accumulation of the seeds of all dharmas, as stated in the first fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*: 'Because it is accumulated by the seeds of the perfuming of various dharmas.'"

Second, it is called "external" because it is the accumulation and growth of the six objective spheres. Third, it is called "collection" because it collects various objects of perception (*ālambana*).
As stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*, we now rely on this sūtra and follow the second meaning.
Therefore, it is called "mind" (*citta*). This has two meanings: first, accumulation; second, growth.

It is so named because it is accumulated and grown by means of objects such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest. According to the third fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, there are seven names.
In addition to the four names mentioned in this sutra, three more are added. What are these three? As that treatise states:
It is said: It is also called the "basis of the knowable" (*jñeyāśraya*), because it serves as the support for all phenomena that are known, whether defiled or pure.
This is explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* within the first of the ten excellences, titled "the basis of the knowable. Vasubandhu’s commentary states:

That which is to be known is called the "knowable" (*jñeya*). This refers to all phenomena (*dharma*) consisting of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*), namely the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
The term "basis" (*āśraya*) carries the meaning of "cause. Anu-vyākhyāna states: "Because it is that which is to be known, it is called the knowable. 'Basis' means the support (*āśraya*).
This term 'support' specifically selects the conditioned phenomena of affliction and purification which depend upon it [the basis], and does not [select the basis itself]."
It takes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object, because that [unconditioned] has the sense of being without a basis.
The basis is precisely the *ālayavijñāna*, because it is the cause of that [unconditioned], and because it can manifest it, as appropriate. To explain according to this:

Master Vasubandhu maintains that the eighth consciousness serves as the basis for all three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Master Asvabhāva, however, [maintains it serves as the basis] only for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
"Nature serves as the basis; it does not serve as the basis for the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) because it is the cause of that.

This means it serves as the basis for the afflicted portion of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). "It can enumerate that" means it serves as the basis for the pure portion of the dependent nature.

Question: How can there be such a contradiction between the two treatises? Answer: Vasubandhu speaks from the perspective of the general basis, and thus [the dependent nature] encompasses all three natures. Asaṅga...
It is called "dependent" (*paratantra*) solely in terms of its immediate basis; thus, each term is based on a single specific meaning and they do not contradict one another.

Alternatively, it is named the "maturation consciousness" (*vipākavijñāna*), because it is the maturation fruit of wholesome and unwholesome karma that draws forth birth and death. The commentary explains: there are three kinds of maturation.
1. It is called *vipāka* because it matures through transformation (*pariṇāma*). 2. It is called *vipāka* because it matures at a different time. 3.
It is called *vipāka* because it matures as a different category: the cause is wholesome or unwholesome, while the fruit is exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*).

Among these three, only the third—maturation as a different category—is taken [as the primary meaning], because the first two names apply to other types of fruits as well. Alternatively, it is called the "Stainless Consciousness" (*amala-vijñāna*). Most...

"Extremely pure. This is because it is the basis for all untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas. The commentary explains: *amala-vijñāna* in the Sanskrit sound is translated here as "stainless consciousness" (*wugoushi*).
It refers to the state of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*), the essence of mind associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), which is named the stainless consciousness.
Because it is the most extremely pure and serves as the support for all untainted path-dharmas, such as the various wisdoms and meditative concentrations, it is so called. Therefore...
The *Tathāgataguṇajñānācintyaviṣayāvatāranirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata’s stainless consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*) is the pure, untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).

It is liberated from all hindrances and is associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). This is explained in detail in the third fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-ṭīkā*.
Vipula-mati, based upon and established by the ādāna-vijñāna, the sixfold group of consciousnesses arises;
namely, eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.
The commentary states: From this point downward is the second section, clarifying the distinctions regarding the simultaneous evolution of the various consciousnesses.

This section contains three parts: first, the doctrine; second, the analogy; and third, the application. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the *ādāna-vijñāna* evolving simultaneously with the six consciousnesses;

second, the detailed explanation of how many consciousnesses evolve together with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) when it is confronted by the five [sensory] consciousnesses. In the first of these, the fundamental and derivative aspects are raised for analysis.

They arise simultaneously. Later, when the mind (*manas*) is contrasted with the five [sensory consciousnesses], their simultaneous arising is examined. However, in the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts, they explain simultaneous arising based on the first meaning for the time being.
Regarding this, one should have discussed the simultaneous arising with the *manas*, yet it is not mentioned;

this is because by citing the first and the last cases, the others can be inferred accordingly. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other works treat the *manas* comprehensively to explain [simultaneous arising].

They arise simultaneously. Of the preceding section, there are two parts: first, a general statement regarding their simultaneous arising; second, a re-explanation in response to difficulties. This is the first part.
Because they take the *ādāna-vijñāna* as their support, the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya*) arise—namely, visual consciousness and the others.

In this regard, with the eye and forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises; and together with that visual consciousness, a conceptual mental consciousness arises simultaneously, having the same object and following along with it.

The commentary states: From this point downward is the second section, which provides a further explanation in response to objections. This section contains two parts: first, it clarifies that visual consciousness must be accompanied by mental consciousness;
second, it clarifies that the four [sensory] consciousnesses are accompanied by mental consciousness. This is the first part.

Regarding the phrase "in this context," it is explained according to the *Nyāyamukha* (Introduction to Reasoning) and possesses two meanings: first, the sense of initiating the subject matter of the treatise;

second, the sense of distinguishing and retaining [the specific point]. Although it was stated above in general terms that all consciousnesses arise simultaneously (*sahabhū*), the specific distinction—that the five [sensory] consciousnesses necessarily depend upon the mind (*manas*), whereas the mind does not depend upon the five—has not yet been analyzed.
It is for the purpose of initiating such a thematic point that the text says, "in this context. Furthermore, regarding their simultaneous arising...
This term contains many meanings and cannot be explained all at once. To exclude other meanings and to grasp this specific meaning, it says "in this context.
Regarding the phrase "the eye possessing consciousness," there are two kinds of eyes: first, the eye possessing consciousness, called the *sabhāga* (homogeneous) eye;
second, the eye lacking consciousness, called the *tatsabhāga* (non-homogeneous). By excluding the *tatsabhāga*, it is termed the "eye possessing consciousness. However, this *sabhāga*...

Regarding the *sabhāga* (homogeneous) and *tatsabhāga* (partially homogeneous), various teachings differ. First, the Sarvāstivāda school, based on the eighteen *dhātus*, explains the meaning of *sabhāga* and *tatsabhāga* as follows:
those among the eighteen *dhātus* that possess functional activity (*karmavipāka*) are termed *sabhāga*; those that lack functional activity are termed *tatsabhāga*.
Thus, the second fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* asks: "Among the eighteen *dhātus*, how many..."
This is the *sabhāga* (homogeneous). How many are the *tatsabhāga* (non-homogeneous)?
The verse says: "The dharma-element is *sabhāga*; the others are both. The commentary says:
This means that the single dharma-element is exclusively *sabhāga*, referring to the various noble ones (*ārya*) from the second moment onward; there is no [tatsabhāga] therein.

My observation through wisdom is that there is no dharma whatsoever that is not universally encompassed by all dharmas; therefore, the *dharmadhātu* is always termed "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*). The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* explains:
"Because all *dharmadhātus* are objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"Because there is no dharma not subsumed within the three time periods that is not an object of the mental consciousness. The full explanation is as stated therein. Question: Regarding the seventeen elements (*dhātu*) and the mental consciousness...

Question: Should all objects of perception (ālambana) be exclusively "with-partner" (sabhāga) and never "without-partner" (tatsabhāga)? Answer: The seventeen elements (dhātu) are not established as "with-partner" or "without-partner" based on the mental consciousness (manovijñāna);
rather, they are established in relation to their respective faculties (indriya) and objects (viṣaya). For example, visible form (rūpa) is related to the eye (cakṣus).
...up to the body being in contact with tangibles, and tangibles being in contact with the body. Question:

If that is so, then the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) should only be established as having the status of "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) or "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*) in relation to the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*). Consequently, those [moments] that take the other seventeen elements as their objects would not be homogeneous.
Answer: It is indeed logically so. However, because the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element are capable of cognizing everything universally, [they are established differently].
Because it is a universal dharma (*sarvadharman*), it is established as "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) based on its own specific function;
for example, since the sense organs such as the eye possess functions such as seeing, they are never established as "non-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*).

Other masters claim that the *dharmadhātu* subsumes all dharmas without exception, because the other seventeen elements are also called "dharmas. They should not make such a statement, for although the name "dharma" applies generally...

However, because the *dharmadhātu* is distinct [from the other eighteen], what was stated previously is logically sound. (The commentary explains: According to this Sarvāstivāda school, all phenomena are subsumed within the *dharmadhātu*).

That is to say, among the remaining seventeen *dhātus*, each possesses both the "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and the "counter-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*). What are these termed "homogeneous" and "counter-homogeneous"?
They refer to whether they perform their own function or do not perform their own function. If they perform their own function, they are called "homogeneous."
That which does not perform its own function is called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*). Among these, the eye-element that has seen, sees, or will see is called the "homogeneous eye.
This is explained in detail, extending thus up to the mind-element; for each, one should explain its respective function within its own sphere.
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīra maintain that the "homogeneous" (sabhāga) eye has only four types:
those that have not seen form and are already past, currently perishing, or destined not to arise; whereas the masters of the Western regions maintain that there are five types.
That is to say, the dharmas that do not arise. These are further divided into two: those associated with consciousness and those dissociated from consciousness.

It should be understood that this applies likewise up to the body-element (*kāyadhātu*). The "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) aspect of the mind-element (*manodhātu*) consists exclusively of dharmas that do not arise. (The commentary explains:

Based on this, the homogeneous aspect of the final aggregate of an Arhat’s mind-element is designated as "homogeneous" in terms of its capacity as an object-possessor. Otherwise, how could it be called homogeneous? As for the form-element (*rūpadhātu*), when it has been seen, is being seen, or will be seen by the eye, it is termed "homogeneous."
Visible forms (*rūpa*) and their counterparts (*tatsabhāga-rūpa*) are likewise of four kinds. This applies even up to the element of the tangible (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*);

for each, one should explain its specific function in relation to its own respective sense faculty. It should be understood that regarding the eye that is "functioning" (*sabhāga*) and the eye that is its "counterpart" (*tatsabhāga*):
if it is functioning with respect to one [object], it is functioning with respect to all others as well; such is the detailed explanation for the counterpart eye, and so on up to the mind (*manas*).
The same applies to the *dhātus*. The *Miśrakābhidharmahṛdaya* is also like this. According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, there are three explanations.

The first master’s view is the same as that in the *Abhidharmakośa* and other texts. Another says: "The eye that perceives forms in relation to its own sentient being is called 'homogeneous' (*sabhāga*)."
The eyes that do not see forms are called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) with respect to other sentient beings;

they are also called "homogeneous" with respect to the sentient being themselves. Furthermore, some say that the eyes which do see forms are called "homogeneous" with respect to the sentient being themselves, but are not "homogeneous" with respect to other sentient beings.
It is not the case that those eyes which do not see forms are "not of that class" (*asabhāga*). Regarding one's own sentient being, those eyes are called "of that class" (*sabhāga*);
regarding other sentient beings, they are neither "of that class" nor "not of that class. One should not say this.
How could there be eyes that are neither "of that class" nor "not of that class"? One should rather say: [this applies] to the three [types of] explanations.
In the middle [section], the first part explains what is logically appropriate, as fully detailed therein. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"Because the eye is not common [to all], its *sabhāga* (homogeneous) and *tatsabhāga* (non-homogeneous) states are established based on a single continuum. Because visible form (*rūpa*) is common, its *sabhāga* and *tatsabhāga* states are established based on multiple continua.
As it is said regarding the realm of visible forms, one should know that the same applies to sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.

Sound may be like visible form; however, the three—odor, taste, and tangible objects—are apprehended only when they reach the sense faculty. Because these are not shared [with other faculties], one is apprehended by that specific faculty alone and not by others;

thus, in principle, they should be treated like the eye and so forth, and should not be explained in the same manner as visible form. Although this logic holds, it is possible for there to be shared apprehension.
Why is this? Because the three objects, such as odor and so forth, can all give rise to their respective consciousnesses—such as olfactory consciousness—whether they are present or otherwise;

the eye and other faculties are not like this, and thus they are explained in the same manner as visible form (*rūpa*). According to the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, it is said that when the eye sees a visible form, it is the "participating" (*sabhāga*) [eye];

when it does not see a visible form, it is the "other-participating" (*tatsabhāga*) [eye]. It is said that when a visible form is visible to the eye, it is the "participating" [form]; when it is not seen...
This refers to the "possessors of the remainder" (*śeṣabhāgin*). As for the distinction: if one eye is a possessor of the remainder, all others are also possessors of the remainder;
if one is a possessor of the remainder, all others are likewise possessors of the remainder. If a visible form that is being seen is a possessor of the remainder, it is not so for others.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body, as well as to sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. In the ultimate sense, this is explained in the same way as the eye.

The conventional enumeration is as explained for the realm of form (*rūpa*). (The commentary states: the mental consciousnesses are not distinct. The *Vibhāṣā* says: "As it is with the realm of form, so it is with the realms of sound, odor, taste, and tangibility;
for their categories of specific and general characteristics (*sabhāga-tatsabhāga*) are all similar.

However, regarding this point, some maintain that only the [respective] olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses perceive the various odors, tastes, and tangibles within their own respective bodies.

Thus it is said: regarding the realms of odor, flavor, and tangibility, according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they are explained in the same manner as the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*).
That is to say, people in the world speak thus: "The fragrance you smell, we also smell; the flavor you taste, we also taste;
the touch you perceive, we also perceive. According to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), however, the realms of odor, flavor, and tangibility are like the eye.
The explanation of the elements (*dhātu*) is as follows: that which is a fragrance-object (*gandha-dhātu*) smelled by one sentient being cannot be smelled by another;

that which is a taste-object (*rasa-dhātu*) tasted by one sentient being cannot be tasted by another; and that which is a tangible-object (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*) perceived by one sentient being cannot be perceived by another.

Question: If two bodies of sentient beings, each situated on one side, are both pressed against the same tangible object (spraṣṭavya-dhātu), would this not be a case of ultimate reality (paramārtha) as described for the form realm (rūpa-dhātu)?
Answer: Such a tangible object consists of many atoms (paramāṇu) that have accumulated together in a single location.

Second, because the two bodies [of the sense organs] come into contact with [their objects], each obtains only one side [of the object], and there is nothing that is obtained by both together; therefore, according to the ultimate principle, it is as explained regarding the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*).
The fragrance-element (*gandhadhātu*) and taste-element (*rasadhātu*) should be understood accordingly.

Furthermore, there are those who wish to maintain that other [beings] and non-sentient things also smell, taste, and touch various fragrances, tastes, and tangibles—whether they have already been used or are being used at the time—according to the conventional principle (*saṃvṛti-nīti*). As...
Regarding the explanation of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*): it is so called because it is said by the world at large that it is commonly obtained.
According to ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), it is like the explanation of the eye-realm (*cakṣurdhātu*), as it is the object of enjoyment for one person and cannot be obtained by another.

If the odor, taste, and touch realms have not yet been enjoyed, they may also be explained according to the principle of ultimate truth in the same way as the form realm; that is to say, while existing in the future, they shall reach the present, and thus many people and so forth [may enjoy them].

Because they share the same meaning. If one follows the former sense, it should be stated as follows: the realms of odor, taste, and tangibility, according to conventional reasoning, are as explained for the realm of form;
according to ultimate reasoning, they are as explained for the realm of the eye. If one follows the latter sense, it should be stated as follows:
regarding the realms of odor, taste, and tangibility, when they have been experienced or are being experienced, according to conventional reasoning, they are as...
Regarding the explanation of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is according to the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).

As with the explanation of the eye-realm (*cakṣurdhātu*), if [the object] has not yet been experienced, according to the ultimate meaning, it may likewise be said to be as explained for the form realm. Therefore, all treatises state this:

as it is for the form realm, so it is for the realms of sound, odor, taste, and tangibles (*śabda-gandha-rasa-spraṣṭavyadhātu*), because odors, tastes, and tangibles can be perceived in common. As for the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñāna*), such as the eye-consciousness and so forth...

Regarding *sabhāga* (homogeneous) and *tatsabhāga* (partially homogeneous), because they are phenomena that either arise or do not arise, it is as explained in the section on the element of mind (*manodhātu*).
Next, the names *sabhāga* and *tatsabhāga* will be explained. According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, there are three meanings; thus, it asks:
"What is the meaning of *sabhāga* and *tatsabhāga*? It is so called because the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness mutually intermingle.
"Part" (*bhāga*) refers to its own activity; alternatively, "part" refers to the contact (*sparśa*) that is produced.
Because they share this same part, they are called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*). That which is contrary to this is called "non-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*).
Because it is not homogeneous, yet shares a commonality of category with the homogeneous, it is named "non-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*); the principle is the same.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* state: "What is the meaning of 'partaking' (*sabhāga*) and 'partaking of the remainder' (*tatsabhāga*)?

Answer: When it partakes [of its function], it is called "partaking. Question: Within the eye-faculty, there are two types: those with activity (*sakarma-sabhāga*) and those without activity (*akarma-sabhāga*).
Can that which has activity be divided into that which lacks activity, and yet still be called "partaking"? Furthermore, can that which lacks activity also become that which has activity?
It is also called "having parts" (*sabhāga*). Both [aspects] possess the characteristic of having parts. According to the Sautrāntika school, the original text has not been seen;
however, by analogy with the Mahāyāna, there is no contradiction in principle. Now, relying on the Mahāyāna, the various treatises differ.

If one follows Vasubandhu’s and Sthiramati’s *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra*, the meaning of "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) is explained solely in terms of the five internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*); thus, that treatise states:
All say: "How many are sabhāga? It refers to the five internal bases with form, because they share the same objects as their respective consciousnesses.

"How many are tatsabhāga? It refers to when those [bases] are devoid of their respective consciousnesses, because they are equal to their own kind. The commentary explains: they are called *sabhāga* (homogeneous) because they share the same objective sphere (*ālambana*).
This is consistent with the third chapter of the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* and the fifth chapter of the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā*, which agree with the treatment in the *Pañcaskandhaka*.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* asks: "What are the *sabhāga* (homogeneous) and *tatsabhāga* (non-homogeneous)? How many are *sabhāga* and *tatsabhāga*?
For what purpose are the *sabhāga* and *tatsabhāga* examined? It states:

"The sense organs that do not exist apart from consciousness, which arise in a continuous stream toward their respective objects, and those that arise in a continuous stream similar to their own kind apart from consciousness—these are the *sabhāga* and *tatsabhāga*."

The first is the *sabhāga* (homogeneous). Because the various sense-faculties arise in a continuous succession that resembles the consciousness [with respect to] their respective objects, they are called *sabhāga* in the sense that the faculties evolve in a manner similar to the consciousness. The second is the *tatsabhāga* (quasi-homogeneous).

Because the various sense-faculties, being separated from consciousness, arise in a continuous succession that resembles their own kind, they are [called *tatsabhāga*] because the faculties do not conjoin with consciousness, but exist solely as themselves.

It arises as a continuous succession of similar entities. The meaning of "similarity" regarding the faculties is explained as *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity). It is a portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), specifically the five material sense bases (*āyatana*) such as the eye, which are portions of the material realms (*dhātu*).
These are classified as *sabhāga* (functioning) and *tatsabhāga* (non-functioning). Furthermore, this is stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 56.

This is also explained based on the five internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*). It says: Question: Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and how many are "counter-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*)?
Answer: The visual element (*cakṣurdhātu*) that possesses consciousness is called homogeneous; the remaining visual elements are called counter-homogeneous.
As it is with the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), so it is for all elements up to the body-element (*kāyadhātu*).

Among the internal elements comprised solely by the faculties (*indriya*), one should consider their "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*) states; this does not apply to the external elements such as visible form (*rūpa*).

It should be understood that regarding all objects of cognition within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), those with an object are as explained for the mind-element (*manodhātu*), while those without an object are as explained for visible form and the other [external] elements. (This passage is missing from the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*; it is found in the Liang translation of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.)

As listed in the treatise, the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (Jiejing) states: "Depending on the eye-faculty that possesses consciousness (*savijñāna*), and taking external form-objects as its condition, eye-consciousness arises. Paramārtha’s commentary explains: "If it were the eyes of a dead person, they would be called 'eye-faculties devoid of consciousness' (*avijñāna*). Therefore, the term 'possessing consciousness' is used to distinguish them from those devoid of consciousness."
This explanation is incorrect, because after one has relinquished life, the eye is no longer established. (The phrase) "there is consciousness, ear, etc. below should be understood accordingly.

Regarding the statement "that which accompanies and follows along with the visual consciousness," this clarifies that when visual consciousness arises, there must necessarily be a conceptual mental consciousness that arises simultaneously as its concomitant, sharing the same object of perception.
There is consciousness. With the ear, nose, tongue, body, as well as sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles as conditions, there arise the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses.

Simultaneously with and accompanying these auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses, a conceptual mental consciousness (manovijñāna) arises at the same time and in the same object-domain.

The commentary states: This is the second explanation that the other four consciousnesses function simultaneously with the mental consciousness; this should be understood according to what has been stated above.

O Broad Wisdom, if at that time a single visual consciousness arises, then at that very moment, there is only one discerning mental consciousness that arises functioning in tandem with the visual consciousness.
The commentary states: From here below is the second section, which provides a detailed explanation of the varying degrees of simultaneous occurrence (*sahabhāva*). This section contains two parts:

first, it clarifies the simultaneous occurrence of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) with the visual consciousness; second, it clarifies the simultaneous occurrence of the mental consciousness with two, three, four, or five of the sensory consciousnesses, such as the visual.
This is the first part, clarifying the simultaneous occurrence of the mental consciousness with the visual consciousness due to the convergence of a single object-condition.
If, at that time, two, three, four, or five groups of consciousness arise, then at that very moment,
there is only a single discerning mental consciousness that arises together with those five groups of consciousness, sharing the same objective domain.
The commentary states: This is the second [section], clarifying the varying number of conditions—such as the objective referent—that conjoin.

It concerns the varying number of instances in which this single mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) operates simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness; their number is not fixed.

The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* speaks of "non-conceptual mental consciousness," while the *Viniscayasamgrahaṇī* and other texts speak of "conceptual mental consciousness"; these are essentially the same.
Therefore, know that conceptual discrimination is primary.
O Vipaśyanāmati, it is like a great torrent of water: if the conditions for the arising of a single wave appear, only one wave will arise.
The commentary states: This is the second section, which provides a further explanation through analogies. It consists of two parts: first, the analogy of the quantity of water waves;
second, the analogy of the quantity of mirror reflections. Regarding the differences between these two preceding analogies, various explanations exist.

One interpretation states that the intended meanings of the two metaphors are distinct, as in the *Tattvasaṃgraha-ṭīkā*: the metaphor of water producing waves illustrates the sense that the six consciousnesses arise and perish simultaneously with the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*);

the metaphor of a mirror producing reflections illustrates that although the various consciousnesses arise, it is not the substance of the fundamental consciousness itself that transforms into the six consciousnesses.
Another interpretation states that the intended meanings of the two metaphors are no different, for both equally reveal the principle that the various consciousnesses evolve simultaneously.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 51) and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (fascicle 17), I shall now explain these two metaphors. The various teachings differ;
in some instances, two metaphors are presented in order to clarify the distinction between the basis (*āśraya*) and that which depends upon it (*āśrita*).
As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 63) states: "What is called the differentiation established by the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-yukti*)? Briefly..."

There are two types of consciousness: first, the ālaya-vijñāna; second, the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna). The ālaya-vijñāna is the basis, while the evolving consciousnesses are that which depend upon it.
These latter consist of seven kinds, namely, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness.
This is like waves depending upon a turbulent current, or like reflections depending upon a clear mirror. Thus is it called "dependence" in the ultimate sense.
The distinction between the basis (*āśraya*) and that which is based upon it (*āśrita*) is established according to reason.

In some places, such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (51) and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (17), it is taught in order to show that the eighth consciousness functions simultaneously with the seven [consciousnesses].

In other places, such as the seventh chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it is taught in order to show that the eighth consciousness is not distinct from the seven; as it says: "The self-nature of the eight consciousnesses cannot be said to be fixed."
First, because their modes of activity (*ākāra*), bases (*āśraya*), objects (*ālambana*), and associations (*saṃprayoga*) differ; and because when one ceases, the others do not necessarily cease;

and because the characteristics of the perfumers (*vāsaka*) and so forth are each distinct. Yet, they are not definitively different, for the Sūtras state that the eight consciousnesses are like water and waves, being without distinction.
If they were definitively different, they would lack the nature of cause and effect, as things such as illusions have no fixed nature. As it is said: [omitted].
The distinctions among the various types of consciousness previously explained are based on conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) and not on ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Within ultimate truth, mind and its objects transcend both thought and expression. As a verse states: "The eight kinds of mind, intellect, and consciousness have distinct characteristics conventionally;

ultimately, their characteristics are without distinction, because there is no distinction between the characteristic and that which is characterized. The intended meaning of this present sutra contains the above points.

This explains various meanings. Alternatively, the intended meaning of the two metaphors in this sutra may differ: the former metaphor signifies simultaneous arising and the uninterrupted continuity of cause and effect.
As stated in the third fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*: "The term 'constant' excludes interruption; its transformation is not non-eternal."
It is like a violent torrent; such is the nature of cause and effect. This is explained in detail as therein.

Subsequently, the analogy of simultaneous arising and the eight non-transformations are reduced to seven, along with the meaning of inexhaustible enjoyment. Within the former section, there are three parts; the first is the analogy of one condition producing one wave.
Next is the analogy of many conditions producing many waves; following that is the analogy of the uninterrupted succession of its own kind.
This is the first analogy: one condition producing one wave.
Whether it be two or many waves, when the conditions for their arising are present, many waves arise and evolve.
The commentary states: This is the second analogy of many conditions and many waves.
However, this turbulent water flows perpetually from its own kind, without interruption or exhaustion.
The commentary states: This is the third analogy of the non-interruption of one's own kind. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* also shares this same intent; therefore, it says:
The verse says:
Just as when the ocean encounters the condition of wind, Various waves arise;
Their manifest activity turns without interruption, So it is with the ocean of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), Struck by the winds of objects and the like.
The waves of various consciousnesses constantly arise and manifest as transformative functions.
It is like a perfectly pure mirror surface: if the conditions for the appearance of a single reflection are present, then only that one reflection arises.

The commentary states: From here below is the second [section], the analogy of the number of reflections in a mirror. This consists of three parts: first, the analogy of one object reflecting one image;
second, the analogy of many objects reflecting many images; and finally, the section beginning with "not being this," which is the analogy of inexhaustible enjoyment.
This is the first: the analogy of one object reflecting one image.
Whether there be two or many reflections, when the conditions for their arising are present, many reflections arise.
The commentary states: This is the second analogy, that of many conditions producing many reflections.
It is not that this mirror surface undergoes transformation into the reflections, nor is there any cessation or exhaustion of its capacity to be experienced.

The commentary states: This is the third analogy for inexhaustible enjoyment. Regarding the statement that "the surface of this mirror does not transform into reflections and so forth," the *Jinzhendi ji* (Record of the True Dharma) says:
"The production of a reflection in a mirror depends upon conditions; the mirror itself does not transform to become the reflection.

As for the six consciousnesses arising in dependence upon conditions and objects, they all arise from the seeds of the preceding six consciousnesses to produce the subsequent six consciousnesses; it is not [the case that] the [seeds] themselves are the fundamental [source].

The essence of consciousness transforms into the six consciousnesses. Now, let us explain that this transformation has two meanings: first, transformation as cause (*hetu-pariṇāma*), wherein the seed-ālaya-vijñāna transforms into the seven [evolving] consciousnesses;
second, transformation as fruit (*phala-pariṇāma*), wherein the manifesting eighth consciousness transforms its own objective aspect (*sva-nimitta-bhāga*).

Yet it cannot transform the seven consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness. In this present sutra, because the meaning refers to transformation as a result (*phala-pariṇāma*), it is not that the surface of this mirror transforms into a reflection.
Furthermore, the fact that reflections appear on this mirror’s surface without ceasing is intended to manifest that the eighth consciousness produces results inexhaustibly.
Question: Why is it that, among the examples of combination, only water and waves are cited? Answer: The meaning can be inferred; it is stated briefly.
Yet it was not so stated. If that is the case, how are the two metaphors combined in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*? The explanation says:
There is this distinction in the Sanskrit original.
Thus, O Viśālamati, because the ādāna-vijñāna serves as the support and the basis, being like a violent torrent... if...
At that time, when the conditions for the arising of a single visual consciousness are present, at that very moment, a single visual consciousness arises.
The commentary states: From here below is the third section, which cites the dharma as an analogy. This section has two parts: first, it clarifies that one condition gives rise to one consciousness;
second, it clarifies that multiple conditions give rise to multiple consciousnesses. This is the first part, clarifying that one condition gives rise to one consciousness.

If, at that time, the conditions for the arising of even the five groups of sensory consciousness (pañca-vijñāna-kāya) are present, then at that very moment, the five groups of sensory consciousness proceed.
The commentary states: this is the second [point] clarifying that multiple consciousnesses proceed based on multiple objects; it should be understood according to the above.

Vipula-mati, although such a bodhisattva is skilled in the secrets of mind, thought, and consciousness by relying upon and being established in the wisdom of the abiding of phenomena (dharmasthiti-jñāna),
the Tathāgatas do not designate him as a bodhisattva skilled in all the secrets of mind, thought, and consciousness based on this alone.
The commentary states: Below this, the second section distinguishes the skillful response regarding the secret [teachings] to the two preceding questions.

This section contains two parts: first, the formal explanation based on the questions; second, from "Next, Vast Wisdom... onwards, the conclusion of the response to the preceding questions. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections.
The first part clarifies that what precedes the stages (bhūmi) was not taught by the Buddha, while the latter part clarifies that what pertains to the stages was taught by the Buddha;

this refers to the former. Regarding "knowledge of the abiding of phenomena" (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*): according to the Sarvāstivāda school, it is called knowledge of the abiding of phenomena because it knows the internal basis upon which the resultant phenomena abide.
Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 110, states: Question: Why is it called "knowledge of the abiding of phenomena"? Answer: ... [text continues] ...

"Dharma" refers to the fruit; "abiding" (sthiti) refers to the cause. Because one knows the cause upon which the fruit-dharma abides, it is called "knowledge of the stability of dharmas" (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*).

That is to say, knowing the causes upon which the fruits—low, middle, and superior—of the three realms abide is called the knowledge of the stability of dharmas. The detailed explanation is as stated therein.

According to the Sautrāntika school, because it knows that dharmas abide eternally, it is called the knowledge of the stability of dharmas. Thus, it is established in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle 2.
Sixteenth, it is said: To know the arising of all phenomena is called the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*).

For example, from birth as a condition for old age and death, down to ignorance as a condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); because this nature remains eternally constant whether a Buddha appears or not, it is called the knowledge of the stability of phenomena.

Now, according to the Mahāyāna, the *Xiányáng shèngjì lùn* (Śrāmaṇyaphala-sūtra-śāstra), fascicle fifteen, states: "The knowledge of the stability of phenomena refers to that which relies upon the sūtras..."

Regarding the wisdom that establishes the gates of the Dharma through mooring-ropes and so forth, it accords with the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and is identical to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*. Thus, the tenth [chapter] asks:
"What is the wisdom of the abiding of phenomena (*dharmasthitijñāna*)? It replies: "It is knowing, without error, according to what the Buddha has designated and revealed.

Furthermore, the ninety-fourth [chapter] asks: "What is the wisdom of the abiding of phenomena? It replies: "It is when, for example, someone among humans follows in accordance with dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)."

Having received the unerring teaching, while abiding in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) regarding the causal states of dependently arisen formations (*pratītyasamutpanna-saṃskāra*), one is then able to reflect correctly through the mental attentions (*manaskāra*) produced by hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

By means of sublime wisdom (*prajñā*), one can penetrate and gain conviction that suffering is truly suffering, origination is truly origination, cessation is truly cessation, and the path is truly the path. All...
Such as these. The sublime wisdom that establishes the factors according to their causes and effects within the Dharma is called the "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*).
The intent of what is explained here is identical to that of the tenth chapter of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

The meaning of this is to say that although Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) understand the conventional distinctions within mind, thought, and consciousness through the power of the knowledge of the stability of phenomena, they have not yet...
They have realized the secret ultimate truth of mind, intellect, and consciousness. Therefore, World-Honored One, you do not designate them as skillful bodhisattvas based on this alone.
O Vast Intelligence, if those bodhisattvas, within their own individual [streams of being], do not see the *ādāna* (appropriating consciousness) as it truly is, nor see the *ālaya*...
The *ādānavijñāna* does not perceive the *ālaya*, does not perceive the *ālayavijñāna*, does not perceive the accumulation [of seeds], and does not perceive the mind.

The commentary states: From here below is the second section, which correctly clarifies that [the stages] above the ground (*bhūmi*) are what the Buddha has prophesied. Within this, there are two parts; first...
This provides a general answer to the two questions. The subsequent section provides specific answers to each question under their respective names.

That is to say, within the preceding answer, there are two meanings: first, the meaning elucidated by the teaching, which answers the first question; second, the establishment of the teaching based on that meaning, which answers the latter question.

Within this [latter part], there are two sections: first, the discernment of "knowing as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) in relation to the three names of the eighth consciousness; second, [the discussion] in relation to the ten...
"Eight elements: one knows them as they truly are; this is the first. However, there are differing explanations regarding this passage. The *Tattvasaṃgraha-ṭīkā* states:
"If a bodhisattva perceives form, consciousness, and so forth in the manner described above, this is based on conventional understanding.

The Buddha did not declare that such a person understands the secret meaning of mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*), because they have not perceived [those things] as they truly are in the manner previously described."

Regarding the meaning of consciousness as clarified: the Buddha has now recorded and taught that this person understands the secret meaning of mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

This clarifies that consciousness is empty, false, and non-existent, which is itself the truth; it is by penetrating the fundamental secret that one finally attains clear understanding regarding the derivative level of the false.
Furthermore, another interpretation states: "Internally distinct" refers to the internal, namely *tathatā* (suchness), the self-nature of all phenomena.
Because it is the essence, it is called "internal. As for "individually distinct": following the expression that reveals the ultimate truth, it is termed "individually distinct.

This means that Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*), relying upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and by means of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), within their own individual internal experience, do not see the function of the *ādāna-vijñāna* as it truly is, nor do they see the essence of the *ādāna-vijñāna* as it truly is, because they have realized the realm of *tathatā*.
The distinction between the essence and function of the *ālayavijñāna* and the mind (*citta*) should be understood according to this principle. Furthermore, another interpretation states:

regarding "each being internal and distinct," within the essential nature of all phenomena such as the *ādānavijñāna*, there exist both specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Among these, because the specific characteristic is the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is termed "internal. Each phenomenon’s specific characteristic adheres to its own individual substance; thus, it is called [internal].
They are distinct. Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (First Chapter) states: "That which is internally experienced is the meaning of 'cognition' (*jñāna*).

This refers to the meaning of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) cognizing its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Second Section) makes this same statement: "Based on cognition, there is verbal expression."
This refers to that which is individually experienced, realized, touched, and attained within; by virtue of these causes and conditions, one explains it to others.
According to this interpretation, both the fundamental [wisdom] and the subsequently attained wisdom are direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Because they know the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of *dharmatā* as they truly are, free from all conceptualization (*vikalpa*), it is called "not seeing. It is not that the absence of conceptualization itself is what is meant by "not seeing."
One does not see the eye, forms, or eye-consciousness; one does not see the ear, sounds, or ear-consciousness; one does not see the nose, odors, or nose-consciousness;
one does not see the tongue, tastes, or tongue-consciousness; one does not see the body, tangibles, or body-consciousness; one does not see the mind, mental phenomena, or mind-consciousness.
The commentary states: Because this explanation does not perceive the eighteen constituents (*dhātus*), one is called a bodhisattva skilled in means.
This is what is meant by a "bodhisattva skilled in the ultimate meaning" (*paramārtha-kuśala*). It is the Tathāgata who designates such a person as a bodhisattva skilled in the ultimate meaning.
The commentary states: This constitutes the second specific response to the two preceding questions. The text consists of two sections.
The first, "one who is called a bodhisattva skilled in the ultimate," reiterates the meaning realized above to answer the former question.
The second, "the Tathāgata designates him as a bodhisattva skilled in the ultimate," reiterates the teaching that expresses [that meaning] above to answer [the latter question].
Later, [the Buddha] asked (or perhaps these two characters "ke shi" [may be so called] encompass both sections):
"Vipulamati, up to this point one is designated as a bodhisattva skilled in all the secrets of mind, thought, and consciousness.
It is up to this point that the Tathāgata establishes one as a bodhisattva skilled in all the secrets of mind, thought, and consciousness."
The commentary states: This is the second response to the preceding question, which may be understood according to the text.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
The commentary states: From here below is the second section, which presents the verses as a brief exposition. This section contains two parts: first, the introduction of the verses;
second, the presentation of the verses as a brief exposition. This is the first part, the introduction of the verses.
The *ādāna-vijñāna* is profound and subtle; containing all seeds, it is like a violent torrent.

I do not reveal it to the foolish and ignorant, fearing they would conceptually grasp it as a self. (As the *Saṃdhinirmocana-gāthā* says: "All seeds, the *ādāna*..."; and the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states: "The *upādāna-vijñāna* is profound and subtle; it can give rise to all phenomena.
I have taught the analogy of water and a mirror, but not for the sake of fools. All seeds flow constantly; I do not speak of this to the foolish, lest they grasp it as a self.")
The commentary states: This is the second verse cited. However, various treatises differ in their explanations of this verse.
According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, Asvabhāva’s commentary states: It is called "profound" because the wisdom and insight of the world's wise ones cannot fathom its depths;
it is called "subtle" because it is difficult for Śrāvakas and others to comprehend. Therefore, it is not [for them...]
This consciousness is revealed to the śrāvakas and others because they do not seek the subtle knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
That which possesses all seeds and flows like a torrent is a continuous succession from moment to moment without interruption, like the current of a river.

"I do not reveal this to the foolish and the ignorant" means that it is not disclosed to those who harbor the view of self (ātmadṛṣṭi), for fear that they would engage in conceptual proliferation (vikalpa).
They conceive of it as a self. How could those types [of beings] possibly distinguish and conceive of a self?
For its mode of activity remains uniform and unchanging until the very end of saṃsāra. Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "Ādānavijñāna" is an alternative name for what has been explained.
"Profound and subtle" means it is difficult to comprehend. "Containing all seeds like a torrential stream" means it evolves in a continuous succession.
All seeds, through their moment-to-moment succession like the flow of a torrential stream, continue in a continuous series.
Fearing that others might conceptually grasp this as a self—since it functions through a single mode of activity—conceptual grasping can indeed occur.

As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) states in Dharmapāla’s commentary: "Because it is able to maintain the seeds of all phenomena and is able to appropriate the material sense organs and their bases..."
It also functions as the basis for grasping and the continuity of rebirth; therefore, this consciousness is called *ādāna*.

Because sentient beings lacking the nature [for liberation] cannot fathom its depths, it is said to be profound. Because those of the lineage intent on tranquility cannot penetrate it, it is called extremely subtle.
It is the true seed of all phenomena; when struck by conditions, the waves of the evolving consciousnesses arise.
It is constant and uninterrupted, like a violent torrent. "Ordinary" means the absence of intrinsic nature; "foolish" means tending toward quiescence.

Fearing that they might give rise to conceptual attachment toward this [reality], thereby falling into the various evil destinies and obstructing the arising of the noble path, my World-Honored One did not reveal it to them.
Commentary on the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra, Scroll Three;
Commentary on the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra, Scroll Four (Sutra Text Volume Two).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuance of Ximing Monastery.

Regarding the explanation of the fourth chapter, "The Characteristics of All Phenomena" (*Sarvadharma-lakṣaṇa-parivarta*) of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the chapter title; second, the interpretation of the textual meaning.
As for the title "The Chapter on the Characteristics of All Phenomena," there are two interpretations. One states that because the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are not identical, it is called "all."
All [phenomena] maintain their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and give rise to conceptual understanding; thus they are called "dharmas" (*dharma*).

"Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to their essential form (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), or to their specific appearances (*ākāra-lakṣaṇa*), such as that which is grasped and so forth. These are the essential natures and specific appearances of all phenomena.

Taken collectively, these three natures are termed "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*); this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. If each individual nature were termed "all phenomena," it would be a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. This is because...
Because each individual nature is not the whole. Regarding the term "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*), there are briefly two explanations:

namely, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Within the latter, there are five categories, such as mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika*). Extensively, there are one hundred dharmas.
This refers to the eight consciousnesses and so forth. However, these three natures constitute the essential nature and characteristics of all phenomena;

therefore, they are called the "characteristics of all phenomena" (*sarvadharma-lakṣaṇa*). According to this interpretation, among the three natures, the first two are termed the "characteristics of all phenomena" by means of a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound, because both natures possess all phenomena.
The latter, the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature), is termed "one... [the remainder of the sentence is omitted in the source].
The term "all dharmas" (*sarvadharma*) is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound, because it refers to the essential nature (*lakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas.

Although there are two such interpretations, the latter is superior, as it does not contradict the principle of the subsequent scriptural passage. As stated in the following sutra: "the grasped and the dependent."
All are said to be the thoroughly established nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). These are all phenomena, the universal suchness (*tathatā*).

Because this chapter extensively elucidates the principles of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) regarding the characteristics of all phenomena, it is titled "The Chapter on the Characteristics of All Phenomena" (the title of the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* refers to it as "The Chapter on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Śrīguṇavibhūti," as there is this variation in the Sanskrit manuscript).

At that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Guṇākara addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said, regarding a bodhisattva who is skillful in the characteristics of all phenomena..."
The commentary states: The second section is the formal explanation of the text. Regarding the objects of observation, there are two types: first, the objects of the ultimate and conventional truths;

second, the objects of the nature of existence and non-existence. The preceding portion has already explained the two objects of the ultimate and conventional truths; hereafter, we shall distinguish the objects of the nature of existence and non-existence.

First, the nature of existence is clarified, which refers to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*); subsequently, the nature of non-existence is taught, which refers to the three absences of nature (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*).
Within these two categories, existence (*sat*) is established as the basis for non-existence (*asat*). The nature of existence (*sattva*) is fundamental and is therefore explained first;
the nature of non-existence (*asattva*) is derivative and is thus discussed later. For this reason, Master Vasubandhu’s *Triṃśikā* states:
"Based precisely upon these three natures, those three absences of nature are established. Within this chapter, the text is divided into two parts; the first concerns the Bodhisattva...
Question: The Tathāgata’s formal response follows the inquiry. Within the inquiry itself, it is further divided into two parts: first, the presentation of the teaching being inquired about;

second, the posing of questions based upon that teaching. This is the first part. The text consists of two sections. The first concerns the differentiation of question and answer according to time. The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states:
"Guṇākara (Merit Forest)" refers to one who has become a person through virtue, just as a forest is formed by trees.

Both the Dharma and the metaphor are presented together; thus he is named Guṇākara (Forest of Merit). As for the present Guṇamati (Root of Virtue), it is because he has long planted the roots of virtue over immeasurable kalpas.
The explanation says: this is a name established based on his cause. Because he has cultivated the two kinds of roots of virtue—merit and wisdom—he is called "Root of Virtue.

Regarding the phrase "the bodhisattva who is skillful in the characteristics of all dharmas," this introduces the teaching that is the subject of the question. As for "the characteristics of all dharmas":
To distinguish the phenomena that are the objects of observation: a bodhisattva who is skillful is one who is able to observe persons.
Regarding a bodhisattva who is skillful in the characteristics of all phenomena—by what criteria is one called a bodhisattva skilled in the characteristics of all phenomena?
By what criteria does the Tathāgata designate such a person as a bodhisattva skilled in the characteristics of all phenomena? Having spoken these words, [he continued:]
The commentary states: This is the second [section], which poses questions based on the teaching. The text consists of two parts: first, the restatement of the teaching that was questioned;
second, "To what extent? which is the actual phrasing of the question. There are two intentions in this question: first, to ask at what stage the bodhisattva’s skillfulness resides;
second, to ask regarding the designation of the term "skillfulness. Alternatively, it may clarify the signified meaning of the former.
[The section on] Meaning. Next, [the Buddha] asks about the teaching that expresses [that meaning].
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Deben.
The commentary states: From here below is the second part, the World-Honored One’s formal exposition. This contains two sections: first, praising the question and granting permission to speak.

The subsequent section on the characteristics of all phenomena consists of a formal exposition in response to questions. The preceding section has three parts: first, the presentation of the interlocutors;
second, the praise of the benefits of questioning; and third, the exhortation to listen and permit the teaching. This [present passage] is the first part.
Excellent, Kuśalamūla! It is well that you are now able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such a profound meaning.
You do so now out of a desire to benefit and bring peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, and out of compassion for the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
This question was posed in order to enable the attainment of benefit and happiness.

The commentary states: The second [section] praises the question for its utility. The text consists of two parts: first, praising the profundity of the meaning of the question; second, praising the question for its utility.
This should be understood according to the above.
"You should listen attentively; I shall explain the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) for you.
The commentary states: This third instruction commands attention and permits the exposition.
That is to say, the characteristics of all phenomena are, in brief, of three kinds.

The commentary states: From this point downward is the second section, which provides the formal explanation in response to the questions. This section contains two parts: first, the differentiation of the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) based on the objects of observation;
second, from "Furthermore, Guṇākara" onwards, the clarification of the skillful Bodhisattva based on the person who observes.

Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, the teaching (*dharma*); second, the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*). Within the teaching, there are three further divisions: first, the presentation of the headings and enumeration of items; second, the questions and answers.

The names are listed here; they will be explained individually in sequence below, and this is the first [section]. However, regarding these brief statements, there are two interpretations. First, the "abbreviation by way of breadth":
although all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are extensive when categorized as the hundred dharmas, they are abbreviated to merely the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Since we are currently contrasting them with the hundred dharmas, it is called "abbreviated. Second, the "abbreviation by way of essentials": as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states, "That which is to be known... [is thus abbreviated].

The characteristics are briefly of three kinds. As explained by Asvabhāva: "Briefly of three kinds" means that all phenomena necessarily possess the distinctions of that which is to be known, that which is to be abandoned, and that which is to be realized.
"What are the three? The commentary states:
this second question-and-answer section enumerates the names. First there is the inquiry, followed by the enumeration;

this [sentence] constitutes the inquiry. "First is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*); second is the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*); third is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*)."
The commentary states: This is a listing of the names. However, regarding the names of the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there are both general and specific senses.
"Three characteristics" is the general name; "three" indicates the number, and "characteristics" refers to their essential nature (*svabhāva*) or their formal appearance (*ākāra*).

This is an example of the "attributive compound denoting a number" (*dvigu* or *saṃkhyāpūrva-dvigu*) among the six types of grammatical compounds, as detailed in a separate chapter. As for the specific names: the first is the "thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita*). [This] encompasses...

The fourth volume of the *Mahāyāna-śāstra* states: "How is the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the nature of being conceptually constructed) established? For what reason is it called the *parikalpita-svabhāva*?

Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) conceptually constructs infinite modes of appearance (*ākāra*), giving rise to inverted characteristics, it is therefore called the *parikalpita-svabhāva*.
Its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not truly exist; only that which is conceptually constructed can be apprehended. Therefore, it is so named."

This refers to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the nature of universal imagination). [The commentary] explains: This passage answers both questions simultaneously; alternatively, it may answer the two preceding questions in sequence. Vasubandhu’s commentary states:

"Innumerable aspects" refers to the aspects of all objective spheres (*ālambana*). "Universal imagination by the mental consciousness" means that the mental consciousness itself is designated as "universal imagination.
"The aspect of arising from perversion" refers to that which can give rise to false and perverted objects.
Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of the objective sphere are in reality non-existent": this means that their substantial entity does not exist at all;

there is only the obtainable [object] as it is grasped by pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*). This means there is only what is obtainable as grasped by deluded consciousness. As Vasubandhu’s commentary explains: "immeasurable aspects" refers to...

This refers to the images of various objects consisting of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*). (One interpretation says: the self and phenomena based on dependent causes and conditions; another says: the self and phenomena that are grasped.
"The consciousness that performs universal imagination" (*parikalpa*) means that the mental consciousness itself is designated as "universal imagination.

"The characteristic of arising from inversion" refers to the causal appearance of the grasped and the grasper (*grāhya-grāhaka*) within the deluded consciousness. (One interpretation says: the objective meaning of the realm universally imagined, which is the cause for the inverted and deluded consciousness to arise. Another says: the immeasurable aspects of what is grasped.)
It is called "thoroughly imagined" (parikalpita) because it is the cause for the arising of the appearance of characteristics based on the dependent nature (paratantra).

This means that the very object-characteristic (artha-lakṣaṇa) which is thoroughly imagined is termed the "imagined intrinsic nature" (parikalpita-svabhāva). Its own characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) does not exist in reality;

there is only the obtainable [object] which is thoroughly imagined. This means that within the truly non-existent self and phenomena, there is only the appearance of an image that is thoroughly imagined.
Because its appearance can be apprehended, it is called the "thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita*). As stated in the eighth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:
"Because it thoroughly calculates (*pariccheda*), it is called 'thoroughly imagined' (*parikalpa*. This refers to the false conceptualization that performs the calculation;
