"conceptualization" refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) that are grasped as either phenomena (*dharma*) or a self (*ātman*), along with their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) and specific characteristics (*viśeṣa*). These are collectively termed the "intrinsic nature of the thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpitasvabhāva*).

Regarding the nature [of the pervasive imagination], there are two explanations. One says that the eight consciousnesses and all mental factors (caitta) that are fully subsumed therein are all capable of pervasive imagination, because they have false discrimination as their intrinsic nature and because they all manifest as the semblance of the grasped object and the grasping subject.
Thus, the ālayavijñāna is said to take the seeds of the false attachment to the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) as its object.

This is due to conditions (*pratyaya*). (This is the interpretation of the master Sthiramati. According to another interpretation, the sixth and seventh mental states (*citta-varga*) that grasp at a self and phenomena are the universal conceptualizers (*parikalpa*).

This is because it is taught that only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is capable of universal conceptualization; the details are as explained therein. (This is the school of the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states:
"The characteristic of false discrimination, the characteristic of causes and conditions, and the characteristic of the ultimate truth" (as translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha).

Regarding the various treatises’ classifications of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*): the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* speaks of "the nature of false appearances," "the nature of dependent origination," and "the nature of establishment. These differences are due to the translators.

Now, when we speak of the "imagined and grasped" (*parikalpita-parigṛhīta*), we cite the agent of imagination (*parikalpa*) to indicate that which is grasped. If it is the "imagined and grasped," it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound, because the grasped depends upon the act of imagining.

If one takes "that which is grasped" (*parigṛhīta*) in relation to "nature" (*svabhāva*), it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative) compound, because that which is grasped is itself the nature. Thus, there are two [ways of understanding it].

Regarding the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "If the dependent nature is, in reality, nothing but consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), which serves as the basis for the manifestation of objects as if they were external, how does it become the 'dependent'?
For what reason and by what causes and conditions is it called 'dependent'?"
That which arises from seeds produced by its own habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) is called "dependent origination" (*paratantra-utpatti*).
Because it lacks the capacity to abide naturally after a single moment has passed, it is called "dependent" (*paratantra*). Vasubandhu’s commentary states:

"Arising from its own causes and conditions, and lacking the power to remain once it has arisen, abiding only for a brief duration is called 'dependent origination'. Asaṅga’s commentary [explains it similarly].
It is said: [The nature of] the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) arises from the seeds of linguistic habitual tendencies (*nāma-vāsanā*).
Because it is produced by others based on its own seeds, it is called "dependent origination" (*paratantra*). This explains that its essence is produced in dependence upon others;
after the moment of production, it lacks the capacity to abide spontaneously. This explains that its essence abides in dependence. For these two reasons, it is so named.

The *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature). Regarding what is called "abiding": according to the system of Sthiramati, a distinct period of abiding is established after the moment of arising; this is termed "dependent abiding. According to the school of Dharmapāla, it is so designated because the moment of arising itself possesses a temporary function;

thus, it is figuratively described as "abiding. All conditioned phenomena arise by depending upon causes and relying upon conditions; this is called the *paratantra-svabhāva*. Therefore, the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The *paratantra-svabhāva* is that which is produced from the discrimination of conditions. Dharmapāla’s commentary explains: "Depend[ing]..."
It arises in dependence upon other conditions; thus it is called *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature).
Third is the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (the perfected nature). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:

"Because it is unchanging, because it is the object of purification, and because it is the most excellent among all wholesome dharmas—it is called 'perfected' (*pariniṣpanna*) in the sense of being the supreme reality. Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "Because it is without..."
Regarding "because of its nature of being changeless": this refers to the quality of being non-deceptive, like a non-deceptive minister.

Regarding "it is called *pariniṣpanna* (the perfected) by way of the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*)": this means it is called *pariniṣpanna* because it is the object of purification and because it is the supreme reality, just as a garment is "perfectly finished" (*pariniṣpanna*).
Anandagarbha’s commentary states: "Its nature is the perfect accomplishment of reality; [this is] an abbreviation."
No analogy is provided; the rest is the same as Vasubandhu’s [commentary]. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"That which is revealed by the two kinds of emptiness, the perfectly accomplished reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), is called the 'perfectly accomplished nature' (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

This reveals that its pervasive and eternal essence is not false or erroneous, thereby distinguishing it from self-characteristics, common characteristics, space, the self, and so forth. The commentary explains: "Revealed by the two kinds of emptiness" briefly indicates its essential nature, which possesses three meanings.

Therefore, it is called "perfectly accomplished reality" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). First, "perfect" (*pari*) signifies the sense of being all-pervasive; this distinguishes it from the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of matter, such as its resistance or obstruction.

Second, "accomplished" (*niṣpanna*) signifies the sense of permanence; this distinguishes it from common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), such as suffering and impermanence, which—though they are indeed common characteristics—are themselves impermanent.
Third, "the true nature of all phenomena" (*dharmatā*) signifies that it is not deceptive or false; this distinguishes it [from conventional reality].
Regarding the outsiders such as the Ākāśika, although they claim that [space] is all-pervasive and eternal, this is false and erroneous. Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Untainted conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*), being free from inversion and possessing ultimate, supreme function that is all-pervasive, also receive this name.

However, among these, when the sūtra speaks of the former and not the latter, those things so named are all explained by the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. As for the "thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)...
Because that which reaches the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) is itself the nature (*svabhāva*).
What is the imagined characteristic (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena?
The commentary states: From here below, the three parts are explained separately in sequence. Regarding the first characteristic:
In the middle [of the text], there is first a question followed by an answer; this is the question:
"All phenomena are designated as having a self-nature and its distinctions, even for the purpose of giving rise to conventional discourse."

The commentary states: This is the answer. It means that all phenomena lack a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); rather, they are merely provisionally established through false conceptualization and linguistic designation as "self" or various "intrinsic natures.
For example, one speaks of a "self," or speaks of the intrinsic natures of phenomena such as "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth.

Some speak of a provisional self (*prajñapti-ātman*), while others speak of a real self (*dravya-ātman*). There are such distinctions among the dharmas of the self, such as visible form versus the invisible, and so forth.

Having thus provisionally established these distinctions of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), even down to enabling worldly sentient beings to engage in conventional discourse, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), fascicle eight, further states:
"That which is falsely grasped as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)," and so on.

Whether it be a self or a phenomenon, the imagined nature and its specific distinctions that are erroneously grasped— this nature and these distinctions taken together are termed the "imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
For a detailed explanation of the meanings of "nature" (*svabhāva*) and "distinction" (*viśeṣa*), see Vasubandhu’s and Asaṅga’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*,
fascicle four, as well as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle seventy-three, and other such texts.
"What is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) of all phenomena?
The commentary states: Below this, the second section distinguishes the dependent nature; it first poses a question and then provides an answer. This is the question.
That is to say, all phenomena have dependent origination as their intrinsic nature: because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises.
That is to say, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise, and so on, until the complete mass of suffering is brought about.
The commentary states: This is the answer. The text consists of two sections. The first provides a general definition of its essential nature:
all defilements of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and birth that arise from conditions are called "dependent" (*paratantra*) because they arise from conditions.
Generally speaking, there are two types of the dependent: first, the defiled; second, the pure. Thus, it is stated in the eighth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
It is said: both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are *paratantra* (dependent origination), because they arise in dependence upon various conditions.
When the verse says "that which is produced by conditions through conceptualization" (*vikalpa-pratyaya-ja*), it should be understood as also referring to the defiled portion of the *paratantra*.

This sutra is likewise; it speaks of the defiled and not the pure. As for the statement "because this exists," and so forth, this refers to specific instances for detailed explanation. However, regarding the first two lines... [there is] existence.
Regarding the distinctions: according to the Sarvāstivāda school, as stated in the ninth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*:
"For what reason did the Blessed One teach the first two phrases—namely, 'because this exists, that exists' and 'because this arises, that arises'?
It was for the sake of knowing with certainty the nature of dependent origination. Based on the existence of ignorance, volitional formations come to exist; they cannot exist apart from ignorance."

Regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*): furthermore, it is to demonstrate the sequential arising of the members (*aṅga*), meaning that based on the existence of this member, that member comes to exist, and from the arising of that member, another member arises.

Furthermore, it is to demonstrate the sequential arising across the three time periods (*traiyadhvika*), meaning that based on the existence of the prior limit (*pūrvānta*), the middle limit (*madhyānta*) comes to exist, and from the existence of the middle limit, the subsequent limit (*aparānta*) arises. Furthermore, it is to demonstrate the immediate [succession].

The transmission has two conditions: namely, there is ignorance (*avidyā*), and conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arise either immediately or through the power of succession.

(One interpretation states: after the limb of ignorance, the limb of volitional formations arises immediately; this is called "arising immediately. Alternatively, after ignorance has arisen, an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*) arises next, and subsequently the limb of volitional formations arises; this is called "volitional formations arising only through the power of succession.")
One interpretation states that ignorance in relation to formations is called "immediate arising," while ignorance in relation to consciousness and so forth is called "successive arising.

Other masters explain these two phrases as being intended to refute the two theories of causelessness and eternal causality (this presentation of proof and refutation is found in full in that treatise). The various masters of the tradition (*ācāryas*) explain these two phrases as follows:
This is to clarify that cause and effect are both uninterrupted and subject to arising;

that is to say, based on the non-interruption of ignorance, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are not interrupted, and precisely because ignorance arises, the formative forces are produced. This should be explained in detail for each subsequent link in the chain.
For a detailed analysis, see the twenty-fifth chapter of the *Nyāyānusāra*. According to the tenth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it asks:
What is meant by the statement, "Because this exists, that exists"? Answer: Because there is the sense that other [factors] arise due to conditions that have not yet been severed.

Question: What is meant by "Because this arises, that arises"? Answer: Because there is the sense that other [factors] arise due to impermanent conditions. According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, Chapter Four:
"Characteristics (lakṣaṇa) refer to arising through non-active conditions and arising through impermanent conditions. [This refers to] power (*śakti*).
Because it arises by way of conditions, this is the characteristic of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). By virtue of this characteristic, the Blessed One said:

"When this exists, that exists; from the arising of this, that arises. This refers to the detailed exposition beginning with "ignorance is the condition for volitional formations" (*avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*), and so forth.

The phrase "when this exists, that exists" reveals the meaning of unconditioned dependent origination: that a resultant phenomenon comes into existence solely by virtue of the existence of its condition, and not [by the action] of the condition itself.
There exists a real, causal activity capable of producing an effect. The principle that "because this arises, that arises" reveals the meaning of dependent origination through impermanent conditions;
it is not the case that a non-arising phenomenon serves as a cause, whereby even a minimal amount of produced phenomena could be established.
Regarding the statement "ignorance conditions volitional formations" (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*) and so forth, this reveals the meaning of dependent origination through functional efficacy.
Although all phenomena are devoid of agency and impermanent, it is not the case that every single phenomenon serves as a condition for the arising of every result. Why is this?
Because the specific capacities of phenomena are as described: by the power of ignorance, volitional formations arise; and so on, up to the power of birth [conditioning aging and death].
Therefore, old age and death come to be. If one were to explain this in detail, it is as stated in the fifth fascicle of the *Maitreyaparipṛcchā-śāstra*.
Regarding the phrase "the gathering of this entire mass of suffering," according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the word "entire" (*kevala*) indicates that there are only formations (*saṃskāra*).
"Without self or what belongs to a self; the phrase 'great mass of suffering' indicates that this accumulation of suffering has neither beginning nor end.
The word 'accumulation' (samudaya) is used to indicate the arising of the various aggregates of suffering. According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 24:
"Furthermore, these twelve links of dependent origination have roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, just like [a tree]."
Great Tree. Herein, the roots are ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); the trunk is consciousness (*vijñāna*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);

the branches are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); the leaves are contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*); the flowers are craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*); and the fruit is birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
This is the tree of the twelve-linked dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). It may have flowers and fruit, or it may be without flowers and without fruit. There is...
Those who possess both flower and fruit are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*). Those who possess neither flower nor fruit are arhats.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Chapter Ten: Question: Within dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), what is the sprout of suffering?

Who nurtures and protects this sprout of suffering? What is the tree of suffering? Answer: Consciousness, conditioned by ignorance and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), up to and including feeling (*vedanā*), is the sprout of suffering.
The "tooth" refers to craving, which is drawn forth by its conditions, up to and including existence (*bhava*); this is the tooth that nurtures suffering.

Birth, along with old age and death, should be known as the tree of suffering. According to the *Saṃgrahaṇī*, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is clarified in terms of eleven consciousnesses;
thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "In this context, what is the dependent characteristic? It is that which has the ālayavijñāna as its seed."

Son, regarding the various consciousnesses subsumed under false conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*), what are they? They are: the consciousness of the body, the possessor of the body, and the experiencer;

the consciousness of that which is experienced; the consciousness of that which experiences; the consciousness of time; the consciousness of number; the consciousness of location; the consciousness of verbal expression;

the consciousness of the distinction between self and other; and the consciousness of death and birth in the good and evil realms. Among these, as for the body, the possessor of the body, and the experiencer...

Consciousness: the consciousness of what is experienced, the consciousness that experiences, the consciousness of time, the consciousness of number, the consciousness of place, and the consciousness of verbal expression—these arise from seeds perfumed by names and conventions.
If it is the consciousness of the distinction between self and others, this arises from seeds perfumed by the view of self.
If it is the consciousness of death and birth in the happy or miserable realms, this arises from seeds perfumed by the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*). Thus...
Regarding the statement, "Thus it is called the *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature)," the fourth chapter of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* explains:

"The 'body' refers to the five elements, such as the eye and so forth. The 'possessor of the body' refers to the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭa-manas*). [As Asvabhāva states: the element of mind (*manodhātu*) which is the support for the five consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, is called the 'consciousness of the possessor of the body.

The 'consciousness that experiences' refers to the element of mind (*manodhātu*). [As Asvabhāva states: the element of mind which is the support for the sixth consciousness is called the 'consciousness of the experiencer. That which is 'experienced by it' refers to..."
The six external objects, such as form and so forth; that which cognizes them is the consciousness-element, namely the six consciousness-elements.

"World-consciousness" refers to the continuous, uninterrupted abiding of birth and death (An-hsiung says: world-consciousness refers to the manifestation of the three periods of time). "Numerical-consciousness" refers to the nature of calculation.

(As Vasubandhu states: "This refers to the manifestation resembling [objects] such as mountains and so forth. The *sthāna-vijñāna* (locus-consciousness) refers to the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*). (As Vasubandhu states: "This refers to the manifestation resembling villages, groves, and so forth.
The *abhilāpa-vijñāna* (discourse-consciousness) refers to the four kinds of discourse: seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.

All such consciousnesses take as their cause the specific latencies of linguistic expression (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-vāsanā*) as explained within the section on the "basis of the knowable" (*jñeya-āśraya*). The *sva-para-viśeṣa-vijñāna* (consciousness of the distinction between self and other)...

This refers to the distinctions based upon this [consciousness]. It takes as its cause the previously mentioned distinctions in the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). (As Asvabhāva states:

"Because there are distinctions such as the continuous, uninterrupted grasping of 'I' and 'mine,' 'other' and 'belonging to others,' within the consciousnesses of the body and so forth. Regarding the consciousness of the good and bad destinies of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), this refers to the various distinctions among the realms of rebirth;
it arises from the previously mentioned distinctions in the habitual tendencies of the members of dependent origination (*bhavāṅga-vāsanā*).

The seed. (As Vasubandhu’s *Bhāṣya* states: "This refers to the appearance of reflections of death and birth as devas, humans, hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts. This is explained in detail in the fourth chapter of Vasubandhu’s and Asaṅga’s commentaries.

Now, regarding the distinctions among these various consciousnesses: according to Asaṅga, the mental element (*manodhātu*) that serves as the support for the five sensory consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, is called the "consciousness of the body";
the mental element that serves as the support for the sixth mental consciousness is called the "experiencer."

"Consciousness. The commentary explains: According to the intention of the *Anabhāvavāda-śāstra*, the mental element (*manodhātu*) that serves as the support for the five consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, is precisely the *ālaya-vijñāna*;

it is called the "consciousness of the experiencer" (*vedaka-vijñāna*). The mental element that serves as the support for the sixth consciousness, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), is precisely the *manas* (the seventh consciousness);

it is called the "consciousness of the experiencer" (*vedaka-vijñāna*). If one follows Vasubandhu, this is reversed: the seventh *manas* is called the "consciousness of the experiencer," while the eighth [consciousness] is... [the consciousness of the body].
The *ālayavijñāna* is termed the "recipient consciousness" (*vedaka-vijñāna*). Thus, that treatise states: "The 'body' refers to the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭa-manas*);
the 'recipient' refers to the mind-element (*manodhātu*). Furthermore, regarding the number of these various consciousnesses, there are differences:

according to the *Liang* commentary and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, they are all said to be eleven; however, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, there are two passages: the former text lists eleven, while the latter lists ten.
The second [category] refers to the consciousness of death and birth in the good and evil destinies (*gati*). Because there are two, there is: first, the consciousness of the good and evil destinies;

and second, the consciousness of death and birth. Thus, that treatise states: "Because the maturation (*vipāka*) of karmic results is immeasurable, and because the deaths and births experienced are immeasurable.
An-hui’s commentary explains: "The good and evil destinies, as well as death and birth, are understood [as such]."
It says, "Because it is taught" and "because it is stated. Thus, one knows there are twelve [categories]. Vasubandhu did not provide an explanation, so [the count] becomes eleven;
this does not contradict reason.
What is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) of all phenomena?

The commentary states: From here below is the third section, the explanation of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Within this, there is first a question followed by an answer; this is the question.
It refers to the true suchness (*tathatā*) that is equal across all phenomena.
The commentary states: This is the answer. Within it, there are two parts: first, the actual presentation of the essence; second, the manifestation of its superior function. This is the first part.
That is to say, as previously stated, the single-flavored *tathatā* (suchness) that pervades all phenomena is taken as the essential nature.

Furthermore, regarding the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature)—whether in the context of the "middle" or the "extremes"—it itself has two types. Therefore, the second [verse] says: "This *pariniṣpanna*..."

In total, there are two kinds, distinguished by the difference between the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). The unconditioned encompasses *tathatā* (suchness) and *nirvāṇa*;
because it is devoid of transformation, it is called the "perfectly established nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). The conditioned encompasses all noble paths (*āryamārga*);
because they are non-erroneous regarding their objects, these are also called the "perfectly established nature. According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the perfectly established nature itself...
There are four kinds. Thus that treatise says: "How should the pariniṣpanna-svabhāva (perfected nature) be known? It should be known by means of the teaching of the four dharmas of purification.
First is natural purity (*prakṛti-vyavadāna*), which refers to suchness, emptiness, the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), the signless (*animitta*), and the ultimate dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Second is purity through the removal of stains (*vaimalya-vyavadāna*), which refers to this very [nature] being free from all obscurations and defilements. Third is the attainment thereof..."
The purity of the path refers to all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), the perfections (*pāramitā*), and so forth.

Fourth is the purity of the objective sphere that gives rise to this [path], which refers to the sublime and correct teachings of the Mahāyāna; it is because of these pure conditions of the Dharma-teachings that [the path arises].
It is not the nature of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because it is of the nature of the outflow from the most pure *dharmadhātu*.
It is not the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). These four dharmas collectively encompass all pure phenomena without exception. Regarding this, there are two verses:
The teaching on "illusion" and so forth concerns arising; the teaching that [things] are non-existent refers to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

If one speaks of the four purities, these are called the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*): namely, natural purity, purity through the removal of stains, the purity of the path, and the purity of the object of focus.
All phenomena that are pure are subsumed within these four characteristics.

This is explained in detail, as stated in the fifth fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Vyākhyāyukti* (Exegesis by Asvabhāva). Up to this point, this sutra has separately explained the meaning of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) with reference to three dharmas.

If one relies on the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, specifically the second chapter, "Establishing Consciousness-Only," and the eighth chapter, they explain the three natures comprehensively in relation to the meaning of the Four Noble Truths.
If one relies on the fifth fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, they explain them in relation to the three categories of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*).

To explain the three natures in general: according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, since the three natures are explained comprehensively with respect to all phenomena, the fourth fascicle of the *Wúxìng shìlùn* (*Treatise on the Non-existence of Nature*) states: "As it is also taught in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*:"
The Buddha told Maitreya: "If, regarding various objects characterized by specific aspects, one universally conceptualizes them as form,
feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, and even as all the Buddha-dharmas— relying upon names, concepts, designations,
and verbal expressions to universally conceptualize them as the intrinsic nature of all forms, and so forth, up to the intrinsic nature of all the Buddha-dharmas— this is called..."
Imagined form, up to and including all imagined Buddha-dharmas: if, regarding those objects of mental activity,
there is only the establishment of the nature of phenomena through conceptualization, and with conceptualization as a condition, various discursive proliferations arise—
concocting names, notions, and verbal designations, such that one says "this is form," up to and including saying "these are all [Buddha-dharmas]."
The Buddha-dharma. This is called the conceptualization of form, up to the conceptualization of all Buddha-dharmas.
Whether Tathāgatas appear in the world or do not appear in the world, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) remains established and the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) remains established.
Because of that form which is conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*), this conceptualized form is, at all times and for all eternity, truly [non-existent].

The nature of things (*tathatā*), the nature of being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), the nature of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), and the nature of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)—this is called the "nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*).

From form (*rūpa*) up to all the Buddha-dharmas as they are conceptually constructed by that [imagination], this discrimination of all Buddha-dharmas exists at all times, at all moments; even unto this, it is called the "nature of phenomena" of all Buddha-dharmas.
As explained at length in the sūtra:

regarding this suchness (*tathatā*), it is by virtue of the bodhisattvas’ courageous diligence as the causal condition, and their correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) and non-erroneous reflection as the causal condition, that they are able to penetrate it. Having attained this penetration, they gradually cultivate and accumulate [realization] therein.
"Up until the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, it is then that [the realization] is fully perfected.

The commentary states: This reveals its superior function; that is to say, regarding suchness, the assembly of bodhisattvas applies courageous diligence during the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) and engages in non-erroneous contemplation during the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*).
By virtue of these causes and conditions, during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-avasthā*),...

One is then able to penetrate it. Abiding in the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one gradually cultivates and accumulates [the practice] until reaching the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhābhūmi*), whereupon one realizes its perfection.
According to the seventy-third [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there are three functions: first, the function of realizing purity (*viśuddhi*).
There are two functions: the function of the two liberations and the two fetters, and the function of inducing the attainment of merit. Thus, that treatise states:
"It can even cause one to realize purity, and can cause liberation from all fetters of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) and fetters of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*)."
It also causes all meritorious qualities to be brought forth. The commentary explains: these correspond respectively to the three paths of seeing and so forth.

However, regarding the breadth or narrowness of the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of these three characteristics, various explanations differ. For now, we shall rely on the explanation of the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha, who said:

The eighth *ālaya*-consciousness is called the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). The seven consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, constitute the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

The non-arising of the dependent and the signlessness of the imagined constitute the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that all eight consciousnesses, including the eye-consciousness and so forth, are the dependent nature.

The manifested image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). That which is non-arising in the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the absence of characteristics in conceptual construction is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the seeing-aspect (*darśanabhāga*) and image-aspect of the eight consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, are termed the dependent nature;

the objects grasped through delusion are the nature of conceptual construction; and the non-arising of the dependent and the absence of characteristics in conceptual construction are the perfected nature, as explained above.

Both interpretations are logically untenable. Since the eight consciousnesses, including the visual consciousness and so forth, as well as their respective objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*), arise from conditions, why is it that only the eighth consciousness, the *ālayavijñāna*, is specifically designated as the "dependent nature" (*paratantra-svabhāva*)?
Furthermore, why are the [other] seven consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, classified as the "imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)?
It is devoid of conceptual construction, dependent on others, and unarisen; it is not different from the two natures.
How then can it be called the "perfected nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)? Such faults could not be fully enumerated. Other external doctrines are omitted for fear of prolixity.
Now, regarding the three natures as taught in the various scriptures, there are generally two approaches. The first is the approach of non-perverted defilement through grasping, namely:
The real self and real dharmas falsely grasped at do not exist at all; they are merely designated in accordance with deluded sentiments, and thus are said to exist.
All such things are termed the "thoroughly imagined" (parikalpita).
All defiled, outflowing dharmas that arise from conditions are termed the "dependent" (paratantra), because they are produced by relying on causes and depending upon conditions. All...

The conditioned uncontaminated Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) and all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are called the thoroughly established nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because both of these two types are non-erroneous.
Regarding the gate of the unchanging aspect of the dependent origination of the two types of grasped objects—namely, the falsely grasped real self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*).

Because it exists according to conceptual attachment, it is called the "imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), whether contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), are the "dependent nature" (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Because all dharmas are the equal *tathatā* (suchness) and are unchanging, it is called the "perfectly established nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Regarding these two gateways, there are differences among the various teachings; some sacred scriptures state the former and not the latter, as in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, chapter [number].
The *Catur-varga-sūtra* states: "Mahāmati, because perfect wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) are indestructible, they are called the 'perfected nature' (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The *Madhyānta-vibhāga-śāstra* also explains it in this same way. Within the sacred teachings themselves, the latter is mentioned before the former;
as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 74, says: Question: By how many [natures] is the second nature subsumed? Answer: It is subsumed by four. Question: The third...
By how many natures (*svabhāva*) is it subsumed? Answer: It is subsumed by one. There are two types according to the sacred teachings (*āgama*).

As stated in the eighth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*: "One should know that [the dependent nature] arises from conditions through discrimination; for now, this refers to the defiled portion of the dependent nature."

This is because the purified portion of the dependent nature is also the perfected nature; or alternatively, because all defiled and purified minds and mental factors are termed "discrimination" (*parikalpa*) since they are capable of cognitive apprehension.
Thus, all defiled and purified dependent natures are subsumed within this [category of] the *paratantra-svabhāva*.
The fourth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Second, the dependent nature is not established as being either defiled or pure."

(Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "Because this very *paratantra-svabhāva* becomes defiled when it is the object of conceptual construction (*parikalpa*), and becomes pure when it is free from conceptual construction; due to these two aspects, a single nature is not established. This is the intended meaning of the explanation regarding "the absence of nature" (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
It is explained in the same way here: this particular section speaks of the latter and not the former, because it speaks exclusively of *tathatā* as the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Alternatively, it may be said to speak of the former and not the latter, because it speaks exclusively of defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) as being dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*). Or, it may be understood to possess both meanings.
Because of the two previous explanations. If one were to analyze this in detail, it is as in the Chapter on the Three Natures.
"Good son, just as the affliction of visual impairment exists within the eyes of a person with cataracts, so is the parikalpita-lakṣaṇa (the imagined nature)."
One should know that it is likewise so. The commentary states:
From this point downward is the second section, which provides a further explanation by means of analogies. This section contains two parts:

first, the analogy of the three characteristics of the object-field of an eye cleared of cataracts; second, from the words "Good son" onwards, the fourfold analogy of the *sphatika* (crystal) gem. Within the former, there are three [sub-sections].

The analogy is divided into three parts: first, the analogy of the affliction of cataracts; second, the analogy of the various appearances caused by cataracts; and third, the analogy of the original object for the clear eye.
Each section contains two sub-divisions: first, the explicit explanation of the analogy; second, the application of the principle to show its correspondence with the analogy.
This is the first part, the analogy of the affliction of cataracts. The intent of this analogy is as follows: because the eye possesses cataracts, it gives rise to [false perceptions].
The consciousness and the simultaneous eye-consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna) constitute the conceptualizing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

By means of these two consciousnesses, they induce a second moment of conceptualizing mental consciousness that produces the cognition of "hairs" (*keśonduka*) and so forth. Now, these hairs are of two kinds:
first, those real hairs and so forth imagined by the conceptualizing mental consciousness; it is precisely this [latter] that is said to be the fault of the visual impairment (*timira*). Because...
This "defect" (ādīnava) serves as a metaphor for the nature of the imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva).

Second, that which is the support and basis for that very conceptualizing mental consciousness—the appearance resembling a mass of floating hairs—is said to be the various signs of the visual impairment (timira); this serves as a metaphor for the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), as will be explained later.
Since this uses the defect as a metaphor for the nature of the imagined, one should know that the term "thoroughly imagined and grasped" (parikalpita) is applied in the same manner.
Alternatively, it may be that the impairment of the visual faculty (*timira*) itself is what is referred to as the "defect.

This means that because of the grasping [at the unreal], the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) arises; it appears like the perception of floating hairs and so forth due to an impairment such as cataracts.
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (73) states: "If the eye has a defect such as an impairment, there appear [unreal objects] such as floating hairs and the like."

The appearance of the cataract can be perceived when it is present; if that affliction were absent, it could not be perceived. There is only the intrinsic nature, free from erroneous grasping. Question:

How is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) illustrated by the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva)? Answer: Because the pure form is used as an illustration for the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), there is no fault.
Question: Does the eye-consciousness of one with cataracts see hair-tufts? Explanation: According to the various [masters] of the West...
The Master has two interpretations. First is the school of Sthiramati: the five eyes, such as the fleshly eye and so forth, also take objects such as floating hairs or a second moon.
Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "One with the disease of kāmalā damages the visual faculty and sees blue as yellow.

The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla asserts that the consciousnesses of the eye and other senses arise taking real objects as their conditions, because they are direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is the position of the teacher Ghoṣaka.
In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Record of the Twelve [Chapters] on Consciousness-Only) based on the Sanskrit original, there are two explanations. One states:
"The five consciousnesses perceive only real objects. Therefore, the *Abhidharmasūtra* says: 'There are no visual or other consciousnesses that arise without perceiving real objects.'"

There are three types of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*): those that take real objects as their conditions and those that take unreal objects as their conditions. Therefore, it is known that the five consciousnesses take only real objects as their conditions.
One school asserts that the five consciousnesses also take unreal objects as their conditions; thus, a sutra states:

"By means of a distracted eye-faculty and eye-consciousness, a distracted mental consciousness is induced to arise; by means of an undistracted eye and eye-consciousness, an undistracted mental consciousness is induced. From this, it is known that the five...
The consciousness perceives a second moon, flowers in the sky, and so forth. The faults and defects mentioned herein follow from the three previous explanations;
they may be understood by analogy.
It is like a person with cataracts perceiving various manifestations of those cataracts—such as tufts of hair, circles, bees, flies, or mustard seeds—or again, blue and yellow.
The various characteristics such as red and white appear distinctly; one should know that the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) is likewise. The commentary states:
The second set of analogies concerning cataracts illustrates the dependent nature; one should know it is likewise.

That is to say, for a person with cataracts, the appearance of a mass of hairs is not real, yet it appears as if real; therefore, it serves as an analogy for the dependent nature. That which does not exist appears as if it exists. One should know [it is thus].
Knowledge is also like this.
Just as a person with clear vision is free from the affliction of cataracts in the eye, so too should one understand that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)—
the object of the natural range of that same clear vision— is likewise free from confusion.
The commentary states: The third analogy concerns the original object of the pure eye.
That is to say, the original objects of the range of that pure eye—such as colors like blue and yellow—are pure by nature and free from defects such as the optical illusion of floating hairs.
One should know that the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) is likewise so: it is pure by nature and lacks the nature of grasping within the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
"Good son, it is like a pure crystal gem: if it comes into contact with a blue dye, it appears like an indranīla or mahānīla mani-jewel.
Because sentient beings falsely grasp it as being an indranīla or mahānīla mani-jewel, they are deluded."

The commentary states: What follows is the second section, the analogy of the four colors of the *sphatika* (crystal) jewel. This consists of two parts: first, the detailed explanation of the four analogies;

second, from the passage beginning "Thus, the root of virtue... onwards, the presentation of the Dharma as being analogous to the metaphors. Within the first part, the four analogies are divided into four sections.
This is the first, the analogy corresponding to the blue color. The text contains five segments, which encompass four types of meaning.
The "intention" (the underlying meaning) illustrates the three natures. The "text" consists of five sections: 1. "Pure crystal" refers to the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature). 2.

"If it comes into contact with blue dye" is a metaphor for the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of verbal expression; this clarifies that the *paratantra-svabhāva* is conjoined with the habitual tendencies of verbal expression.
3. "That which appears as sapphire, great-blue, and so forth" is a metaphor for the *paratantra-svabhāva*, [arising] due to the self...
1. By the power of the seeds of linguistic conventions for the conceptual differentiation of phenomena, although they reside within internal consciousness, they appear as if external. 4.
"By means of erroneous grasping, such as [the perception of] sapphire and so forth" is a metaphor for how, due to false attachment, one clings to things as being substantially existent. 5.
"Deluding sentient beings" is a metaphor for how a false teacher, taking what he himself has clung to, deludes sentient beings and causes them to give rise to [the notion of] substantial existence.

Explanation: Regarding the statement that "the meaning contains four," according to the corresponding text below, there are four elements within the analogy. First, the *sphatika* (crystal) represents the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
Second, its being joined with the dye of blue represents the fusion of the perfuming of linguistic designations (*nāma-vikalpa-vāsanā*) with the dependent nature.

Third, the adherence to the three types of *yāya* (error) and so forth serves as a metaphor for that which is grasped. Fourth, the fact that those very objects of grasping exist conventionally but lack ultimate reality serves as a metaphor for the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).
Regarding the meaning of these three: they refer to the application of blue dye, up to and including the deluding of sentient beings.
The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is illustrated by the analogy of a crystal gem; the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is illustrated by the analogy of a crystal gem;

and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is illustrated by the analogy of a genuine indranīla sapphire. One should understand that all three lower analogies encompass these various meanings.

For example, regarding "a pure crystal gem," this refers to the substance of the gem itself; since it has no name in this [Chinese] context, it is not translated. One should follow the phonetic transcription of the term from the sutra.
It is called "water-jade" (shuiyu) here, or sometimes "white pearl. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* refers to it as "pure vaidūrya," which is due to a different translation convention.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, is composed of four jewels:
namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), and crystal (*sphaṭika*). This crystal corresponds here to the red color. Furthermore, that same text speaks of the solar disc.
The crystal jewels (*sphaṭika*) below are composed of fire-gems (*tejo-maṇi*); the crystal jewels below the lunar disk are composed of water-gems (*vāri-maṇi*).
According to these passages, those crystal jewels likewise possess all colors. Now, in this sūtra...
Furthermore, white is mentioned as a contrast to the four colors; for this reason, white is not discussed in the subsequent text.
If it is dyed blue, its color is seen to undergo transformation: that is, when crystal (*sphaṭika*) comes into contact with blue, it resembles a *indranīla* or *mahānīla* mani-jewel.
Regarding "Indranīla" and so forth, these refer to the blue of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the mahānīla. Maṇi... [text ends]
“Nirbhāsa” (appearance) here refers to the *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem); that is to say, it refers to *sphatika* (crystal), which is called “wish-fulfilling.
Alternatively, it may refer to gems such as *indranīla* (sapphire) and the like, which are indeed *maṇi*.

Regarding the phrase “due to false attachment,” this reveals how worldly people grasp at what is merely similar [to reality] as being real, and proclaim this to others, thereby deluding sentient beings. The intended meaning is as follows: the *ālayavijñāna*.
Due to the power of the habitual tendencies of grasping at a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-abhiniveśa-vāsanā*), [the ālayavijñāna] manifests as if it were a self and phenomena.
Sentient beings grasp this as a real self, thereby deluding themselves. In reality, there is no actual blue color or the like upon a crystal;
one should know that the absence of the nature of what is grasped upon the ālayavijñāna is likewise so. This shall be analyzed later.
If it is combined with red dye, then by means of an image of a *musāragalva* mani-jewel,
and because of grasping that *musāragalva* mani-jewel as being [a real] *musāragalva*, sentient beings are deluded.
The commentary states: This is the second analogy concerning the correspondence with the color red. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* says:
"If it is placed amidst red [objects], then a red *padma* mani-jewel emits its radiance and appears before one."
If it is combined with green dye, it resembles a mārakata mani jewel;
because sentient beings mistakenly perceive it as a mārakata mani jewel, they are deluded.
The commentary states: The third is the analogy of the green-colored [jewel], the *mala-keta*.
Since it has no name in this [language], it is not translated. Some say that this means "the jewel that destroys color," because by means of this jewel, all colors are destroyed and ruined.
According to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, however, it simply says "green."
"If it is combined with a yellow dye, it resembles a golden image; because of the false apprehension that it is a genuine golden image, it deludes sentient beings.
The commentary states: Regarding the fourth analogy of correspondence with the color yellow, the difference from the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* is as follows: this [text] says...
The golden image: he says it is a jewel of golden *maṇi*. The latter three metaphors may be understood by analogy with the first.
In this way, the root of virtue is like the coloring applied to a pure crystal;
one should know that the linguistic habituation (*vāsanā*) of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is likewise so.
The commentary states: From here below is the second section, which cites the dharma and its analogy and combines them with the four preceding meanings, dividing them into four parts:
first, combining the seed; second, combining the grasping at characteristics; third, combining the dependent nature; and fourth, combining the perfected nature. These are the four meanings.
In the preceding analogy, although there are five textual elements, there are four meanings; thus, the four meanings are combined with the preceding analogical text.
This is the first [point]. Now, regarding these four meanings, there are two interpretations. One says: the first is the grasping of conditions (*ālambana*).

The next three correspond respectively to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). One interpretation states that the first two illustrate the nature of the grasped (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because white seeds and manifest grasping constitute the grasped;
this refers to the first [analogy]. That is to say, it concerns the meaning of the application of colored dyes upon a crystal.
Just as an image resembling blue appears upon the crystal, so too does [an image] appear upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Because the seeds of false attachment serve as the causal condition, there appear upon the ālayavijñāna images of form, sound, and so forth that are dependent in nature,
just as [images of] indranīla, mahānīla, musāragalva, and marakata appear upon a pure crystal.
The grasping at [gold] and so forth; one should know that the grasping at the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is likewise.
The commentary states: This is the second section, which synthesizes the grasping of active manifestation.

That is to say, by virtue of the seeds of grasping as previously described, the dependent nature produces appearances resembling form and so forth; through the grasping of active manifestation, one clings to those [appearances] as being real. It is for this reason [that the two are combined].
The meaning of these two preceding sections is to clarify that among the three natures, it is the thoroughly imagined nature [that is being discussed].
One should know that the dependent nature is likewise like that pure crystal gem.
The commentary states: The third [aspect] corresponds to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

This means that just as a crystal appears as if it were blue and so forth, so too the dependent nature, by virtue of its seeds, manifests in various forms resembling color, sound, and other such phenomena.
Just as the appearances of sapphire, great-blue gem, amber, musāragalva,
and refined gold upon that pure crystal are at all times and for all eternity without reality and without intrinsic nature.

The commentary states: The fourth [point] corresponds to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Within this, there are two parts: first, the repetition of the previous analogy; second, the explanation that the phenomena correspond to the analogy.

This is the first part. Upon the crystal (*sphaṭika*), there is no actual blue and so forth; this is called "the absence of reality" (*avastukatva*) and is also called "the nature of being without intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Alternatively, "the absence of reality" may be understood as negating the reality of the blue and so forth. It does not exist.
Regarding the nature of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvatva*): although there is no reality such as blue and so forth, there is the nature of crystal.
That is to say, upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), by means of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*), at all times and for all eternity.
There is no reality; the nature of being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) and the perfected character (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*) should be understood in the same way.
The commentary states: This is the second explanation of the analogy for the dharma. Upon the dependent nature (*paratantra*), there is no such thing as the grasped reality of a self and so forth;
this very absence is called the nature of being without intrinsic nature. Alternatively, it may mean that upon the dependent nature, there is no...
Regarding the statement that "the entities grasped as real possess the nature of being without intrinsic nature at all times and for all eternity," there are two interpretations.
One says: the word "always" (*nitya*) is used because they are absent in each preceding moment, and [the word "eternally"] is used because they are absent in each succeeding moment.

Regarding the repeated use of the terms "constant" (*nitya*) and "eternal" (*śāśvata*): one explanation states that "always existing" (*sadā asti*) is said to reveal the absence of true reality, while "at all times" (*sarvakālam*) is said because of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Question: How are these three natures (*trisvabhāva*) subsumed within the seven aspects of suchness (*saptavidhatathatā*)?
Answer: As stated in the eighth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it says: "In this way, these three natures [are related] to the seven aspects of suchness..."

How are they subsumed? Regarding the seven kinds of *tathatā* (suchness): first is the *tathatā* of transmigration, which refers to the true nature of the transmigration of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

[There are two types of "conditioned": first, that which is produced by the four characteristics; second, that which is produced by afflictions (*kleśa*). This refers to the latter. Second is the *tathatā* of the real mark, which refers to the true nature manifested by the two forms of selflessness (*anātman*).
Third is the *tathatā* of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*), which refers to the defiled and the pure.

The reality of phenomena is the true nature of consciousness. (The present wisdom of the contemplation of consciousness-only, which takes as its object the defiled and pure aspects of the perceived and the perceiver, is itself suchness. Fourth is the established suchness.
That is to say: (1) the suchness of the reality of suffering; (2) the suchness of the reality of the five types of wrong practice, which refers to the reality of origination;

(3) the suchness of purity, which refers to the reality of cessation; and (4) the suchness of right practice, which refers to the reality of the path. These seven realities of nature are subsumed under the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (the perfected nature), because they are the objects of both fundamental and subsequently attained wisdom (*mūla-jñāna* and *pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
As for their inclusion according to their characteristics: the three [realities] of flow, transformation, suffering, and origination are the former [the *paratantra-svabhāva*].

Two natures are subsumed [under the dependent nature] because they consist of false attachments and defilements. The remaining four are all subsumed under the perfected nature. The second fascicle of the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states:

"The reality of differentiation consists briefly of seven kinds: namely, the reality of cyclic existence (*pravṛtti*), the reality of true characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the reality of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), the reality of establishment (*vyavasthāna*), the reality of wrong practice (*mithyāpratipatti*), the reality of purification (*viśuddhi*), and the reality of right practice (*samyakpratipatti*). How should these seven realities be understood? They are based upon three [natures]."
Is this established as the fundamental reality? The verse says: "Cyclic existence and its establishment, and erroneous practice depend on the first two;

the true nature, consciousness-only, and purity depend on the latter one. (This is from) the third fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and the seventy-seventh [fascicle] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
This should be understood accordingly; it does not contradict the principle. Subsequently, he again asks how the three natures and the five categories are mutually inclusive.

The various sacred teachings state that their mutual inclusion is not fixed. First, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (74) states that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) includes the characteristics (*nimitta*), names (*nāman*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*).
The perfected and real nature (*pariniṣpanna-tathatā-svabhāva*) includes suchness (*tathatā*). As for the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)...

The "Grasping" [section] does not include five matters. It states that the contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), which manifest as if they were the signified (*lakṣya*), are called "characteristics" (*nimitta*).
That which manifests as if it were the signifier (*lakṣaṇa*) is designated as "name" (*nāman*). The transforming mind and so forth are established as "discrimination" (*vikalpa*).

Because uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds and so forth are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), they are collectively termed simply "correct knowledge" (*samyag-jñāna*), which does not speak of the signifier or the signified. These four [arise] from...

All that is dependently originated is subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). This is explained in the second fascicle of the *Madhyāntavibhāga*. The dependent nature comprises both the "aspects" (*nimitta*) and the "discrimination" (*vikalpa*);

the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) comprises only their names (*nāman*). Correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) are subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

That [text] explains that the "aspect-portion" (*nimittabhāga*) of contaminated minds and mental factors is called "aspects," while the remaining names are called "discrimination. The imagined nature is comprised of these.

Because that which is grasped has no substance whatsoever, it is conventionally designated as "name" in order to manifest its non-existence. Second, because it is non-erroneous, it is subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Third, according to the seventh fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) subsumes only conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) comprises those signs (*nimitta*) and names (*nāman*); correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) comprise the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

That which consists of the objective and subjective aspects (*grāhya-grāhaka-bhāga*) of contaminated minds and mental factors is collectively termed "discrimination" (*vikalpa*), because its intrinsic nature is false discrimination.
The signified and the signifier of the imagined nature are established as the two entities—name and sign—in accordance with conventional usage. (4)

According to the fourth fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, "name" (nāman) belongs to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), while "referent" (artha) belongs to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Those contaminated mental states and mental factors, such as the aspects of the object (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subject (*darśana-bhāga*), become the objects of universal conceptualization through the power of names;
therefore, they are called "names. The imagined nature is a horizontal construction that follows names, yet its essence is not real.

There is. This is a designation established by way of conventional meaning. As explained in the four preceding teachings regarding the inclusion of the five categories (*pañcavastu*) within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), although the phrasing differs, there is no contradiction in their meaning.
The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla takes the first [explanation] as superior because it is not confused.
Furthermore, a question is asked: "In various sacred teachings, five characteristics (*pañcalakṣaṇa*) are taught; how do these correspond with the inclusion within the three natures?"

The expressed (the signified) and the expresser (the signifier) each possess the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). That is to say: that which is falsely conceptualized belongs to the first nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

The characteristics (*nimitta*), names (*nāman*), and conceptualizations (*vikalpa*)—as appropriate—are, as the expressed and the expresser, included within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

True suchness (*tathatā*) and correct gnosis (*samyagjñāna*)—as appropriate—are, as the expressed and the expresser, included within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). This is because subsequently attained gnosis transforms and appears as the aspect of the expresser. Second.

The characteristic of mutual connection (*saṃbandha-lakṣaṇa*) is subsumed solely within the first nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because the false attachment to objects and names is necessarily connected.

That characteristic of attachment (*abhiniveśa-lakṣaṇa*) is solely the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is false conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*).

The characteristic of non-attachment (*anabhiniveśa-lakṣaṇa*) is solely the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because its intrinsic nature consists of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and so forth. According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (81), two natures are that which is expressed (*lakṣya*).
The nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is the signifier (*vācaka*). [Treatise on Manifestation, Chapter 16, Verse 74].
Both signifier and signified (*vācya*) pervade all three natures. A detailed analysis is fully set forth in the commentary on the eighth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Furthermore, Guṇamati, because the association of characteristics (*nimitta*) and names (*nāman*) serves as a condition, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) can be cognized.
The commentary states: From this point downward is the second section, which, based on the perspective of the contemplator, clarifies the skillful bodhisattva. Within this, there are two parts.
First, there is an extensive explanation in prose; subsequently, it is briefly stated in verse. Within the former [prose section], there are two parts:

first, a brief discernment of the three characteristics to exhort beings to understand them; second, based on those three characteristics, the correct manifestation of the gate of contemplation. Furthermore, this explanation is divided into two sections.

The first part correctly elucidates the gates of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*). The second part, beginning with "Thus, the root of virtue... and so forth, reiterates the preceding contemplation to answer the previous question. Within the first part, there are three sections:

first, it clarifies that the Bodhisattva thoroughly understands the three natures (*trisvabhāva*); second, from "Good son" onwards, it shows that by knowing the three natures, one thoroughly understands the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*);
third, from "Good son" onwards, it shows that by knowing the three characteristics, one severs defilement and realizes purity.
Although there are two sections, we shall follow the latter explanation for now. This constitutes the first [section]: the thorough knowledge of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Because the three natures are distinct, they are divided into three parts; this is the first. That is to say, because the signified characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the signifying name (*nāman*) are mutually connected as conditions, the falsely grasped characteristic—the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)—can be thoroughly known. Therefore...
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 73, states: "What should be known as the object-condition for the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)? Answer:
It should be known that it conditions the association between signs (*nimitta*) and names (*nāman*). For a detailed analysis, one should consult the *Tri-svabhāva-nirdeśa*. Its first chapter says:
Regarding the nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*): it has no essential substance or characteristic, because it is not subsumed within the five factors, such as names and so forth.

An opponent asks: "If there is no substance, how can there be conceptualization? The answer is: "Because there is only the object [of the concept]. Why is this? It is like how, in the world, names are established for objects;
ordinary people (*bāla*) cling to these names and conceptualize the nature of the object, asserting that the name is itself the nature of the object. This is an error.

This is an inversion. It consists merely of the conceptual differentiation of names, for there is no substantial reality. Why is this so? Because these names and their referents are mutually adventitious.
How is this known? It can be understood through three points: first, the non-arising of cognition prior to the name;
second, the fallacy of contradiction regarding multiple entities; and third, the error of contradiction regarding a mixed entity. This is explained in detail in that treatise, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, this is identical to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Taking the grasping at the characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*) upon the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*) as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), the characteristics of the dependent nature can be fully understood.
The commentary states: This explanation concerns the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

It means that because one grasps the imagined characteristics (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*) through conceptualization as being the causal condition, the dependent nature arises. Thus, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, chapter sixteen, says:

"Because of clinging to the first nature within the dependent nature, the wisdom of perfuming (*vāsanā-jñāna*) arises, whereby defilement (*saṃkleśa*) is established. It further says: "In regard to..."
Because it is the grasping that arises from the characteristics of what is grasped, it should be understood as the *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature).
Because that which is capable of grasping arises from conditions, the second volume of the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* states: Question:

By virtue of what cause is the *paratantra-svabhāva* established? Answer: It is manifested by virtue of the condition of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the imagined nature). Question: The *paratantra*...
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) arises as both defiled and pure.

How is it that it can be understood solely by taking the grasping at the characteristics of what is clung to (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa-grāha*) as its condition? This difficulty is resolved as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 74.
Thus, it says: "Question: If the dependent nature is also subsumed within correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*), for what reason was it previously..."
It is said that one should understand that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) takes the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as its object through grasping. The answer is:
that intention refers only to the defiled portion (*saṃkleśa-bhāga*) of the dependent nature, not its purified portion (*vyavadāna-bhāga*).
As for the purified portion, it should be understood that one should know there is no grasping when taking it as an object; this is what should be understood.
Because one takes as a condition the non-apprehension of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) can be understood.
The commentary explains that this clarifies the perfected nature by means of the absence of the imagined nature within the dependent nature.
It is real; therefore, it is said to be "without grasping. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 73, states:
"One should know that [the object] which has the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as its objective condition is ultimately unreal within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Alternatively, "without grasping" may refer to the noble path itself; because one does not grasp, it is called "without grasping. This meaning explains that it is the path of non-grasping.
Because it serves as the cause, one realizes the pure *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Bhagavān, in another sutra you said:
'One should know that this nature is to be understood by taking non-attachment to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* as the object-condition.'"
This is explained according to the attainment of purity, not according to characteristics. The commentary states: "Other sūtras" refers to this very sūtra.
"According to the attainment of purity" means that based on the internal realization of the noble path of suchness, the realized principle is manifested;
or, by the power of the noble path, one severs defilement and realizes pure suchness, thereby manifesting the realized principle based on the realizing path.

Regarding "not explained by way of characteristics": this passage does not rely on the elimination of the imagined characteristic (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*) to reveal the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

If one relies on the previous explanation, the phrase "other sūtras" refers to those remaining sūtras. Some say that "without grasping" (*nirgrāha*) means there is no grasper (*grāhaka*)—namely, the dependent nature (*paratantra*)—nor the grasped, which is the conceptualized nature (*parikalpita*);
therefore, it is called "without grasping. Thus, the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* asks: "What is reality?"
Question: By what cause is this nature established? Answer: It is manifested because the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is utterly non-existent when analyzed.
Explanation: This is an error by the translators, for to negate the dependent nature contradicts the Yogācāra school’s own tenets.
"Good son, if bodhisattvas can, with respect to the dependent nature (paratantra-lakṣaṇa) of all phenomena,
truly understand the imagined nature (parikalpita-lakṣaṇa), they will then be able to truly understand all phenomena as being without characteristics (animitta)."

The commentary states: This is the second [section] below, which, by knowing the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), brings about the thorough knowledge of the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*). Since these three characteristics are distinct, they are divided into three parts.
This is the first: by knowing what is grasped (*parikalpita*), one thoroughly knows the absence of characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*).

That is to say, as previously stated, because the characteristics and names are associated and serve as conditions, one knows the reality and thoroughly knows that the names and characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*) are merely conventional designations.
One establishes that there is no real intrinsic nature; by means of this, one is then able to understand, as they truly are, all phenomena grasped through conceptualization as being signless.
If bodhisattvas understand the dependent nature as it truly is, they are then able to understand everything as it truly is.
Regarding the "phenomena characterized by affliction" (*saṃkleśalakṣaṇadharma*):
the commentary states that this is the second [point]. Because one realizes the dependent nature (*paratantra*), one knows the characteristics of affliction;

that is, one is able to realize that all [phenomena] arising from the grasping of signs are dependent, and thus one is able to realize that affliction itself is dependently originated (*paratantra*). The former was...
The former is general observation; the latter is specific observation. The two preceding aspects should be understood according to this principle. Furthermore, it is said:

the first distinguishes the observation of the dependent nature by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); the latter distinguishes the observation of the dependent nature by way of its particularity (*viśeṣa*). It is further said: the former relies on the nature of "exhaustive extent" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*);
the latter is the nature of "suchness" (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
If bodhisattvas understand the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) as it truly is, they are then able to understand all phenomena characterized by purity as they truly are.
The commentary states:
this is the third [stage], understanding the perfected nature and knowing the characteristics of purity; that is to say, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Because there is no grasping as a condition, one is able to understand that all pure phenomena are the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Son of good family, if bodhisattvas can, upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), know as it truly is the phenomenon that is signless (*animitta-dharma*),
they will then be able to sever and extinguish phenomena characterized by affliction (*saṃkleśa-lakṣaṇa*).
The commentary states: This is the third section below, concerning the knowledge of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), through which one abandons defilement and realizes purity.
Within this, there are two parts: first, realizing the signless (*animitta*) to abandon defiled phenomena; second, by abandoning defilement, one attains purity. This is the first part.

Now, regarding the signless nature (*animittadharma*), there are three interpretations. One says: it is the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*), so called in accordance with conventional sentiment.
It exists; yet according to principle, it is non-existent. Because its characteristics are eternally absent, it is called "signless" (*animitta*). Thus, the *Madhyāntavibhāga* states:
"The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is fundamentally without these characteristics; therefore, it is called signless.

According to this interpretation, because one is able to realize the signless dharma, the defiled characteristics of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) cannot arise; therefore, it is said to be able to sever [them].
Regarding phenomena characterized by affliction (*saṃkleśa-lakṣaṇa-dharma*): if there were no grasping, phenomena characterized by affliction could not arise.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 74, states: Question: How many functions can the nature of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) perform?
Answer: Five. First, it can produce the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Second, it can give rise to verbal expression regarding that very nature. Third, it can produce... [text continues]
