1) Grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*); 2) the four [graspings] that can give rise to grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*); 3) the capacity to appropriate the latencies (*vāsanā*) and heaviness (*dausthulya*) of those two types of grasping.

One explanation states: because the suchness (*tathatā*) manifested by the absence of grasping upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is free from all characteristics, it is called "signless" (*animitta*).
Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says: "Suchness is eternally free from all characteristics, such as form (*rūpa*), and so forth."

Therefore, it is called "signless" (*animitta*). Furthermore, the *Śataśāstra* states: "The principle of emptiness of true suchness (*tathatā*) is free from all dharmic characteristics, such as existence and non-existence;
therefore, it is called signless. According to this interpretation, it means that one is able to thoroughly understand the dharma of signlessness.
One can immediately sever and extinguish the phenomena characterized by defilement within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
One interpretation states that both the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) are termed "signless" (*animitta*) for two reasons.

According to this explanation, because one is able to realize the signless nature of the imagined, one is thereby able to penetrate the signless dharma of the perfected nature. Through this realization...

Because one enters into the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), one is able to sever and extinguish the phenomena characterized by defilement within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 74, states: Question: When a practitioner of contemplation realizes the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as it truly is, into which nature should it be said that they have entered? Answer: The perfected nature. Question: If a practitioner...
When one enters into the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), what kind of nature should be said to be eliminated? Answer:
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
If one can sever and extinguish phenomena characterized by affliction (*saṃkleśa-lakṣaṇa*), one will then be able to realize phenomena characterized by purity (*vyavadāna-lakṣaṇa*).
The commentary states: This refers to the second [aspect], the abandonment of defilement (*saṃkleśa*), by which one realizes *nirvāṇa*.
That is to say, through the cessation of defiled phenomena, one is able to realize the pure *nirvāṇa*. Question: Upon what stage (*avasthā*) are these three aspects of contemplation based?

If they pertain to the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), how can one abandon the phenomena characterized by defilement? It requires the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) alone to be capable of such abandonment.
Because they have been severed. If one is on the ground [of the path], at the time of entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), one realizes the principle of the two kinds of emptiness;
how then could one previously give rise to the contemplation of the two natures? The explanation says: this contemplation of the three natures is divided into two stages.

The first two, the contemplations of the *parikalpita* (imagined) and *paratantra* (dependent) natures, rely on the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*) to perform the four investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*) and the four types of knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*). The third, the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) nature, resides in the ten stages. This is so.
Therefore, in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, Asaṅga establishes the contemplation of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) to explain the intent of this sūtra. In its sixth fascicle, the treatise states:
"In this way, the bodhisattva enters into the appearance of objects as mental verbalization; thus, he enters into the nature of the imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Because he enters into representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), he enters into the nature of the dependent (*paratantra-svabhāva*). How does he enter into the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)?"

Regarding the true nature (*tattva*): when the conceptualization of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra*), which is of the same category as the mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) and the permeation of hearing the Dharma (*dharma-śruta-vāsanā*), has already been eliminated, at that time the Bodhisattva has discarded the conceptualization of objects (*artha-saṃjñā*).
Since no semblance of an object can arise, a semblance of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) also cannot occur.
By this cause and condition, one abides in the designation "non-conceptual regarding all objects. (As for "non-conceptual designation," it is that which is able to...)

The names that express the truth of ultimate equality are called "names of non-conceptualization" because they are established based on the ultimate reality (*tathatā*) they express—the principle that is free from conceptual differentiation regarding all objects. Since these names are established according to what they express, they are termed "non-conceptual names.

Furthermore, since this expressed ultimate reality is designated by means of its expression, it is likewise called "non-conceptual. Within the *dharmadhātu*, one then attains direct vision and abides in correspondence with it.

At that time, the Bodhisattva’s non-conceptual wisdom—characterized by the absolute equality of the object of cognition (*ālambana*) and the subject of cognition (*ālambaka*)—has already arisen. By means of this...
This bodhisattva is said to have already awakened to and entered the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).
According to this very text, the contemplation of the perfected nature exists only on the [supramundane] stages (*bhūmi*). Therefore, the ninth verse of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"When, with respect to the object of cognition, wisdom finds nothing at all to be apprehended, at that time one abides in consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), because of being free from the characteristics of the two graspings."
Thus, Guṇamati, because bodhisattvas understand, as they truly are, the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),

and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), they understand, as they truly are, all phenomena that are signless, as well as phenomena characterized by affliction and phenomena characterized by purification.
The commentary states: From here below is the second section, which restates the gates of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*) to answer two questions.

This section contains two parts: first, the restatement of the gates of contemplation; second, from this point onward, the actual answers to the two questions. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections:

first, restating that because one knows the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), one thoroughly understands the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*); second, restating that because one knows the three characteristics, one immediately severs defilement and realizes purity.
This is the first [point]. Having cited the aforementioned knowledge of the three natures, one thoroughly understands the three characteristics; this may be understood by analogy with what precedes.
Because one knows the characteristicless phenomena (*animitta-dharma*) as they truly are, one eliminates all phenomena characterized by affliction (*saṃkleśa-lakṣaṇa*).
Because one eliminates all phenomena characterized by affliction, one realizes all phenomena characterized by purification (*vyavadāna-lakṣaṇa*).
The commentary states: From here on is the second section, which restates the preceding point that because one knows the three natures, one abandons defilement and realizes purity.

This means that by understanding the meaning of the signlessness of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), one gradually and successively realizes the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Through this, one attains pure nirvāṇa. Furthermore, it is explained that this is because one understands the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the signlessness of the thoroughly imagined nature.
One is able to sever all defilements and realize the fruit of nirvāṇa.

Up to this point, one is called a bodhisattva skilled in the characteristics of all phenomena. It is up to this point that the Tathāgata designates one as a bodhisattva skilled in the characteristics of all phenomena.
The commentary states: This is the second [section], which answers two questions by means of the aforementioned method of contemplation.
That is to say, the Buddha, based on his superior understanding of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) for the assembly of bodhisattvas, designates them as "skillful bodhisattvas.
The Tathāgata, relying upon these skillful bodhisattvas, establishes the sacred teachings and names them "skillful bodhisattvas. Now, regarding these bodhisattvas' skill...
Regarding the skillful demarcation [of the stages], various explanations differ. One says that from the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) upward, all are termed "skillful.

Another says that within the ten levels of transference (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), the tenth transference is called the "path of preparation" (*prayoga-mārga*), because it is based on that stage that one gives rise to the four investigations and the knowledge of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
Yet another says that from the first [stage] upward, one realizes the purity of both the ultimate nature (*tathatā*) and conventional characteristics.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse, saying:
[The commentary states: From here on is the second section, which briefly explains the meaning through verses. Within this, there are two parts; first, the introductory verses.
The verse is subsequently cited as a brief summary; this is its first [line].
"If one does not understand phenomena that are signless (*animitta*), one cannot comprehend phenomena characterized by affliction (*saṃkleśa*).

Because one does not sever phenomena characterized by affliction, one destroys the realization of phenomena characterized by subtle purity. Failing to contemplate the manifold faults of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), one is harmed by the fault of negligence (*pramāda*)."
"Sentient beings, through indolence, abide amidst both stable and fluctuating phenomena; they suffer ruin and destruction and are thus to be pitied. The commentary states:

This is the second [verse], which provides a brief explanation in verse. The preceding prose section has provided a direct explanation for understanding the virtues of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*);
this verse, conversely, reveals the loss resulting from failing to understand the signless (*animitta*). How can this be said to provide a reverse and direct explanation?

In reality, both the prose and the verses contain both the direct (anuloma) and the inverse (pratiloma) sequences. However, for the sake of brevity, each is presented according to one side, with the other being implied through ellipsis.
As for the claim that, according to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, both the verses and the prose provide only direct explanations, this is due to the particularity of the translators.
There are two verses, which are divided into two parts. The first verse correctly explains the failure to realize the signless (*animitta*).
The latter verse reiterates the explanation of the failure regarding the non-contemplation of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). Within the former [verse], there are two sections.

First, the initial two lines cite the lack of realization to reveal the failure of not severing affliction (*saṃkleśa*). Second, the final two lines, based on the non-severance of affliction, reveal...
The failure to realize the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) constitutes a loss. "Destruction" (*vipraṇāśa*) means to lose or ruin;
it refers to the loss and ruin of the attainment of the pure characteristics of subtle *tathatā* because one does not sever defilements. This "loss" signifies the inability to realize [the goal].

Regarding the commentary on the latter verses, there are two distinct parts: the first two lines clarify the loss resulting from negligence (*pramāda*), while the latter two lines clarify that resulting from laziness (*kausīdya*).

"Loss. Regarding the statement "not observing the various faults of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and so forth," this means that due to ignorance, one is unable to observe the faults of conditioned phenomena;
consequently, heedlessness arises, which harms sentient beings.
Regarding the statement "indolence abiding amidst stable and unstable phenomena," this clarifies the second fault of indolence: namely, that indolence is the cause of all faults.

This is an obstacle to merit. Regarding "abiding phenomena" (*sthita-dharma*): this refers to *nirvāṇa*, which is eternally abiding and imperishable; therefore, it is called "abiding. Regarding "moving phenomena" (*cala-dharma*):

these are the phenomena of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), which arise before and perish after, circulating through the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*); therefore, they are called "moving phenomena.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that "abiding phenomena" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while "moving phenomena" refers to distraction (*vikṣepa*). It is said that there is no loss [in either case].
"Ruined and pitiable" means that due to indolence, they lack the qualities of stability and possess the qualities of instability;
because of this lack, they undergo ruin. Because they are ruined, they are deeply pitiable. This is the detailed explanation of ruin.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicles 36 and 73 (the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* says: "To know all phenomena as they truly are is to abandon the characteristics of defiled phenomena;

having abandoned the characteristics of defiled phenomena, one realizes pure phenomena. Without observing the faults of the conditioned, and being unharmed by indolence or negligence, the dharmas are eternally immovable; one who is free from such characteristics is called a Bodhisattva").

Regarding the fifth chapter of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, "The Chapter on the Characteristics of the Lack of Intrinsic Nature" (*Niḥsvabhāva-lakṣaṇa-parivarta*), there are two points for its explanation: first, the interpretation of the chapter title; second, the explanation of the textual meaning.

As for the title "The Chapter on the Characteristics of the Lack of Intrinsic Nature," it refers to the three types of lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*): first, the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Second is the naturelessness of arising; third is the ultimate naturelessness. The term "naturelessness" reveals these three types of naturelessness;
thus, it is called "naturelessness. "Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to essential characteristics, or what are termed "phenomenal appearances.

These three types of naturelessness take the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) as their respective essential characteristics in their proper order. This chapter extensively elucidates these three types of naturelessness.

Because it concerns the essential nature, substance, characteristics, and marks [of phenomena], it is called the "Chapter on the Absence of Self-Nature Characteristics" (the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* refers to this as the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Paramārthasiddhi";
these are names established based on the person [who asks the questions], due to the differences among translators).
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Paramārthasamudgata addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One. [The commentary] explains:

From this point downward, the meaning of the text is correctly explained. Regarding the explanation of the objects characterized by the lack of intrinsic nature of sentient beings, the explanation of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) as objects has already been completed above.
From here on, secondly, the three absences of intrinsic nature (*trividhā niḥsvabhāvatā*) are explained. Within this chapter, there are...
Five divisions: First, the section on the Bodhisattva’s inquiry; second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" downward, the section on the Tathāgata’s correct exposition;
third, from "At that time, Paramārthasamudgata" downward, the section on understanding and upholding the teaching;

fourth, from "Then the Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata" downward, the section on comparative evaluation and praise of excellence; fifth, from "At that time, Paramārthasamudgata" downward, the section on practicing according to the instructions.
Regarding the section on posing questions, the text is divided into three parts. First, the question and answer are introduced; second, from "I once...

onwards, the matter to be questioned is set forth; third, from "I do not yet understand... onwards, the question is posed in accordance with the teaching. This is the first part, the introduction of the question and answer.
Regarding the term "arising of the ultimate" (*paramārtha-udbhava*): the "ultimate" (*paramārtha*) refers to the object to be realized, the domain of supreme wisdom;

thus it is named the "ultimate. "Arising" (*udbhava*) refers to the wisdom that is capable of realizing it; because this wisdom arises by taking the ultimate as its object, it is called "arising. Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states:

Because it is realized and experienced therein, it is called "arising. Since superior wisdom arises with respect to this object of focus, its name is established based on both the means of realization and that which is realized;
thus, it is named "Arising of the Ultimate" (Paramārthasamudgata).
"I once dwelt alone in a quiet place, and such reflections arose in my mind.

The commentary states: From this point downward is the second section, which sets forth the matter of the inquiry. This contains two parts; first, the presentation of one's own doubts and reflections.

Next, the teaching that was asked about is presented; this is the first [section]. It means: formerly, while I was alone in a mountain forest, a quiet room, or a secluded place, I reflected in this way:
"How is it that the World-Honored One first taught the existence of nature (*svabhāva*) and later taught the non-existence of nature? The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states:

"In a place of empty seclusion, one who gives rise to the mind of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*)... This is as previously analyzed; the difference arises from the particularity of the translators.

In general, there are four kinds of investigation (*vitarka*). First, the tainted (*sāsrava*) conceptual mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) of the three realms. Second, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*); thus, the *Gambhīrārtha-samgraha* states: "In a secluded place, the mind of applied and sustained thought arises. Third, applied thought alone; thus, the sixth chapter of the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* says: "For one who practices investigation, the object of mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation is the basis. Fourth, sustained thought alone; thus, the same treatise states: "For one who practices sustained thought, the object of mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation is the basis. Furthermore, the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā* explains: "The first refers to the nature of the dharma itself. The second refers to the function of the dharma. The third refers to the coarse aspect of the dharma. The fourth refers to the subtle aspect of the dharma. Regarding the first, the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states: "What is the investigation of the nature of phenomena? It refers to the investigation of all dharmas, whether conditioned or unconditioned, by means of their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and so forth. Regarding the second, the same work states: "What is the investigation of the function of phenomena? It refers to the investigation of the functions of all dharmas, such as arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. The *Śarīra-prakaraṇa*, fascicle 22, states: "One whose mind is frequently distracted by vitarka is called a 'vitarka-carita' (one whose conduct is dominated by applied thought).

Such a person is able to correctly enter into cultivation by relying on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*). Alternatively, it may be explained generally that both vitarka and vicāra are termed 'vitarka-carita. Fourth is the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā-saṃskāra*)."
Just as with the four thorough investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*), which are taught in various places, here in this context the fourth is preeminent.

For the Blessed One has, through immeasurable gateways, previously explained all the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the aggregates, as well as their characteristics of arising and cessation, their permanent abandonment, and their full comprehension (*parijñā*).

The commentary states: From this point downward is the second section, which sets forth the teachings requested [by the interlocutor]. This section contains two parts: first, the presentation of the teaching on the existence of nature (*sattva-dhātu*);
second, from "Furthermore, the World-Honored One said" onwards, the revelation of the teaching on the absence of nature (*asattva-dhātu*).

Within the preceding text, there are thirteen topical gates, which are subsumed into five sections: (1) elucidating the teaching on the aggregates (*skandha*); (2) elucidating the teaching on the truths (*satya*); (3) elucidating the various elements (*dhātu*); (4) elucidating the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

The five [aggregates] and the eightfold noble path—this is the first section analyzing the teaching on the aggregates (*skandha*). Within this, there are two parts: first, the explicit explanation of the teaching on the aggregates;
second, the analogical manifestation of the three teachings. This constitutes the holy teaching that analyzes the aggregates through five aspects. Regarding the "innumerable gates":

There are two explanations for this. The first says: because the individual and general characteristics (svalakṣaṇa and sāmānyalakṣaṇa) contained within the aggregates (skandha) comprise manifold categories, they are called "immeasurable" (apramāṇa).
The second says: because there are manifold categories such as visible and invisible, or material and immaterial, they are called "immeasurable."

Therefore, they are called "immeasurable. Their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are themselves their individual characteristics (*pṛthaglakṣaṇa*); for example, as it is said that form (*rūpa*) is characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*), so too consciousness (*vijñāna*) is characterized by cognition (*vijñapti*).

The characteristic of arising and the characteristic of cessation are universal characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), because form and the other aggregates all possess the characteristics of arising and cessation.

Permanent abandonment and thorough knowledge are the characteristics of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*); this is because one permanently abandons the afflictions of suffering and its origin within the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of Origin. Thorough...

Because one knows the truth of suffering as the fruit of birth and death. Alternatively, that which constitutes its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is precisely its characteristic of individual differentiation (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
These two characteristics pervade arising and ceasing; their permanent abandonment and thorough knowledge are as explained in the section on "Understanding" (*avabodha*) below.
As it has been taught regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), the bases (*āyatana*), and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), so it is with the nutriments (*āhāra*).

The commentary states: this is the second category of explanation for the two gates. That is to say, just as the five characteristics explained within the [section on] the aggregates apply, one should know that they likewise apply to the teaching on the twelve bases, dependent origination, and the nutriments.
Specifically, the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the base [of the eye] is that which sees visible forms; this is called "name" (*nāman*).

That which is the eye is called "form" (*rūpa*) because it is what is seen by the eye. Likewise, up to that which can cognize phenomena (*dharma*), is called "mind" (*manas*) because it is what is known by the mind;

that which is known by the mind is called "phenomena. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is a distinct mental factor (*caitta*) characterized by the nature of obscuration, which stands in opposition to the wisdom that perceives the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of dependent origination. As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 56: [text follows].

The gradual decline and sudden cessation [of the faculties] is termed "aging and death" (*jarāmaraṇa*). All food that is swallowed in distinct portions is each called "edible food" (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).

Up to the point of discerning and maintaining [the continuity of existence] is termed "consciousness-food" (*vijñānāhāra*). The permanent cessation and thorough knowledge of the two characteristics of arising and ceasing should be understood according to the above.
Question: How are the aggregates (*skandha*) analyzed by means of the six aspects within the section on the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)?
[The text] explains the Four Truths in full. Within this chapter, however, only Suffering and its Origin are mentioned, rather than Cessation and the Path. The commentary states:
In the preceding chapter, all four truths were explained in full because it was intended to distinguish the various aspects of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).

In the present chapter, there is a distinction between the two teachings concerning those with potential and those without; therefore, [the other truths] are omitted here. This is due to the attainment of the aggregates (*skandha*).

"Regarding cessation and reliance upon realization, through immeasurable gateways, he has previously taught all the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the truths, as well as their full comprehension (*parijñā*), permanent abandonment (*prahāṇa*), realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Commentary:
The second section distinguishes the teaching on the Four Noble Truths. It consists of five phrases. Regarding "all their specific characteristics," there are two [aspects].

The explanation follows the above and should be understood accordingly: that which oppresses is called "suffering" (duḥkha); that which gathers is called "origination" (samudaya); that which is extinguished is called "cessation" (nirodha);

that which enables passage is called the "path" (mārga). The four [aspects] beginning with thorough knowledge specifically reveal the Four Noble Truths: thoroughly knowing the truth of suffering, permanently abandoning the truth of origination, realizing the truth of cessation, and cultivating the truth of the path.

"By means of immeasurable gateways, [the Buddha] has previously explained all the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the various realms (*dhātu*), as well as their manifold natures and their non-uniform nature, regarding their permanent abandonment and thorough knowledge. Commentary:
This third section distinguishes the various realms. All their specific characteristics should be understood according to what was stated above. Next, the two...
"Phrases" refers to the eighteen elements (*dhātus*). Their mutually distinct characteristics are called "various elements.
These same eighteen elements, as the bases for the distinctions among immeasurable sentient beings, are called "non-unitary elements," as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 56.

According to fascicle 83, this is the opposite of what was stated above, as noted in the commentary on the first fascicle. "Permanent abandonment through thorough knowledge" should be understood by analogy with what precedes.

Through immeasurable gateways, he has previously explained all the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), as well as their remedies and the objects they counteract, and their cultivation— how to cause those not yet arisen to arise,
how to ensure those already arisen remain firm and stable, and how to practice with faith so that they are not forgotten, but rather increase, expand, and become vast.

The commentary states: The fourth section distinguishes the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Within this, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the foundations of mindfulness;
second, the classification according to five gates. Regarding the former, there are five phrases. As for the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of each, there are two interpretations;

these should be understood by analogy with the aggregates (*skandha*). These four foundations of mindfulness have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essential nature. While one should say "wisdom abides" because they abide upon objects such as the body, they are called "foundations of mindfulness. Why? [Because... (text continues).

They are called "foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*) because mindfulness is associated with them and abides upon objects such as the body; among these six types of etymological explanation (*nirukti*), this is the *sāmīpika* (proximate) explanation.
As for the latter four phrases: first, they counteract the four inversions; second, they cause what has not yet arisen to arise; third, they cause what has already arisen to remain firm.
The four applications of mindfulness are practiced with redoubled effort, increasing and expanding as explained in the first fascicle.
As it was said regarding the applications of mindfulness, the same applies to the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment.
The commentary states: This is the second category of explanation regarding the five gates.

That is to say, just as the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) have five phrases, so too do the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), and the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) each possess five phrases.
It should be understood as corresponding to what was stated above.

By means of immeasurable gateways, the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the remedies (*pratipakṣa*) and their objects (*vipakṣa*), and the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the Noble Eightfold Path have already been explained:
causing that which has not yet arisen to arise; once arisen, ensuring its firm stability, non-forgetfulness, repeated practice, increase, and expansion.
The commentary states: The fifth [section], the eight branches of the noble path, consists of five phrases; these should be understood according to the preceding [explanation].
These subsequent seven gates are the contemplation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*); their meaning is as explained in a separate chapter.
The World-Honored One further taught that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), being without arising or cessation, primordially quiescent, and by nature in *nirvāṇa*.
The commentary states:
the second [section] clarifies the teaching on the absence of intrinsic nature; that is to say, according to the subsequent sūtra, regarding the Wheel of Dharma in three stages, in the first...
At that time, he taught the doctrine of the Four Noble Truths. In the second period, he taught the doctrine of signlessness (*animitta*).

In the third period, he taught the definitive (*nītārtha*) doctrine, explaining that all phenomena (*dharma*) are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), are without arising or ceasing, are primordially quiescent, and are by nature in *nirvāṇa*—that is, their very nature is the absence of intrinsic nature.
Now, within this context, with reference to the second period in contrast to the first period:

It serves as the basis for the inquiry. Previously, "possessing characteristics" (*sanimitta*) was taught; subsequently, "without characteristics" (*animitta*) was taught. This term "without characteristics" contradicts the prior "possessing characteristics";
therefore, "without characteristics" is taken as the basis for the inquiry. If one asks: according to this sutra, does it not initially teach only existence?
Later, it speaks only of non-existence. However, in both the earlier and later sections of the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, both emptiness and existence are taught.

Thus, that sūtra says: "Good son, when I rose from beneath the King of Trees and went to the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī to turn the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for the five men, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya, I also spoke of how all dharmas are originally quiescent."

In the interim, at this location and in various other places, for the sake of the bhikṣus and the assembly of bodhisattvas, he analyzed, expounded, and proclaimed the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) and the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
He also taught that all phenomena are primordially empty and quiescent, explaining them in full detail as previously described.
How, then, are these two sūtras to be harmonized? The explanation states: as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says, "The Buddhas..."
The Dharma has two aspects: first, the secret; second, the manifest. The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* relies upon the secret gate, whereas this present sūtra relies upon the manifest gate.
Each is based on one side [of the teaching], yet they do not contradict one another.
I do not yet understand, Blessed One, based on what underlying intention you have made such a statement:
that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, unarisen and unceasing, primordially quiescent, and by nature in a state of nirvāṇa.
The commentary states: The third section concerns the inquiry based upon the teaching. This consists of three parts: first, the presentation of one’s own doubts;
second, the request for an explanation; and third, the citation of the sūtra to be explained. This is the first part.

It means that the Buddha previously taught thirteen dharma-gates, such as the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu), all of which lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva); subsequently, he further stated that all dharmas are without [intrinsic nature].
Regarding the self-nature being without arising or ceasing and so forth: the former teaching speaks of existence, while the latter speaks of non-existence. These two teachings appear contradictory;

I do not yet understand, Blessed One, with what underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) you have made such statements as "the absence of self-nature" and so on. (If one follows the *Guhyasūtra*, there are five sections.)

1. All phenomena are originally without realization; 2. all phenomena are originally unarisen; 3. all phenomena are originally without cessation; 4. all phenomena are originally quiescent; 5. all phenomena are originally by nature in nirvāṇa.
I now inquire of the Tathāgata regarding this matter; I only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately explain it.
The commentary states: This is the second explanation of the various vows.
The underlying intention behind the teaching that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, unarisen and unceasing, primordially quiescent,
and by nature in a state of nirvāṇa.
The commentary states: The third section sets forth the teaching that has been explained.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata.
The commentary states: From here below is the second part, the Tathāgata’s formal exposition. This contains two sections: first, the praise of the question and the granting of permission to speak.

Regarding the passage "Furthermore, Paramārthasamudgata, you should know that... and below, it is based on the formal exposition following a question. Within the preceding section, there are two parts: first, praising the benefit of the question;
second, commanding [the audience] to listen and permitting the exposition. Within the first part, there are four sections: (1) identifying the speaker;
(2) praising the question as being appropriate; (3) praising the profound meaning of the question; and (4) praising the benefit of the question. This [present section] is the first of these.
Excellent, excellent, Paramārthasamudgata! What you have investigated is most consistent with reason.
The commentary states: This is the second praise of the question as being appropriate.
"Excellent, excellent! Son of good family, it is well that you are now able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such a profound meaning.
The commentary states: This constitutes the third praise for the inquiry into the profound meaning. The preceding two types [of inquiries] were excellent both in phrasing and in meaning;
therefore, he says "excellent, excellent" twice.
You have now raised this question out of a desire to benefit and bring peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, out of compassion for the world and its devas,
humans, and asuras, and in order to enable them to attain meaningful benefit, peace, and happiness.
The commentary states: This is the fourth praise-question regarding the benefit. It should be understood accordingly:
"Listen attentively; I shall explain for you that all dharmas which have been taught are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature."
"Without arising and without cessation; originally quiescent; by nature in nirvāṇa"—this is the intended meaning.
The commentary states: this is the second command to listen and permission to speak.

Paramārthasaṃvartanīya, you should know that it was with reference to the three kinds of lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) that I spoke with intentional meaning (*saṃdhi*), saying that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature. Commentary:
This is the second section, the formal exposition in response to the question. It contains two parts; first is the extensive explanation in prose.

The following section cites the verse to repeat the explanation. Within the preceding portion, there are five parts: first, an explanation of various phrases from the sūtra based on the three kinds of non-nature;
second, following the phrase "furthermore, the ultimate meaning arises," a discussion establishing the intent behind the three kinds of non-nature by means of the contemplation of the three natures;

third, following the phrase "furthermore, the ultimate meaning arises," a discussion establishing the intent behind the three kinds of non-nature by means of the [spiritual] stages; fourth, following the phrase "furthermore, the ultimate meaning arises"...
Distinguishing the meaning of the One Vehicle through the contemplation of the three kinds of non-nature (*trividhā-niḥsvabhāvatā*).

Fifth, following the section on the arising of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), distinguishing the differences in comprehension based on the teaching of non-nature. This is the first [section]. Explaining various phrases from the sūtras by means of the three kinds of non-nature.

Within this, there are two parts. First, explaining how all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are said to lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) within the various sūtras by means of the three kinds of non-nature.

Regarding the nature (*svabhāva*): it should be understood that from the passage "Later, Paramārthasamudgata... onwards, the non-arising, non-ceasing, and so forth of all phenomena are explained by way of the three types of non-nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*)—the first and the last.

Within the preceding section [of this explanation], there are three parts: first, the brief statement of the headings; second, the detailed explanation through question and answer, beginning with "Good son...";
and third, the concluding summary after the explanation, beginning with "Good son...". Within the first of these, there are two parts: first, based on the three types of non-nature...
This reveals the intended meaning (*abhiprāya*) of the Sūtra. Subsequently, the names of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are enumerated according to their number; this is the first [of those].

That is to say, when the Blessed One stated that "all phenomena (*dharma*) lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)," I now explain that all phenomena are entirely without intrinsic nature by relying fully upon the three types of lack of intrinsic nature.
All phenomena are precisely the three natures; it is upon these three natures that the three [lackings of intrinsic nature] are established.
Because they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), various sūtras state that all phenomena are devoid of self-nature. Therefore, the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says:
"Based precisely upon these three natures, those three absences of nature are established; thus, with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*), the Buddha taught that all phenomena are without nature."
These are the so-called naturelessness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*), naturelessness of production (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*), and ultimate naturelessness (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).

The commentary states: this is the second [section], which enumerates the names according to their number; that is to say, the three types of naturelessness, beginning with the naturelessness of characteristics.
"Good son, what is the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in the characteristics of all phenomena?

The commentary states: From here below is the second section, which provides a detailed explanation through questions and answers. This section contains two parts; first is the correct exposition based on the Dharma.
The following provides a further explanation through an analogy. Within the preceding discourse on the Dharma, the three kinds of non-nature are divided into three parts;
this is the first. This section contains five components: first, the question; second, the answer; third, the inquiry; fourth, the explanation; and fifth, the conclusion. This is the question.
This refers to the characteristics of that which is thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*).

The commentary states: this is the second [point], the correct answer to the question; namely, that among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the thoroughly imagined is taken as the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Why is this? The commentary states:
This is the third inquiry. For what reason is it said that the characteristics of the grasped (parikalpita-lakṣaṇa) are called "characteristics" yet lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva)?
It is because these are established as characteristics by way of conventional designation (prajñapti), and not established as characteristics by way of their own specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
The commentary states: The fourth section provides a detailed explanation based on an inquiry.

Regarding the phrase "this is established as a characteristic by means of conventional designation," this explains the term "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa), meaning that it is a characteristic established in dependence upon names and expressions. It is not established as a characteristic by way of its own intrinsic nature (svalakṣaṇa).

The commentary by Asvabhāva explains the general meaning as follows: Because the characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which exist only conventionally, are non-existent according to reasoning, they are said to be "without nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*).
For this reason, it is stated that the very characteristics grasped by that [nature] constitute its own nature. Thus, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* says:

"Because the essence and characteristics of the grasped nature do not exist, it is called 'the nature of being without self-nature' (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). Furthermore, there are three types of naturelessness.
It is said: "As it appears, this characteristic does not truly exist; therefore, the nature of the imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) is characterized by the absence of characteristics.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 73, states: "What is the naturelessness of characteristics? It refers to the nature of all phenomena as expressed through conventional designations (*vyavahāra*)."
Therefore, it is called the "lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
The commentary states: this is the fifth concluding passage; it may be understood accordingly.
What is the "lack of intrinsic nature in terms of the arising of phenomena" (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*)?

The commentary states: From here below is the second section, explaining the lack of intrinsic nature in arising (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*). The text consists of five segments, which may be understood by reference to the preceding [section].
This is the question:
namely, regarding all dependently originated characteristics (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*).

The commentary states: This is the second [section], the correct answer based on the question. That is to say, among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), it takes the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as its own essence. Why is this?
The commentary states: This is the third inquiry. For what reason is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) called "the naturelessness of arising"?
It exists by virtue of the power of other conditions; it does not exist inherently.
The commentary states: This is the fourth [section], which provides a detailed explanation based on the inquiry.

Regarding the phrase "it exists by virtue of the power of other-dependent conditions," this explains the term "arising"; that is to say, it is called "arising" because it exists by virtue of the power of other-dependent conditions.

The phrase "not existing inherently" explains the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). To summarize the intended meaning: other-dependent phenomena are said [to exist] by virtue of causes and conditions.
Its arising is not produced by false causes such as *svabhāva* (nature), *īśvara* (the Lord), or other such [deities]; therefore, it is called "non-arising.
Thus, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is produced by the power of conditions; because it is not produced spontaneously, it is 'non-arising'."

Furthermore, regarding the three natures of non-essence (*trividha-niḥsvabhāvatā*), it is said that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) arises through the power of conditions and does not arise by itself;
therefore, its nature is the non-arising of that which depends on others. As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Stages of Yoga Practice), fascicle 73:

"What is the nature of the non-essence of arising? It refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) which are produced by various conditions and exist by the power of conditions, rather than existing spontaneously."
Therefore, it is called the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of arising (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
The commentary states: the fifth [section], which concludes the text, is thus to be understood.
What is the ultimate nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in all phenomena (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*)?
The commentary states: Below this is the third section, which explains the absence of intrinsic nature in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*). This consists of two parts:

first, explaining the absence of intrinsic nature in the ultimate sense by way of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); second, as follows below, explaining the absence of intrinsic nature in the ultimate sense by way of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The preceding section has five parts; they should be understood according to the above. This is the question:

namely, because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature by virtue of their "nature of lacking intrinsic nature," they are said to be "without intrinsic nature"; that is to say, they are dependently originated phenomena.
It is also called the "ultimate naturelessness. The commentary states:
the second [section] provides the correct answer to the question. The text consists of two parts. First, in order to explain the third [nature], it cites the preceding second [nature];
the explanation of its meaning is as before. Second, regarding the phrase "that which arises dependently," etc., based on the second nature, the third [nature] is established.

The three kinds of non-nature. This means that because the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) does not exist upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), dependently arisen phenomena are not only designated as being "natureless by way of arising" (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*), but are also called "natureless by way of the ultimate" (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Thus, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: "The dependent nature is also established as being natureless by way of the ultimate due to its distinct characteristics. Why is this?"
Because it lacks ultimate reality. Why is this?
The commentary states:
This is the third inquiry. For what reason is dependent origination also called the "ultimate naturelessness"?
Among all phenomena, whatever is an object of pure observation, I demonstrate that as the ultimate nature of lack of intrinsic existence (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
The dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), however, is not an object of pure observation.
The commentary states: The fourth section provides a detailed explanation based on specific inquiries. The text consists of two parts: first, it explains the pure ultimate truth that does not exist;
second, it clarifies that the dependent nature lacks that pure ultimate truth. This explains the object of focus for the pure wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness).
It is called the "pure ultimate truth" (*viśuddha-paramārtha*). Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (*Xianyang lun*) states:
"One should know that the ultimate truth is the objective referent (*ālambana-svabhāva*) of purity. Why? Because by taking this object as a referent, one attains the purity of the mind."
Therefore, it is also called the "ultimate lack of intrinsic nature" (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
The commentary states: the fifth [point], which concludes the text, is thus to be understood.
Furthermore, there is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, which is also called the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature.
The commentary states: Hereafter, the second section explains the three natureslessnesses (*trividha-niḥsvabhāvatā*) by way of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

This section contains four parts: first, the heading; second, the inquiry; third, the explanation; and fourth, the conclusion. This is the heading: namely, the perfected nature among the three natures.
"It is taken as the intrinsic nature. Why is this?
The commentary states: This second [question] investigates the reason. Why is the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) further described as "supreme" (*parama*)?
Meaning (*artha*) is also called "the absence of nature" (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).

The dharma-nature of selflessness (*dharmanairātmya*) of all phenomena is termed the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and it is also designated as the "nature of the absence of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Because these are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of all phenomena, they manifest as the nature of being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
The commentary states: The third section provides a formal explanation based on the inquiry. The text consists of two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation.

That is to say, the nature of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) has two meanings: first, it is called "ultimate" (*paramārtha*); second, it is called "the nature of being without intrinsic nature. These are all phenomena.

Because it is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), and because it is the principle revealed by the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) in all phenomena. Thus, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:

"It refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) as the ultimate absence of nature. For this reason, its own-nature is the ultimate, and it is also the very nature of the absence of nature in all phenomena.
Furthermore, it says: "For this reason, this own-nature is itself the ultimate and is also the absence of nature."
Because the nature of self and phenomena is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), it is explained differently according to the *Treatise on the Three Non-natures*.

Thus, it says: "Regarding the nature of reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), it is called 'non-nature' because that very reality is non-existent [as a separate entity]. This refers to the nature of reality.
There is no other nature; rather, the very absence of the preceding two natures is the true nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Because this true nature is without characteristics (*animitta*) and without arising (*anutpāda*), all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) do not transcend these two natures—the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the dependent (*paratantra*).
Since these three natures are truly without characteristics and without arising, by virtue of this principle, all dharmas are of one and the same [nature].
"Non-existence. This single non-existence is truly non-existent and truly existent;
it is truly non-existent. These two—the imagined and the dependent—are truly existent; these two—the imagined and the dependent—are [also] non-existent.

Therefore, one cannot say they are non-existent, nor can one say they are existent, and so forth, as explained at length. The commentary states: because this universally negates the dependent nature, it is not the same as this [case].
For this reason, it is called the "ultimate naturelessness.
The commentary states: this is the fourth [point]; the concluding text is clear. Question: If, according to this sūtra, there is ultimate naturelessness...
There are two types of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): first, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); second, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Why does the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* speak of the latter and not the former? The explanation is that, according to the actual reality, both meanings are fully present; therefore, this scriptural passage as well as the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* [state so].

All [masters] say this: because the *paratantra-svabhāva* lacks ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it can also be described as being "without nature in terms of the ultimate" (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāva*).
However, among the various treatises, the former [the *parikalpita-svabhāva*] is not explicitly clarified. In the ninth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, Dharmapāla explains:
"Because it would be confused with the second [nature], it is not mentioned here. Question: The intent of this sūtra is to establish the three [natures] based upon the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Non-nature. Its essence is the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Why is there a *Tri-svabhāva-nirdeśa*? Because within the single true suchness (*tathatā*), the three absences of nature are established.
Thus, the first fascicle of the *Tri-svabhāva-nirdeśa* states: "Based on these three natures, the three absences of nature are taught.

By means of the three absences of nature, one should know that this is the principle of the single absence of nature. Regarding the conceptualized nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it is taught as the absence of nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
It is called "naturelessness. Regarding the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), it is called "natureless" by virtue of its naturelessness in terms of arising (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*).

Regarding the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature), it is called "natureless" because of its naturelessness in terms of reality (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*). This is as explained therein. The commentary states: "There are two interpretations of this."
The Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Tang dynasty states: "As in the *Vyākhyāyukti* and other texts, it is based on the three [natures]. The Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of the Sui dynasty states:

"Because the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are negated within the single True Suchness (*tathatā*), they are taught as the three kinds of lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). Among these, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is subsumed under the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*), whereas all three types of lack of intrinsic nature are non-established (*avyavasthāna*).

This is as explained in the *Tri-svabhāva-nirdeśa*. The Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang dynasty states: "As in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and others, it is precisely based on the three [natures]."
Regarding the nature [of phenomena], the three non-natures are established; this is taken as the correct view. Why is this so?
The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, in his *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, composed this verse: "Based precisely upon these three natures, those three non-natures are established;

therefore, with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*), the Buddha taught that all phenomena are without nature. Dharmapāla’s commentary states: "In terms of both existence and non-existence, they are collectively said to be without nature."

Therefore, it is called "intentional" (*saṃdhāya*). Furthermore, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Exposition of Manifestation), composed by Asaṅga, reveals the same meaning as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other such works.
Moreover, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* extensively cites this sūtra and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), encompassing both existence and non-existence.

Thus, one knows that the *Tri-svabhāva-nirdeśa* (Treatise on the Three Natures) is a mistranslation by the translator. Why is this so? [Because] the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*... the three natures... [is consistent with these].
Regarding the *Treatise on the Nature* (*Xinglun*), it was composed by Vasubandhu. How can there be such a difference between these two treatises?
Furthermore, since that Vasubandhu relied upon the school of Maitreya as well as Asaṅga and others, we know they are the same person, Vasubandhu; thus, Paramārtha is mistaken.

Alternatively, if one examines Paramārtha’s *Treatise on the Three Non-natures* (*San wuxing lun*) now, it is clear that it is not the *Manifestation of the Doctrine* (*Xianyang lun*) composed by Asaṅga, which lacks the [section on] non-self-nature.
Chapter on Nature. However, that [section] was translated as a separate version by Paramārtha (one should consult the catalog and the *Abhidharmasamudaya-śāstra* for further details).
"Good son, it should be known that the nature of the absence of self-nature in characteristics is just like a flower in the sky."

The commentary states: From here on is the second section, which provides a further explanation by means of analogies. This explanation of the three natures of non-self-existence (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is divided into three parts;
this is the first, explaining the nature of non-self-existence in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*).

It is like a flower in the sky (*khapuṣpa*): due to ophthalmia (*taimira*), the appearance of a flower manifests within empty space. In reality, there has never been a flower in that empty space. The same applies to the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
It is likewise. Because that which is grasped is itself, from the outset, without intrinsic nature, it is called the "naturelessness of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*);

one should know that it is also thus. Just as with a magical illusion, the "naturelessness of arising" (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*) should be known to be likewise. This is the "ultimate naturelessness" (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*) in one respect.
The nature (*svabhāva*) should be understood in the same way.

The commentary states: the second [explanation] clarifies the lack of intrinsic nature in arising (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*) and a portion of the lack of intrinsic nature in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).

As stated in the *Abhidharmasūtra*, the eight similes such as the illusion (*māyā*) manifest the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); here, this second [explanation] concerns the lack of intrinsic nature in arising.
The nature [of phenomena] and one portion of the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) both take the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as their own essence;

therefore, they should be understood as being just like illusory forms. Question: In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras, illusions and the like are used as metaphors for the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
How is it that this sūtra uses them as metaphors for the dependent nature? Answer: Illusions and the like possess two meanings. First, they are not...
There is existence that resembles existence; these two lack substantial images and so forth. Therefore, the two sūtras each rely on one specific meaning and are thus not contradictory.
For example, space is manifested solely by the absence of intrinsic nature in various forms and pervades all places; this is one aspect of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

The nature of being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) should be understood in the same way, for it is manifested by the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and because it pervades all things.
The commentary states: This is the third explanation of one part of the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature, which is like space.
It has two meanings: first, it is manifested by the absence of form; second, it pervades all locations. Such is the ultimate reality of *tathatā*.
The nature of nature (*dharmatā*) should be understood in the same way. This is because it is manifested by the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), and because it pervades all phenomena.
Therefore, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* employs ten metaphors of space to illustrate the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); this [nature of nature] is likewise so. Question:

Regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, which state that space (*ākāśa*) is the absence of matter (*rūpa*), and the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, which state that space is the absence of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*):

how are these to be reconciled? The explanation is as follows: The *Yogācāra* and *Abhidharma* treatises follow the "conventional gate of reasoning" (*saṃvṛti-yukti-mukha*), which is identical to the Sarvāstivāda school.
The *Vijñaptimātra* and other such treatises follow the "ultimate gate of reasoning" (*tattva-yukti-mukha*). Each [approach] is consistent within its own context.
According to one sense, there is thus no contradiction.
Son of good family, it is based on these three kinds of naturelessness that I have spoken with intentional meaning,
saying that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.
The commentary states: This concludes the third explanation.

Paramārthasamudgata, you should know that it was with reference to the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇaniḥsvabhāvatā*) that I spoke with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*), saying that all phenomena [are without intrinsic nature].
"Without intrinsic nature; without arising or ceasing; originally quiescent; by nature in nirvāṇa.

The commentary states: From here on, the second section explains the phrases "all phenomena are without arising," and so forth, by way of their lack of intrinsic nature at both the beginning and the end.
Within this, there are two parts. First, the explanation of the phrases such as "unborn" by means of the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Second, from the words "Good son" onwards, the explanation of the phrases such as "unborn" by means of the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).

Within the first part, there are four sections: first, the thesis; second, the inquiry; third, the explanation; and fourth, the conclusion. This is the first [section], which establishes the tenet through reasoning, stating that various sūtras say:

Regarding the statements that "all phenomena are unarisen" and so forth, these are taught as being unarisen and so on with reference to the lack of nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇaniḥsvabhāvatā*) among the three natures. Why is this?
The commentary states: This is the second objection raised by the opponent.
If all self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) were entirely non-existent, then there would be no arising; and if there were no arising, then there would be no cessation.
If there is neither arising nor ceasing, then it is primordially quiescent;
if it is primordially quiescent, then it is by nature in nirvāṇa, because within it there is not even the slightest thing that could further be brought to parinirvāṇa.

The commentary states: This third explanation consists of four sections: first, the explanation of non-arising; second, the explanation of non-ceasing; third, the explanation of primordial tranquility;
and fourth, the explanation of natural nirvāṇa. These may be understood from the sūtra itself, so they will not be explained in detail here.

Therefore, based on the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*), I have spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*) that all phenomena are unarisen and unceasing,
primordially quiescent, and by nature in a state of nirvāṇa.
The commentary states: This is the fourth concluding passage; it may be understood as follows.

"O son of good family, it is also by relying on the ultimate naturelessness—which is manifested through the selflessness of phenomena—that I have spoken with intentional meaning that all dharmas are unarisen, unceasing, primordially quiescent, and by nature in a state of nirvāṇa."
The commentary states: From here below is the second section, which explains the phrases "non-arising" and so forth in terms of the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
This section contains four parts: first, the heading; second, the inquiry; third, the explanation; and fourth, the conclusion. This is the first part.

That is to say, within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there are four meanings: first, non-arising; second, non-ceasing; third, original... [text fragment ends].

It comes to rest in tranquility. Because it is by nature nirvana, the various sūtras also speak of non-arising and so forth based on the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which is the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*). Why is this?

The commentary states: Second, the opponent raises a counter-objection. That is to say, although the opponent has raised a counter-objection by stating four points, he has not yet distinguished their underlying cause.
Based on what cause are they termed "non-arising" and so forth?
The ultimate nature of lack of intrinsic nature, which is manifested by the selflessness of phenomena, is at all times and for all eternity the dharmatā of all phenomena;
it abides unconditioned, because it is dissociated from all afflictions.

The commentary states: From here below is the third section, which provides the formal explanation based on the preceding inquiry. This section is divided into two parts. First, the three causes are presented in general to answer the inquiry.
Second, the three causes are cited to explain "non-arising" and so forth. This is the first part. It consists of two sub-sections.

The first sets forth the nature of the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*), which is of two kinds: first, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); second, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Indeed. In this context, we take the latter [definition] and not the former. Regarding the phrase "at all times, at all moments," etc., it correctly clarifies the three reasons.
First, because the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) of all phenomena abides at all times and at all moments, it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because it is twofold unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there is neither arising nor ceasing; this is because it is abiding and because it is unconditioned.

These two reasons establish the two meanings of "neither arising nor ceasing. Because it is dissociated from all defilements (*saṃkleśa*), the third reason establishes the two meanings found in the sūtra:
"primordial tranquility" (*ādi-śānta*) and "naturally extinguished" (*prakṛti-parinirvṛta*).
Because a single character contains three meanings, it constitutes three reasons.
Since the dharma-nature of all phenomena remains established at all times and for all eternity, it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because it is unconditioned, it is without arising and without cessation.
The commentary states: From here below is the second section, which provides a double explanation of the three causes. It explains non-arising and so forth, which consists of two parts:

first, the explanation of non-arising and so forth by means of two causes; second, the explanation of the original quiescence and intrinsic nirvāṇa by means of the cause that is dissociated from all afflictions (*saṃkleśa*).
This is the first part. That is to say, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
This principle is established as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) because the dharma-nature of all phenomena abides at all times and for all eternity.
By virtue of being unconditioned, the two meanings of neither arising nor ceasing are established.
"Because it is dissociated from all defilements, it is primordially quiescent and by nature in *nirvāṇa*.
The commentary states: This constitutes the second reason for its dissociation from all defilements, establishing two points:
first, that it is primordially quiescent; and second, that it is by nature in *nirvāṇa*. Question: Regarding the words "non-arising" and so forth spoken in the Sūtra...

How is it that [the teaching of] "lack of nature" (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) relies solely on the first and the last [of the three natures]? The answer is: Generally speaking, there are two types of lack of nature.
First, the lack of nature taught in common by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna Piṭakas; second, the lack of nature taught exclusively in the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.

Regarding what is taught in common, as stated in the fifth fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, it refers to the intended meaning of the statement that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Now, that which is "naturally non-existent" shall be demonstrated.

Because all phenomena lack an intrinsic nature that exists independently of conditions, this is called the first sense of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). As for "the non-existence of self-essence," because phenomena, once ceased, do not arise again, they lack intrinsic nature;
this is the latter sense of the absence of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, their intrinsic nature does not persist.
Because phenomena, as soon as they arise, lack the power to remain even for a single moment after that, they have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Such a principle of the absence of intrinsic nature is shared with the Śrāvakas. As for what is called "unshared," that same treatise states:

"If one asserts the absence of intrinsic nature because the grasping [at objects] does not exist, this absence of intrinsic nature is unshared with the Śrāvakas. This is because, according to the [Mahāyāna] perspective...
The nature of the imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva), which is grasped by foolish people, does not exist in that way.

It is with this intention that, according to the principles of the Mahāyāna, it is said that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva). The *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*, and the *Tattvasiddhi* also share this same intent.
Although there are these two [different] explanations, in this present sūtra, it is taught through the uncommon approach that phenomena lack intrinsic nature and so forth.

However, regarding the explanation of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) and so forth through the "unshared gate" (*asādhāraṇa-mukha*), various sūtras differ based on the three absences of intrinsic nature (*tri-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
There is indeed a sacred teaching that, relying on the first absence of intrinsic nature, states that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature and lack arising or cessation.

As the tenth fascicle of the *Śata-śāstra-vyākhyā* (*Vigrahavyāvartanī-vyākhyā*) says: "The Buddha himself definitively judged: 'I rely upon the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)... [and so forth].
In other sutras, it is taught that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), unarisen, unceasing, primordially quiescent, and naturally in a state of nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, this is stated identically in the seventy-fourth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the fifth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, and the fifth fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*.
The Liang dynasty version of the *Saṃgraha* relies comprehensively upon the three kinds of absence of intrinsic nature.
The [teachings on] nature, such as the statement that there is no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and so forth, differ from this.

There is indeed a sacred teaching which, based on the three kinds of non-nature, states that all phenomena (*dharma*) are devoid of intrinsic nature; and based on the first kind of non-nature, it speaks of "no intrinsic nature" and so forth.
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 73, says: "Question: With what underlying intention (*saṃdhāya*) did the Blessed One say that all phenomena are..."
"Without intrinsic nature. Answer: "The three kinds of lack of intrinsic nature are taught by virtue of the capacities of those to be trained.
Furthermore, it is asked: 'Bhagavān, with what underlying intention did you say that all phenomena are unarisen, unceasing, primordially quiescent, and by nature in nirvāṇa?
Answer: 'It was said thus with reference to the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics.'"
There is scriptural authority: based on the three kinds of non-nature (*trividha-niḥsvabhāvatā*), it is taught that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Based on the first and the last [of these three], it is taught that they are unarisen and so forth, as in this very sutra and the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. There is also scriptural authority:

based on the three kinds of non-nature, it is taught that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, unarisen, undestroyed, and so forth, as in the tenth chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*.

The second explanation states: "All phenomena" refers to the three natures, namely: the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The imagined nature is definitively devoid of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Because it lacks its own characteristic, it is called "the absence of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāva*). Because it is the absence of characteristics, it is called "the lack of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*). As for the dependent [nature]...
Because the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) arises in dependence upon various conditions, it does not arise spontaneously.

Since there is no spontaneous arising, and because it lacks the nature of spontaneous arising, it is called "the naturelessness of arising" (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*). Because it is the naturelessness of arising, it is described as being without intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, because the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the pure object of focus, the characteristic of the imaginatively constructed nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*) is absent within the dependent nature; this is what is revealed as the [perfected] self-nature.
Therefore, the ultimate (*paramārtha*) is its own essence. Furthermore, because it is manifested by the absence of nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it is called "ultimately without nature.
Because it is ultimately without nature, it is termed "without nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*). By this principle, the Tathāgata has said that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self-nature.
It is not that they are called "without nature" because their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are entirely non-existent in every respect. Moreover, that...
It is said: "All phenomena are without arising and without cessation; they are quiescent from the beginning and by nature in *nirvāṇa*. With what underlying intention (*saṃdhi*) was this said?
Just as there is no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), so too is there no nature (*abhāva*). Just as there is no arising, so too is there no cessation.
Just as there is no arising and no cessation, so too are they quiescent from the beginning. Just as they are quiescent from the beginning, so too are they by nature in *nirvāṇa*.

The *Vasubandhu-śāstra* (Pán) is also like this. Furthermore, that same text states: "The secret of characteristics refers to the teaching regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, unarisen, and unceasing.
The sixth fascicle of the Liang translation of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* is the same as the *Saṃgraha*.
The reason why these various teachings differ is that the nature being negated here is exclusively the nature of false attachment (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); thus, it is stated in the *Śata-śāstra*.

And so forth. It is solely with reference to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) that it is said that all phenomena (*dharma*) lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and are without arising or cessation, in order to demonstrate that the meaning of dependent origination is not non-existent.
Therefore, this sutra universally relies upon the three natures of non-nature (*tri-niḥsvabhāvatā*) to state that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature;
however, it employs phrases such as "without arising" specifically in reference to the first and the last two types of non-nature.
However, although the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) arises in dependence upon other factors, it lacks the sense of being self-existent or arising without a cause.

Therefore, works such as the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* fully explain, by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and are without arising or ceasing.
The meaning of the three absences of intrinsic nature is detailed in a separate chapter.
