Therefore, with reference to the ultimate nature of lack of self-nature as manifested by the selflessness of phenomena, I have spoken with intentional meaning that all dharmas are unarisen,
unceasing, originally quiescent, and by nature in nirvāṇa.

The commentary states: The fourth conclusion may be understood as it stands. Question: Regarding the various intentional expressions (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*) mentioned above, upon which of the four types of secrets (*caturvidha-abhisandhi*) are they based?
Answer: According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, there are four secrets. As that treatise says: first, the secret of introduction (*avatārābhisandhi*);
second, the secret of characteristics (*lakṣaṇābhisandhi*); third, the secret of remedy (*pratipakṣābhisandhi*); and fourth, the secret of transformation (*pariṇāmābhisandhi*).
"Esoteric. These four kinds [of esoteric meanings] briefly encompass all the secret principles taught by the Tathāgata within the Mahāyāna, enabling those who enter the esoteric to do so.
Regarding the "esoteric of expression": this refers to teaching that all phenomena such as form possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) within the Śrāvaka vehicle;
this is for the purpose of ensuring they have no fear and may gradually enter the holy teachings. Regarding the "esoteric of characteristics," it refers to the three... [text fragment ends].
Regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): it is taught that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, without arising, and without cessation.
Regarding the secret counteractive measures: this refers to the Tathāgata’s proclamation of various secrets for the purpose of subduing various faults.
For example, he taught the Supreme Vehicle (*uttarayāna*) as a counteractive measure against eight kinds of obstacles. What are these eight? First, disparaging the Buddha; second...
These are: (1) disparaging the Dharma; (2) laziness; (3) being satisfied with a small amount of virtue; (4) conduct dominated by craving; (5) conduct dominated by pride;
(6) regret; and (7) an unstable nature. These serve as obstacles to counteracting the disparagement of the Buddha.
It is said that the Buddha Vipaśyin of the past was none other than my own self. This was taught in order to counteract the obstacle of disparaging the Dharma;

[it shows that] only by practicing the Mahāyāna under immeasurable Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, does one attain understanding. It was taught in order to counteract the obstacle of indolence;
[it shows that] there are sentient beings who vow to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss, and all of them will attain rebirth there by reciting [the name].
One who hears the name of the Buddha Vimalacandraprabha will certainly attain unsurpassed bodhi.
In order to counteract the obstacle of being satisfied with little merit, he sometimes praises and sometimes disparages practices such as giving.

In order to counteract the obstacle of conduct characterized by craving, he praises the richness, bliss, and adornments of the buddha-fields. In order to counteract the obstacle of prideful conduct, [he does likewise].
The praises of the Buddhas may be further enhanced as an antidote to the obstacle of remorseful conduct.

Furthermore, for those sentient beings who harbor harmful intentions toward the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it is taught that even such beings who practice disparagement can still be reborn in the heavens;
this serves as an antidote for those of indeterminate lineage, causing them to abandon the inferior aspirations of the Śrāvakas and to be prophesied for the Great [Vehicle].
Śrāvakas shall attain Buddhahood; furthermore, it is said that there is but a single vehicle (ekayāna) and no second.
Regarding "transformative secrets" (pariṇāmanābhisandhi), this refers to the cryptic terminology used in the sūtras. For example, it is said: "Awakening is not firm; one dwells well in perversion;
being tormented by extreme afflictions, one attains supreme bodhi. The intended meaning here is that within non-distraction, one gives rise to firmness.
It is indeed superior awakening. Why is this so? "Firmness" (*dṛḍha*) has two meanings: first, reality; second, agitation.

Because of this agitation, it causes the mind to become rigid and unruly; thus it is also called "firm. Those who dwell well in perversion invert the four perversions of permanence, pleasure, self, and purity into impermanence and so forth;
therefore, they are called "perversion. Because one does not retreat from this [state], it is so named.
It is named "Abiding Well. Those who are afflicted by extreme afflictions refer to those who, having practiced diligent asceticism for a long period, are oppressed by extreme exhaustion.
Regarding those who attain supreme enlightenment: if one possesses the three matters described above, one will certainly and swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi.
The hidden intention (*saṃdhāya*) clarified in this sutra is as follows: just as in the world...
The Venerable One has taught through immeasurable gateways that the thirteen dharma-gates, beginning with the aggregates (*skandha*), all possess their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*);

this corresponds to the "secret of entry" among the four types of secrets. Furthermore, the World-Honored One has taught that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and are without arising or ceasing;
this constitutes the "secret of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-guhya*) among the four. (From Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Chapter on the Summary.)
Fifth: Regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the teaching of "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) is the secret [of the characteristics].

In the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (12) and the sixth chapter of the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, based on the three absences of nature (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*), the teaching of "non-arising" (*anutpāda*) and so forth is called the secret of names and characteristics (*nāmalakṣaṇa*). This refers precisely to those texts, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, which accord with the wording of this sūtra.

Furthermore, Paramārthasamudgata, it is not because sentient beings within the realm of sentient beings perceive the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as their own essence that I establish the three kinds of naturelessness;
nor is it because they perceive the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) as their own essence that I do so.
It is for these reasons that I establish the three kinds of naturelessness.
The commentary states: From here below is the third section, concerning the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), which establishes the intent behind the three non-natures (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*).
This section has two parts: first, an explanation by way of negation; second, a positive explanation beginning with "However, by means of... This is the first part.

"Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) means either "contingent observation" or "thorough investigation. The meaning here is as follows: sentient beings do not [perceive] the three natures through some other contemplation, as [is shown in the verse]:...

The sequence [of these] is established by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Why is this so? It is not merely that the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇaniḥsvabhāvatā*) negates the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*);
rather, the other two [natures] also negate the imagined nature. However, they do not negate the dependent (*paratantra*) and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) natures;
thus, the latter two kinds of lack of intrinsic nature are established. The dependent and the perfected [natures] cannot...
Furthermore, another interpretation is that the three [natures] are established here in order to eliminate the faults of the attachments held by sentient beings;
thus, the three natures without essence are posited. It is not that those sentient beings individually grasp each of the three natures as having three distinct intrinsic natures.

To eliminate those [misconceptions], the three natures (trisvabhāva) are established. However, sentient beings do not understand the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) and the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva);
consequently, they give rise to superimpositional attachments regarding these two natures. Based on this, the three kinds of "three-naturelessness" (trividha-niḥsvabhāvatā) are established.
Between these two explanations, the latter is superior because it accords with the literal sense of the text; thus, it does not contradict this sūtra, following the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*.

Nevertheless, because sentient beings superimpose the nature of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*),
I establish the three kinds of non-nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
The commentary states: Below this is the second section, the "Conformity with Explanation," which contains two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation.

This is the heading. Its intended meaning is as follows: regarding the two natures, because the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is not established as a characteristic by way of its own intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the "characteristiclessness of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*) is established.
Regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), there is no arising by itself.
Because it is augmented [by conceptualization], the nature of birth-lack-of-intrinsic-nature (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*) is established.

Because this grasped nature does not exist within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the ultimate lack-of-intrinsic-nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*) is established. This is not to say that one separately contemplates the three natures as being intrinsic natures;
therefore, the three kinds of lack-of-intrinsic-nature are taught.
By means of the characteristic of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*),
those sentient beings give rise to linguistic expressions with respect to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The commentary says: This is the explanation. The general meaning is as follows: By means of the characteristics that are grasped, verbal expression arises;
by means of verbal expression, the three kinds of causes are established; by means of these three causes, various attachments arise; and by means of attachment—
The dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) gives rise to the faults of the threefold defilement (saṃkleśa), the wandering through the six destinies, and the cycle of birth and death.
For this reason, within this context, the three natures (trisvabhāva) are established based on the imagined characteristic (parikalpita-lakṣaṇa). Among these, there are two parts.

First, the imagined characteristic gives rise to attachment; second, as explained below, from that attachment the phenomena of cyclic existence (pravṛtti-dharma) arise. Within the first part, there are two further divisions.
Initially, one gives rise to verbal expression based on the characteristics of what is grasped;
subsequently, as it truly is, attachment arises due to that verbal expression—this is the first point. In reality, both natures are devoid of names and expressions;
however, because of the characteristics of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), verbal expression arises within these two characteristics.
Just as verbal expressions arise accordingly, so too, by means of the mind being perfumed by verbal expression, by means of the subsequent conceptualization of verbal expression,
and by means of the latent tendencies of verbal expression [does this occur].
The commentary states: This is the second [point], whereby attachment is produced through verbal expression. Within this, there are two parts:
first, how three types of causes are established through verbal expression; second, how attachment is produced by means of those three causes. This is the first part.
Regarding the term "tathatā" (suchness), it reveals the dharma being taught. Since that which is taught is not singular, it is called "tathatā. It follows...
That suchness gives rise to all verbal expressions; therefore, it is repeatedly stated as "thus and thus. Through these verbal expressions, three kinds of causes are established:
first, because the mind is perfumed by verbal expressions—this clarifies the perfuming of names and phrases (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*) among the three types of perfuming;
second, because of the subsequent realization (*anuvyavasāya*) of verbal expressions—this explains the conceptualization of subsequent realization regarding names and phrases. As [it says]:
Regarding "those among humans and devas who understand speech": this refers to three types [of conceptualization] that arise due to the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of speech.

These are not like the conceptualization of those who do not understand the latent tendencies of conventional designations (nāma-vyavahāra-anuśaya), such as oxen and sheep, which arise through latent tendencies alone.
This demonstrates that by virtue of giving rise to speech, three kinds of causes are established.
Regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), one clings to the characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The commentary states: this clarifies that clinging occurs by means of three causes. Among these three causes, the first cause is as follows:
The first cause reveals the apprehension of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). The latter two causes reveal the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
By means of these three causes, one clings to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) within the two natures.
In whatever way one clings, in that very same way one clings to the imagined nature upon the dependent nature and the perfected nature.
The commentary states: Below this is the second [section], concerning how the phenomena of saṃsāra arise due to grasping.
Within this, there are two parts: first, citing the preceding subject of grasping to reveal the cause of saṃsāra; second, properly clarifying how grasping produces the result of saṃsāra.
This is the first part. The term "tathatā" (suchness) reveals the object of grasping. Since the objects of grasping are not singular, it is called "tathatā. It follows...
That suchness gives rise to various forms of attachment; therefore, it is said again and again that "it is suchness.
Due to this attachment, one clings to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) within the two natures. By means of this attachment, one becomes a cause for cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
"By reason of these causes and conditions, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) arises in a future life.
Commentary: From here below is the second section, which clarifies the fruit of transmigration (*pravṛtti-phala*). This contains two parts; first, the arising of the dependent nature.
The three subsequent defilements constitute the first [of the four types of defilement]. Question: What is the distinction between dependent defilement (*paratantra-kleśa*) and the others? Answer:

There is a difference in terms of being general or specific, or rather, they differ in their breadth and narrowness. Dependent [defilement] is broad, because all things arising from conditions are dependent;
however, it does not encompass the nourishment of the five sense faculties (*indriya*) and so forth within the three defilements. Thus, there is a difference in scope.
Due to these causes and conditions, one is defiled by the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), or defiled by the defilement of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*),
or defiled by the defilement of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*); thus, within saṃsāra, one gallops for a long time and wanders for a long time without rest.
The commentary states: Below this is the second section, concerning the arising of the three types of defilement (*saṃkleśa*).

This section has two parts: first, the circulation through birth and death (*saṃsāra*) by means of the three defilements; and second, the circulation through the six destinies (*ṣadgati*) by means of the three defilements.
This is the first part. That is to say, with this grasping as the causal condition, the three defilements arise. As for the three defilements, they refer to [the defilements of] karma and birth.
Bound by the two fetters associated with conditions, it is therefore called "mixed and profound.

Due to this defilement, one gallops and wanders through the two types of birth and death—segmented and transformational—without rest (the meaning of the two types of birth and death is as explained in a separate chapter).
Whether in the hells, or among animals, or among hungry ghosts, or in the heavens, or among the asuras,
or among human beings, they undergo various sufferings and afflictions.
The commentary states: This refers to the second [point], wherein one transmigrates through the six destinies (*ṣadgati*) due to the three types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).

Regarding the term *naraka*: according to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 21, *ka* is a name for pleasure; *na* means "non-" or "absence"; and *ra* has the sense of "bestowing" or "endowment. Thus, that which is devoid of the endowment of pleasure is called *naraka*.
Alternatively, *loka* (from which *nara* is derived) has the sense of "rescue" or "relief," while *na* signifies "impossible" or "unattainable. Therefore, it is called *naraka*.
It is beyond remedy; thus it is named *naraka*. According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (Taishō 1545), fascicle 172:
"Nara" means person (*manuṣya*), and "ka" means evil (*pāpa*). A place where evil persons are born is called *naraka*. According to the *Abhidharma-śāstra* (Taishō 1546), fascicle 8:
"Because it is not delightful, it is called hell. Regarding "animals" (*tiryag-yoni*): the *Abhidharma-śāstra* states that their bodies...
They are called *tiryag-yoni* (animals) because they move horizontally. The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "In that realm, the bodies of most beings dwell horizontally;
or rather, within that realm, there may be some who move sideways. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "Because their form is horizontal, their movement is also horizontal;
because their movement is horizontal, their form is also horizontal; therefore, they are called *tiryag-yoni* (those who move sideways). Others say it is because they pervade all places."
They are called *tiryag-yoni* (animals). This is because they exist throughout all five destinies (*gati*). Regarding those called *preta* (hungry ghosts), the *Abhidharma-śāstra* states:

"Because they seek [sustenance] from others, they are named *preta*. The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Because they mostly harbor inferior qualities, their forms are emaciated and withered, and their bodies and minds are flighty and restless;
therefore, they are named *preta*. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Because hunger and thirst are intensified, they are named..."

Regarding *preta* (hungry ghosts), some say they are called "ghosts" (*pīśāca*) because they are driven into service; they are constantly driven about in various places by the devas and are perpetually running to and fro.
As for what is called a "deva," the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "They are called devas because of their radiance. The *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"A deva is so named because they are honored and lofty, possessing sovereign spiritual power, and are the object of prayers from the multitude; therefore, they are called devas. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* [states...].
The *Śāstra* says: They are called "devas" (*deva*) because their radiance increases; for their natural bodily light constantly illuminates day and night alike.
Regarding *asura*, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: *sura* means "deva," in the sense of being "sovereign" (*īśvara*). The prefix *a-* signifies negation, indicating that they are not devas.
Because their sovereignty is diminished compared to the devas, they are called *asuras*. The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: *Sura*...
Because they are gods (*deva*), yet are not [true] gods, they are called *asura*. Furthermore, "sura" means "handsome"; because they are not handsome, they are called *asura*.
Regarding what is called "human" (*manuṣya*): the *Abhidharma-śāstra* states that they are called humans because their minds are tranquil;
the *Nyāyānusāra* states that they are called humans because they possess much deliberation; and the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that they are so called because they are capable of tranquility.
The Great Master [Vasubandhu] states that among the five destinies, none possess a mind capable of such tranquility as that of humans; this is explained in detail therein.
For a full exposition, one should consult the *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, as presented in their respective chapters.
Furthermore, Paramārthasamudgata, if there are sentient beings who, from the very beginning, have not planted roots of virtue, have not purified their obscurations,
have not matured their mental continuums, have not extensively cultivated resolute conviction, and have not been able to accumulate the two types of provisions— merit and wisdom.
The commentary states: From here below is the third section, which establishes the intent behind the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) by way of their stages. This contains two parts:
first, the explanation of the nature of the lack of self-nature in production (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*) by way of the five stages;

second, from "Even though it is thus" onwards, the explanation of the latter two kinds of naturelessness by way of the stages of application (*prayoga*) and so forth. Regarding the gateways of contemplation, there are five stages, as established in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle nine, states: "What are the five stages of entering into consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*)? First is the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), which refers to cultivating the Mahāyāna factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*).
The commentary explains: this begins from the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) up to the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

Second is the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), which refers to cultivating the Mahāyāna factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*). The commentary explains: this occurs at the end of the tenth stage of dedication."

Mind. Third is the stage of thorough penetration, which refers to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) wherein bodhisattvas abide. Fourth is the stage of cultivation, which refers to the path of meditation (*bhāvanāmārga*) wherein bodhisattvas abide.
Fifth is the ultimate stage, which refers to abiding in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Now, based on this sūtra, these are divided into two sections. The first, concerning the five stages, distinguishes the nature of non-self-existence in arising; that is to say:

The first [of the three natures] refers to the stage of the initial accumulation of merit (*sambhāra-avasthā*) and the stage prior to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), which are the positions for planting the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).

The latter two natures are established by way of the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*) and so forth; these correspond to the three intermediate stages within the system of Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*).

Excluding those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), for they are not the intended audience. This constitutes the first [section]. Within this, there are three parts: first, clarifying the purpose of the teaching;

second, "I [teach] for their sake," etc., which is the formal teaching according to the capacity of the listeners; and third, "Having heard that," etc., which distinguishes the benefits of the teaching.
This is the first part. Now, regarding the intended audience, there are five stages. The first is the stage of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). That is to say:
The stage prior to the ten faiths is the stage of planting the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya-kuśala-mūla*).
The method for planting these roots of goodness conducive to liberation is as explained in the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*. Second is the stage of purity, which refers precisely to the ten faiths;
this is because one is able to purify karmic offenses to a certain extent. Thus, the second fascicle of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "Those whose karmic offenses have not yet been purified..."

The *Sūtra on the Origination of the Purification of Karmic Obstacles* states: "Because the unique ignorance of ordinary beings within the internal [Dharma] has been eternally severed, they do not create karmic obstacles.

Third is the stage of the maturation of the continuum, which refers to the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*), for it enables the accomplishment of the continuity of faith and the other [faculties].
As the *Gambhīrārtha-samcaya* states: "By the power of those matured roots of goodness... Fourth is the stage of... [text fragment ends].
The stage of cultivating resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) refers to the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*), because resolute conviction is predominantly manifest therein.
The stage of accumulating the provisions of merit and wisdom refers to the ten stages of dedication (*daśapariṇāmana*), because it fully possesses both provisions of merit and wisdom.
The intent here is to say that those who have not yet planted roots of goodness are caused to plant them, and so on, until those who have not yet completed the provisions are caused to complete them.

Because [the previous explanation] is sufficient. For these reasons, it is said that there is "non-nature in arising. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that this passage distinguishes the five matters within the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*);
it does not establish five stages by correlating them with the forty mental states (*citta*). The distinction between the five matters is as analyzed previously.
"For their sake, I have taught all phenomena based on the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in arising (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*).

The commentary states: This is the second correct teaching according to the capacities of sentient beings. That is to say, since beginningless time, sentient beings have failed to realize the principle of the dependent origination of phenomena;
they falsely cling to the notion that things arise without cause or spontaneously. Therefore, the World-Honored One...
Based on the nature of the lack of self-existence in terms of arising (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*), it is taught that all phenomena arise from causes and do not exist spontaneously.
Having heard this, one is able to partially comprehend, within all dependently arisen formations (*saṃskāra*), that they are impermanent and non-eternal.
"Having understood that these are unstable and subject to transformation," the commentary explains:
this is the third benefit of hearing the teaching. The four benefits are divided into four parts:

first, the benefit of comprehending impermanence; second, the benefit of fear and revulsion; third, the benefit of ceasing evil and cultivating good; fourth, [the benefit of... five... [text fragment].
The fulfillment of the objective is the first [of the three]. This refers to what the World-Honored One taught:
that from ignorance as a condition arise volitional formations, and so on, up to old age and death; they do not arise from Īśvara or other such causes.
By means of this, sentient beings partially comprehend that all phenomena are impermanent and lack constancy. Because they are impermanent, they are unstable, unlike *nirvāṇa*.

Because it is free from arising and ceasing, it is that which is "dwelling in peace. Furthermore, regarding all conditioned phenomena— which are characterized by the prior cessation and subsequent arising of things,
and by the gradual process of decay, ruin, and transformation—
one gives rise to fear toward all formations and develops a profound sense of weary detachment.
The commentary states: This is the second benefit of fear and revulsion, as can be understood from the text.
Having given rise to fear in the mind and developed deep revulsion, one restrains all evils; regarding all unwholesome dharmas, one is able to refrain from committing them.
Regarding all wholesome dharmas, one is able to diligently practice them.
The commentary states: this is the third benefit, which is the cessation of evil and the cultivation of goodness. This can be understood from the text.
Because one practices the causes of goodness, those who have not yet planted roots of goodness are able to plant them, and those whose obscurations have not yet been purified are able to purify them.

Purifying it, they cause the immature continuum to reach maturity. By means of these causes and conditions, they cultivate resolute conviction extensively and also extensively accumulate the two kinds of provisions: merit and wisdom.

The commentary states: This is the fourth [of the] five things that constitute complete benefit. The characteristics of these five things should be understood by analogy with what was explained above.
Although they thus plant various roots of goodness, even accumulating the two kinds of provisions—merit and wisdom—until they are fully gathered.
However, regarding the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in arising, they have not yet been able to understand, as it truly is,
the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in characteristics and the two kinds of ultimate lack of intrinsic nature.
The commentary states: Below this, the second section concerns the stages of application (*prayoga*) and so forth, explaining the latter two types of lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).

This section contains three parts: first, clarifying the purpose for which the teaching is given; second, "The Tathāgata, for their sake... and below, the actual teaching according to the capacities of the disciples;
and third, "Having heard this... and below, distinguishing the benefits of the teaching. This is the first part. Within it, there are two sections; the first is as follows:
This clarifies two kinds of non-nature that have not yet been fully understood. Subsequently, it distinguishes the nature of that which is not yet understood as being without nature.

That is to say, sentient beings, upon hearing it taught that all phenomena arise from conditions and are not produced by a creator god (Īśvara) or other such causes, thereby comprehend meanings such as impermanence.
They accumulate the two provisions of merit and wisdom, yet they are still unable to fully realize the nature of all existents.
Because all conditioned phenomena are like illusions and do not possess a real intrinsic nature, one might instead cling to the notion that all phenomena definitely possess a real intrinsic nature.

This is largely due to a failure to understand the lack of nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇaniḥsvabhāvatā*), or alternatively, a failure to understand the two kinds of ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*paramārthaniḥsvabhāvatā*) as explained above.
Regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), they have not yet correctly developed revulsion, have not yet correctly become dispassionate, have not yet correctly attained liberation,
and have not yet fully liberated themselves from the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), the defilement of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), and the defilement of birth (*jāti-saṃkleśa*).
The commentary states: This is the second [point], clarifying the fault of non-comprehension. It refers to the failure to comprehend that phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Consequently, one is unable to correctly cultivate revulsion toward all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth. "Correct revulsion" refers to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*); "correct detachment from desire" refers to the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*);
and "correct liberation" and so forth refer to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), as well as the path of advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*). [This pertains to] the afflictions...
The karma of affliction gives rise to the three types of defilement, as explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and other such texts.

For their sake, the Tathāgata further taught the essential points of the Dharma, namely: the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*) and the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
The commentary states: From here below is the second section, the formal teaching according to the capacity of the audience. This section contains two parts: first, the formal teaching itself;

second, the clarification of the purpose of the teaching. This is the first part. That is to say, those at the stage of the final preparatory practice (*prayoga*) at the conclusion of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) are suitable to hear this teaching; therefore, it is taught for their sake.
This is for the purpose of enabling them to correctly feel revulsion toward all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), to become correctly dispassionate, to attain correct liberation,
and to transcend all afflictive obscurations (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), to transcend all karmic obscurations (*karma-saṃkleśa*),
and to transcend all obscurations of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*).
The commentary states: This second section clarifies the purpose of teaching.

It is intended so that those in the stages of application (*prayoga*) and so forth may swiftly accomplish the path of application and the like, and so that they may transcend the three kinds of affliction (*saṃkleśa*). For this reason, two further types of lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) are explained.

Having heard this teaching thus expounded, regarding the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in arising, they are able to correctly believe in and understand the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in characteristics and the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in the ultimate sense;
they investigate and contemplate it, and penetrate it as it truly is.
The commentary states: Below this is the third section, which distinguishes the benefits of the teaching. This section contains two parts:

first, clarifying the benefits obtained during the stage of application (*prayoga*); second, following the section on the *paratantra-svabhāva*, distinguishing the benefits obtained in the two stages [the first and second] of the grounds (*bhūmi*).
This is the first part. Herein, the primary focus is on the benefits obtained during the stage of application. Now, as for the stage of application...

Regarding the stage of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), various explanations differ. Some say it belongs to the second *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, because it is the proximate preparation (*sāmantaka*) for the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), just as the "not-yet-attained" concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) belongs to the first dhyāna.

Others say it is precisely within the tenth stage of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) of the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, because one has not yet entered the [bodhisattva] stages (*bhūmi*). Although there are these two views, the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla maintains the latter.
Explanation: As stated in the ninth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it is called "preparatory application" (*prayoga*) because it is proximate to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Within this stage, because one hears the teachings on the two kinds of lack of nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), one performs the four investigations (*paryeṣaṇā*) and the four correct realizations (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*).

One retains the consciousness that acts as the grasper (*grāhaka-vijñāna*) while discarding the emptiness of the grasped (*grāhya-śūnyatā*); this is precisely the nature of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasvabhāva*), which is manifested by that very absence of nature.
The ultimate truth is called the "ultimate naturelessness. If explained in detail, it is as stated in the ninth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Therefore, it is said here: the analytical contemplation regarding the two kinds of naturelessness constitutes the four thorough investigations (*catvāraḥ paryeṣaṇāḥ*).
"Thoroughly penetrating reality as it is" refers to the four types of knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-parijñāna*).

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that "discriminative reflection" refers to the stage of the four investigations (*catasraḥ paryeṣaṇāḥ*), while "thoroughly penetrating reality as it is" refers to the stage of penetration (*prativedha*) from the first bhūmi upward.
Regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), one is able to refrain from adhering to the characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Commentary: Hereafter is the second section, which distinguishes the sixfold benefits obtained during the two stages of the *bhūmis*. There are six such benefits.

This is divided into six parts: first, the elimination of the grasped characteristics; second, the non-arising of the three causes; third, the cessation of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);
fourth, the severing of the cause of future suffering; fifth, the ability to lead to the three paths; and sixth, the separation from the three defilements (*saṃkleśa*). This is the first [part].

This refers to the two stages of the *bhūmi*s. Because they have heard what was previously explained regarding the two kinds of naturelessness, they are able to refrain from clinging to the *parikalpita-svabhāva*.
This is due to the wisdom that is not permeated by verbal expression, the wisdom that does not follow after the conceptualization of verbal expression, and because it is free from verbal expression.

"Because of the knowledge of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). The commentary states: This refers to the second [set of] three causes for non-arising, namely, because of non-appropriation (*anupādāna*).

Since these three causes are not established, and because the causes are not established, three kinds of knowledge arise. Regarding the "three kinds of knowledge": first, the knowledge that verbal designations (*abhilāpa*) are unconditioned (*avāsita*); second, [the knowledge that]...
Discourse does not follow discursive cognition (*buddhi*). Third, discourse is free from latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) through wisdom.

Regarding these three types of wisdom, there are two explanations. First, they are designated according to their objects; that is, the subsequently attained wisdom arises by taking three objects as its conditions, and thus the names of the three wisdoms are established.
Alternatively, it is said they are designated according to their causes; that is, the two kinds of wisdom regarding the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) arise from three kinds of causes.
Because it is that from which [the dependent nature] arises, three names are established.
It can extinguish the characteristics of the *paratantra-svabhāva*.
The commentary states: This refers to the third [stage], the extinction of the *paratantra*, meaning that by not giving rise to the three causes, one accomplishes the three kinds of wisdom.
By means of the three knowledges, one is able to extinguish that which depends on others.
Sustained by the power of knowledge within the present life, one is able to permanently sever and extinguish the causes for future lives.
The commentary states: This is the fourth [stage], the abandonment of the cause of future suffering.

Because the dependent nature (*paratantra*) has been extinguished by the three preceding types of knowledge, within the present body there exists the knowledge of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*). Since it is sustained by this knowledge of skillful means, that fundamental knowledge (*mūla-jñāna*) [is established].
One is able to permanently eliminate the causes for future existence.
By means of these causes and conditions, one is able to correctly feel revulsion toward all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), correctly become free from desire, and correctly attain liberation.

The commentary states: This refers to the fifth [topic], which cites the three paths—namely, the path of preparation (*prayoga*), the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya*), and the path of liberation (*vimukti*).
These are capable of universally liberating one from the three types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*): those consisting of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and birth (*janman*).
The commentary states: This is the sixth [topic], the separation from the three types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*). It may be understood according to the text.

Furthermore, Paramārthasaṃudgata, sentient beings belonging to the lineage of the Śrāvakayāna also realize the unsurpassed, secure *nirvāṇa* by means of this path and through these tracks of practice.
So too do sentient beings belonging to the lineage of the Pratyekabuddhayāna and the Tathāgatas...
Sentient beings belonging to the various spiritual lineages (*gotra*) also realize the unsurpassed, secure *nirvāṇa* by means of this path and through these tracks of practice.

The commentary states: From here below is the fourth section, which establishes the meaning of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) in terms of the three natures of non-essence (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). This section contains three parts.

The first section establishes the meaning of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) by way of the Noble Path. Next, from "Good son" onwards, it clarifies that *śrāvakas* who are inclined toward quiescence (*śama*) will certainly not attain Buddhahood.
Finally, from "If they turn back" onwards, it clarifies that *śrāvakas* who do turn back will certainly attain Buddhahood. The general purport of the explanation is as follows:
In the first segment, with reference to the three lineages (*gotra*), the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya*) taught them as the One Vehicle. Regarding...
This is the true principle. It possesses the three vehicles (*triyāna*), each of which realizes the ultimate *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

The intent of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* is also the same as this explanation. Regarding the meaning of the second section: those of fixed nature among the two vehicles realize only the *nirvāṇa* without remainder of the two vehicles;

there is absolutely no principle that they will later attain Buddhahood. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "That which is realized by the two vehicles is [the state of] without remainder..."

Nirvana consists solely of the pure *dharmadhātu* of *tathatā*. The meaning of the third section is that those of indeterminate lineage who have turned toward the Śrāvaka vehicle will certainly attain Buddhahood.

Therefore, the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paṛivarta*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that for those of the two-vehicle lineages, it is in principle certain that they shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
If one relies on this teaching, the three vehicles are taught as expedients; in terms of reality, [there is but one].
It is because [the teaching] is one. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna);

there is no second, nor is there a third, except for the Buddha’s skillful means. While the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda* each rely on one specific meaning, this present section contains the meanings of both;
therefore, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* is the most definitive in meaning (*nītārtha*). (The meaning is as discussed in a separate chapter). Within the first section, it is further divided into...
This consists of three parts: first, it clarifies that each of the three vehicles realizes the nirvana without remainder specific to its own vehicle;
second, it explains their unity by way of the skillful means of the noble path; and third, it clarifies the actual distinction between the three vehicles. This is the first part.
That is to say, those of the three vehicles’ spiritual lineages each realize the realm of the wondrous nirvana without remainder through the wondrously pure path of non-nature. However, that...
Because the Noble Path has the sense of "leading through," it is called the "Path" (*mārga*). Furthermore, because the various noble ones travel along it, it is also called a "track" (*pratipad*).
By means of this path and track, one leaves behind all afflictions and the body of outflow-tainted suffering, and realizes the bliss of eternal, quiescent cessation;
therefore, it is described as the "secure *nirvāṇa*."
All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas share this single, wondrously pure path; they all equally attain this ultimate purity.
There is no second vehicle. It is based on this that, with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*), it is said that there is only one vehicle (*ekayāna*).
The commentary states: This is the second explanation concerning skillful means. First, regarding the term "śrāvaka" (hearer): in the holy teachings of all Buddhas, sound is the primary medium.
Having heard these sounds of the teaching from teachers and friends, one practices and realizes them through successive stages, thereby attaining eternal transcendence from the mundane world.

Because they practice minor deeds and attain minor fruits, they are called *śrāvakas* (Hearers). As for those called *pratyekabuddhas* (Solitary Realizers), they constantly delight in tranquility and do not wish to dwell in company.
Having perfected their preparatory practices (*prayoga*) without the instruction of teachers or friends, they naturally awaken alone and transcend the world forever.

Because they practice middling deeds and attain middling fruits, they are called *pratyekabuddhas*. Alternatively, because they awaken to the fruit of sainthood by observing conditions (*pratyaya*), they are also called *pratyayabuddhas* (Condition-Realizers). Thus it is said:
A Bodhisattva is one who aspires to great enlightenment and feels compassion for sentient beings;

or one who seeks bodhi with firm and fierce resolve, practicing and realizing it over a long period of time, forever transcending the mundane world, and attaining great conduct and great fruit—therefore, they are called a Bodhisattva.
This is explained in detail in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. To state the general meaning: it refers to those of the three vehicles, all of whom possess this single, wondrous, and non-dual [nature].
Regarding the path of nature (*prakṛti-mārga*): this very path is called ultimate purity (*atyanta-viśuddhi*).
Since there is only this path and no second, it is designated as the "One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*) based on this single path. Therefore, the *Gambhīrārtha-samgraha* states: "There is only one pure path;
there is no second," yet it does not separately mention "ultimate purity. Thus, we know that ultimate purity is itself the Sublime (*sūkṣma*).

It is also the path of purification (*viśuddhimārga*). Furthermore, it is said that "one" has three meanings: first, it is called "one" because the path is one; second, it is called "one" because the fruit is one;
third, it is called "one" because the principle is one. According to this text, there are two [meanings] here.
The wondrously pure path is the oneness of the path; ultimate purity is the oneness of the fruit. Based on these two kinds of oneness, there is no second;
therefore, with a profound underlying intent, it is said that there is only the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

This is not the same as the explanation of the One Vehicle in the fourth fascicle below, which speaks of the One Vehicle because there is no distinction in principle. However, the One Vehicle refers exclusively to the Single Buddha Vehicle (*eka-buddhayāna*).
Therefore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas all enter the Mahāyāna; the Mahāyāna is itself the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*).
Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "In the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle;
there is neither a second nor a third. Alternatively, the Dharmakāya may be used to clarify the One Vehicle; thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra* says: "By means of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya..."
It is no different from the *dharmakāya* of the śrāvakas; therefore, they are granted the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). This will be explained in detail later.

This is the "explanation by enumeration" (*saṃkhyānirukti*) among the six types. Regarding its essential nature (*svabhāva*): if it refers to the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), its essential nature consists of the aggregates and so forth subsumed under the categories of the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna-cittavarga*).
If, however, it is taken as the *dharmakāya*, then true suchness (*tathatā*) is its essential nature; this is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) for identifying its essence.
Within the gateway of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit are taken as the One Vehicle. However, this sacred teaching of the One Vehicle is vast and manifold;
its translators were numerous, and its underlying intent is profound and far-reaching. For this reason, new and old schools have vied with one another to raise disputes.
A certain class of masters, such as Paramārtha and others, relying upon the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other sūtras and śāstras, all maintain this position. First.
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. Thus, the seventh fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* asks:
"In the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), is there a self? The Buddha replied: "Good son, 'self' is the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha.
That all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature is precisely the meaning of 'self. Furthermore, the twenty-fifth [fascicle] says: "Sentient beings and Buddhas..."
The nature [of all things] is neither identical nor different. The Buddhas are equal, like empty space; all sentient beings equally and universally possess it.
(This explains the nature of reality. Furthermore, the twenty-seventh [chapter] states: "Lion's Roar" means definitive teaching:
all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. It further says: For example, suppose there is a person whose house contains milk and curd. Someone...
He asked, "Do you have ghee? He replied, "I have it. Although the curd is not actually ghee, because it will certainly be obtained through skillful means, he said, "I have ghee.
Sentient beings are likewise; they all possess a mind. For anyone who possesses a mind...
They will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. For this reason, I definitively declare that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
(This explains the nature of practice. Furthermore, in the thirty-third [chapter] it says: "All sentient beings equally possess Buddha-nature;
they are all identical in the One Vehicle, identical in liberation, identical in cause, identical in fruit, and identical in sweetness."
"Śāriputra, all shall attain the eternal, blissful, self, and pure. This is called the single flavor. (This explains both principle and practice. Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle; there is neither a second nor a third, except for what the Buddhas teach as skillful means.
It also says: "Only this one reality is true; the other two are not real. Furthermore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "The voice..."
Those who hear of the Pratyekabuddhas all enter the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Questions of the Devaputra Susīma* states:
Mañjuśrī said, "All shall certainly attain Buddhahood; you must not harbor doubts. Why is this?
Because all shall attain the awakening of a Tathāgata. This is explained at length therein. Moreover, the second chapter of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* clarifies the five... [text ends].
The *Shengxing lun* (Treatise on the Nature of the Vehicle) states: "There are two types of icchantikas: first, those who have incinerated all roots of goodness;
second, those who, out of compassion for all sentient beings, make a vow to exhaust [the world]. Of these two, one will certainly not attain Buddhahood. The full explanation is as stated therein.
The first fascicle of the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra* states that although the wording differs, the meaning is the same as the previous version.

According to such scriptures, sentient beings without the [Buddha-]nature can also attain Buddhahood. Furthermore, the fifteenth fascicle of the *She dasheng lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya) by Liang says:
"The fifth is to have the activity of rescuing through the vehicle," and so on, until it says: "He is able to establish those śrāvakas whose faculties are not yet determined."

"Because one practices the Mahāyāna. The commentary explains: Up to and including the attainment of the five faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*), they are not called the "faculties of certainty" (*niyata-indriya*), because one has not yet attained the state of an Ārya.

If one attains the three faculties beginning with "the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), they are then called the "faculties of certainty," because one has attained the state of an Ārya.
If one reaches the stage of the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*), it is not called the "state of certainty," because one has not yet escaped the four evil destinies. If...
Upon reaching the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), one is said to have attained a "fixed nature" (*niyata-gotra*), because one has escaped the four miserable realms.

According to the interpretation of the Hīnayāna, if one has not yet attained this fixed nature of the faculties, one may turn from the Small Vehicle to the Great Vehicle; however, once the fixed nature of the faculties is attained, it cannot be changed.
In such a case, for these Śrāvakas, there would be no sense in transforming the Small into the Great. How, then, can the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) be taught? Now, according to the Mahāyāna...
[Answer: Those who have not yet exclusively cultivated the Bodhisattva path are all termed "those of indeterminate faculties.

Therefore, every Śrāvaka possesses the potential for their small vehicle [path] to be transformed into the Great Vehicle. Having thus established these persons of the Small and Great Vehicles, one causes them to practice the Mahāyāna.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 84, states: "There are four kinds of paths: the path of humans and devas, and the paths of the three vehicles."
There are four [reasons]. It is the duty of a bodhisattva to lead sentient beings onto the Great Path.
If they are capable of entering the Great Path, he establishes them therein; if they are not capable of entering nirvana, he establishes them in the blessings and joys of humans and devas.
They act as the causes and conditions for nirvāṇa. Furthermore, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* states: "There are four kinds of śrāvakas: first, those who are fixed;
second, those with overweening pride; third, those who have regressed from bodhicitta; and fourth, emanated śrāvakas.

Regarding two kinds of śrāvakas, the Tathāgata bestows upon them the prediction of enlightenment—namely, the emanated śrāvakas and those who, having regressed, subsequently give rise to bodhicitta again."
Regarding the two types of śrāvakas who are fixed [in their destiny], because their faculties are not yet mature, the Tathāgata does not bestow upon them a prophecy.
As for the bodhisattvas to whom he does bestow a prophecy, it is as a skillful means to cause them to resolve their minds toward enlightenment.

According to these passages, there are certainly no sentient beings devoid of the potential for awakening (agotra), nor are there any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas of fixed nature who will definitely fail to attain buddhahood; thus, the *Saṃdhinirmocana*...

Regarding the statement that [the attainment of Buddhahood] is definitely not achieved according to the *Sūtras* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, this is said in reference to the period when one's faculties (*indriya*) are not yet mature;
it does not mean that Buddhahood is definitively unattainable. Therefore, the second volume of the *Ratnagotravibhāga* asks:
"As previously stated, icchantikas never enter nirvāṇa and lack the nature for nirvāṇa. What is the meaning of this? It is intended to demonstrate the refutation [of the Mahāyāna]."
Because it is the cause of the Mahāyāna, and so forth, up to "relying upon immeasurable time," it is thus stated.

Since that pure nature (*viśuddha-dhātu*) truly exists, one cannot say that it is eternally and ultimately devoid of a pure mind. Question: According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle eighty, it is said:
"In the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*), one is far removed from all activities of generating and proceeding."

All karma and all functional efforts are completely stilled. If it is as stated above—that even those who are determined śrāvakas can attain Buddhahood—how then should one interpret the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*?
Answer: According to the third fascicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it says:
"After my parinirvāṇa, there will be further disciples who have not heard this sūtra; they do not know and do not realize the conduct of bodhisattvas."
Regarding the merits they have attained, they conceive the thought of extinction and enter into *nirvāṇa*.
I shall become a Buddha in another land under a different name. Although these people conceive the thought of extinction and enter into *nirvāṇa*, they shall seek the Buddha’s wisdom in that land.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 93, also states this. Furthermore, regarding *nirvāṇa*...

The *Pāṇḍaravāsinī-sūtra*, fascicle 23, states: "The abodes of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—measuring eighty thousand, sixty thousand, forty thousand, twenty thousand, and ten thousand [yojanas]—are termed 'nirvāṇa.
Only the abode of the Unsurpassed Dharma-Lord, the Holy King, is named 'Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the fourth verse of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says:
Just as a piece of wood floating on the ocean Is driven along by the turning waves, So too are the śrāvakas: tossed about by the winds of signs,
Though free from the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), They remain bound by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of affliction,
Relishing the bliss of meditative absorption (*samādhi-sukha*), Abiding in the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), Without any ultimate destination.
Nor shall they ever regress; they attain the body of all samādhis. For immeasurable kalpas they remain unaware, like a person who is intoxicated;
only when the wine has worn off do they awaken. Having attained the unsurpassed essence of Buddhahood, this is my true Dharmakāya.
The second [case] and the second [instance] likewise share this same meaning. Furthermore, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* states:

"In reality there is nothing, yet those with overweening pride (adhimāna) perceive it as existing; because they possess worldly *samāpatti* while there is in fact no *nirvāṇa*, they give rise to the notion that it is *nirvāṇa*."
To counteract this, it should be understood that the parable of the conjured city is taught. Furthermore, it says: "The fourth person is one who is skillfully led into the city of nirvāṇa.
As for the city of nirvāṇa, it is the city of the various dhyānas and samādhis; having passed beyond that city, [one proceeds further].

This is because it causes one to enter the city of Great Parinirvāṇa. According to such passages, the "nirvana without remainder" (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa) taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi* is identical to the "samādhi of the bliss of samādhi" (*samādhisukha-samādhi*) taught in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
Because it is free from the [rebirth] of fragmented existence (*pariccheda*), it is called "without remainder."
It is not that there is no remainder at all, because there is transformation. The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states that there is no [nirvana] without remainder; thus that sūtra says:
"Therefore, Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have a remainder, because the dharmas of birth are not yet exhausted. Since there is birth, there is a remainder."

Because the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been accomplished; because impure matters have not been fully exhausted; because there is still that which must be done; because one has not yet crossed over to the further shore;
and because there is still that which must be abandoned—due to this non-abandonment, one remains far from the realm of *nirvāṇa*.
Even the statement that "one attains *nirvāṇa*" is the Buddha’s skillful means (*upāya*). Only the Tathāgata attains *parinirvāṇa*; this should be understood accordingly. [Eighty thousand...]

Regarding the kalpas and so forth: entering the bliss of samādhi is conventionally termed "nirvana without remainder. In reality, when both body and wisdom are extinguished without remainder, it is nirvana without remainder.

(However, those such as the srotāpanna are designated by their original names, though they are in fact those beyond training. Therefore, the followers of the two vehicles will certainly attain Buddhahood.

Based on these various sutras, the One Vehicle is taught in its true sense, while the Two Vehicles are taught as a provisional designation. Second, the Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang, relying upon various sutras and śāstras...
It is established that there are five classes [of beings]. Sentient beings without lineage (*agotra*) lack the nature for *nirvāṇa*.
Those of fixed nature among the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) will certainly not attain Buddhahood. Thus, the first fascicle of the *Bhadraśīla-sūtra* states:

"If one lacks the bodhisattva lineage, even if they resolve their mind [for enlightenment] and diligently cultivate with vigor, they will ultimately be unable to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*...

The first fascicle of the *Śāstra* states: "Because those who lack the lineage possess no seed-nature (*gotra*), even if they resolve their minds and diligently cultivate with vigor, they will certainly not reach the ultimate state of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The thirty-fifth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* agrees with the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Furthermore, this sūtra says: "Even though a person belonging to the śrāvaka lineage who is solely oriented toward tranquility..."

Even if they were to receive the guidance of the various skillful means and courageous applications established by all the Buddhas, they would ultimately never be able to sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, the second chapter of the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "Those persons who have perfected the *śrāvaka* nature of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-nirvāṇa*)... All [the Buddhas]...
Even if a Buddha exhausts all his power to teach and transform them, he cannot cause them to sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and attain unsurpassed bodhi.
I call such persons "śrāvakas of quiescence. Furthermore, the fifth fascicle of the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra* states:

"Beings of right determination are the true vessels of the Dharma; whether the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma or does not preach the Dharma, they all attain liberation. [Those of] wrong determination...
It is determined that such sentient beings are not vessels for the True Dharma.

Whether the Tathāgata were to preach the Dharma for them or not to preach it, they would ultimately be incapable of realizing liberation. Having known those sentient beings as truly being non-vessels for the Dharma, the Tathāgata simply abandons them.
The third fascicle of the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* states: "The three groups of sentient beings are distinct."
This refers to the Śrāvaka-yāna. The Mahāyāna consists only of two groups: those who are curable and those who are incurable.
As for what is called "wrongly fixed" (*mithyātva-niyata*), it refers to those icchantikas. "Rightly fixed" (*samyaktva-niyata*) refers to Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, and those of the two vehicles.
Furthermore, the third fascicle of the *Śīla-sūtra* states: "There are four kinds of ways in which sentient beings are disciplined: first, those who possess the nature of a śrāvaka."

First, those who attain the path of the śrāvaka; second, those of the pratyekabuddha nature who attain the path of the pratyekabuddha; third, those with the buddha-nature who immediately attain the path of the Buddha;
and fourth, those with the human-and-deva nature who attain the bliss of humans and devas. These are called the four. The Śrīmālā-sūtra says:
Furthermore, it is like the great earth, which bears four heavy burdens. What are these four? First, the great oceans; second, the various mountains;

third, the grasses and trees; and fourth, sentient beings. In this same way, sons and daughters of good family who uphold the True Dharma establish themselves as the great earth, capable of bearing these four kinds of heavy responsibilities, just like that great earth. Why is this so?

These constitute four [categories]. That is to say, for those sentient beings who lack virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and have not heard the Dharma, one brings them to maturity through the roots of goodness of humans and devas.
To those who seek the vehicle of the śrāvaka, one imparts the Śrāvaka-yāna; to those who seek the pratyekabuddha, one imparts the Pratyekabuddha-yāna;
and to those who seek the Mahāyāna, one imparts the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, fascicle 593, states:
If there are classes of sentient beings whose nature is determined for the Śrāvaka Vehicle, having heard this Dharma, they will swiftly realize their own stage of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*).
Those whose nature is determined for the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, having heard this Dharma, will swiftly attain liberation by relying on their own vehicle.
Those whose nature is determined for the Unsurpassed Vehicle, having heard this Dharma, will swiftly...

They realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. As for those classes of sentient beings who, though they have not yet entered the state of rightness and departure from birth, are indeterminate regarding the three vehicles—upon hearing this Dharma, they all resolve to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The ninth chapter of the *Daśacakra-sūtra* shares the same intent as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. According to the second fascicle of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, it states:
"Regarding those who achieve [enlightenment] as human beings, there are briefly four types: those with the lineage of the śrāvaka, who achieve it by means of the Śrāvaka-yāna;
those with the lineage of the pratyekabuddha, who achieve it by means of the Pratyekabuddha-yāna; and those with the lineage of the Buddha."
They are brought to fulfillment by means of the unsurpassed Mahāyāna. Those who lack the spiritual lineage (*agotra*) are brought to fulfillment by means of the happy realms (*sugati*).

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) in the *Yogācārabhūmi* are also the same as those in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*. Furthermore, the second fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
Those who lack the dharma for nirvāṇa are deficient in the seeds of the bodhi of the three vehicles. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 67, states:
"One who abides in the absence of lineage is called one who ultimately lacks the dharma for parinirvāṇa," and so on, as explained at length.

Furthermore, the fifty-second [fascicle] states: "If, within the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of the thorough penetration of *tathatā*, there exist seeds of ultimate obstruction, one establishes such as a person (*pudgala*) of the lineage that does not attain *parinirvāṇa*.
If it is otherwise, one establishes them as persons of the lineage possessing the nature for *parinirvāṇa*. Also, the first fascicle of the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* [states]:
It is said: There are two kinds of lack of nature (*abhāva*). First, the temporary absence of parinirvāṇa; second, the ultimate absence of parinirvāṇa.

Regarding those whose nature is the temporary absence of parinirvāṇa, there are four types: first, those who exclusively practice unwholesome conduct; second, those who have universally severed all wholesome dharmas;
third, those who lack the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*); and fourth, those whose wholesome causes are meager and incomplete.
[This is] sufficient. Those who ultimately lack the dharma of *nirvāṇa* have no nature for parinirvāṇa because they lack the cause;
they seek only birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and do not seek *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, the fourteenth fascicle of the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) from the Liang dynasty states:
"Because those obstructing causes are incomplete, all within the realm of sentient beings abide in two kinds of fixed states (*niyata*). The Buddhas have no mastery over them. — Vasubandhu.
The commentary states: Sentient beings who lack the nature for nirvāṇa are said to be "deficient in causes. Within this state, the Buddhas are unable to cause them to attain parinirvāṇa;
they also lack mastery over supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), are greedily attached to saṃsāra, and have no faith or delight in the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (translated during the Great Tang) says:
The realm of sentient beings is pervasive; though possessed of obstructions, they lack the cause.
These two types [of karma] proceed with certainty (the two certainties of creating karma and experiencing its fruit).
Regarding this, the tenth fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Vyākhyāyukti* states: "If there are sentient beings in the realm who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa, they are called..."
"Lacking the cause" means that because they lack the cause for nirvāṇa—namely, the absence of the spiritual lineage (agotra)—the Buddhas have no sovereign power over them.
The *Mahāvyutpatti* also shares this same intent. Furthermore, the *Anabhilāpya-śāstra* states:

"Because they possess the obstacles of afflictions, karma, and maturation, they are called 'possessing obstacles. Because they lack the cause for nirvāṇa—the absence of the spiritual lineage—they are called 'lacking [the cause].'"
Regarding the cause: the Buddhas do not possess the sovereign power to bring all sentient beings mentioned above to nirvana, as explained at length elsewhere.
According to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, there are five lineages (*gotra*), the meaning of which is as commonly explained. It continues until it states:
"Because the fifth lineage lacks the causal conditions for supramundane merit, it ultimately has no time of liberation."

Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle eleven, states: "The group of those with false certainty (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*) is called 'those lacking the nature for parinirvāṇa' (*aparinirvāṇa-dharmaka*).
Based on such passages, sentient beings without the [Buddha] nature lack the cause for nirvāṇa, and those of the two vehicles with fixed natures will certainly not become Buddhas.

If this is so, how can it be said that there is a Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*), and how are the scriptural citations previously quoted to be reconciled? The explanation says: As in the *Nirvāṇa*... [text continues].
Baonun said: "Good son, 'I' is precisely the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Furthermore, all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, which is eternally abiding and without change. Moreover, the first fascicle of the *Ratnagotravibhāga* states: Question:
How is it known that all sentient beings possess the *tathāgatagarbha*? Answer: It is based on the equality of all Buddhas.
The *dharmatā-kāya* (Dharma-nature body) knows that all sentient beings possess the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Passages such as these refer to the Buddha-nature of the *tathatā-dharmakāya*. This is precisely the teaching that the five natures all possess Buddha-nature. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"For example, there is a person... because they will certainly attain it. Teachings such as these refer to the nature of practice (*pratipatti-gotra*), which is certain to be attained.
This is because it is obtained. It is spoken with reference to a small portion of those whose lineage (*gotra*) is indeterminate. Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"In the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*); there is neither a second nor a third, except for what is taught as a skillful means (*upāya*) by the Buddhas.
Regarding the interpretation of this scriptural passage, various explanations differ. Kumārajīva and others say that the statement "there is no second" means there is no Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha.
Regarding "the absence of three": it means there are no Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or those Bodhisattvas who practice the six perfections in isolation within the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, some say that "the absence of two" refers to the absence of a second [vehicle], which is the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
and "the absence of three" refers to the absence of a third, the Śrāvaka vehicle. One interpretation states that these previous two explanations pertain only to the Hīnayāna.

Nevertheless, seeing that the Buddha-vehicle possesses the nature of the ultimate fruit, I have not intentionally refuted it. Now, I am correctly determining that there are neither two nor three vehicles.

This meaning is revealed by means of the three bodies of the Buddha. As for what is called "no two," there is only the single vehicle of the Tathāgata’s *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body), and there are no those two vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* says: "The vehicle of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas..."
"All who enter the Mahāyāna" refers precisely to the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*). The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"This alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real. What is meant by "there are no three" is that there is only the single vehicle of the Tathāgata’s *dharmakāya*, and no three vehicles consisting of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "When a bodhisattva has not yet entered the second stage, they give rise to..."

This refers to "conception" (*saṃjñā*), meaning the distinctions among the three practices of those belonging to the Three Vehicles, which lead them to be deluded regarding the principle of the One Vehicle.

The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "There is not even a second vehicle, let alone a third. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas share the same Buddha-nature and the same untainted nature (*anāsrava*).
The former [passage] refutes duality to return to oneness; the latter refutes smallness to enter greatness, while the subsequent [passage] refutes the threefold refuge.

First: This involves the submergence of phenomena into principle (*li*). Although there are three interpretations, the second is correct. Therefore, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Fa-hua lun) states at its conclusion:

"The second [chapter], the 'Expedient Means' (*Upāya-paṛivarta*), manifests the destruction of duality and the clarification of oneness" (some editions read "destruction of triad and clarification of oneness," yet most versions state "destruction of duality and clarification of oneness").
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, in its tenth, twenty-eighth, and sixtieth [chapters], all state that there is no duality.
Regarding the name "vehicle" (*yāna*): furthermore, the third fascicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "In the world, there are no two vehicles by which one attains extinction (*nirvāṇa*);
it is only through the single Buddha-vehicle that one attains extinction. It further states: "There is only the single Buddha-vehicle; it is spoken of as two because they are places of rest.
The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty states: "The five faculties, such as faith (*śraddhā*), are not called 'fixed faculties' (*niyata-indriya*) and so forth. [End of] Daye.
Neither of the two versions of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* from the Great Tang contains these words; therefore, they cannot be relied upon. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"If one is not fit to enter nirvāṇa, one remains within the blissful rewards of humans and devas, creating the causes and conditions for nirvāṇa.
Within the bliss of humans and devas, there are naturally two kinds: first, those who ultimately lack the nature for nirvāṇa, [remaining] merely as humans and devas..."
And they bring it to fruition. Second, there are those who temporarily lack the nature of *nirvāṇa*, yet as humans or devas, they accomplish the causes for *nirvāṇa*.
Although there are these two types, that treatise speaks from the perspective of one side—that of the temporary absence of the nature [of *nirvāṇa*].

Alternatively, it may be that it reveals the compassionate vows of Bodhisattvas, who desire to lead [beings] to *nirvāṇa* without remainder, rather than intending that all without exception enter [it].
Regarding *nirvāṇa*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra* states: "The two types of *śrāvakas* who are fixed [in their course] do not receive a prediction because their faculties are not yet mature.
When a bodhisattva grants them a prediction, it is an expedient means intended to cause them to resolve their minds [toward enlightenment].
This means that when a bodhisattva grants them the prediction of attaining buddhahood, it is because he desires to inspire faith in them regarding the Mahāyāna. This...
This is merely a skillful means; it is not the actual attainment of Buddhahood. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"Although this person gives rise to the thought of extinction and enters into nirvāṇa, they seek the wisdom of a Buddha in other lands. According to the fourth fascicle of the *Zhengfahua jing* (Sanskrit: *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*), it says:
"All have their minds set upon the thought of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), thinking that they shall enter extinction; only then will they proceed to other [lands]."

In the Buddha-world, it is further stated in the third [section] that when [the Buddha] was about to enter parinirvāṇa, the Buddha stood before him and instructed him with the essential Dharma, causing him to resolve upon the bodhicitta:
neither remaining in saṃsāra nor dwelling in nirvāṇa, and realizing the emptiness of the triple world. The meaning of the text in the fourth fascicle is the same as this.
Since this text states "when about to enter parinirvāṇa," based on this one should know that he dwells in non-abiding.

Regarding the "remaining support" (*sopadhiśeṣa*): when one is about to enter the state without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*), one generates the bodhicitta; it is not the case that one can generate this mind after having already entered that state.

This explains the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*; one should understand other points according to this principle. Furthermore, regarding the statement in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* that they "dwell for eighty thousand kalpas" and so forth, the Tripiṭaka Master explains:
