"World-Honored One, at one time, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana near Vārāṇasī, you taught for those who had set out solely in the Śrāvaka Vehicle by means of the four..."
"Turning the Wheel of Dharma according to the characteristics of the truths. The commentary states:
From this point downward is the fourth section, the portion on the comparative evaluation and praise of excellence. Within this, there are two parts: first, the Bodhisattva’s inquiry;

second, from "At that time" onwards, the World-Honored One’s formal exposition. In the former part, there are two sub-sections: first, clarifying the superiority and inferiority of the three turnings.

This is different. From the passage "Later, the World-Honored One [said], 'If a son of good family... onwards, the text correctly introduces the inquiry that distinguishes the superiority and inferiority of merit.
Within the preceding section on the three wheels, it is divided into three parts; this is the first, the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, which itself contains two sections.

The first part correctly elucidates the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). Although the subsequent section is inferior and reveals that this teaching is of lesser grade, this [present section] constitutes the first part.

The text consists of five sections: first, the identification of the interlocutors; second, the clarification of the time of the teaching; third, the revelation of the location of the teaching; and fourth, the explanation of the purpose for which it was taught.
Fifth, the explanation of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). The phrase "at that time," etc., identifies the persons involved in the dialogue.
The phrase "first, at one time" refers to the time when the sutra was spoken; that is, it refers to the time when the first wheel among the three wheels of Dharma was taught.
The phrase "in Vārāṇasī," etc., indicates the location where the sutra was spoken. The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "In the city of Vārāṇasī, at the Assembly of Seers..."

It is situated in a place frequented by various birds and beasts. According to the *Jiejiji* (Record of the Unraveling of the Knots) based on the *Paramārtha-satya*, during the first period, [the Buddha taught] at the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī, a gathering place for rishis.
Because this location possesses three virtues, three types of people constantly assemble there. As for these three virtues:
the first is the virtue of the grove; the branches of the trees provide dense shade, shielding against the rain in spring and [heat] in summer.
It can ward off heat; in winter, it further wards off the wind. Second is the virtue of water: it constantly possesses five qualities—lightness, coolness, softness, sweetness, and fragrance.
Third is the virtue of others: all birds and beasts from the forests and wilderness outside gather there, eating and drinking without fear.
Furthermore, beneath this ground lies a great treasure trove, forty *li* wide and forty *li* deep, which contains...
It appears at that time, yet no one may take it; only when a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) appears in the world can this treasure be used.
Furthermore, "Deer Park" (Mṛgadāva) has two meanings: first, it is said that in ancient times there were immeasurable deer on this site.

When the king wished to capture the deer, the deer king said, "If you kill one deer every day, we shall provide an inexhaustible supply of meat broth. Subsequently, each day another deer was killed in turn.
A doe was carrying a fawn. The king of the deer felt compassion for her and went in her place to face death. When the king saw this, he looked around and investigated the matter.
The Deer King continued to preach the Bodhisattva path for him. Upon hearing this, the king immediately attained understanding and realization, and he subsequently released all the deer.

(The detailed account of the Deer King sacrificing his life in place of his mother is as described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 16. Second, regarding the time of the turning of the Wheel of Dharma:

there were three deer that constantly came to the Buddha’s presence to listen to the Dharma. As for the three types of people: before the Buddha appeared in the world, the sages of the world [were such].
First, when this stage [of the Buddha's teaching] was established, those who practiced the path of the *ṛṣis* all gathered at this place to cultivate the way of the *ṛṣis*.

Second, before the two Buddhas had appeared in the world, all *pratyekabuddhas* gathered at this place to cultivate the path of the *pratyekabuddhas*. Third, after the Buddhas had appeared in the world, they gathered here together with the *śrāvakas*.

According to the *Mahāvyūha-sūtra*, it is named the "Abode of the Fallen Ṛṣis" (*Ṛṣipatana*) and the "Deer Park" (*Mṛgadāva*). Regarding the first [name], the *Ekajātipratibaddha* (those bound to one more birth) [gathered there].
When the Bodhisattva was about to descend to be born, a certain devaputra descended to Jambudvīpa and addressed a pratyekabuddha, saying:
"Venerable one, you should abandon this land. Why is this? Twelve years hence, a Bodhisattva shall descend in spirit and enter a womb.
At that time, five hundred pratyekabuddhas of the city of Vārāṇasī, having heard these words from the deva, rose from their seats.
He rose and leaped into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees, where he entered the fire of self-immolation and attained *nirvāṇa*.
Only his *śarīra* (relics) descended from the sky; therefore, this place is named "The Place Where the Rishi Fell.
Furthermore, in the past, there was a benevolent king who granted safety to the herd of deer; for that reason, that land is also named [the Deer Park].

Regarding the "Instruction":

the commentary explains that from this point downward is the second section, the formal inquiry concerning the superiority or inferiority of merit. This section contains two parts: first, the Bodhisattva’s question;
second, the Tathāgata’s formal response. Within the former, there are two further divisions: first, citing the instruction to be questioned by way of the person [who asks].
Having heard [the teaching] later, one believes and accepts it. Next, in accordance with the instruction, one asks about the amount of merit produced by the ten types of dharma-practice;
this is the first [point]. To clarify the explicit terminology regarding the aforementioned nature of lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), he says:
"The profound, definitive teachings that have been expounded."
Having heard it, one believes and understands it, writes it down, protects and maintains it, makes offerings to it, disseminates it, receives and recites it, and reviews it;
by practicing it according to principle and initiating application through these modes of cultivation, how much merit is generated? Having said these words, [he asked].
The commentary states: This is the second [section], which correctly asks about the amount of merit produced by the ten dharma-practices arising from reliance on the teaching.
These ten dharma-practices have already been explained as before.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata, saying:

"Paramārthasamudgata, the merit produced by such a son or daughter of good family is immeasurable, incalculable, and difficult to know even through analogies; I shall now briefly explain a small portion of it for you."
The commentary states: From here below is the second section, the Tathāgata’s formal exposition. This consists of two parts: first, praising its excellence and promising to speak;
second, providing the formal exposition in response to a question. This is the first part, which may be understood according to the text.
It is like the dust on a fingernail compared to the dust of the great earth: it does not equal even one part in a hundred, nor one part in a thousand, nor one part in a hundred thousand;
by calculation, reckoning, analogy, or even the *upaniṣad* (ultimate) fraction, it does not approach even a single part.

The commentary states: From here below is the second section, the Tathāgata’s formal exposition. This consists of two parts: first, the presentation of two similes to distinguish their relative superiority and inferiority;
second, from "In this way" onwards, the presentation of the corresponding dharmas to the similes to distinguish the superiority and inferiority of merit. Within these two similes:
It is divided into two parts. The first is the analogy of a small amount of soil on a fingernail; the second is the analogy of a small amount of water in a cow’s footprint. This is the first.
Now, according to this sutra, the superiority and inferiority [of these] are measured by eight divisions: first, the hundredth part; second, the two-thousandth part;

third, the three-hundred-thousandth part; fourth, the numerical part; fifth, the calculable part; sixth, the reckonable part; seventh, the analogical part; eighth, the *aupaniṣadika* (proximate) part.
Regarding the *Śārdūlakarṇa-avadāna*, both the *Anupamā-sūtra* and the *Adbhuta-dharma-sūtra* explain it as having eight parts, which is identical to this sutra.
However, according to the twelfth fascicle of the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, although the number is likewise eight, they are subsequently divided into five parts.

All these are established in the Sanskrit language. Thus, that sūtra says: "The portion of *saṃkhyā*, the portion of *kāla*, the portion of *gaṇanā*, the portion of *upamā*, and the portion of *upanisad*.
Among these, if one follows the various teachings, the first four correspond respectively to number (*saṃkhyā*), calculation (*gaṇanā*), analogy (*upamā*), and metaphor (*upaniṣad*).
However, according to the direct text of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, they correspond respectively to number (*saṃkhyā*), calculation (*gaṇanā*), analogy (*upamā*), and metaphor (*upaniṣad*).

The analogy of calculation: According to the *Prajñāpāramitā-nirdeśa-sūtra* (or *Nengduan banruo jing*) and the *Daśacakra-sūtra* (or *Zhijiben jing*), the fifth chapter states that there are ten parts, meaning one hundred thousand followed by *koṭi* and *nayuta* parts.
According to the fourteenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it states there are thirteen parts, meaning one hundred thousand followed by five [additional units].

[It is] divided into portions: namely, a *koṭi*-fold portion, a hundred-*koṭi*-fold portion, a thousand-*koṭi*-fold portion, a hundred-thousand-*koṭi*-fold portion, and a hundred-thousand-*koṭi*-nayuta-fold portion.
Now, regarding the explanation of the distinctions between these various portions, according to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as translated by Paramārtha:
"A hundredth part does not equal it; ten million, a billion, or ten trillion parts do not equal it; even to the point of exhausting [all divisions], [it cannot be reached]."
In terms of calculation, it does not even equal one part of it; indeed, it cannot be reached by any analogy corresponding to its categories of power.
Paramārtha’s commentary states: Generally, five points are raised to demonstrate that this is superior and that is inferior:
first, it is superior with respect to quantity; second, it is superior with respect to power; third, it is superior with respect to categories; fourth, it is superior with respect to correspondence.
It is superior. Fifth, it is superior because of its analogies. Regarding its numerical quantity: even exhausting all possible numbers, one cannot reach it. As the Sūtra says:
"A hundredth part does not equal it," meaning that even exhausting all calculation, one cannot reach even a single fraction of it. Second, regarding its majestic power (*prabhāva*):
it means that whatever one desires, the supreme fruits of the three vehicles are spontaneously accomplished; it surpasses even the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*). Hypothetically...

Even if there were wish-fulfilling jewels like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, filling the great trichiliocosm, they would lack this power, for one cannot attain the fruits of the three vehicles through them.
Regarding the superiority of the three categories, there are five types of categories, which correspond to the meaning of the five treasuries:
first, the Tathāgata; second, the True Dharma; third, the Dharmakāya; fourth, supramundane dharmas; and fifth, intrinsic purity.
Purity. These five meanings of the "store" (*garbha*) are the meaning of "categories. Within the single *tathatā* (suchness), there are these five meanings of the store:
first, it reveals the essential nature; second, it reveals the cause; third, it reveals the fruit; fourth, it reveals the qualities; and fifth, it reveals the unique [attributes].
Because these are attainable only through non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), these five kinds constitute the meaning of "categories. As for that merit of material giving:
It lacks these five meanings; therefore, it is inferior. Fourth, regarding "correspondence" (*samyoga*): this clarifies the correspondence between cause and effect.
That is to say, faith and delight in the Mahāyāna can evoke *tathatā*, whereas the merit of giving cannot correspond to suchness.
Because it lacks this correspondence, it is inferior. Fifth, regarding "analogy": this very *tathatā* is the foremost dharma; there is nothing else...
Because no other dharma is equal to this dharma, there is nothing that can serve as a simile; the full explanation is as stated therein.
According to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* translated by Bodhiruci, it says: "A hundredth part does not equal it; a thousandth part does not equal it;
a hundred-thousandth part does not equal it; a *kalā* part does not equal it; a numerical part does not equal it; an *upaniṣad* part..."
The portion of the śrāvakas does not equal even a fraction of it; indeed, it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
According to Vasubandhu’s *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the relative superiority and inferiority are compared based on four kinds of excellence. Thus, the verse says:
The power of its number is incomparably superior; likewise, its cause is incomparable.
No worldly phenomenon can serve as a metaphor for this—what is the meaning of this statement? It demonstrates that the aforementioned merit is supreme. How is it supreme? First, by way of number.
First, superiority in number; second, superiority in power; third, superiority by way of dissimilarity; and fourth, superiority of cause. Therefore, the verse says:
"No phenomena of the entire world can serve as a metaphor. Regarding superiority in number, it is as the sutra states:
"One hundredth part does not equal it," up to "beyond what can be reached by calculation or analogy. This is because numbers have no limit. [This concludes the section on] inclusion.
One should know that the remaining numbers are attained. Regarding "superiority by power," it is as the sutra says: "it does not reach even a *kalā*.
Regarding "superiority by resemblance," the numbers within this merit are not comparable; because this merit is incalculable, it cannot be reached, as the sutra says.
Regarding "superiority by cause," the cause and effect are not similar; this cause and effect surpasses that cause and effect.
Therefore, as the sūtra states, it does not even approach a fraction—down to a *upaniṣad*—of this [merit].
Because this dharma is supreme and there is no worldly dharma that can serve as a metaphor for it, the verse says: "No worldly dharma can be found to serve as a metaphor.
Thus, within this merit, that [other] merit is infinitesimal; therefore, there is no [worldly] dharma [that can compare].
This may be illustrated by the *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra*, which states: "A hundredth part does not equal one," and so forth. The treatise explains that this refers to the superiority of calculation;
it clarifies that contaminated merit (*sāsrava-puṇya*) is a phenomenon subject to exhaustion and therefore has limits.

It clarifies that uncontaminated wholesome phenomena (*anāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) are inexhaustible phenomena and therefore have no limits. This is why they are superior. A *kalā* part does not equal one.
As for "force-victory" (*balavijita*), the treatise states that it means "victorious in power. *Kala* is the correct pronunciation in the Western [Indic] lands;

it is like dividing a single hair into one hundred parts, where one such part is called a "kala-part. This meaning is translated as "force-victory," because the power and merit of untainted wholesome dharmas (*anāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) surpass those of tainted wholesome dharmas (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*);
thus it is named "force-victory. It does not even approach a numerical fraction [of the former].
The treatise states: "It is called 'superior by dissimilarity' because, within that very number, it becomes increasingly subtle and increasingly fine until it reaches a mere trifle;
since it does not even equal one [unit], it is named 'superior by dissimilarity. This clarifies these untainted wholesome dharmas."
If there were any form or shape, it could not be contained within the dharma-realm of empty space; for form is a phenomenon subject to exhaustion, whereas the unconditioned is inexhaustible.

Even if one were to take a tiny fraction of something dissimilar—such as dividing a mustard seed into ten thousand parts and comparing it to Mount Sumeru—the former would be wasted in its own essence, for they would never be comparable. Upāniṣad.
"Less than a fraction of a *śatadru* grain" is explained in the treatise as meaning "superiority by cause. This clarifies that the cause and effect are dissimilar.
Worldly wholesome dharmas (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) yield only retribution within the three realms; thus, both cause and effect are inferior.

Unworldly wholesome dharmas (*anāsrava-kuśala-dharma*), however, ultimately attain the fruit of Buddhahood; thus, both cause and effect are superior. Therefore, they are called "dissimilar in cause and effect."
Furthermore, regarding this sutra, its first three parts may be understood from their titles.
As for the term "Saṃkhyā-vibhāga" (Analysis of Numbers): *saṃkhyā* is *saṃkhya* in Sanskrit, which here means "number.

According to the seventh fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vyākhyāna*, "numbers" refers to such calculations as one and one making two, and two and two making four, and so forth. This is based on Guṇaprabha’s [commentary on] the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
If one consults the *Lun* (Treatise), it states: "As for 'number,' this refers to sixty stages; beyond this, numbers cannot reach. The commentary explains:
according to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, the number gradually increases through sixty revolutions; according to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, there are one hundred and twenty revolutions.
For now, following the *Abhidharmakośa*, it says "sixty. According to the *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra*, this refers to the first five parts.
All are termed "numerical divisions. Thus, regarding the statement that "one hundredth part does not equal it" and so forth, the *Śāstra* says that calculation (*gaṇanā*) is superior.
As for the term "calculated division," the Sanskrit original is *gaṇanā*, which is translated here as "calculation. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "As for calculation..."
"One vertical and ten horizontal," and so forth. According to the *Vibhāṣā*, fascicle 126, it asks: "What dharma is designated by the term 'calculation' (*gaṇanā*)?
It answers: "It is the mental action (*manas-karman*) that transforms in accordance with reality, along with the various skillful wisdoms (*upāya-jñāna*) upon which it relies."
In this context, "number" does not refer to the count of objects to be counted, such as rice, sesame, or the number one hundred thousand; rather, it refers to the faculty that performs the counting.
Because it is this faculty that performs the counting, it is called "number. As it says further: "The intrinsic nature of number consists of these four aggregates.
What dharma is designated as 'calculation'? The answer is: "It is vocal action transformed in accordance with reason, and this..."
Regarding the various skillful means of wisdom that serve as the basis:

herein, "calculation" does not refer to the objects being calculated—such as the numbers one, ten, hundred, thousand, ten thousand, hundred thousand, or ten million—but rather refers to all the methods capable of calculating. Because these are the methods of calculation, they are called "calculation."
"...up to the phrase 'those clouds. Regarding the statement that 'these five aggregates constitute the nature of calculation,' the commentary explains:

if one follows this text, then the skillful wisdom capable of counting and calculating, and so forth, constitutes the act of calculation. Although this interpretation exists, for now we shall rely on the previous explanation."
Regarding the term "ji-fen" (計分): the Sanskrit original is *kalā*, which here means "count" (*ji*). Guṇaprabha states that it is "not reached by *kalā*" (*ge-lo bu ji*);
"that which cannot be reached by calculation" (*jiao-ji bu-ji*) is explained according to the subtle meaning of *kalā*.

This means that although the merit of upholding [the precepts] is most subtle, its virtue is already so great that it is not reached by what precedes it; even when one exhausts all calculation, there is ultimately nothing equal to it. It is subtle.

If even a subtle [particle] is thus, how much more so the case for all things? (The terms *kalā* and *kṣaṇa* differ in their Sanskrit pronunciation; they should not be divided into two distinct types. This is according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
Calculating the two parts is also called "enumeration. Thus, the *Ekādaśa-sāhasrikā* states: "There are two kinds of enumeration:
first, calculating enumeration; second, definitive enumeration. Calculating enumeration refers to the six *pāramitās*. Definitive enumeration refers to..."
This refers to the pāramitās, which in number are exactly six, neither more nor less.
Regarding the term "analogy" (dṛṣṭānta): the Sanskrit word is *upamā*, which here is translated as "analogy.
Guṇaprabha states that what is "inadequate as an analogy" is like a young girl who is called "moon-faced"; for how could a woman's face truly correspond to the moon?
Because it possesses a degree of brilliance and shares a small portion of similarity, that previous analogy of a mass of merit is not like this;
there is not even a slight resemblance that can serve as a metaphor.
As for the term *aupaniṣadika-bhāga*, this is translated here as "the ultimate" (*parama*); it refers to a numerical calculation or a metaphorical reckoning.
Among the four [types of numbers], it is said that the last is the ultimate; thus, after the categories of number and so forth, the *aupaniṣadika* portion is taught.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the *aupaniṣadika* portion refers merely to the limit of number.

This is the name for the final number at the end of the greatest numbers in the Western regions (India), which resembles the names of the *kāra* units in this land (China) but is not actually those *kāra* units themselves, as the numbering system of this land...
The Dharma is brief; there are only fifteen [verses]. In the West, however, there are sixty names for the numbers.
Vasubandhu’s treatise states that it is "due to excellence" (*hetu-viśeṣa*). Guṇaprabha says that *upaniṣad* means "cause" (*hetu*). What is its meaning?

This small portion of merit becomes the causal nature for the most excellent fruit, whereas the total accumulation of previous merit does not constitute a cause, being unable [to produce such a result].
Because it attains the fruit of ultimate reality.
Or, for example, the water in a cow’s footprint compared to the waters of the four great oceans does not equal even one hundredth part;
as explained at length, it does not even equal one *upaniṣad* (infinitesimal) part.
The commentary states: This is the second analogy of the small amount of water in a cow’s footprint; it may be understood by reference to what preceded.
In this way, having heard and gained faith and understanding in those sūtras of provisional meaning, and so forth, as extensively explained up to their aspect of cultivation.
The merit obtained from initiating the preparatory application is compared to the merit accumulated from hearing and gaining faith and understanding in the definitive sūtra teachings here explained;
this comparison extends, as explained at length, even to the merit accumulated from initiating the preparatory application by means of the aspect of cultivation.
"A hundredth part does not equal it; to speak more extensively, even a *upaniṣad* part does not equal it.
Having said these words, the commentary explains:
This is the second instance of citing a phenomenon as a parallel example (*dṛṣṭānta*) to compare their relative superiority and inferiority—that is, by hearing the two sūtras.
One obtains merit. Based on the two preceding metaphors, the distinction between their relative superiority and inferiority, as well as their numerical differences, may be understood from the sutra.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, within this Dharma-door of the profound meaning..."
"What should this teaching be named? How should I uphold it? The commentary states:
From here below is the fifth section, the Section on Upholding the Teaching. Within this, there are two parts: first, the Bodhisattva’s inquiry;
second, the Tathāgata’s formal response. This is the first part. The inquiry concerns two matters: first, asking for the name of the teaching; second, [asking how to uphold it].

[The Bodhisattva] asked for the instruction on how to uphold [this teaching]. The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata: "Son of good family, this is called the teaching of the definitive meaning of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
You should uphold this teaching of the definitive meaning of the ultimate truth."
The commentary states: From this point downward is the second section, the Tathāgata’s direct response. This contains two parts: first, the direct response based on the questions;
second, the explanation of the benefits of the teaching. This is the first part. That is to say, he declares that this teaching is named the "Teaching of the Ultimate Definitive Meaning.
Based upon this name, you should uphold it.
When this teaching of the definitive meaning of the ultimate truth was spoken, six hundred thousand beings within that great assembly resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The commentary states: From here below, the second section explains the benefits of teaching the Dharma. There are four superior benefits, which are divided into four parts; this is the first benefit.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 46, there are five benefits. It says:
"When the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas proclaim the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, it should be known that there are five great fruits of benefit. First..."
First, there is a class of sentient beings who, upon hearing the true Dharma, become free from dust and defilement, and the Dharma-eye arises within them regarding all phenomena.
Second, there is a class of sentient beings who, upon hearing the true Dharma, attain the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).

Third, there is a class of sentient beings who, upon hearing the true Dharma, immediately give rise to the mind of right aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Fourth, there is a class of sentient beings who, upon hearing the true Dharma, realize the supreme dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*) of a bodhisattva.
Fifth, there is a class of sentient beings who, having heard the true Dharma, receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice it correctly;
through these successive skillful means, they cause the eye of the true Dharma to endure for a long time without perishing. These five types should be known as [the recipients of] the various...
Regarding the great fruits and supreme benefits of the True Dharma taught by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, this present sutra contains four such benefits;
however, the final one is omitted because it is easily understood and is therefore not frequently mentioned in other sutras.
These four benefits are divided into four sections, and this is the first: the benefit of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*). (Based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 53)
The "Chapter on Non-arising" asks: What are the five kinds of bodhi? It answers: First, the patience of compliance (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*);

second, the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); and [the remaining] three kinds of bodhi. (The commentary explains that these consist of the bodhis of those prior to the stages, those within the stages, and the bodhi of the three vehicles’ stage of no-more-learning. Furthermore, there are another five kinds of bodhi:
first, the bodhi of generating the mind (*cittotpāda-bodhi*), which is the generation of the mind amidst immeasurable births and deaths for the sake of [attaining] Arhatship...
Because it is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is called "bodhi. This refers to the designation of the fruit within the cause.
Second is the bodhi of subduing the mind: by suppressing all afflictions (*kleśa*) and conquering one's own mind, one practices the various *pāramitās*. Third is the bodhi of clear knowledge:
observing the beginning, end, general characteristics, and specific characteristics of all phenomena throughout the three periods of time, and discerning and weighing them all.
The Dharma is ultimately pure; this is what is called the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Having set out toward enlightenment by means of the four [bases of psychic power], because one has attained the power of skillful means within the *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not even cling to the *prajñāpāramitā* itself.

It extinguishes all afflictions (*kleśa*), beholds all Buddhas of the ten directions, attains the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), emerges from the triple world (*traidhātuka*), and reaches omniscience (*sarvajñā*).

Fifth is unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*): sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), severing the habitual tendencies of afflictions (*vāsanā*), and attaining unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The Tripitaka Master Chang-er (Dīrghakarṇa) explains: that which precedes the stage of the habituation-seed (*vāsanā-bīja*) is called the stage of generating the mind (*cittotpāda*). Next...
The thirty stages of mind are called the stage of subduing the mind (*vinaya-citta*). From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage is called the stage of illumination (*vidyā-bhūmi*).
The eighth, ninth, and tenth stages are called the stage of emergence (*niṣkrānta-bhūmi*). Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is called the unsurpassed stage (*anuttara-bhūmi*).

Now, relying on these five [stages] to explain the meaning of the sūtra: that which is here termed "Anuttara-bodhi" is the bodhi sought; as for the term "arousing the mind" (*cittotpāda*), it refers to this.
Because it gives rise to the mind that seeks [enlightenment], it is called "arousing the bodhicitta. This refers to the first two of the five types of bodhi.
One interpretation states that the third clarifies bodhi. Why is this? Vajrasena says: "Because the bodhicitta is aroused at the first stage (bhūmi).
Alternatively, it may be understood that while there are five kinds of what is sought, the mind that seeks them exists only in the causal state.
"Three hundred thousand śrāvakas, having removed themselves from dust and abandoned defilement, attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena. The commentary states:
This refers to the second benefit, namely the removal of dust and defilement; that is to say, by hearing this teaching, they obtain two kinds of benefits.
First, the benefit of being far removed from dust and free from defilement; second, the benefit of attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Regarding these two benefits, there are differing explanations in various teachings. According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 182, it says:
"As stated in the Sūtra, when the Buddha taught this Dharma-gate, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya and eighty thousand devas were far removed from dust and free from defilement regarding all [phenomena]..."
Within the Dharma, the pure Dharma-eye arises. Herein, "distant from dust" means being distant from the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that accompany the eye;
"free from defilement" means being free from the defilements of active entanglements (*paryavasthāna*). "Among all dharmas" refers to among the Four Noble Truths. "The pure Dharma-eye arises" means:
This refers to seeing the Four Noble Truths, whereby the pure Dharma-eye arises. As stated in the ninth fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*:
"As the Sūtra says, 'Distant from dust and free from defilement, the true Dharma-eye arises regarding all phenomena,' this is said in reference to the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
The various *dharmakṣāntis* (patiences) distance one from dust, and the various *dharmajñānas* (knowledges) free one from defilement; because these first [arise] regarding all..."
Within the truths, the sublime noble eye of wisdom constitutes their intrinsic nature. Regarding "the patience toward phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*) being able to distance one from dust":

this is because through these various patiences toward phenomena, all the dust of afflictions is forever severed. Regarding "the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) being able to leave behind defilement":

this is because through these various knowledges of phenomena, having already severed the stains of obstructions, [this state] arises based upon that attainment. Furthermore, regarding these two stages of patience and knowledge, in their respective order...
Because of thorough knowledge, because of permanent abandonment, and because the path has attained purity; it is based on these that one speaks of being "distant from dust and free from defilement.
This is stated in the fifth chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, which agrees with the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. The commentary explains:

"Because of thorough knowledge, because of permanent abandonment, and because the path has attained purity" is a general explanation of the purification of the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣurviśuddhi*). Furthermore, according to the eighty-third fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: "Moreover..."

Regarding "distant from dust and free from defilement": "dust" refers to the already-arisen but not yet perfected wisdom that can obstruct clear realization (*abhisamaya*), whether it occurs intermittently or continuously, and the active manifestation of the conceit of self (*asmimāna*).
"Defilement" refers to the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) belonging to those categories as well as the categories to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*).
Because these are made to cease forever, it is called "distant from dust and free from defilement. Furthermore, "dust" refers to the conceit of self and [the afflictions] associated with views.
It severs all afflictions (*kleśa*). "Impurities" refers to the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to both categories.

"Among all phenomena" means among those phenomena that abide in their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common-characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). "The Dharma-eye" refers to the direct realization of reality as it is, which is solely the wisdom of the Dharma.
"Seeing the Dharma" refers to seeing [the truths] such as suffering (*duḥkha*) as they truly are. "Attaining the Dharma" refers to...
This refers to the successive realization of the fruits of śrāmaṇya; the details are as explained therein. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 86, states:
"Moreover, it should be known that the noble ones’ eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) is purified by two characteristics:

namely, by being 'distant from dust' (*vīta-rajas*) and by being 'free from defilement' (*vigata-mala*). Because they have attained dissociation (*visamyoga*) from the various afflictions (*kleśa*) and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) that were to be abandoned, it is called 'distant'."
"Dust" (*rajas*): Because one attains dissociation from those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), it is called "free from stain" (*vītaraja*).

Furthermore, while in the process of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), a coarse sense of self (*asmimāna*) enters and operates continuously amidst the mental attentions (*manasikāra*). If one thoroughly understands that the grasped object and the grasping subject are equal in their objective referent (*ālambana-samatā*), that [sense of self] is immediately severed.
Because it is thus extinguished, it is called "distant from dust. This applies to all paths of vision (*darśanamārga*).

Because the latent tendencies of the afflictions have been severed, it is called "stainless. The ten kinds of benefits, such as "seeing the Dharma" and "attaining the Dharma," are fully explained therein.
One hundred and fifty thousand śrāvakas completely exhausted all outflows, and their minds attained liberation.
The commentary states: This is the third benefit of attaining liberation. First, by the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*), one attains liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*);

by being permanently free from the hindrances to meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*), one attains liberation through mind (*citta-vimukti*). Alternatively, because one is freed from the three outflows, it is called the "permanent exhaustion of all outflows."
Because one is forever free from craving, the mind attains liberation. According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (Treatise on the Great Abhidharma), fascicle 94:

"The exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) means that all outflows are forever exhausted. Question: Since the phenomena conducive to the outflows (*āsrava-saṃprayukta-dharma*) are also forever exhausted, why is it said only that "those outflows are exhausted"?
Answer: Because the exhaustion [of the outflows] is primary, one should understand that this also implies the exhaustion of the phenomena conducive to them.
Furthermore, the outflows (*āsrava*) are difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend; they are not in accordance with the factors that lead away from the outflows.

For these reasons, they are specifically discussed. Furthermore, the faults of the outflows are numerous, predominant, and firm; they are not in accordance with the factors that lead away from the outflows.

For these reasons, they are specifically discussed. The details are as explained there. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle three, states: "The three kinds of outflows within the triple world have already been exhausted and are non-existent."
...the remainder. Thus it is said that "all outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted. The commentary explains: the mind attains liberation, as previously explained in detail. Question:
How can this profound Mahāyāna bring about the benefit of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*)? The commentary explains:
according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are two kinds of teachings taught by the Tathāgata: first, the explicit (*nītārtha*); second, the secret (*neyārtha*). If one relies upon...
It is clearly revealed that one realizes only the great fruit, yet there is a secret [intention]. Therefore, it encompasses the benefits of both the Great and Small Vehicles. Thus, a sutra says:
"The Buddha preaches the Dharma with a single voice, and sentient beings each understand it according to their kind.

Furthermore, the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* states: "The Tathāgata preaches the three wheels of the Dharma with a single voice. Also, the *Mahāsīmā Sūtra* says: "The Tathāgata, with a single..."

Within its sounds, it expounds an ocean of immeasurable sūtras. Furthermore, this sūtra states that it is taught for the sake of those who have set out upon all vehicles as a definitive exposition (nītārtha).
Therefore, one should know that there is no logical contradiction in attaining the fruits of the three vehicles by hearing this.
Seventy-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The commentary states: This is the fourth benefit of attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena. Furthermore, this non-arising itself is of two kinds.

First, a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*bhūmi*) is said to have attained the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There are two kinds of patience:

first, the patience of compliance (*anuloma-kṣānti*); second, the patience regarding non-arising. The commentary explains: "The patience of compliance resides in the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*);
the patience regarding non-arising begins from the first stage upward. Second, from the eighth stage upward, one attains the non-existence of all phenomena...

Regarding the patience of birth (*janma-kṣānti*), the *Ratnaketuparivarta* (Renwang jing) speaks of five kinds of patience: first, the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*); second, the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*);

third, the patience of conformity (*anuloma-kṣānti*); fourth, the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*); and fifth, quiescence (*śānti*). According to their respective order: the thirty minds prior to the [ten] stages constitute the stage of the patience of subduing;
the first, second, and third stages constitute the stage of the patience of faith; the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages constitute the stage of the patience of conformity; and the seventh...
The eighth and ninth stages are the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); the tenth stage and the Buddha-stage are the patience of tranquility (*śānta-kṣānti*).

These are explained in detail as in that [text]. The *Bodhicaryāvatāra-ṭīkā* (or *Bodhisambhāra-śāstra*), chapter three, states: "The Bodhisattva who has attained the stage of the patience of non-arising dharma is the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).
The twentieth fascicle of the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* states: "O Śāriputra, at the time of my receiving the prophecy, I realized..."
He attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Śāriputra, what kind of patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena does he realize?

It is the realization of the patience that perceives no attainment in all form-phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*); the realization of the patience that perceives no attainment in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*);

and the realization of the patience that perceives no attainment in the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*). Śāriputra, that which is called "attaining patience" is precisely named...
This is for the sake of enduring that all phenomena are ultimately unattainable. Why is this? Because at the time one realizes such patience (*kṣānti*), worldly phenomena no longer manifest;

nor do the phenomena of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the phenomena of those in training (*śaikṣa*), the phenomena of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the phenomena of solitary buddhas (*pratyekabuddha*), or the phenomena of bodhisattvas. Furthermore, any phenomena that are not the Buddha-dharma do not manifest.
Why is this? Because all phenomena do not manifest, it is called "attaining patience" (*kṣānti*).
Because all phenomena are ultimately unobtainable and there is nothing to be obtained, it is called "attaining patience.

Furthermore, this patience exhausts all marks (*nimitta*) and all objects of cognition (*ālambana*) in a single instant; therefore, it is called "attaining patience. Moreover, this patience does not tolerate...
Regarding the eye, one does not destroy the eye nor its various objects; therefore, it is called "attaining patience.
One does not find dissatisfaction with the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, yet does not destroy the mind. Such patience has an inexhaustible sphere of activity. Such patience—
Because it is not an object of the [ordinary] destinies (*gati*), it is called "attaining patience" (*kṣānti*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 74, states: Question:

As it is said in the sūtras, how is the "patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) established? Answer: It is established by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

That is to say, by means of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), one establishes the patience regarding the original non-arising of intrinsic nature; by means of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)...

Therefore, the patience regarding the non-arising of the spontaneous (*svabhāva*) is established by virtue of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). The patience regarding the non-arising of the defilements of affliction and suffering is established [by virtue of the dependent nature].
It should be known that this patience is irreversible; this is also consistent with the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* in its sixth chapter.
Furthermore, the *Xiǎnyáng* states: "These three kinds of patience exist on the stage of non-retrogression.
The *Dàjí* and the *Gōngdéshī Jīnɡāng Lùn* agree with the *Xiǎnyáng*. The sixth fascicle of the *Fódì Lùn* explains: "From the eighth stage upward..."

It is called the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*). Furthermore, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* presents two alternative explanations: one states that from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
the other states that from the eighth stage upward, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena. These are explained in detail therein.

As for the "patience regarding the non-arising" mentioned here, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it refers to the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena from the first stage upward. If...

According to the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, those on the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). For a detailed analysis, see what is explained in the tenth fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
(From the *Sūtra on the Profound Secrets* Commentary, Fascicle Five)
Commentary on the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra, Scroll Six (Sūtra Text Three), composed by the Śramaṇa Yuance of Ximing Monastery.
Chapter Six: The Analysis of Yoga (*Yogācāra-vibhaṅga*).
In explaining this chapter, there are briefly two parts: first, the explanation of the chapter title; second, the explanation of the main text.

Regarding the explanation of the chapter title: the Sanskrit term *yoga* is translated here as "correspondence" (*xiāngying*). However, regarding this *yoga*, there are two different interpretations based on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
One interpretation states that it refers generally to the objects, practices, and fruits of the three vehicles (the word "etc. includes the teachings that express these). All of these...
All phenomena are termed "yoga," because they all possess the sense of being associated with skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). Regarding the yoga of the object (*ālambana-yoga*):
it refers to all objects being non-erroneous, non-contradictory, conformable, and leading to the ultimate.

(The commentary explains: this refers respectively to their intrinsic nature, their non-contradiction with reason, their conformity with all dharmas, and by virtue of these, their ability to lead to the attainment of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*)—in accordance with correct principle and teaching.

Because it is the union of practice and its fruit, it is called *yoga*. Although this *yoga* of the object (*ālambana-yoga*) applies universally to all things, various sūtras and śāstras provide diverse explanations according to their specific characteristics and the capacities of beings.

Some speak of the four principles, such as dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*), and so on, up to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the truths (*satya*).
All of these are termed *yoga*, and they collectively possess the four natures (*catur-lakṣaṇa*).
Because it accords with the four dharmas, the practitioner of yoga is so called.

This means that all practices are mutually concordant, they accord with correct principle, they accord with the authentic teaching, and they lead toward the authentic fruit; thus, they are termed "yoga.

Although this practice of yoga applies to all activities, various sūtras and śāstras provide diverse explanations according to their specific characteristics and the capacities of beings. Some speak of the correct cultivation of various...
Practice is called yoga. Alternatively, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are called yoga.
Alternatively, the balanced operation of śamatha and vipaśyanā is called yoga.
In this way, it is further stated that the simultaneous and equal functioning of the bodhisattva’s extraordinary wisdom and compassion is called yoga.
Because it possesses the four types of meanings described above, it is called "yoga of the result" (*phala-yoga*).
This means that all results are mutually concordant, accord with correct reasoning, conform to the authentic teachings, and correspond to the true cause; thus they are designated as "yoga.

Although this yoga of the result applies generally to all results, various different explanations are given according to the specific sūtras and śāstras, their characteristics, and the capacities of beings. Or...
In some places it is said that the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), such as the powers (*bala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), are called *yoga*.
In this manner, even up to the point where conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) merits are spoken of, they are all termed *yoga* because they possess the aforementioned meaning.

Such sacred teachings (*āgama*) are also called *yoga* because they accord with correct principle (*nyāya*), conform to correct practice (*pratipatti*), and lead to the correct fruit (*phala*). One [commentary] says:

The correct undertaking of the contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā*) of the three vehicles is termed *yoga*. This is because it involves repeated cultivation in accordance with reason, proceeding in a manner that attains superior fruits.
It is [termed *yoga*] because the objects, fruits, and sacred teachings are the objects of *yoga*, the fruits of *yoga*, and the expressions of *yoga*, respectively.
It is also called *yoga*, yet it is not the primary *yoga*. The commentary explains: although that treatise contains two explanations, the *yoga* of this sutra corresponds to the second explanation.
Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), its essence consists of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
As in the *Ṣaḍāyatana-sūtra*, it is designated as *yoga* because it refers to the path of the equal operation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Within this chapter, [this is] explained in detail.
It elucidates the meaning of the yoga of correct contemplation; therefore, it is called the "Discrimination of Yoga.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, upon what does a bodhisattva rely and in what do they abide while practicing śamatha and vipaśyanā within the Great Vehicle?"
The commentary states: The preceding four chapters have distinguished that which is observed. Next, there are two chapters explaining the practice of the observer. Within these, there are two parts:
first, the *Viniścaya-yoga*, which clarifies the gateways of the practices of śamatha and vipaśyanā; second, the *Bhūmi-pāramitā*, which clarifies the ten stages and the ten perfections.
Of these two chapters, śamatha and vipaśyanā are the general [subject], and thus they are explained first; the ten perfections are the specific [subject].

Therefore, it is explained later. Alternatively, because *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are concise, they are clarified first; the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) are extensive, which is why they are explained later.
Within the section on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the text is divided into two parts: first, the formal explanation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; second, from "At that time, Maitreya...

onwards, clarifying the reliance upon the teaching and its observance. Within the former, there are two sections: first, an extensive explanation in prose; second, the citation of verses for reiteration.
It is said: according to one interpretation, this chapter is divided into three sections. First, an extensive explanation in prose; second, a brief exposition by means of verses;

and third, the formal acceptance and upholding of the teaching. Within the prose section, it is further divided into two parts. The first extensively distinguishes the characteristics of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
After the World-Honored One had spoken these words at that time, he concluded with a summary and exhortation to study. Within the detailed exposition, there are eighteen sections:

first, the section on the analysis of the basis and dwelling of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; second, the section on the distinctions among the objects of focus (*ālambana*) for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
1. The gate of discerning the ability to seek the methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. 2. The gate of mental attention (*manasikāra*) that accords with *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. 3.

The gate of the similarities and differences between the two paths of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. 4. The gate of discerning *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* through the perspective of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

(Alternatively: the gate of discerning the identity or difference between mind and objects. 5. The gate of practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* either individually or combined. 6. The gate of the distinctions in the categories and numbers of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. 7. The gate of reliance and non-reliance.

1. The Gate of the Cessation and Contemplation of Dharmas; 2. The Gate of Tenfold Distinctions such as Vitarka and Vicāra; 3. The Gate of Distinctions among the Characteristics of Cessation, Exaltation, and Equanimity;
4. The Gate of Distinctions between Knowing Dharmas and Knowing Meanings; 5. The Gate of How Cessation and Contemplation Encompass All Samādhis; 6.
The Gate of the Causes, Effects, and Functions of Cessation and Contemplation; 7. The Gate of Distinctions in How Cessation and Contemplation Remedy Obstacles.
Sixteen is the gate of realizing bodhi through śamatha and vipaśyanā; seventeen is the gate of eliciting vast majestic power;
eighteen is the gate of the cessation of sensation within the nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa. This constitutes the first gate of the analytical reliance and abiding upon śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Within this, there are two parts: first the question, and subsequently the answer. This is the first, the inquiry of the Bodhisattva. Regarding the term "Maitreya":
according to the correct Sanskrit, it should be *Maitreya*; here it is translated as "Compassionate One" (*Cishi*). It possesses three meanings.
First, his name is established according to his clan. His mother’s clan was the Maitreya clan; because he takes his name from his mother’s clan, he is called Maitreya.
His personal name is Ajita, or alternatively Aśita, which translates as "Invincible," meaning that no one can surpass him.
The old transcription "Ajita" is erroneous. Second, his essential nature is compassion. This is named...
Maitreya, therefore the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Because he first attained the Samādhi of Compassionate Mind, he is named Maitreya.
Thirdly, the name is established based on his vow. The *Sarvajñāprabha-ṛṣi-sūtra* states that in the past, Maitreya was the ṛṣi Sarvajñāprabha;
he encountered the Buddha Maitreya, who preached the *Samādhi Sūtra*, and made a vow that when he would attain Buddhahood in the future, he too—

He is named Maitreya Buddha. Based on these three meanings, he is called Maitreya (the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* says Maitreya; the *Saṃghāṭa Sūtra* says Maitrīyi; the Wei translation says "Compassion"). Question: There are two points of inquiry.
First, upon what basis does one rely when practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*? Second, abiding in what dharma does one practice *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*?
The Sanskrit term *śamatha* is translated here as "calm abiding" (*zhi*). *Vipaśyanā*... [is translated as "insight" (*guan*)].

This is called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā). It is precisely concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā). Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, Chapter 24, "Chapter on Calm Abiding and Contemplation," states:
"Calm abiding is named concentration; contemplation is named wisdom. Furthermore, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, Volume 1, states: "Calm abiding refers to samādhi; contemplation refers to prajñā.
Moreover, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Chapter 568, states: "Calm abiding refers to the non-distraction of the single mind."
"Contemplation" (vipaśyanā) refers to seeing phenomena as they truly are. Furthermore, the seventh fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states:
"Śamatha is the meditative concentration that serves as the antidote to all distractions; vipaśyanā is the wisdom that serves as the antidote to all inversions.

[This is also found in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* 24, the *Awakening of Faith*, the first and tenth fascicles of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*, the second fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, the third fascicle of the *Upāsakaśīla-sūtra*, the nineteenth fascicle of the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, and the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-sūtra*].
The *Saṃyuktāgama* in twenty-four fascicles; the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* in thirty-one fascicles. [These] explain two distinct characteristics; fearing prolixity, they are not described here.

The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: "Good son, you should know that the provisional designation of the dharmas of a bodhisattva, as well as the non-abandonment of the vow for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, serve as the basis and support upon which one practices within the Mahāyāna."
Regarding *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the commentary states:
this is the second correct response of the Tathāgata, namely that bodhisattvas employ the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).

One practices *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* by relying upon provisional designations (*prajñapti*). Furthermore, one practices *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* while abiding in and not abandoning the great vow for enlightenment.
Regarding "provisional designations of phenomena": all phenomena are beyond names and expressions, yet the twelvefold teaching is provisionally established.
Thus, the first [chapter] of this sutra says: "Precisely within these things that are beyond expression..."
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Because one desires to cause others to manifest perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*), one provisionally establishes names and concepts.

Furthermore, the first fascicle of the *Bao’en jīng* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness) states: "Phenomena are beyond verbal expression; the Tathāgata, through wondrous skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), is able to express through names and signs those phenomena that are devoid of names and signs.
Moreover, the thirty-sixth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* asks: "For what reason, regarding a single..."
All phenomena possess a nature that transcends verbal expression, yet verbal expressions arise regarding them. [Question:

If one were not to employ verbal expressions, one would be unable to explain to others that all phenomena possess a nature transcending verbal expression, and others likewise would be unable to hear such a meaning.

If there were no hearing, they would be unable to know this nature of all phenomena that transcends verbal expression. It is for the purpose of enabling others to hear it [that verbal expressions are used].

One knows that all phenomena have an ineffable intrinsic nature (*nirabhilāpya-svabhāva*). Therefore, with respect to this ineffable intrinsic nature, one gives rise to verbal expressions while abiding in the vow for enlightenment (*bodhicitta-praṇidhāna*).
As stated in the second fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavāca-śāstra*: "Regarding the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*):

it refers to the bodhisattvas' arousal of the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). If bodhisattvas abide in the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) of bodhisattvas, they do so desiring to benefit [sentient beings]."
All sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, by virtue of those powerful causal conditions and modes of practice,
give rise to great vows for unexcelled bodhi and receive the dharma of generating the mind of awakening, thinking:
"I shall certainly realize unexcelled bodhi in order to deliver all sentient beings of the ten directions, so that they may be freed from all afflictions and freed from all suffering."
Because it is difficult [to attain], this generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is further of two kinds. First is the conventional generation of the mind (*saṃvṛti-cittotpāda*).
This refers, for example, to someone who stands respectfully before a wise person, gives rise to a superior intention (*adhyāśaya*), and makes a vow, saying:
"Venerable sir, please remember me," or "Noble one, please remember me," or "Upādhyāya (meaning 'Preceptor'), please remember me; I, who am named so-and-so..."
From this day forth, I shall teach the unsurpassed bodhicitta for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
From now on, whatever practices of the six perfections I cultivate shall all be for the purpose of realizing unsurpassed bodhi.
I now go forth in harmony with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas; may the Honored One bear witness to me.
This Bodhisattva does likewise in the second and third [assemblies].

They realize the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), meaning that as if having already passed through the first incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) and attained the Bodhisattva’s first stage, the "Extremely Joyful" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they proceed until, by virtue of this, they become irreversible from their vow for great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
This is called the generation of the mind through realizing the nature of phenomena. Alternatively, it may be understood as follows:
"Dwelling in the vow for enlightenment" refers to the four types of mind found in the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* by Śrīguṇaprabha says: "What is meant by 'dwelling'? It is the mind that dwells in aspiration and seeks after a fruit characterized by such-and-such qualities.
This passage reveals the four kinds of minds associated with the benefits of the Bodhisattva's fruition. What are these four? First, the boundless...
1. The mind [of universal compassion], as in the sūtra: "All classes of sentient beings," and so forth. 2. The two supreme minds, as in the sūtra:
"I shall cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to liberation. 3. The mind of inclusive reception, as in the sūtra:
"Thus I have liberated immeasurable sentient beings; yet, in reality, there is no sentient being who has been liberated. 4. Right Knowledge.
Regarding the mind: as the sutra states, "If a sentient being still harbors the notion of a self, they cannot be called a bodhisattva," it is explained in detail therein.
Vasubandhu’s *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: first, the vast mind; second, the foremost mind; third, the constant mind; and fourth, the non-perverted mind.
As for "within the Mahāyāna," this refers to the cultivation of the gates of śamatha and vipaśyanā, which encompasses both piṭakas while distinguishing itself from the Śrāvaka-piṭaka. Therefore...

It is called the Mahāyāna. It is named the Mahāyāna because it encompasses the principles, teachings, practices, and fruits; it is that which is mounted by great beings (*mahāpuruṣa*) and possesses superior functional utility.

(Now, regarding this Mahāyāna: the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* explain the Mahāyāna through three meanings; the first chapter of Asvabhāva’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* explains the Mahāyāna through two meanings and seven meanings;

the *Dvādaśamukha Śāstra* explains the Mahāyāna through six meanings; the *Bhadrapāla-śīla-sūtra* [fascicle] 7, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* [fascicle] 8, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* [fascicle] 8, the *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* [fascicle] 11, the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* [fascicle] 12, and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* [fascicle] 46 explain the Mahāyāna through seven meanings.)
The *Mahāyānaguṇaparikīrtana-sūtra* explains the Mahāyāna through thirty-seven meanings. Regarding the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*:
since calm abiding and insight are primary among the practices of a bodhisattva, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna;

according to the Dharma he has attained, adorned with the power of concentration and wisdom, he delivers sentient beings by means of this. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 17, says:
Just as with a chariot, if one wheel is strong and the other weak, it will not be stable; so too it is when wisdom (*prajñā*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are unequal.

Therefore, a bodhisattva practices both calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) together. (The *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, chapter ten, contains four propositions: first, having concentration but no wisdom; second, having wisdom but no concentration;
third, having both concentration and wisdom; fourth, having neither concentration nor wisdom. These should be discussed here.)
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying: "As the World-Honored One has spoken of the four kinds of objects of focus. [Commentary:
This is the second section, the gate of the distinctions among the objects of focus for śamatha and vipaśyanā. Within this, there are two parts: first, the question, and second, the answer.
In the question, there are three sections: first, the heading indicating the activity and citing the number; second, listing the names according to that number; and third, the actual inquiry.

This is the first of the interrogative statements. Regarding the term "objective entity" (*viṣayavastu*): "objective" (*viṣaya*) refers to the field of perception; "entity" (*vastu*) refers to the substantial nature.
Since all four types of objects of cognition possess a substantial nature, they are termed "objective entities."
First, the objective referent that is a conceptual image; second, the objective referent that is a non-conceptual image;
third, the objective referent that is the limit of phenomena; and fourth, the objective referent that is the accomplishment of what was to be done.
The commentary states: Second, the enumeration of names according to their number. There are four types of objects of focus (*ālambana*) for the fetters (*saṃyojana*):

first, the pervasive object of focus; second, the object of focus for purifying conduct; third, the object of focus for skillfulness; and fourth, the object of focus for purification of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Regarding these four types, various sūtras differ. According to this sūtra and the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, however, only the four pervasive objects of focus are enumerated.

The text cites these but does not explain them. If one follows the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapters thirteen and sixty-five, it enumerates in full the four types of objects of focus, such as pervasive, complete, pure conduct, and so forth, yet provides no explanation.
This is also the case in the sixth chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and the twelfth chapter of the *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Xianyang lun), chapter sixteen, and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter twenty-six, extensively explain the four kinds of objects of focus (*ālambana*) in succession;
therefore, they are now compared and analyzed here. Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "What is the object of focus regarding phenomena (*dharma*)? Briefly stated in detail, there are four:

namely, the pervasive object of focus (*vyāpyālambana*), the object of focus for purifying conduct (*caritaviśodhanālambana*), the object of focus for skillfulness (*kauśalyālambana*), and the object of focus for purifying ethical discipline (*vyañjanālambana*). [First,] the pervasive object of focus..."

Furthermore, there are four kinds: namely, the object of focus consisting of the conceptual image (*savikalpa-pratibimba*), the object of focus consisting of the non-conceptual image (*nirvikalpa-pratibimba*), the object of focus consisting of the limit of phenomena (*vastuparyanta*), and the object of focus consisting of the fulfillment of what is to be done (*kāryapariniṣpatti*). Regarding the conceptual object of focus:
it refers to the objective domain of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* that arises through the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*). (The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states:)
*Adhimukti-manasikāra* (attention through resolute conviction) is exclusively mundane attention. Regarding the object of non-conceptual images (*nirvikalpa-bimba*):
this refers to the objective domain of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* resulting from *tattvamanasikāra* (attention to reality). [The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states:

"Tattvamanasikāra is exclusively supramundane attention and the attention subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) therefrom. Regarding the object of the limit of phenomena (*vastuparyanta*): this refers to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) in their entirety (*yāvadbhāvikatā*).

Nature (*svabhāva*). Regarding the nature as it is (*yathāvadbhāvatā*) and the nature in its full extent (*yāvadbhāvatā*): these refer to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*). (The *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* states:

"In order to reveal that the substance and entities of all knowable phenomena have only such a measure and limit, the three—aggregates, elements, and bases—are established. The nature as it is refers to the four noble truths and their sixteen aspects, suchness (*tathatā*), and the [three seals]:
that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all conditioned phenomena are suffering, and all phenomena are without self.

Nirvāṇa is quiescent, empty, wishless, and signless. (The *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* states: "By means of such distinctions of meaning and categories, one thoroughly understands the objects of knowledge; therefore, it is called 'the nature as-it-is' (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).

Regarding the object of focus for the accomplishment of what is to be done, this refers to the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*). [The *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* states: "For one who has already attained the transformation of the basis, there is no manifestation of inverted objects of focus.

Furthermore, there are five kinds of objects of focus for pure conduct: namely, those whose conduct is dominated by desire take impurity as their object; those whose conduct is dominated by hatred... [and so forth].

One whose temperament is characterized by hatred should cultivate the object of loving-kindness; one whose temperament is characterized by delusion should take as objects the superior natures of beings and the various factors of dependent origination;

one whose temperament is characterized by pride should take as objects the differentiation of the elements; and one whose temperament is characterized by discursive thought should take as objects the mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation.
[The *Abhidharmahṛdaya* 8, *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* 22, *Nyāyānusāra* 59, *Mahāvibhāṣā* 40, and *Yogācārabhūmi* 26 provide extensive explanations of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*).

[The *Abhidharmahṛdaya* 7, *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* 29, *Nyāyānusāra* 79, *Mahāvibhāṣā* 82, *Yogācārabhūmi* 27 and 30, and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* 15 explain the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrīkaruṇābhāvanā*). [The *Yogācārabhūmi* 27 explains the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpādabhāvanā*). [The *Abhidharmahṛdaya* 5 [explains the contemplation of the elements (*dhātubhāvanā*)].]

The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (75), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (27), the commentary on the *Dharmaskandha-śāstra* (8), the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (22), the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (60), the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (26), and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (27) extensively explain the skillful objects of focus (*ālambana*) regarding the contemplation of inhalation and exhalation (*ānāpānasmṛti*).

There are five kinds of these skillful objects of focus: namely, skill in the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*), skill in the elements (*dhātu-kauśalya*), skill in the sense bases (*āyatana-kauśalya*), skill in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*), and skill in what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*). How should one contemplate them? One should do so according to dependent origination.
Regarding skill in observation: what is the distinction between skill in the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*) and skill in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*)?
If, by means of all phenomena, one causes phenomena to be deeply moistened so that they arise free from causelessness and unequal causes, this is skill in dependent origination.

If [one understands] that arising is governed by the correspondence between cause and effect, this is skill in the possible and the impossible. (The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "That is to say, by means of ignorance...")

The profound penetration of all phenomena such as these, and that those phenomena do not arise without cause, nor are they produced by an unequal cause such as Īśvara, and so forth—such investigative wisdom is called skill in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).

That is to say, although only phenomena serve as causes, it is only through the apprehension of corresponding causes that corresponding effects can arise; for example, virtuous conduct brings about desirable maturation (*vipāka*), while unwholesome conduct brings about undesirable maturation. Such analogies and investigative wisdom are called skill in the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).

These five types of skill are explained in detail in the twenty-seventh [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*. Regarding the object of pure ethical discipline (*śīla*): it refers to the coarseness of the lower realms.

Nature. The nature of tranquility in the higher stages; suchness (*tathatā*) and the four noble truths. (The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "The coarse nature of the lower stages and the tranquil nature of the higher stages" is spoken in reference to the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), because by means of this one subdues the various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).

"Suchness and the four noble truths" is spoken in reference to the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*); suchness is mentioned briefly and the four noble truths extensively, because by means of this one eternally eradicates the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
For details, see *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* 27). If analyzed in detail, it is as found in *Abhidharmasamuccaya* 11, *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* 16, and *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* 2.
Sixteen and seventeen. Subsequently, regarding the three objects, various treatises are largely in agreement; therefore, they will not be explained separately.

Regarding the four pervasive objects (*kṛtsnāyatana*), there are differences among the various teachings, and thus they shall now be compared and analyzed. In this present sutra and others, these are taught according to their preeminence;
for this reason, the four types of pervasiveness are specifically highlighted. These four objects have both general and specific names. As for the general name, it refers to the "four types."
Because they are all termed "pervasive objects of focus" (*vyāpyālambana*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 26, states:
"These four kinds of objective referents pervade all things and enter into every object of focus.
They have been proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past, future, and present; therefore, they are called pervasive objects of focus. Furthermore, regarding these...

It is called "pervasive" because it pervades the category of vipaśyanā, the category of śamatha, all objects, true objects, and the objects of the causal relationship between phenomena. This refers to what is called the "discriminated image."
That which is described here as the category of *vipaśyanā* (insight) refers to the non-conceptual image (*nirvikalpa-pratibimba*).

That which is described here as the category of *śamatha* (calm abiding) refers to the limit of phenomena (*vastuparyantatā*). That which is described here as the reality of all things (*sarvavastu-tattva*) refers to the limit of phenomena.
That which is described here as the accomplishment of what was to be done (*kāryapariniṣpatti*) refers to the matter of the connection between cause and effect (*hetuphalasambandha*), and so forth.
He said: "One should know that such an object of pervasive focus conforms to the pure teachings and accords with correct reasoning;
this is called the 'pervasive object of focus. As for its alternative names, they differ across various teachings.
According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the objective domain of calm abiding and insight associated with the mental application of resolute conviction is termed the 'discriminated image.'"

Because it is the object of exclusively mundane mental attention (*manasikāra*), the objective sphere of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) associated with true mental attention is called the "non-conceptual image" (*nirvikalpa-pratibimba*).
Because it is the object of exclusively supramundane mental attention and that which is subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*),
the substantial reality of all phenomena— limited to such a measure and boundary as the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-fields (*āyatana*)— is called [the "object of reality"].

The object of focus regarding the limits of phenomena (*vastuparyantālambana*) is so called because it is the objective domain for one who has already attained the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*);

its full explanation is as stated there. According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, regarding the conceptual image (*savikalpapratibimba*), this refers to an image that corresponds to the object of knowledge (*jñeyavastu*), which is investigated through the practice of insight (*vipaśyanā*) on the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhitabhūmi*).
