Discerning, thoroughly discerning, extensively investigating, and extensively examining the objects of knowledge—namely, the objects of focus for pure conduct, the objects of focus for skillfulness, and the objects of focus for pure ethical discipline—their respective objects of knowledge appear as similar manifestations.
By this principle, they are called "images concordant with the objects of knowledge. Because the practitioner of meditation investigates these, [he...]
Regarding those objects of knowledge that are his natural domain, he examines and definitively ascertains their qualities and faults;

this is called the "discriminated image. As for the "non-discriminated image," it refers to when a practitioner of meditation, having received the characteristics of such an image, no longer examines, discriminates, intensely discriminates, thoroughly investigates, or extensively scrutinizes it; rather, he simply...
Regarding this objective image, one quiets the mind through *śamatha*; this is called the "non-conceptual image.
As for the "limit of phenomena" (*vastuparyantatā*), it refers to the object of focus in its entirety (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and its suchness (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
The nature of the full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and the four noble truths.

The nature of the mode of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*) refers to that which is the object of focus (*ālambana*), namely, the nature of reality (*tattvabhāva*), the nature of suchness (*tathatābhāva*), and the nature of the four principles (*catur-yukti-bhāva*).

The accomplishment of what is to be done (*kāryapariniṣpatti*) refers to the various activities regarding the images of conditions (*pratyaya-pratibimba*) performed by a practitioner of meditation (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) on account of having cultivated serenity (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) as their causal conditions.

The mind attains full perfection in all respects. Because of this perfection, one achieves the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). All coarse heavinesses (*dauṣṭhulya*) are completely extinguished.

Having achieved the transformation of the basis, one transcends mental images; thus, regarding the objects of knowledge, there arises a direct perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣa-jñāna-darśana*) free from conceptual differentiation as to whether things exist or not.
For one who enters the first dhyāna, at the time of attaining that dhyāna, regarding the objects of the first dhyāna—

Regarding the sphere of activity: even for one who enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, at the time of attaining that meditative absorption, they attain the sphere of activity associated with that very absorption;
this is called the accomplishment of the basis of abiding. The full explanation is as stated therein. These are the four types.
In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter eleven, among the forty modes of mental abiding (*manasikāra*), four types of attention (*manasikāra*) are named.

In the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, chapter sixteen, and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter sixty-seven, among the sixteen types of cultivation, these are three kinds of cultivation. Since their explanations of the meaning are largely identical, they are not described separately here.

(Regarding the four types of mental engagement (*manasikāra*): first, mental engagement with conceptual images; second, mental engagement with objects that are non-conceptual images; third, mental engagement with the limit of phenomena as the object; and fourth, mental engagement with the accomplishment of what is to be done. Regarding the three types of cultivation:

first, cultivation of images—this is because conceptual images and non-conceptual images are combined into one; second, cultivation of the limit of phenomena; and third, cultivation of the accomplishment of what is to be done.
According to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, "conceptual images" refers to the insight (*vipaśyanā*) that is the objective domain of samādhi, which is concordant with the objects of knowledge.
Regarding the "object": the non-conceptual image refers to the mental object that is the sphere of activity of samādhi, which is of the same nature as the knowable thing (*jñeya-vastu*).

Regarding the "limit of things" (*vastuparyanta*): it refers to the nature of exhaustiveness (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and the nature of suchness (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*). Regarding the "accomplishment of what is to be done" (*kāryapariniṣpatti*):

it refers to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) and the non-conceptual knowledge based upon this. (The *Treatise on the Three Non-natures* contains many errors and thus is not consulted here. These various...
In this explanation, what is set forth accords with the sūtras and not with the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and similar treatises;

for in those works, both the first and second [stages] are said to be common objects for both śamatha and vipaśyanā. Furthermore, that which differs from the sūtra in the *Yogācārabhūmi* concerns the various dhyānas and so forth.

Because they are established through penetration, I shall now explain the four [objects] mentioned in the sūtra. Since their meaning is the same as that in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā*, I will not explain them separately.
Among these four, how many are the objective referents (*ālambana-vastu*) of śamatha, and how many are those of vipaśyanā?
Regarding the objects of focus: how many are the objects of focus that are shared?
The commentary explains: this is the third section, consisting of the formal inquiry.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: "Good son, there is one object of focus for *śamatha*, namely—"
Non-conceptual images: first, the objective referent of vipaśyanā, namely conceptual images;

second, the objective referent common to both [śamatha and vipaśyanā], namely the culmination of the limits of phenomena (vastuparyantatā) and the accomplishment of what is to be done (kāryapariniṣpatti).
The commentary states: This is the second part, the Tathāgata’s direct response concerning the distinct characteristics of the four objects, as previously explained.
Among these four, the second is the object of *śamatha*, because *śamatha* is non-conceptual.

Among the four, the first is the object of *vipaśyanā*, because *vipaśyanā* involves conceptualization. The latter two among the four are the common objects of both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. *Śamatha*...

Because contemplation universally takes two kinds of objects as its domain. However, regarding the specific distinctions between the stages of these four contemplations, various explanations differ. One school asserts: the first two are objects of the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*).
When practicing in reliance upon the teachings, one contemplates the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the mental image that appears as the objects of all phenomena transformed by one's own mind.

Contemplating while actively seeking and investigating is called "with discrimination" (*savikalpa*); contemplating with a concentrated mind (*samādhi-citta*) while seeking and investigating is called "without discrimination" (*nirvikalpa*).

It is distinct. The third is the objective sphere (*ālambana*) of correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) in the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*); for it is only upon reaching the ten stages that one can fully comprehend the limits of the object.

The fourth objective sphere exists only in the stage of Buddhahood (*buddha-bhūmi*), because it is the objective sphere of the accomplishment of what was to be done through the attainment of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Question: If this is so, how is it that the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* speaks of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*)?

Regarding the "object of focus consisting of images" (*pratibimba-ālambana*): it refers to the objects of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

The commentary explains that because this treatise establishes the principle of universal penetration, its meanings differ from those in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts. One interpretation states:

the first two [types of objects] are common to both the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*) and the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*), as they both possess the objective realm of images; the explanation is the same as previously stated. Another interpretation states: the first three...
All [of these] pertain to the stages prior to the bhūmis as well as the ten bhūmis, because [the categories such as] "exhaustive" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and so forth apply to all stages.
The explanation is as previously stated. One interpretation holds that all four types pertain to all stages, as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (67) states:

"What is the cultivation for the accomplishment of what is to be done? It refers to having already entered into the fundamental dhyānas, or the various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), or the worldly..."

Whether it be mundane concentration (*laukika-samādhi*) or supramundane concentration (*lokottara-samādhi*), all such cultivation is termed "cultivation for the accomplishment of what is to be done" (*kārya-pariniṣpatti-bhāvanā*).
This is stated in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (XVI), and the same is found in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (XI and XXVI). One interpretation states: "All these explanations do not contradict reason."
According to the subsequent scriptural passage, those prior to the stages possess only the first two; those on the ten stages possess the first three; and those on the Buddha stage possess all four.
Therefore, the scripture below states: "At that previous time, they had already attained the two kinds of objects of focus;

now, because they have attained the path of seeing, they further realize the object of focus that is the limit of phenomena (*vastuparyantālambana*), and so forth, up to the realization of *anuttara* [samyaksambodhi]."

...for the sake of *samyaksambodhi*. Furthermore, one attains the object of focus (*ālambana*) wherein that which is to be accomplished is fulfilled; this is explained in detail as therein [stated]. Question:
Does the category of untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) transform into an image (*pratibimba*)? If it does not transform, how can it be reconciled with the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* cited previously?
If it does transform into an image, how then is the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* to be interpreted? It says therein: "When, regarding the object..."
Regarding the phrase "wisdom has nothing at all to apprehend": the answer explains this meaning as stated in the ninth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
It says: "Next, what are the characteristics of the stage of thorough penetration (*prativedha*)? The verse states:

'When, with respect to the object of cognition, wisdom has nothing at all to apprehend, at that time one abides in representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), because of being free from the characteristics of the two appropriations. The commentary states: When the Bodhisattva, with respect to..."

Regarding the object of focus (*ālambana*), wisdom finds nothing at all to be apprehended, because it does not grasp the various signs of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); this is explained at length.
One interpretation holds that this wisdom lacks both parts [of subject and object], because it is said to be devoid of the characteristics of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).

Another interpretation holds that this wisdom possesses both the aspect (*nimitta*) and the vision (*darśana*), for it arises bearing those aspects and is thus called "taking that as its object. If it lacked those aspects, it would be...

Regarding that which takes [an object] as its condition: the cognition of form and so forth should be called the cognition of sound and so forth. If there were no seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*), it would be unable to take [an object] as its condition;

how then could it be said to be the cognition that takes *tathatā* (suchness) as its condition? Let it not be the case that *tathatā* itself is also called a cognizer. Therefore, one must admit that, apart from this, there definitely exists a seeing-portion.

According to one interpretation, the seeing-portion of this cognition exists while the image-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) does not; it is described as "taking without an image" (*animittagrahaṇa*). It is not [the case that the image-portion is absent].

Because it grasps signs (*nimitta*), although there is a seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), it is non-conceptual and is said not to be a grasper (*grāhaka*). This does not mean that grasping is entirely absent.

Although there is no image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), it can be said that this [consciousness] arises bearing the likeness of suchness (*tathatā*), because it is not separate from suchness—just as when the self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) takes the seeing-part as its object, it does so without transformation.
This case should be understood in the same way. If it were to take [its object] through transformation, it would not be [the self-witnessing part].
Direct realization, like subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), should involve conceptualization; therefore, one must admit that this [wisdom] has vision but no aspect (*nimitta*).
Do all subsequently attained wisdoms possess two parts? One interpretation holds that both are absent, because they are free from the duality of subject and object (*grāhya-grāhaka*).

Another interpretation holds that this wisdom has vision but no aspect, because it is said that the category of this wisdom involves conceptualization. All noble wisdoms (*ārya-jñāna*) are capable of observing, and they are capable of observing.
Because it illuminates the object, there is one interpretation that this wisdom possesses both parts (the subjective and objective aspects).

It is said that while this contemplative investigation resembles the aspect of True Suchness (*tathatā*), it does not perceive the actual nature of True Suchness. This is explained at length in the third chapter of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, which shares the same intent as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Although there are various theories, according to the school of Dharmapāla, non-conceptual wisdom perceives existence as its aspect and non-existence as its essence; all subsequent [wisdoms]...
One attains wisdom; thus, the [mental] image and the vision both exist together. Question: If this is so, how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*?

That treatise states: "The object of focus consisting of the non-conceptual image refers to the objective domain of calm abiding and insight resulting from authentic mental attention (*bhūta-manaskāra*).
Authentic mental attention is exclusively supramundane, as well as that which follows it..."

Regarding the attainment of *manasikāra* (attention), the commentary explains that Asaṅga speaks only of "true attention" (*tattvamanasikāra*) and does not mention "supramundane wisdom" (*lokottarajñāna*).
Therefore, one should know that the phrase "supramundane and so forth" refers to the intention of Siṃhabuddhi; it was not spoken by Asaṅga. Thus, there is no contradiction.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva, by relying on these four kinds of objects of focus for śamatha and vipaśyanā, succeed in seeking śamatha and becoming skilled in vipaśyanā?"
The commentary states: From here below begins the third section, the detailed analysis of the gates for seeking śamatha and vipaśyanā.
This section contains two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. This is the question. The question has two intentions. First:
how does a bodhisattva, relying upon these four types of objects for śamatha and vipaśyanā, seek śamatha? Second: how does he become skilled in vipaśyanā? These are the words [of the question].

Regarding the phrase "seeking the wholesome" (*kuśala*), there are three interpretations. First, some say that both "seeking" (*paryeṣaṇā*) and "wholesome" (*kuśala*) carry the sense of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

The term "seeking the wholesome" is spoken in order to distinguish between *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). Second, some say that "seeking the wholesome" applies to both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Therefore, Sthiramati states:

"One practices *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and skillfully knows *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Third, some say that "seeking" (*paryeṣaṇā*) carries the sense of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), because it refers to the progressive cultivation of *śamatha*; thus, it refers exclusively to *śamatha*.
It is not contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). "Skillful" means skillfully knowing; because *vipaśyanā* skillfully knows the meaning, it is exclusively contemplation and not tranquility (*śamatha*).
Therefore, this sutra says: "One is able to seek *śamatha* and is able to be skillful in *vipaśyanā*."
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: "Good son, the Dharma that I have taught for the sake of the bodhisattvas is a provisional designation, namely:
the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, itivṛttakas, jātakas, vaipulyas, adbhutadharmas, and upadeśas."
The commentary states: From this point downward is the second section, the Tathāgata’s direct response. This contains two parts: first, clarifying the teachings upon which cultivation is based;
second, revealing the correct cultivation based on those teachings. This is the first part. The Buddha told Maitreya:
"I have established twelve divisions of the Dharma for the sake of bodhisattvas through conventional designation, namely: from the *sūtra* up to the *upadeśa*. However, these ten..."
The various teachings are extremely numerous; for now, I shall describe what is stated in the sixth chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*. It says:
"Sūtra" refers to that which is composed in prose (*gadya*) to briefly explain the meanings that ought to be explained.

"Geya" (Verses) refers to those passages within the sūtras that are either in the middle or at the end, restated in verse (*śloka*), as well as those sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) that require further explanation through verse; therefore, they are called Geya.

Verse. *Vyākaraṇa* (Prophecy/Elucidation) refers to those passages where the noble disciples (*ārya-śrāvaka*), having passed away into the past, have their merits, faults, and the distinctions of their places of rebirth prophesied.
Furthermore, sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) are also called *vyākaraṇa*, because they reveal and elucidate the profound, hidden intent (*saṃdhi*).
*Geya* (Chanted Recitation) refers to that which is proclaimed in verses (*pada*) within various contexts, consisting of either two or three lines.

Either four, five, or six [categories]. (The commentary states: according to the *Vyākhyāyukti*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, and other texts: "Spontaneous utterance" (*svayambhāṣita*) refers to those instances in the various sūtras where the Tathāgata speaks spontaneously out of his own inclination.
"Dependent origination" (*nidāna*) refers to speaking in response to a request, as well as due to specific causes and conditions.
The establishment of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) is also called the "origin" (*nidāna*). The "illustrative tales" (*avadāna*) refers to those discourses (*sūtra*) that contain analogies.
The "past events" (*itivṛttaka*) refers to the proclamation of accounts concerning the previous lives of the noble disciples (*ārya-śrāvaka*) and others.

The "birth stories" (*jātaka*) refers to the proclamation of accounts concerning the previous conduct of the Bodhisattva. The "extensive teachings" (*vaipulya*) refers to discourse associated with the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
That which is called *Vaipulya* is also called *Vaitulya* and *Vaidalya*. For what reason is it called *Vaipulya*?
Because it is the basis for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, and because it proclaims the vast and profound Dharma.
For what reason is it called *Vaitulya*? Because it can extensively demolish all obstacles. For...
For what reason is it called "Incomparable" (*anupama*)? Because there are no phenomena that can serve as its counterpart. Regarding "Marvelous Teachings" (*adbhutadharma*):
it refers to those instances where the most extremely rare, extraordinary, and marvelous dharmas of the śrāvakas, the great bodhisattvas, and the Tathāgatas are proclaimed.
Regarding "Discourses" (*upadeśa*): it refers to those instances where all things are explained without error.

The profound and hidden characteristics. (Based on the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the Sanskrit names are listed in full but not translated here; thus that sūtra says: "Those so-called sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, and gāthās...")
Udāna, Nidāna, Avadāna, Itivṛttaka, Jātaka, Vaipulya, Adbhutadharma, and Upadeśa.
If these were to be analyzed in detail, they would be as fully set forth in a separate chapter.
The Bodhisattva listens well to this, receives it well, masters it thoroughly through speech, investigates it well with the mind, and penetrates it well through insight.

The commentary states: From here below is the second section, which concerns correct cultivation based on the teaching. This contains two parts: first, a general explanation of the methods for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;
second, following this, a specific explanation of the two gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Within the first part, there are two sections; the first...

This clarifies the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Next, the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) will be explained; this is the first [of those]. Now, this wisdom derived from hearing possesses five characteristics:
first, listening well; second, receiving well; third, verbal mastery; fourth, mental investigation;
and fifth, insight through thorough penetration. This means that bodhisattvas, regarding these teachings, listen with focused attention and are able to receive them well.
One upholds it, recites it until it is mastered, contemplates it well with the mind, and penetrates it well with wisdom.

If one follows the twenty-fifth [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) is explained by means of four aspects; these include the aspect of initial listening mentioned in this sutra.
If one follows the thirtieth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are six aspects, adding the aspect of awakened wisdom (*buddhi*) to the latter five aspects.
The names differ slightly, but the meaning corresponds to this sutra. Thus, that treatise states: "What is the stage consisting of what is heard (śrutamayī bhūmi)?

It refers to the immeasurable distinctions of the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables within the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), which are first apprehended through wisdom and then received through hearing."
To recite, chant, and keep in mind; to understand without error—these are explained as corresponding respectively to the five [factors] of this sutra:
"listening" corresponds to listening well; "receiving" corresponds to receiving well; "reciting with mastery of terminology" corresponds to being well-versed and proficient;
"recalling and reflecting" corresponds to the mind’s thorough investigation; and "seeking only to understand" corresponds to the thorough penetration of vision.
"One then dwells alone in a secluded place, attending to and reflecting upon these very dharmas that have been well-considered.
The commentary explains: this is the second [stage], which clarifies the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

That is to say, one dwells alone in a secluded place, attending to and reflecting upon the meanings of the dharmas heard through the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), by means of two kinds of mental images (*pratibimba*). Thus, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:
The sixteenth [chapter] asks: What is the stage consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī bhūmi*)?
It refers to someone who, dwelling alone in a secluded place, reflects with careful discernment upon the principles of all phenomena as they were heard and as they have been thoroughly mastered.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter thirteen, states: "If that is so, then in a secluded place one can induce the mind to abide in correct *śamatha*."
Furthermore, if the mind abides in right śamatha, one is able to induce vipaśyanā.
Then, regarding this very mind capable of reflection, one attends to it with mental attention within the continuity of the internal mind.
Because one thus correctly induces and dwells in it extensively, there arises physical pliancy (praśrabdhi) and mental pliancy; this is called śamatha.

The commentary states: From here below is the second section, the individual explanation of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). This consists of two parts: first *śamatha*, then *vipaśyanā*.
Within the former, there are two parts: first, the actual explanation of the gate of *śamatha*; second, the concluding response to the preceding question.
Regarding the first gate, there are two interpretations. One says: within this text, there are four sections: first, the object of focus (*ālambana*); second, the subject that focuses...
1. Mind; 2. Its object; 3. The manifestation of faith; 4. The conclusion of its name.
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, that very mind capable of contemplation is the object of focus (*ālambana*)," there are two interpretations of this passage. One says:

within the sphere of these dharmas and meanings, the mind associated with the wisdoms of hearing and reflection that correctly contemplates them is the object of focus. Another says: [the mind itself is the object].
The mind associated with these two types of wisdom serves as the objective referent (*ālambana*).
Herein, it is intended that in the gate of *śamatha*, the mind is made to abide in a single object; therefore, the mind itself is taken as the referent.

In *vipaśyanā*, because one desires to discern the objects of knowledge, the *nimitta-bhāga* (reflected image) transformed by the two types of wisdom—those arising from hearing and reflection—serves as the objective referent. Internally...
Regarding "contemplating the mental continuum through attention": this distinguishes the cessation of the subjective perceiver. The term "inner mind" refers to the inclusion of the perceiving mind;
because it remains within meditative concentration, it is called the "inner mind. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on Yoga Practice), fascicle 63, states:
"By binding the mind to an internal object of focus, it does not flow outward toward external objects. This explains the characteristic of right mind.

Continuing to apply mental attention, because one dwells extensively in such correct practice associated with the mind of hearing and reflection, one gives rise to physical pliancy (*kāya-praśrabdhi*) and mental pliancy (*citta-praśrabdhi*).
This indicates that state, namely *śamatha*, because it possesses the nine stages of correct practice beginning with "internal abiding.
Regarding the arising of physical and mental pliancy: physical pliancy refers to the four... [text truncated]
It is the great derived factor of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). As for "pliancy of mind," it refers to the factor of pliancy among the eleven wholesome mental factors.
The *Tattvārthā-ṭīkā* states: "Lightness and tranquility, possessing the capacity for efficacy—this is the characteristic of pliancy.
Thus, the state of physical and mental pliancy is established as *śamatha*. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle thirteen, says: "If one is able to..."
Regarding the nine types of mental abiding within, this is called the correct śamatha of internal mental abiding.
As for the nine mental abidings, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Compendium of Abhidharma), chapter five, merely lists the nine names without providing an explanation.

The *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* (Commentary on the Compendium of Abhidharma), chapter ten, cites and explains them in sequence; thus that treatise states: "Śamatha is the gathering of the mind within so as to cause it to abide."

Equilibrium (*samasthāpanā*), stabilization (*avasthāpanā*), close stabilization (*upasthāpanā*), subduing (*damana*), pacification (*śamana*), complete pacification (*vyupaśamana*), one-pointed concentration (*ekotīkaraṇa*), and even-minded maintenance (*samasamasthāpanā*).
These nine modes of practice cause the mind to abide; this is *śamatha*. Regarding "abiding" (*sthāpanā*):

it refers to withdrawing from external objects of focus and remaining free from internal distraction by initially binding the mind. Regarding "equilibrium" (*samasthāpanā*): it refers to initially binding [the mind] when it is coarse...
Once the mind has been moved, because one continuously binds the mindfulness to the object, making it subtle and gradually more concise, there is "abiding.
Because at times one loses mindfulness and the mind wanders outward, but one immediately withdraws and gathers it back, there is "close abiding.
From the very beginning, in order to cause the mind not to be scattered outward, one draws it near and causes it to abide; thus, there is "taming. From the outset...

Having already [attained this], by means of the predominant power of perceiving the defects within the phenomena of form and so forth—which are causes of distraction—one tames the mind so that it does not flow outward.

As for "tranquility" (*śamatha*), because one perceives deep-seated defects within the afflictions of discursive thought and mental agitation—the distractions of a disturbed mind—one restrains the mind so that it does not flow outward. Most extremely...
"Tranquil" means that whenever forgetfulness, distraction, discursive thoughts, and so forth suddenly manifest, one immediately subdues them so that they do not arise again.
"One-pointed concentration" means dwelling continuously in superior samādhi through diligent application that is uninterrupted and flawless.
"Equanimous maintenance" means because of having cultivated [the practice] well, it does not [arise] by means of...
The preparatory application (prayoga) is free from effort; it is a continuous flow of concentrated mind, turning away from distraction.
A detailed analysis is as found in the thirtieth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the seventh [chapter] of the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
"This is called śamatha" concludes its name. One interpretation states that within this passage, it is divided into two parts; first, again, regarding these very [points]...
The preceding section explained the skillful means for *śamatha* (calm abiding). The subsequent passage beginning with "In this way" and so forth correctly explains *śamatha* itself.

This clarifies that the superior grade of *śamatha* and *prajñā* takes as its objective condition the internal continuum of mind consisting of the two grades—middling and inferior—of the wisdoms derived from hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*).
The correct explanation of the characteristics of *śamatha* is identical in meaning to the previous interpretation.
"In this way, the bodhisattva is able to seek śamatha.
The commentary states: This is the second response to the preceding question.
Because he takes as his basis the attainment of physical and mental pliancy (praśrabdhi), he [directs his attention] toward the dharmas exactly as they have been well-considered.
"The mental image traversed by internal samādhi; through the contemplation of resolute conviction, one abandons the characteristics of the mind.
Commentary: From here below is the second section, the detailed explanation of the gate of contemplation. This contains two parts: first, the formal explanation of the gate of contemplation.

The subsequent section concludes by answering the preceding question. Within the previous section, there are two explanations. First, it is said that this passage is explained based on the state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*) as a whole, which has two interpretations.
One interpretation explains this passage solely in terms of the mental image (*pratibimba*).
This contains two parts: first, the exclusion of what is not the object of focus; second, the cultivation of insight based on the object. This is the first part. The text consists of two [sections].

Section. First, regarding "by obtaining that, etc.," this distinguishes the basis for insight (*vipaśyanā*). That is to say, by taking as a basis the pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) obtained through prior calm abiding (*śamatha*), one is able to give rise to insight.
Regarding "subsequently, precisely upon that, etc.," this excludes what is not the object of focus.

That is to say, just like the objects of hearing and reflection, one contemplates the phenomena (*dharma*) and gives rise to an internal samādhi that perceives an image (*pratibimba*) concordant with those [phenomena].
Regarding this image, one gives rise to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) and reflects upon it with discernment.
This is for the purpose of generating the mental sign (*nimitta*) that serves as the object of focus for vipaśyanā while relinquishing śamatha. As for the "mental sign," the mind itself is the sign;
therefore, it is called the "mental sign."
Regarding the objects of knowledge within the images of such samādhi, that which is able to correctly discern,
most thoroughly discern, universally investigate, and universally examine— whether it be acceptance, delight, wisdom, view,
or contemplation— is called vipaśyanā.
The commentary states: This is the second [section], which concerns the cultivation of contemplation based on the object. The text consists of four sections. First, "Regarding that very...

and so forth, distinguishes the object of contemplation; namely, the aforementioned images that are the objects of internal samādhi, which serve as the objects of knowledge and are thus the objects of contemplation.
Second, "One who is able to correctly discern... and so forth, explains the characteristics of the practice of contemplation; that is to say, this...
The four aspects of wisdom within the middle [category] are as explained in the tenth fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*.
Thus, that treatise states: "Discerning all phenomena" is by way of their full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*); "thoroughly discerning" is by way of their suchness (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*);
and "universal investigation" is the establishment of phenomena through wisdom accompanied by conceptual mental attention (*savikalpamanasikāra*).
Regarding "by way of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇataḥ*): "thoroughly and carefully observing" means investigating with complete detail.
This is largely identical to the thirty [stages] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. That text states: "What are the four kinds of *vipaśyanā*?
It refers to a bhikṣu who, relying upon internal *śamatha*, is able to correctly discern, most thoroughly discern, and universally seek among all phenomena."
Reflecting and investigating thoroughly—these are called the four kinds of vipaśyanā. What is meant by "correctly investigating"?

It refers to being able to correctly discern, in terms of the nature of things as they are (yāvadbhāvikatā), the objects of focus for pure conduct, or the objects of focus for skillfulness, or the objects of focus for pure ethical discipline. What is meant by...
"Ultimate investigation" refers to the ultimate investigation of that very object of focus regarding its nature as it truly is (*yathāvadbhāva*).

What is called "thorough searching"? It refers to thoroughly searching that very object of focus by means of a conceptual mental attention (*manasikāra*) accompanied by wisdom (*prajñā*), grasping its characteristics (*nimitta*).
What is called... [the remainder of the sentence is omitted in the source].
"Thorough investigation" (*parimārgaṇā*) refers to the careful and precise seeking after, and the thorough investigation, of that very same objective referent (*ālambana-viṣaya*).
As stated in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Xianyang shengjiao lun), Chapter 4, these are respectively termed the four kinds of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Third, from "if patience, etc.

below, there is an analysis of the alternative names for contemplation, which consists of five types: "patience" (*kṣānti*) means patient understanding; "delight" (*ruci*) means experiencing pleasure; and "wisdom" (*prajñā*) is simply discrimination (*viveka*).
"Seeing" (*darśana*) refers to seeking; "viewing" (*prekṣā*) refers to observation. These five types are identical in meaning but differ in name. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (82) states:

"Wisdom (*prajñā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), seeing (*darśana*), clarity (*vidyā*), and viewing (*prekṣā*) are distinctions of name. Their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists of the mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*) that discriminates the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*).
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (13) is likewise the same as the *Yogācārabhūmi*. These four are their names.
Vipaśyanā is a synthesis. Both [explanations]—the primary and the reflected—are applied to explain this passage.

Regarding the phrase "precisely upon that which is as it is," etc., this refers to the reflected image and the primary reality (the object). Regarding "internal samādhi," etc., this means that the reflected image arises based on the primary reality, and one relies upon that reflected image for observation.
Regarding "precisely upon such as this," etc., it means that by virtue of observing the reflected image, one realizes the primary reality of the object to be known.

Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 26, states: "The practitioner of contemplation, because they investigate the reflected image, examines and ascertains the virtues and faults within the objects of knowledge that constitute its fundamental nature," thereby explaining the remaining phrases.
The meaning is as explained previously. One interpretation states that this passage is explained by encompassing both the meditative and non-meditative states.

Within this, there are two parts: first, the analysis of the preparatory means for insight (*vipaśyanā*); second, the explicit elucidation of fundamental *vipaśyanā* itself, which follows immediately below.

In the former part, there are two sub-sections: first, the analysis of the basis upon which insight relies; second, the explicit elucidation of the preparatory means itself, which begins with the words "by virtue of having attained the body."
Because mental pliancy (*citta-praśrabdhi*) serves as the basis, one relies on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to develop insight (*vipaśyanā*).

However, that which is generated must necessarily rely on the distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta) as its preliminary means, namely the wisdoms of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) and reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*). This passage precisely clarifies the preparatory means of hearing and reflection.

Why is this so? Because the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the two doors of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) have already been presented previously; thus, even though one has already attained concentration, one further arouses the distracted mind as a means for hearing and reflection.
Regarding "internal samādhi": concentrating the mind so that it does not scatter is termed "internal. It is called "internal" because it does not refer to being actually in meditative absorption;
thus the term "internal" is used. The rest is as explained previously. Furthermore, for both this preparatory stage (*upāya*) and the fundamental stage (*maula*), there are two interpretations.
The first [type] refers exclusively to the mental image; the second applies to both the basis and the image. Their meanings are the same as explained previously.
Thus, "the bodhisattva is able to skillfully practice vipaśyanā.
The commentary states: this is the second conclusion that answers the preceding question.

Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if bodhisattvas take the mind as their object and internally contemplate the mind, what should all those acts of attention be called until they have attained physical and mental pliancy?"
The commentary states: From here below is the fourth section, the gateway of mental attention (*manasikāra*) that accords with calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).

This section contains two parts: first, the explanation of mental attention that accords with calm abiding; second, the mental attention that accords with insight. Within the former, there are two sub-sections:

first, the question; second, the answer. This is the question. It refers to what was previously explained: subsequently, one is able to contemplate the internal continuity of the mind within this very state.
Regarding mental attention: what should this mental attention be called prior to the attainment of pliancy?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Maitreya: "Good son, it is not the mental attention of śamatha;
rather, it is the mental attention associated with the resolute conviction that accords with śamatha."

The commentary states: The second part is the Blessed One’s direct answer. This is the attention (manasikāra) that accords with śamatha, but it is not actual śamatha, because pliancy (praśrabdhi) is absent.
Blessed One, as long as bodhisattvas have not yet attained physical and mental pliancy, regarding all that they have contemplated...
"One contemplates the mental image that is the object of internal samādhi regarding all phenomena. What should such a form of attention be called?
The commentary states: This is the second [section], "Attention of Subsequent Observation" (*anupaśyanā-manasikāra*). It consists of two parts: first the question, and then the answer. This...
This is the question: Regarding what was previously explained— that is, within the meditative object (samādhi-gocara-bimba) of the dharmas as they have been well-considered,
one observes and resolves upon them while relinquishing the mental image—
what should this mental engagement (manasikāra) be called prior to the attainment of pliancy (praśrabdhi)?
"Good son, it is not the mental engagement of vipaśyanā; rather, it is the mental engagement associated with conviction that accords with vipaśyanā.

The commentary explains: This is the Tathāgata’s second correct response. It is the mental engagement that accords with contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), but it is not the actual contemplation itself. There is none.

Because of [the attainment of] pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). According to this very passage, it is proven that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* exist only within the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-avasthā*).

Furthermore, by virtue of this text, one should understand that the statements in the preceding section regarding the "succession of internal mental attention" (*manasikāra*) and so forth are merely its preparatory means (*upāya*), while the present [teaching] constitutes the definitive meaning (*siddhānta*).

The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, should it be said that the path of śamatha and the path of vipaśyanā are different, or should it be said that they are not different?"
The commentary states: From here below is the fifth section, the chapter on the similarities and differences between the two paths of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).

This section contains two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. This is the question: "Regarding these two types—*śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*—they are the domains traversed by all practitioners.
Because they can induce the various dharmas of the noble paths, they are called 'paths. Are these two paths identical or distinct?"
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: "Good son, one should say that they are neither different nor non-different.
The commentary states: From this point downward is the second section, the Tathāgata’s formal response. This contains two parts; first, the general indication based on the question.
The subsequent questions and answers provide a detailed explanation; this is the first [point].
Why is it not different? Because the mind that takes the object of vipaśyanā as its objective support is itself the objective support.
Why is it not non-different? Because the conceptualized image is not the objective support.
The commentary states: This is the second detailed explanation of the question and answer. Regarding this passage, there are two interpretations. One says:

"There is no difference" refers to the substantial entity (*bhāva*). For example, when calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) proceed together, they both take as their substantial object the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) derived from hearing and reflection, as well as the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of the mind that takes it as its object. [This is so] because of the substance...
Because they are the same, it is said that "there is no difference. That it is not the case that "there is no difference" is explained in terms of the images (*pratibimba*).

This is because when *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* take the same object, the transformed images are each distinct—namely, there are images with conceptualization and images without conceptualization—and since there is such a distinction, it is said that "it is not the case that there is no difference.
One interpretation states that "there is no difference" refers to *śamatha*.

Although it cannot take as its object the focal domain of the *vipaśyanā* that consists of the image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) derived from hearing and reflection, it can take as its object the mind’s seeing-aspect (*darśanabhāga*) which is directed toward the focal domains of those two wisdoms of hearing and reflection; therefore, they are not different.
That they are not non-different means the same as explained previously. Between these two explanations, the latter is superior because it accords with the preceding text.

The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding the images that are the objects of the various samādhis of vipaśyanā, should one say they are different from this mind, or should one say they are not different?"
The commentary states: From here below begins the sixth section, the "Analysis of the Gate of Consciousness-Only regarding Calm Abiding and Insight" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā-vijñaptimātra*).

Alternatively, it may be titled the "Analysis of the Gate of the Identity and Difference between Mind and Objects. This section contains six parts: first, the question; second, the answer; third, the inquiry; fourth, the explanation; fifth, the objection; and sixth, the resolution.
This is the first inquiry of Maitreya. Regarding the intent of this question, there are three interpretations. The first states:
here, the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is cited to inquire about the object of focus (*ālambana*) of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

This is as in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, which speaks only of the "images" (*pratibimba*) that are the objects traversed by various *samādhis*, but does not mention "contemplation. As this sutra states later: "The images traversed by *samādhi* appear."

Because it is the object of focus for the *vipaśyanā-samādhi*. The intent of this question is as follows:

Regarding this image, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it is like the images of the mute, the blind, and so forth. According to the *Saṃgraha* of the Liang dynasty, among the ten universal bases (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*), the first eight consist of form (*rūpa*), namely:

Blue, yellow, red, and white; earth, water, fire, and wind. According to the Sautrāntika school, as in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, the unmanifest is exclusively non-obstructive (*anidarśana*) and non-resistant (*apratigha*).

Form is not mind. The form that constitutes the objects of various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) is subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). This is largely consistent with the Mahāyāna;
thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter thirteen, states: "The Sautrāntikas say:

Furthermore, regarding the sūtras which speak of 'three kinds of form,' the Yogācāras explain that when one cultivates dhyāna, the form that is the object of concentration produced by the power of meditative concentration is not an object of the eye-faculty; therefore, it is called [unmanifest form]."
It is "non-obstructive" (anidarśana) because it does not obstruct a location; thus it is called "non-resistant" (apratigha).

If one asks, "If that is so, how can it be called 'matter' (rūpa)?"—the explanation of this name is the same as for the unmanifest (avijñapti). Furthermore, regarding the "outflow-free matter" (anāsrava-rūpa) mentioned in the Sūtras, the Yogācāras say:
Regarding the matter-form produced by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), that which relies on untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) is itself designated as untainted.

As for those who argue that the "intermediate" refers to the meaning of a gap—as the Vibhajyavādins maintain regarding the reflection in a mirror—the Sthaviras likewise hold this same view.
Second, it is obstructed but not real; however, through the power of the harmony of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-sāmagrī*), all phenomena are made to appear as such.

(The *Nyāyānusāra*, fascicle 23, extensively refutes this position, which can be understood by consulting that text. Now, relying on the Mahāyāna, there are two passages. First, according to the "Chapter on Mind, Intellect, and Consciousness" (*Cittamanovijñāna-varga*) of this very sutra:

As for the Sautrāntika school, they hold that one sees one's own face reflected; thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 36, states: Question:

All possess facial features; thus, they are not a single facial image. For this reason, one does not see the original image again.

Regarding those who see their own faces: according to the Sautrāntika school, the reflection is used as a metaphor for the *nimitta-bhāga* (the objective aspect);

this is not the Mahāyāna doctrine. Second, regarding the school of Maitreya, there are two positions. One says: within the mirror there is a distinct reflected image (*pratibimba*), which arises conditioned by the reflection when visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*) occurs.

Among the five kinds of "matter included within the sphere of mental objects" (*dharmāyatana-saṃgṛhīta-rūpa*) described in the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, this refers to "matter produced by conceptual construction" (*parikalpita-rūpa*). (The five kinds are:

the mirror is a metaphor for meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the substance is a metaphor for the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), and the reflection is a metaphor for the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*). This is the intended meaning here.

This means that because the self-cognizing portion manifests as the seeing and the objectified portions, and because the seeing perceives the object while that object and the seeing do not depart from the self-cognizing portion, it is called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).

"The various sūtras state that 'there is only consciousness' (vijñapti-mātra) in order to cause one to contemplate consciousness and abandon those external objects (*bāhya-artha*). Once external objects are abandoned, the deluded mind subsides accordingly.
Because the deluded mind subsides, one realizes the Middle Way. Therefore, the sūtra says: 'As long as one has not realized that objects are mind-only, one gives rise to the two-fold division.'"
Distinguished. Once one has realized that objects are merely mind, conceptualization no longer arises. By knowing that all phenomena are but mind, one abandons the appearances of external objects.

Through this, conceptualization ceases, and one awakens to the equality of true emptiness. Foolish ordinary beings, however, crave the flavors of sensory objects and indulge in various sensual pleasures;
lacking the resolve to renounce them, they transmigrate through birth and death, casting themselves into the ocean of the three realms of existence and undergoing all manner of sufferings.

There is intense suffering, and liberation would have no cause. Out of compassion, the Tathāgata employs skillful means to teach that all phenomena are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), causing [beings] to abandon external objects.

Therefore, a sutra states: "Just as in the world there is a skilled physician who administers excellent medicine for various ailments, so too do the Buddhas;

The commentary states: The Tathāgata correctly explains that "uninterrupted mind" refers to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) associated with the two types of wisdom—listening and reflection—which take as their object the meaning of the dharmas in an uninterrupted succession. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle ten, states:
"Uninterrupted attention (*manasikāra*) means that it proceeds at all times in an uninterrupted, unbroken, and continuous succession. Thus, one should know that "uninterrupted" is...
It is the continuity [of mind], namely *śamatha*. Because it prevents the mind from being distracted, it takes only the mind as its object.
Regarding the "uninterrupted mind" (*anantara-citta*), there is an interpretation that it takes the immediately preceding, uninterrupted mind as its focal object.
Although there are these two explanations, the former is correct (as the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "the characteristics of the mind are uninterrupted").
"Bhagavān, to what extent may it be said that a bodhisattva’s śamatha and vipaśyanā proceed in union?
The commentary states: This is the third question concerning the characteristics of their proceeding in union.
"O son of good family, if one correctly contemplates one-pointedness of mind.
The commentary explains: "As the Tathāgata has correctly taught, 'one-pointedness of mind' refers to the object of focus upon which both śamatha and vipaśyanā operate simultaneously."

However, regarding this single phrase, various explanations differ. One school says: "One-pointedness of mind" (*cittaikāgrya*) means that, in the conventional sense of *vijñapti-mātra*, the object does not exist apart from the mind;
thus it is called one-pointedness of mind. Alternatively, it refers to the state of being a single mind, which is also called one-pointedness of mind.

"The nature of one-pointedness of mind" (*cittaikāgryatā*) refers to ultimate *vijñapti-mātra*; that is, all phenomena are nothing other than the single true nature, which is called the nature of one-pointedness of mind. First.
It is said that the term "nature" (*svabhāva*) also applies to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, fascicle nine, states:

"The nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā-svabhāva*) is briefly of two kinds: first, the conventional, which refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); second, the ultimate (*paramārtha*), which refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
(The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* says: "Contemplate the mind as the one mind.")
"What is the characteristic of the mind, Blessed One?
The commentary states: From this point downward is the second section, which provides a further explanation of the distinctions among the three types of objects of focus.
This explanation of the three objects of focus is divided into three parts; this question constitutes the first.
"Good son, it refers to the conceptual image that is the object of samādhi and the focal object of vipaśyanā.

The commentary explains: This is the Tathāgata’s correct explanation; that is to say, the aforementioned characteristics of the mind are themselves the image that is the object of samādhi, and they are also the objective sphere traversed by the contemplation of the mind.
"Bhagavān, what is the uninterrupted mind?
The commentary says: This asks about the second object.
"Son of good family, it refers to the object of śamatha, which is the mind taking that image as its objective support."

The commentary states: The Tathāgata correctly explains that the mind consisting of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) associated with the two types of wisdom—those arising from hearing and reflection—which takes that image as its object, is the objective sphere (*ālambana*) of *śamatha*.
“World-Honored One, what is one-pointedness of mind?
The commentary states: This is the third question.
“Good son, it is the thorough realization that the images which are the objects of samādhi are nothing but consciousness; or, it is the thorough realization of this.”
"Having done so, one further contemplates suchness (*tathatā*).
The commentary explains: This refers to the Tathāgata’s correct teaching; that is to say, at this time, one penetrates the realization that all phenomena are not separate from consciousness.

Having observed in this way, one further contemplates suchness, meaning that the previous two types [of contemplation] involve observing the mind and objects separately, wherein calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) do not occur simultaneously.

This third gate involves the convergence of mind and object as conditions, wherein calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) proceed together. (The extensive explanation of the two paths of calm abiding and insight proceeding together is as found in the thirty-first [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*;
the extensive explanation of one-pointedness of mind is as found in the thirtieth [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*).
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how many kinds of vipaśyanā are there? The commentary states:
From here below begins the eighth section, the gate of the distinctions in the number of types of śamatha and vipaśyanā. Within this, there are two parts: first, vipaśyanā, and subsequently, śamatha.
Regarding vipaśyanā, there are two parts: first, the question, and subsequently, the answer. This is the question.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: "Good son, there are briefly three kinds. The commentary states:
The World-Honored One now correctly explains the second [point], which contains three parts: stating the number, enumerating the names, and providing individual explanations.
This is the first [of those three].
First, vipaśyanā with signs; second, vipaśyanā through seeking; third, vipaśyanā through investigation.
The commentary states:
the second [category] lists the names according to their number.
"What is vipaśyanā with signs? The commentary states:
From here on, the third section provides a sequential and detailed explanation. This explanation of the three distinct characteristics is divided into three parts;
this is the first question.
That is to say, it is the vipaśyanā that consists of conceptual images which are the objects of pure mental attention within samādhi.
The commentary explains: this precisely explains the first characteristic, namely, that it consists of conceptual images through pure mental attention.
That which resembles phenomena (*dharma*) and resembles meanings (*artha*), being named after its object, is called "with signs" (*sanimitta*).
What is the vipaśyanā of thorough investigation?
The commentary states: this asks about the second [type].
That is to say, by means of wisdom, one attends to and contemplates vipaśyanā for the sake of thoroughly understanding all those various phenomena that have not yet been well understood.

The commentary states: This is the formal explanation. That is to say, by means of wisdom, with respect to all images and objective spheres possessing signs, one applies mental attention for the purpose of thorough comprehension regarding those points not yet well-understood.
"What is investigative vipaśyanā?
The commentary states: This is the third question;
it refers to the thorough and complete understanding of each and every phenomenon through wisdom, for the sake of attaining realization.
"Because of ultimate liberation, one attends to and contemplates with *vipaśyanā*.

The commentary explains: this is the correct explanation; that is to say, having already thoroughly understood that object, one attends to and contemplates it with the desire to realize ultimate liberation.
This is largely identical to this sūtra based on the thirtieth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Therefore, that treatise says: "What is called 'insight (vipaśyanā) that proceeds solely by way of the characteristics' (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*)?

It refers to the brief contemplation, by means of appropriate mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*) in the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhitabhūmi*), of the teachings one has heard and upheld, or of the various dharmas of instruction and admonition—contemplating them without yet having reflected, measured, inferred, or investigated. This is called 'solely...'"
Vipaśyanā that proceeds by way of following characteristics is [vipaśyanā].
Furthermore, when one reflects upon and investigates those [characteristics], it is then called vipaśyanā that proceeds by way of following examination (*vitarka*).
Moreover, once one has investigated them, if one further scrutinizes them as they abide, this is called vipaśyanā that proceeds by way of following investigation (*vicāra*). However, this...
Regarding the distinction between *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), as stated in the thirteenth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:

"What is *śamatha*? It refers to the nine stages of mental abiding (*navākārā cittasthiti*). What is *vipaśyanā*? It refers either to the contemplation of three things, or the contemplation of four modes, or the contemplation of objects distinguished by six categories.

As for the contemplation of three things: first, the contemplation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vipaśyanā*); second, the contemplation of seeking (*paryeṣaṇā-vipaśyanā*); third, the contemplation of investigation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-vipaśyanā*). [The fourth is omitted in the source fragment.]

"Practicing observation" refers to practicing observation through the discernment of phenomena (*dharmas*), practicing observation through extreme discernment, practicing observation through pervasive investigation, and practicing observation through pervasive analysis.
Regarding "observation of objects distinguished by six matters": first, observation of the object as meaning; second, observation of the object as thing;
third, observation of the object as characteristic; fourth, observation of the object as category; fifth, observation of the object as time... [and so forth].

Regarding the observation of the object (*ālambana-vipaśyanā*): the observation of the object through the six principles (*ṣaḍ-yukti-ālambana-vipaśyanā*) is as stated in the fourth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, which is identical to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

The commentary states: "The nine types of mental abiding (*navākārā cittasthiti*), the two types of observation of things (*vastu-vipaśyanā*), and the four types of observation of practice (*prayoga-vipaśyanā*) have already been explained previously.
Since the six types of observation of things [remain], they shall now be explained. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle thirty, asks: "What are the distinctions among the six things?"
Vipaśyanā with respect to the object of focus refers to the time of investigation, when one investigates six matters:
first, investigating the meaning, which is correctly investigating that such-and-such words have such-and-such meanings;
second, investigating the entity, which is correctly investigating the two entities of the internal and the external; third, investigating the characteristic... [the text continues].
There are two characteristics of phenomena (*dharma*): first, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); second, the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Fourth is the thorough investigation of categories (*pakṣaparyeṣaṇā*), which means correctly investigating the two categories of all phenomena: first, the dark category (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*); second, the white category (*śuklapakṣa*).

One investigates the faults and disadvantages of the dark category, and one investigates the virtues and benefits of the white category. Fifth is the thorough investigation of time (*kālaparyeṣaṇā*), which means correctly investigating...
Regarding the three times—past, future, and present—one investigates such matters as follows:
one investigates that "such a matter existed in the past," one investigates that "such a matter will exist in the future," and one investigates that "such a matter exists now in the present.
Regarding the six modes of investigation, they refer to correctly investigating four kinds of principles: first, the principle of dependence; second, the principle of efficacy... [text continues]
By means of reasoning: (3) the reasoning of logical proof, and (4) the reasoning of the nature of things (*dharmatā-yukti*).
Question: For what reason are these six distinct categories of *vipaśyanā* established? Answer: They are established based on three types of realization (*avabodha*).

What are the three realizations? First, the realization of the meaning; second, the realization of the limits of phenomena; third, the realization of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-avabodha*). Upon investigation...

Because one contemplates the meaning, the awakening to the meaning arises. Because one investigates the particulars and their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the awakening to the limits of phenomena (*vastuparyantatā*) arises.
Because one investigates common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), categories, time, and principles, the awakening to reality as it is (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*) arises.

For a practitioner of yoga, the objects of knowledge are limited to these alone: namely, the meaning of words and the things to be known, in their entirety (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and their suchness (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
The nature of all things is explained in detail as therein described. The four types of reasoning will be explained later.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how many kinds of *śamatha* are there?"
The commentary states: From here below is the second section, which distinguishes the number and categories of *śamatha*. First the question is posed, then the answer follows;
this is the question.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: "Son of good family, you should know that it is precisely by following that uninterrupted mind..."
In this regard, there are also three types. The commentary explains:
hereafter follows the formal explanation, which consists of three parts. First, the three types of *śamatha* are elucidated; second, the eight types of *śamatha* are elucidated;
and third, the four types of *śamatha* are elucidated. This is the first [section], concerning those characterized by signs (*sanimitta*).
Third, regarding the phrase "following that": the previously mentioned mental image (*nimitta*) is the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) which is followed;
the immediately preceding mind is the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) of the mind that follows it.

The intended meaning here is that because there are three types of *vipaśyanā* that take that mental image as their object, there are likewise three types of *śamatha* minds that take the immediately preceding mind as their object.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds, namely the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, as each possesses one type of śamatha.
The commentary states: the second [section] clarifies these eight meditative absorptions, which are termed the "eight śamathas. However, these eight absorptions are divided into...
Second: first, an explanation of the four dhyānas; subsequently, an elucidation of the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*). Regarding the four dhyānas, there is a twofold classification:
first, the explanation of their names; second, the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the explanation of the names [of the dhyānas], there is first the general explanation and then the specific one.

As for the general name, according to the Sarvāstivāda school, there is its own interpretation as found in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 141, which states: "Question: For what reason are these four called 'dhyānas' (*静虑*, *zhìnglù*)?

Answer: 'Dhyāna' (*静*, *jìng*) means tranquility (*寂靜*, *jìjìng*); 'lū' (*虑*, *lù*) means deliberation (*籌慮*, *chóulù*). Because within these four stages, concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are in equilibrium, they are called dhyānas."
It is designated as "dhyāna" (meditative absorption). If any of these [factors] are lacking, it does not receive this name.
According to the seventy-third [treatise], the *Nyāyānusāra*, there are two interpretations. It asks: "By what meaning is the name 'dhyāna' established? The answer is:

"Because by relying on this tranquility (*śamatha*), one is then able to engage in careful consideration (*pravicaya*). Careful consideration has the sense of "thoroughly knowing. (*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Chapter 20).

The eight [limbs] are also the same. One explanation states: this concentration (*samādhi*) is called *dhyāna* (meditative absorption) because it maintains excellence, universal objectification, and correct reflection (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
The term "excellence" excludes the desire realm; "universal objectification" excludes the formless realm; and "correct reflection" excludes false inversion.
That which can maintain this concentration is a sublime *samādhi*, designated as *dhyāna*. This statement demonstrates the balanced practice of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Only non-erroneous meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is designated as *dhyāna*. According to the eighty-first volume of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, there are three interpretations:
first, the ability to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*); second, correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*); and third, possessing both meanings. Thus, that treatise asks:
"In what sense is it called *dhyāna*? Some say: "It is called *dhyāna* because it can sever the fetters. [The text] then asks:
The various formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are also able to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*); thus, they should be called *dhyāna*. Answer:

If an absorption is able to sever both types of fetters—the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the neutral (*avyākṛta*)—it is named *dhyāna*. Since the various formless absorptions sever only the neutral and not the unwholesome, they are not named *dhyāna*.
(There are two further explanations regarding the severing of fetters; fearing prolixity, they are not recounted here. Furthermore, some say that because it is able to...
Because it is right contemplation, it is called *dhyāna*. Question: If that is so, then the *samādhi* of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is also capable of right contemplation;

should it not also be called *dhyāna*? Answer: If a *samādhi* possesses both the name "concentration" (*samāpatti*) and the function of concentration, and is capable of right contemplation, it is called *dhyāna*.
Although the *samādhi* of the desire realm has the name "concentration," it lacks the function of concentration, like a rafter made of mud.

The *liang* (measure) exists in name only and lacks utility; therefore, it is not meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). (There are three further explanations regarding the ability to correctly contemplate within [this state], but fearing prolixity, they are not set forth. Thus it is said.
It must possess two characteristics to be properly termed *dhyāna*: namely, the ability to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the ability to engage in correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).

Although the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) can engage in correct contemplation, they cannot sever the fetters. Although the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) can sever the fetters, [they lack correct contemplation].
Yet because one cannot observe correctly, it is not *dhyāna*. Furthermore, the various formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) possess tranquility (*śamatha*) but lack discernment (*vipaśyanā*);
the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of the desire realm possess discernment but lack tranquility; whereas the concentrations of the form realm possess both, and are therefore called *dhyāna*.

"Tranquility" refers to meditative equipoise (*samāhita*), and "discernment" refers to universal observation; thus they are called *dhyāna*. (Within these two meanings, there are further two interpretations, which I shall not describe here for fear of prolixity. If one relies on the *Mahā-* [vibhāṣā]:
The vehicle. This meaning is the same as that in the *Nyāyānusāra*. The first alternative explanation is therefore stated in the thirty-third fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:
"As for what is called 'dhyāna' (meditative concentration), because one binds the mindfulness to a single object of focus and engages in calm, correct, and discerning reflection, it is named dhyāna.
Regarding its specific names, the first, second, third, and fourth [dhyānas] are its specific names. Thus, the seventy-seventh fascicle of the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "All..."
The general characteristics of meditative absorption (*samādhi-dhyāna*) are not distinct; however, in order to manifest the differences between the stages (*bhūmi*), they are designated by number.

Therefore, they are called the first through the fourth. Question: If the four dhyānas are established as being comprised of the nature of wholesomeness (*kuśala*), consisting of one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*) together with its attendants, by what characteristics are the first, second, third, and fourth established?
Answer: The first is established as possessing applied thought (*vitarka*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*).

Gradually departing from the preceding factors, one establishes [the meditative states] as two, three, and four. There are two types of departure from *vitarka*: (in the second dhyāna, there is departure from *vitarka*, while *prīti* and *sukha* both remain);

there is departure from two [factors] and the presence of *sukha* (in the third dhyāna, there is departure from both *vitarka* and *prīti*, while only *sukha* remains); and there is complete departure from all three [factors] (in the fourth dhyāna, there is departure from *vitarka*, *prīti*, and *sukha*).

Because they proceed in this sequence, one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*) is divided into four kinds. Question: Is it not the case that the various dhyānas lack qualities such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*)?
[Question: There are names and characteristics that are not shared [with other stages], yet here you establish distinct names based only on the first four numbers.

[Answer: It is not that there are no unshared names and characteristics herein; however, because there is no name that exclusively and universally encompasses a single stage, we establish distinct names based only on the number.
The *Abhidharmakośa* is the same. Furthermore, a verse in the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "The first possesses vitarka, vicāra, prīti, and sukha; thereafter, gradually..."
[The first] factor is excluded. Question: Why does the verse not state that it possesses *vitarka*? Explanation:
As stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, this already clarifies that it also possesses *vitarka*, because [the two] necessarily function together, just as smoke and fire are inseparable.

It is not the case that *vicāra* can be accompanied by joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) without being conjoined with *vitarka*. According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 141, regarding the four dhyānas:

This refers to the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna. Some say that the dhyānas associated with vitarka (applied thought), prīti (joy), sukha (bliss), and upekṣā (equanimity) constitute the four respectively.
Now, according to the Mahāyāna, we list their names by number; this accords with the *Nyāyānusāra*. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"Based on the sequential order of counting, they are called the first up to the fourth. As for explaining their essential nature:

According to the Sarvāstivāda school, as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle eighty, the four dhyānas each have as their nature the five aggregates—wholesome, defiled, and non-obscured-neutral—belonging to their own respective levels.
Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle one hundred forty-one, states:

"The substance of the four dhyānas is of two kinds: first, that acquired through cultivation (*bhāvanā-labdha*); second, that acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*). As for that acquired through cultivation..."
That is the one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgratā) pertaining to that specific stage. If accompanied by its attendants, it consists of the nature of the five aggregates (pañcaskandha).
As for that acquired at birth (upapattilābhika), its nature consists of the other five aggregates bound to that particular stage. (*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* 28; *Nyāyānusāra* 77).
The intent is the same as that of the *Vibhāṣā*. Now, following the Mahāyāna, it is largely the same as the *Vibhāṣā*:

[the acquisition] of birth and of fixed birth has the five aggregates—whether wholesome, defiled, or neutral—as its nature; the acquisition of the wholesome has the five contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) aggregates as its nature.
The four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) shall be briefly analyzed by way of two gates: first, the explanation of their names;
second, the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*). Regarding the explanation of the names, there is first the general [explanation] and then the specific.

As for the general name, according to the Sarvāstivāda school—as stated in the *Nyāyānusāra*, fascicle 77—there are three meanings: first, the sense of restraint (*niyama*); second, the sense of manifesting the ultimate (*parama*).
The third [syllable] simultaneously reveals the meaning of "existence" (*asti*). Thus, that treatise says: "By what meaning is the name 'formless' (*ārūpya*) established?
The syllable *rū* reveals the meaning of "being capable of being manifested. Based on this capacity for manifestation, it is called "form" (*rūpa*).

The syllable *ā* reveals the meaning of "restraint" (*niyama*). This is intended to show that even within the ocean of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), there are places where form is temporarily restrained.

Based on the sense of restriction, it is called "non-existent" (*arūpa*). Because within that realm, transformation and manifestation are restricted, it is termed *ārūpya* based on the meaning of "formless.
Alternatively, the syllable *ā* here also conveys the sense of "extreme.
Although there are also phenomena in other realms that cannot be transformed or manifested, the formless realm is the extreme among those that cannot be so manifested; it does not exist elsewhere.
