The eighth fascicle states: "When non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) arises and its activity manifests, all objective referents do not appear.

Furthermore, according to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (顯揚聖教論), fascicle 20, when one eliminates the grasped [object] during the contemplation of suchness (*tathatā*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) does not appear;
this is termed "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*). Thus, that treatise says: "Third, regarding non-apprehension through non-manifestation... [This refers to] the investigation...
When seeking all phenomena, one does not perceive an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This is not because they are entirely non-existent in every respect;

rather, when nothing is apprehended regarding the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), one likewise does not observe the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). (Because it is not observed, the dependent nature does not manifest.)
Just as it is with respect to names, so it should be understood for phrases (*pada*), syllables (*vyañjana*), and all meanings (*artha*).
The commentary explains that there are two types of explanations regarding phrases and so forth: the first type explains phrases, syllables, and the ten kinds of meaning;
the latter, from "subsequently" onwards, explains five meanings, four meanings, and three meanings. Alternatively, the preceding text may be interpreted as follows.
As for the four meanings and so forth, the following categories explain three meanings. This constitutes the first category of explaining the phrases, sentences, and ten types of meanings.
That is to say, when one does not apprehend the names and the intrinsic nature of those names, one likewise does not observe the characteristics upon which they depend.
In this manner, each of the phrases, sentences, and up to the ten meanings—each and every intrinsic nature—is [unapprehended].
There is nothing to be apprehended. Furthermore, one does not observe the characteristics of that which serves as its basis, as should be understood from what precedes.

This continues until, when there is no apprehension of the elements (*dhātu*) and the self-abiding nature of the elements, one likewise does not observe the characteristics of their bases. In this way, they are eliminated.

(Consulting the manuscript of the Sūtra and the manuscript of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, both state "and knowing the elements and the self-nature of the elements"; however, other sūtras and śāstras all state "up to the elements. Taking the meaning as the basis for the text, [the reading] is "up to" [the elements]).
(Excellence).

The commentary states: the second category explains the five meanings and so forth; that is, from those five meanings, four meanings, and three meanings, the meaning of the "meaning of the text" extends up to the five elements (*dhātu*).
Alternatively, it may be that the meaning of the "meaning of the meaning of the text" extends [further].
Regarding the meaning of the *dhātu*, there are two aspects: first, observing that its own nature is unapprehendable; second, not observing the characteristics of its basis.
This should be understood according to the above. Such a method of observation is as explained in the ninth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

Therefore, I shall now briefly describe the essential meaning of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. That treatise, for its part, relies upon the four kinds of thorough investigation (*paryeṣaṇā*) and the four kinds of knowledge of reality (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*) to examine those names and objects.

Specifically, during the stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), one relies on the four thorough investigations to observe that the self-nature and specific differences of the names and objects—which are the "appropriated"—are all unattainable.
Through the four kinds of knowledge of reality, one observes the consciousness which is the grasper of those names and objects.
It, too, cannot be apprehended. Thus, that verse says:
"To posit a slight object before oneself, Claiming it to be the nature of consciousness-only— Because there is something apprehended, one does not truly abide in consciousness-only."

The prose commentary explains: In order to enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and abide in the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), one further cultivates the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) to suppress and eliminate the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*).
These refer to the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*): Heat (*uṣmagata*), Peak (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

These four roots of goodness are established based on the four investigations (*catasraḥ paryeṣaṇāḥ*) and the four cognitions of reality (*catasro yathābhūtaparijñānaḥ*), being positioned at the initial and final stages [of the preparatory path]. The four investigations consist of investigating the names (*nāman*), objects (*artha*), intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), and specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) as mere designations (*prajñapti*).

That which exists [as the dependent nature] is truly non-existent [in its grasped nature]. To know these four as they truly are—that both the object and consciousness do not exist—is called "knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).

Based on the *ālokalabdha-samādhi*, one initiates the lower stage of investigation (*vitarka*) and contemplates the absence of the grasped object; this is established as the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
This means that in this stage, one first observes that the four phenomena—the name and so forth—which are the objects of apprehension, are all transformations of one’s own mind;

they exist only as provisional designations and cannot be found in reality. Based on the *vṛddhāloka* (Increasing Clarity) concentration, one gives rise to superior investigation (*vitarka*) and observes the absence of an object of apprehension; this is established as the *mūrdhan* (Summit) stage.
This means that in this stage, one again observes that the four phenomena—the name and so forth—which are the objects of apprehension, are all transformations of one’s own mind. Provisionally...

That which is conventionally designated exists, yet in reality it cannot be found. Relying on the seal (*mudrā*) to cultivate meditative concentration, one gives rise to the lower stage of knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
One definitively seals and maintains the absence of anything to be grasped (*grāhya*), and within the absence of a grasper (*grāhaka*), one likewise accords with joy and patience.

Since there is no real object apart from the grasper-consciousness, how could there be a real consciousness apart from the grasped object? For the grasped and the grasper are established in mutual dependence. Based on this non-existence...

In the intermediate stage of certainty (*antara-niyama*), one gives rise to the superior knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) and seals both types of grasping as empty, thereby establishing the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

This means that while the preceding stage of "superior patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) sealed only the emptiness of the grasper (*grāhaka*), the present Supreme Mundane Dharma seals the emptiness of both simultaneously.

Thus, in the stages of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) and "summit" (*mūrdhan*), one relies on the consciousness that acts as the grasper to contemplate the emptiness of the grasped (*grāhya*). When the lower stage of patience arises, one seals the characteristic of the emptiness of the object; this is the transitional stage of middle patience (*madhyama-kṣānti*).

Regarding the grasping consciousness (*grāhaka-vijñāna*), just as the object is empty, one accords with and accepts this through the stage of "patience" (*kṣānti*). At the stage where "supreme patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) arises, one confirms the emptiness of the grasper.

During the "highest mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*), both aspects are confirmed as empty; yet because these all still involve conceptual images (*nimitta*), they have not yet realized the truth.
Therefore, it is said that within these four stages, the Bodhisattva still establishes a slight thing before them, namely, that which is called "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
Regarding ultimate reality (*paramārthatā*): because the two aspects of emptiness and appearance have not yet been eliminated, the mind that observes with these aspects still possesses apprehension;
thus, one does not truly abide in the principle of true consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). Only after those aspects have ceased does one truly abide [in it].
Based on this meaning, there is a verse that says:

When the Bodhisattva is in the state of meditative equipoise, he contemplates that the reflected image is nothing but mind. Once the conceptualization of external objects has been eliminated, he scrutinizes that there is only his own mental representation.
Thus abiding in the inner mind, he knows that the apprehended object does not exist;
subsequently, he realizes that the apprehending subject is likewise non-existent. Finally, he touches upon the state of non-apprehension.
To explain these two verses, as stated in the sixth chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* and the eleventh chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it is explained as follows:

The Sūtra says that "the absence of names" and so forth refers to the two stages of *uṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summit), wherein one contemplates the emptiness of the grasped (*grāhya*) and does not contemplate the characteristics of its basis (*āśraya*).

Furthermore, at the stages of *kṣānti* (Patience) and *laukikāgradharma* (Supreme Mundane Dharma), one contemplates the emptiness of the grasper (*grāhaka*). One interpretation states that this passage concerns the contemplative gate (*darśanamārga*) of those on the stages (*bhūmi*). Why? Because...

Answering the previous question: it is said that when bodhisattvas on the stages enter true contemplation (*bhūta-darśana*), they perceive neither the name, the self-nature, nor the characteristics of the basis;
that is to say, they realize the equality of object and wisdom as a single flavor, because they are far removed from the characteristics of the grasper and the grasped.
“World-Honored One, regarding all the characteristics of the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness) that are fully understood, can these characteristics of *tathatā* also be eliminated?

The commentary states: This is the third inquiry; it asks whether the *tathatā* that was previously described as the object of focus for the mental attention (*manasikāra*) upon *tathatā* can also be eliminated.
"O son of good family, within the meaning of the *tathatā* (suchness) that is to be realized, there are no signs whatsoever, nor is there anything to be apprehended;
what, then, could there be to be eliminated?
The commentary states: The fourth [section], the Tathāgata’s explanation for clarification, contains two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the re-explanation. This...

This refers to the very first [stage]. However, there are two interpretations regarding the explanation of this passage. One says that this text explains the resolution of external objections based on the contemplation prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
That is to say, when contemplating suchness, there are no phenomena at all. Because there are no marks (*animitta*), there is also nothing to be attained; what, then, is there to be eliminated?
Another says that this text explains the resolution of external objections based on the contemplation of the stages. That is to say, upon entering...
At the time of true contemplation, there is absolutely no attainment of the characteristics of either the grasper or the grasped. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Next, regarding the stage of thorough penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*), what are its characteristics? The verse says:"

"When at that time, regarding the object of focus, wisdom perceives nothing whatsoever; at that time, one abides in consciousness-only, because of being free from the characteristics of the two graspings.
The long prose commentary explains: "When at that time, regarding the objective realm, the non-conceptual wisdom of the Bodhisattva perceives nothing whatsoever..."
Yes. Because one does not grasp at the signs of various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), as explained at length therein.
Noble son, when one thoroughly understands the meaning of *tathatā*, one is able to subdue the signs of all phenomena and their meanings;
this realization cannot be subdued by anything else.
The commentary states: This is the second detailed explanation of the characteristics of *tathatā* (suchness). It is not something to be discarded by anything else.
The intended meaning here is that all other characteristics, being characterized as such, are discarded by *tathatā*. At the time of realizing *tathatā*, the *tathatā* that is realized—
It is entirely devoid of marks; no other dharma can eliminate this *tathatā*.
This corresponds to what is taught in the *Anantārthasūtra* regarding the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as being "markless" (*alakṣaṇa*) and "non-mark" (*avilakṣaṇa*). To explain:
"markless" means that there are no marks to be eliminated; "non-mark" means that one does not eliminate the markless.
World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said, just as the metaphors of a turbid water vessel, an unclean mirror,
and a stirred-up pond are unfit for observing the reflection of one's own face— whereas that which is fit is the opposite of these.

The commentary states: From here below is the second section, which consists of questions and answers regarding the capacity for investigation. This section has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer.

Within the question, there are two parts: first, the question concerning the scriptural basis; second, the questions raised based on that scriptural basis. Within the former, there are two parts: first, the analogy; second, the response.
This is the presentation of the analogy, which contains two sections. The first concerns that which is not capable of investigation.

The analogies. Next are the analogies for being unfit for observation. That is to say, the Blessed One taught three kinds of analogies—the analogy of a vessel with turbid water, the analogy of an unclean mirror, and the analogy of a stirred-up pond—stating that these are unfit for observing the reflection of one’s own face.
Thus, the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* says: "If the vessel is not clean, the mirror is not clean, or the waters are turbid, the features of the face will not be seen. When [the vessel] is clean...

The analogy of a water vessel, the analogy of a clean mirror surface, and the analogy of a clear spring or pond—these three correspond, in their respective order, to the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Although a clean water vessel can reflect an image, it does not equal a mirror; therefore, it serves as an analogy for the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

Although a clean mirror is bright, it lacks the nature of serene stillness; therefore, it serves as an analogy for the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). The nature of water is supple and gentle, and it possesses clarity...
Because its nature is tranquility, it serves as a metaphor for the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Alternatively, each [of these] may serve as a metaphor for all three types of wisdom.
Thus, if one does not cultivate the mind, one is incapable of correctly observing suchness (*tathatā*) as it truly is;
if the mind is well-cultivated, one is capable of such observation.
The commentary states: This second synthesis follows the sequence [of the previous].

When the three types of wisdom have not yet been attained, if one does not properly cultivate the mind, one is incapable of observing the characteristics of *tathatā* (suchness) as they truly are, just as one cannot see one's own face in turbid water.
If one properly cultivates the mind, one is capable of such observation, just as one can see one's own face in clear water.
"What kind of mind capable of observation is being described here? Based upon which *tathatā* (suchness) is this statement made?
The commentary states: This second question is posed based on the teaching. There are two intentions to the question:
first, it asks what kind of observing mind is referred to when such a statement is made; second, it asks upon which *tathatā* the observed object depends for such a statement to be made.
It is said:
"Good son, these are the three kinds of minds capable of observation:

namely, the mind capable of observation formed through hearing, the mind capable of observation formed through reflection, and the mind capable of observation formed through cultivation. These rely upon the *tathatā* (suchness) of discernment."
Thus it is said. The commentary states:
The second part is the Tathāgata’s direct response, which consists of two sections. The first answers the subject that contemplates, namely the mind of the three types of wisdom;

therefore, the *Gambhīrārtha-samuccaya* refers to this as "contemplation by means of the three kinds of mind. The latter answers the object contemplated, namely the realization within the sevenfold true suchness (*saptavidha-tathatā*).

The distinct *tathatā* (suchness). However, this *tathatā* itself is of two kinds. The first refers to the fact that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are exclusively of the nature of consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*);
thus it is called *tathatā*. This is the conventional observation of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*). The second is the nature of consciousness-only itself.

This is called the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*). This is precisely the ultimate contemplation of consciousness-only. If one is still on the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi, one contemplates the characteristics of consciousness-only;
from the first bhūmi upward, one contemplates the nature of consciousness-only. Within this, both types of contemplation are explained in general.
"Bhagavān, for a bodhisattva who thus understands the meaning of phenomena and diligently practices application in order to eliminate all signs,
how many kinds of signs are difficult to eliminate, and who is able to eliminate them?"

The commentary states: From here below is the third section, which analyzes through questions and answers the various characteristics that are difficult to eliminate. This section contains three parts:

first, the analysis through questions and answers regarding the characteristics that are difficult to eliminate; second, from "The Blessed One dispels these ten characteristics" onwards, the analysis through questions and answers regarding liberation through the elimination of characteristics;
and third, from "At that time, Maitreya... onwards, the analysis through questions and answers regarding the general characteristics.

Regarding emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as that which removes what is difficult to eliminate: first there is the question, and then the answer. This constitutes the characteristics of the correct inquiry for removing difficulties, the enumeration [of those difficulties], and the emptiness that is capable of removing them.
"Good son, there are ten kinds of characteristics that emptiness can remove."
The commentary states: From here below begins the second section, the Tathāgata’s formal exposition. This consists of three parts: first, a brief answer indicating the number;
second, the Bodhisattva’s inquiry; and third, the Tathāgata’s detailed explanation. This is the first part.

Regarding the "ten kinds of characteristics," this answers the initial question; that is, there are briefly ten kinds of characteristics that are difficult to eliminate. These ten characteristics are to be eliminated through the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

This is not like the individual contemplations of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and so forth, which, though not the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), nevertheless eliminate notions of purity and the like.
To distinguish it from those, the text employs the term "difficult" (*duṣkara*). Question: According to the subsequent scriptural passage, there are sixteen aspects (*lakṣaṇa*);
why then are only ten types of aspects mentioned? Answer: In reality, there are sixteen distinct aspects; however, the meanings to be understood [in this context] consist of ten types.

Therefore, they are subsumed into ten characteristics. Regarding "emptiness as that which can dispel," this answers the second question. There are seventeen types of emptiness that are capable of removing [obstructions].
According to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, there are eighteen types of emptiness, because five types of emptiness are included within the eighth characteristic.
"What are the ten?
The commentary states: This is the second inquiry posed by the bodhisattva.
First, because of the thorough knowledge of the meaning of phenomena (*dharma-artha*), there are various characteristics of syllables (*vyañjana-lakṣaṇa*).
The commentary states: From here below is the third section, the Tathāgata’s extensive explanation. He explains ten kinds of signs (*nimitta*) by means of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as their antidote.
This antidotal removal of the ten signs is divided into ten parts; this is the first. Within each sign, there are two sections: first, the designation of the sign to be removed;

second, the clarification of the emptiness that removes it. This is the first [of those two]. Regarding the phrase "the meaning of phenomena" (*dharmārtha*): "phenomena" (*dharma*) refers to the taught doctrine (*deśanādharma*).
“Meaning” (*artha*) has the sense of “object. Since the phenomenon (*dharma*) is itself the meaning, this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

Regarding the “characteristic of syllables” (*vyañjana-lakṣaṇa*), it refers to the collections of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*); these are collectively termed “syllables. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 81, states:
“The essence of a sūtra is briefly of two kinds: first, the syllable; second, the meaning. The syllable is the support; the meaning is that which is supported. What is the syllable?”

This refers to the body of names (*nāmakāya*), the body of phrases (*padakāya*), and the body of syllables (*vyañjanakāya*); thus, one should know that "phrasing" (*vyañjana*) here refers precisely to name, phrase, and syllable.

The intended meaning here is as follows: when bodhisattvas first engage in contemplative practice, for the purpose of understanding the twelve divisions of the scriptures as their objective referents, various manifestations of the characteristics of letters and syllables appear.
This is because all phenomena are empty, which can correctly eliminate [all conceptualizations].
The commentary states: This is the second [section], the analysis of the emptiness that eliminates. However, regarding these various types of emptiness, there are differing explanations.

First, according to the fifty-first chapter of the first division of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it explains the meaning of twenty kinds of emptiness and four kinds of emptiness. Therefore, that...
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, Subhūti, the characteristics of the Great Vehicle of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are as follows:

internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, and common-characteristic emptiness."
"All dharmas are empty: the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
This is called the mark of the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, what is internal emptiness?
The Buddha said, "Subhūti, 'internal' refers to internal dharmas, namely the six internal bases. Among these, the eye, by means of the eye..."
It is empty. Why? Because it is neither permanent nor an object; such is its intrinsic nature. The same applies to the ear and the other [senses].

"External" refers to that which is outside the mind, namely the six external bases (*āyatana*). This should be understood according to the above. "Internal and external" refers to internal and external phenomena, namely the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*).
In this context, the six internal sense bases are empty of the six external sense bases. Why? Because they are neither permanent nor objective entities; such is their intrinsic nature.

The six external sense bases are empty of the six internal sense bases. What is the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*)? The Buddha said: "Emptiness" refers to the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*).
This emptiness is empty by means of emptiness. Why is it neither permanent nor an objective entity? Because such is its intrinsic nature. The Buddha...
[Subhūti] said: "Great emptiness refers to the emptiness of the ten directions. The Buddha said: "Ultimate truth refers to nirvāṇa; this ultimate truth is empty by virtue of being the ultimate truth.
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, 'conditioned' refers to the three realms. Within these, the desire realm is empty of the desire realm."
The same applies to the formless realm. The Buddha said: "The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) refers to that which has no arising, no abiding, no change, and no cessation.
This unconditioned is empty of the unconditioned. "Ultimacy" (*atyanta*) refers to the fact that all phenomena are ultimately unobtainable. The Buddha said:
"Limitlessness" (*anantya*) refers to the fact that no beginning, middle, or end can be found, nor can any limit of coming or going be found. The Buddha said: "Dispersion" (*vibhava*) refers to...
[The interlocutor asks: "Is there anything that can be obtained through relinquishing, abandoning, or casting off? The Buddha said: "There is no alteration;
that is to say, nothing can be obtained through relinquishing, abandoning, or casting off. The Buddha said: "Intrinsic nature refers to the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.

Whether it be the nature of conditioned phenomena or the nature of unconditioned phenomena, none are created by the three vehicles, nor are they created by anything else. The Buddha said: "It is their own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)."
This refers to the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena (*dharma*). For example, resistance and transformation are the specific characteristic of form (*rūpa*);

experiencing is the specific characteristic of feeling (*vedanā*); grasping images is the nature of perception (*saṃjñā*); conditioning is the specific characteristic of formations (*saṃskāra*); and cognizing is the specific characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Such are the specific characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and the specific characteristics of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*). The Buddha said: "The common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is..."

All common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). For example, suffering is the common characteristic of all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*); impermanence is the common characteristic of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*);
and selflessness is the common characteristic of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*). There are immeasurable such common characteristics. The Buddha said:

"All phenomena refer to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*). Whether they are with form or formless, visible or invisible..."
[He] sees: the resistant and the non-resistant, the outflowing and the non-outflowing, the conditioned and the unconditioned.
The Buddha said: "They are unobtainable. Within this, all phenomena are unobtainable; that is to say, the three times are unobtainable. If in the past, the other two times cannot be obtained;
if in the future, the other two times cannot be obtained; if in the present, the other two times cannot be obtained. The Buddha—
It is said: "The emptiness of non-existence" means that within this, not even the slightest existence can be found. The Buddha said:
"Intrinsic nature" refers to the fact that the intrinsic nature of the various phenomena that could come together cannot be found. The Buddha said: "Non-existence cannot be found. The Buddha said:

"The intrinsic nature of non-existence" means that among all phenomena, there is no nature capable of coming together, yet there is a nature of that which has come together. The explanation says: "Non-" [refers to the absence of such a nature].

"Nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to the absence of an intrinsic essence in all phenomena. "Intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to the fact that apart from the essence of phenomena, there is no other capacity for synthesis.

"The absence of nature and intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva-svabhāva*) is a collective term for these two types. Furthermore, there are four kinds of emptiness: namely, existence-nature (*bhāva-svabhāva*), non-existence-nature (*abhāva-svabhāva*), intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*).
Existence-nature refers to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); non-existence-nature refers to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); and intrinsic nature refers to all phenomena.
Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is empty. This emptiness is not produced by wisdom, nor is it produced by anything else. Regarding extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*):
whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, all phenomena abide as phenomena (*dharmasthiti*) up to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
they are empty because of this extrinsic nature. If one follows the second section, which explains the eighteen kinds of emptiness at length (413), it is consistent with the preceding two [sections].

Regarding the ten emptinesses (*śūnyatā*), there are differences in their opening and closing, yet in meaning they are neither broad nor narrow. When combined with the twenty [emptinesses], the "emptiness of the scattered" (*avakāra-śūnyatā*) and the "emptiness of the non-scattered" (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*) are merged to form the "emptiness of the scattered and non-scattered.

The "emptiness of self-characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) and the "emptiness of common characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) are merged and termed the "emptiness of self and common characteristics.
According to the third section [of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*], four hundred and seventy-nine [emptinesses] are enumerated, though they are not explained therein; among them, the first ten—
The six emptinesses are the same as the latter sixteen. However, the final three emptinesses do have distinctions, namely:

the emptiness of the object of focus (*ālambana-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of increase (*upādāna-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of mutual non-existence (*itaretara-śūnyatā*). According to the four hundred and eighty [verses] of the third section, sixteen emptinesses are taught.

Among the twenty kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the combination of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is termed "emptiness of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).

Excluding [the categories of] "emptiness of dispersion," "emptiness of the unobtainable," and "emptiness of intrinsic nature," they are called "identity and difference. Here, "non-dispersion" is substituted for "non-transformation. This explains the characteristics as being identical to the twenty kinds of emptiness.
According to the four hundred and third fascicle of the second division, it is taught that there are seven kinds of emptiness: first, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Twenty-two bases (*āyatana*), thirty-eight elements (*dhātu*), four truths (*satya*), twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), all phenomena such as the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and seventh, intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*).
[The term] "intrinsic nature" is cited but not explained. Chapter Seven of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the eighteen emptinesses (*śūnyatā*) and the four emptinesses.
According to the forty-sixth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it explains the eighteen emptinesses and...

In the fourth volume, it is asked: Within the eighteen kinds of emptiness, such as internal emptiness and the others, it is subsequently stated that they are "neither permanent nor subject to cessation.
What is the meaning of this? It is answered: If a person does not practice this emptiness, they will inevitably fall into one of two extremes—either permanence or cessation.
Why is this so? If all phenomena were substantially existent, they would lack the quality of cessation and would fall into the extreme of eternalism.
It is like a person who leaves one house and enters another; although the eyes do not see him, he is not said to be non-existent. Phenomena are likewise:
they pass from the future world into the present world, and from the present world into the past world. In this way, they do not cease. Because practitioners [perceive] existence...

This becomes a source of affliction. One uses emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to destroy existence (*bhava*), yet the mind then comes to prize emptiness. To be attached to emptiness is to fall into nihilism (*uccheda*).

For this reason, one practices this emptiness to destroy existence, yet does not cling to emptiness either. Free from these two extremes, one practices these eighteen kinds of emptiness by way of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).
With a heart of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one acts for the sake of delivering sentient beings. Therefore, following the eighteen emptinesses...
All say that it is neither permanent nor subject to extinction; this is called the Mahāyāna.

If one differs from this, they are a person of frivolous discourse and madness who has gained nothing at all within the Buddha-dharma—like a person who, amidst a heap of precious jewels, picks up a crystal bead;
though it looks good to the eye, it has no value. It is asked: "The eighteenth emptiness already encompasses all [others]."

"Emptiness. Why is it said that there are four emptinesses? The answer is: within the eighteen kinds of emptiness, the present emptiness fully encompasses them all. The Buddhas have two ways of teaching the Dharma:
either beginning with brevity and ending with detail, or beginning with detail and ending with brevity. Beginning with brevity and ending with detail is for the sake of explaining the meaning;
beginning with detail and ending with brevity is for the sake of ease of retention. Or, it is for the sake of those sentient beings in future assemblies who require brevity.

To state the essentials: either by means of verse or by means of prose, the Buddha has now extensively explained the eighteen emptinesses before us, followed by a brief explanation of the four emptinesses.
The extensive explanation is as found there. Furthermore, according to the sixteenth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the eleven emptinesses are explained;

and according to the seventh chapter of the forty-eighth great section of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, the eighteen emptinesses as well as the four emptinesses are explained. This is based on the *Xian* [Sūtra].
The *Yang* (likely referring to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*) in its fifteenth [fascicle] and the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* speak of sixteen emptinesses (*ṣoḍaśa-śūnyatā*).
The first chapter of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and the thirty-sixth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* speak of seven emptinesses. Based on the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there are four emptinesses.
The *Aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā-śāstra* speaks of eighteen emptinesses. The seventeen, sixteen, fourteen, and two emptinesses are fully detailed in separate chapters. Thus far.
Having already set forth the various teachings, I shall now correctly explain the text. According to this sutra, there are seventeen kinds of emptiness.

Among the twenty kinds of emptiness, it lacks the two emptinesses of "scattered" (*pṛthak*) and "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*). By combining the "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*) and "common characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) from among those twenty into a single "emptiness of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇaśūnyatā*), there are thus seventeen.
In the eighteen kinds of emptiness, it lacks the "emptiness of intrinsic nature. This is the first of all [the emptinesses].

The emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, "the emptiness of all phenomena" refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).

Whether they are with form or formless, visible or invisible, resistant or non-resistant, outflowing or non-outflowing, conditioned or unconditioned—all these phenomena are empty by virtue of the emptiness of all phenomena. This is based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 30.

One interpretation states: "All phenomena are empty" means that all phenomena refer to the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and so forth, as explained in detail therein.
According to the *Aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā-śāstra* and the *Madhyānta-vibhāga-śāstra*, "all phenomena" refers to such qualities as the ten powers (*bala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
This emptiness of all phenomena is established for the sake of purifying all Buddha-dharmas. Now...
Relying on this sūtra, one wishes to encompass all teachings that express the truth;
therefore, by means of written characters, the emptiness of all phenomena is revealed. Question: Why does this sūtra speak only of ten aspects and seventeen kinds of emptiness? Answer:

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, if [the categories] were too brief, they would be incomplete; if too extensive, the matters would be overly cumbersome. Thus, there are only eighteen. This [sūtra] is the same as that.

Second, because one thoroughly understands the meaning of the established *tathatā* (suchness), there is the characteristic of a continuity that evolves through the nature of arising, ceasing, abiding, and changing.

The commentary states: This distinguishes the second characteristic. First the characteristic, then the emptiness; this is the first [of those]. That which is explained herein is "established" (*vyavasthāna*).
That which is established as *tathatā* (suchness) is, among the Four Noble Truths, the Noble Truth of Suffering;
and among the seven types of suchness, it is the "established suchness" (*vyavasthāna-tathatā*) as previously described, because it is established by karma, afflictions, and so forth.

Alternatively, it may be called "established" because it is the first to receive that designation among the Four Truths. It is named "suchness" (*tathatā*) because it maintains its own nature without change. For this reason, it is the Truth of Suffering.

The continuity and successive transformation of the characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth are also termed *tathatā*. Alternatively, it may be understood that there are two aspects herein:

first, the four characteristics such as arising; second, the characteristic of continuity and successive transformation throughout the three periods of time. Through these two types of emptiness, one aspect is respectively eliminated from each.
This is correctly eliminated by the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of being without priority or posteriority (*apūrva-apara-śūnyatā*).

The commentary states: This explains the second emptiness that serves as an antidote. It is of two kinds: first, the emptiness of characteristics; second, the emptiness of being without priority or posteriority.
Based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, this emptiness of characteristics is further divided into two types of emptiness: first, the emptiness of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).

Second is the emptiness of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). Thus, that sutra states: "Emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) refers to the specific characteristics of all phenomena;

for example, that transformation and resistance are the specific characteristic of form (*rūpa*), and that experiencing is the specific characteristic of sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth. As for "common characteristics," this refers to the common characteristics of all phenomena;
for example, that suffering is the common characteristic of all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), and so forth. This is explained as the emptiness of being without priority or posteriority.

It is called the "emptiness of the limitless" (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*). Thus, that sutra states: "As for the emptiness of the limitless, it is because the three limits (*trikāla*) cannot be apprehended," and so forth.

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, its characteristics are explained as being empty; the name is the same as in this sutra, and the meaning is identical to the *Prajñāpāramitā*. A detailed exposition is as found therein.

Regarding the "emptiness of no before or after," that [sutra] calls it the "emptiness of the beginningless" (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*); thus, that treatise says: "As for the emptiness of the beginningless..."
Whether it be sentient beings or phenomena in the world, all are without beginning; therefore, it is called "emptiness of the beginningless. This is explained at length as stated therein.
However, according to this present sutra, it differs from that explanation because it eliminates the four characteristics and is thus called "emptiness of characteristics.
Because it eliminates the process of saṃsāric flow, it is called "emptiness of no priority or posteriority. As stated in the first chapter of the *Madhyāntavibhāga*: "Birth and death..."
It is long-lasting, having neither beginning nor end. The *Eighteen Emptinesses Treatise* states: "The emptiness of no before or after is also called the emptiness of no beginning.
A detailed exposition is as found therein.

Third, because of the thorough knowledge of the object that is grasped (*grāhya*). There are the characteristics of attachment to the body and the characteristics of the conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*).
The commentary states: this clarifies the third characteristic; first the characteristic, then its emptiness. This is the first [of two types]. It is of two kinds.
This refers to the aspect of attachment to the body and the aspect of the conceit of "I.

By means of these, one understands the two types of aspects arising from the five sense faculties and the mind and mental factors mentioned above as the grasper (*grāhaka*). First is the aspect of attachment to the body, which means that the self, the sense faculties, and so forth, are the grasper of all phenomena.
Second is the aspect of the conceit of "I," because the mind and so forth consider themselves superior to others.
This is correctly dispelled by means of internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).
The commentary states: this explains the emptiness that is capable of dispelling. This is of two kinds: internal emptiness and the emptiness of non-apprehension.

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, "internal emptiness" refers to the emptiness of the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-adhyātma-āyatana*); as for the "emptiness of non-apprehension," it is said therein that they are unobtainable.
"Emptiness. Because the three periods of time cannot be apprehended, it is called "unapprehendability. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Internal emptiness" refers to the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), which are without self and without what belongs to a self, and lack such phenomena as the eye; they are unapprehendable.

"Unapprehendable emptiness" means that all phenomena and their causes and conditions are ultimately unapprehendable; this is called the emptiness of the unapprehendable. Now, based on this sutra, by virtue of...

When one is able to discern that the six sense faculties are capable of grasping, there arises attachment and clinging toward the internal body; by contemplating internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), this can be correctly eliminated.

Because of the grasping at a self (*ātman*), the pride of "I" (*asmimāna*) arises; by contemplating the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), this can be correctly eliminated, for no self is to be found.
How, then, could pride arise? Furthermore, it is explained that through these two kinds of emptiness, both [types of pride] are universally eliminated.
Characteristic.
Fourth, because of the thorough knowledge of the objects to be grasped, there is the characteristic of attachment to wealth.
Commentary: This explains the fourth characteristic. First the characteristic, then the emptiness; this is the explanation of the characteristic. This arises from what was stated above.
It is said that among the objects of apprehension, such as the six external bases (*bāhyāyatana*), there is the characteristic of attachment to wealth;
this is correctly eliminated by means of external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*).

The commentary explains that this distinguishes the emptiness that acts as the eliminator, based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. Regarding external emptiness: it refers to the six external bases, according to the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The treatise states: Regarding external emptiness, it refers to the six external sense bases being devoid of self and what belongs to a self, as well as being devoid of the six phenomena.
This sutra is identical to that [teaching], by virtue of excluding the six external [bases].

Fifth is the thorough knowledge of the meaning of enjoyment (*paribhoga*). Because it corresponds to the service of men and women and the requisite articles, there is the characteristic of internal bliss and the characteristic of external purity and excellence.

The commentary explains: this distinguishes the fifth characteristic; first the characteristic, then the emptiness. This is the explanation of the characteristic, namely, by means of thoroughly knowing enjoyment...

This is because, within the context of "utilization," one enjoys men, women, and material requisites. Regarding men and women, since they are sentient beings, one gives rise to the perception of internal bliss.
Regarding material requisites, since they are not sentient beings, one gives rise to the perception of external purity and excellence.

Alternatively, "internal" may refer to the six internal sense bases (*ādhyātmika-ṣaḍāyatana*) and "external" to the six external sense bases; thus, one gives rise to the perception of bliss regarding the six internal sense bases.
Regarding the six external bases, one gives rise to perceptions of purity and excellence;
these can be correctly eliminated by means of internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
The commentary states that "discerning the antidotes" refers to emptiness, which is of two kinds: internal and external emptiness and the emptiness of intrinsic nature. This is based on...
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* states that the six internal and external bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are called "internal and external emptiness" (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*).

That the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of all phenomena—whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—is not produced by the Three Vehicles or anything else, is called "emptiness of intrinsic nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, "internal and external emptiness" refers to the six internal and external sense bases being without self (*anātman*) and without what belongs to a self (*anātmīya*), and lacking an interior.

Regarding external phenomena (*bāhyadharma*) whose intrinsic nature is emptiness (*prakṛtiśūnyatā*): this means that the *dharmatā* (the true nature of phenomena) is eternally empty. Because they arise through conventional continuity, they appear as if they were not empty.

For example, the nature of water is naturally cool and clear; it becomes hot only because of fire. When the fire is extinguished and has remained so for a long time, the water returns to its natural cold state.
The nature of all phenomena is likewise: before they have arisen, they are empty and non-existent, just as the nature of water is eternally [cool].
Cold. All phenomena exist because of the conjunction of various conditions, just as water becomes hot when it encounters fire.

If those various conditions are absent or non-existent, then no phenomenon exists, like water that cools once the fire has been extinguished. Question: What is the difference between this and ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*)?
The treatise itself explains: "Emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) destroys the inherent nature of all phenomena; for example, within that water, there is no [inherent]..."

Regarding the nature of heat: it is not that the characteristic of water is absent. As for "ultimate emptiness" (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), it destroys the characteristic of non-existence and, furthermore, even the characteristic of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Now, in explaining this sūtra, various interpretations differ. One school says: internal emptiness removes the characteristic of internal security; external emptiness removes the characteristic of purity and excellence;
and essential nature emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) universally removes both characteristics. Another school says: [internal and external]...

The emptiness of the internal (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) eliminates the aspect of internal peace and bliss. Within the emptiness of the external (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), one portion eliminates the aspect of purity and excellence.

The emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) universally eliminates both aspects. One interpretation states: the emptiness of the internal and external (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) eliminates the aspect of internal peace and bliss;

it is called "internal" because it pertains to the category of sentient beings, and "external" because it is outside of one's own body. The emptiness of intrinsic nature eliminates the aspect of purity and excellence. Another interpretation states: the internal and external...

The emptiness that excludes internal signs of peace and bliss refers to the emptiness of the internal and external, because [beings] such as men and women possess the twelve sense bases (*dvādaśāyatana*).

The emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) excludes signs of purity and excellence. Question: Why are external signs of purity and excellence not said to be excluded by the emptiness of the external?
Answer: In reality, the emptiness of the external is indeed employed here; however, it was already discussed previously, and therefore it is not mentioned again.
"Sixth, because of the meaning of establishing [the world], there are immeasurable characteristics.
Commentary: This explains the sixth characteristic. First the characteristic, then the emptiness. This explains its characteristic:

namely, by virtue of the meaning of establishing the characteristics of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) as previously described, there are immeasurable characteristics such as the three-thousandfold world system.
This is correctly eliminated by means of the "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*).
The commentary explains that this distinguishes the emptiness that serves as the antidote. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The *prajñāpāramitā* is called 'Great Emptiness'."

Based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, that which is called "great emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*) refers to the emptiness of the ten directions. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains this in the same manner as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

However, the distinction lies in the fact that the treatise fully explains the name "great emptiness" by means of six meanings. Thus, that treatise states: Question: [What is the meaning of great emptiness?]
The emptiness of the ten directions. Why is it called "Great Emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā*)? The answer is: because the eastern direction is boundless; because it exists in all places;

because it pervades all forms; because it is eternal; because it benefits the world; and because it prevents sentient beings from becoming confused or distressed. For these reasons, it is called "Great.
In this way, the ability of the great direction to break [limitations] is named Great Emptiness. The full explanation is as stated therein. Now...
Based on this sūtra, it is largely the same as the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Seventh, because of the thorough knowledge of formlessness (*arūpa*), there is the characteristic of internal tranquility and liberation.

The commentary explains: To distinguish the seventh characteristic, first [the characteristic of] signlessness (*animitta*) and then emptiness (*śūnyatā*) are presented; this explains its characteristic, namely that which was previously distinguished as the sixth.

While the characteristics of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) of the desire and form realms have been explained, we shall now distinguish the characteristic of internal tranquility (*śamatha*) in the formless realm.

Specifically, when a practitioner of meditative concentration attains a formless absorption, they regard it as a peaceful liberation and nirvāṇa; therefore, it is called the "characteristic of liberation."
This is correctly eliminated by the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).

The commentary explains that this distinguishes the emptiness that serves as the antidote (*pratipakṣa-śūnyatā*), based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. Regarding "emptiness of the conditioned," it refers to the emptiness of the three realms (*tridhātu*).

The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (or *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*) states that "emptiness of the conditioned" refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth, which arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; it possesses two meanings.

Therefore, it is called "the emptiness of conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). First, it is empty because things such as a self (*ātman*) or what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*) cannot be apprehended.
Second, it is empty because the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma-lakṣaṇa*) are empty—being neither arising nor ceasing and being non-existent.
As explained extensively in that [text], here too, according to this sutra, it is identical to the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

Eighth, because of understanding the meaning of the suchness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇatathatā*): there are the characteristic of the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmyalakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyalakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of representation-only (*vijñaptimātralakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārthalakṣaṇa*).
The commentary explains: To distinguish the eighth characteristic, there is first the characteristic and subsequently emptiness; this is the explanation of the characteristic.

That is to say, because of the aforementioned characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness), there are four characteristics: namely, the characteristic of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), the characteristic of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), the *tathatā* of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*), and the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

This is correctly dispelled by means of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

The commentary explains that these are the emptinesses that serve as antidotes; according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, "ultimate emptiness" refers to the fact that all phenomena are ultimately [non-existent].
"Unobtainable" means that not even the slightest nature can be found.
"Emptiness of the natureless" means that all phenomena lack any nature of synthesis or any self-nature resulting from synthesis. "Emptiness of the ultimate" refers to *nirvāṇa*.
According to the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, "emptiness of the absolute" means that by means of the emptiness of the conditioned and the emptiness of the unconditioned, one deconstructs all phenomena.

There is nothing remaining; this is called "emptiness of the ultimate" (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). Regarding "emptiness of non-existence" (*abhāva-śūnyatā*): because that which is called "non-existence" is the absence of phenomena that have already ceased, it is called the emptiness of non-existence.

"These two sutras teach that although dependently originated phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they are not contradictory, because there are two kinds of dependently originated phenomena."
The first is the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); the second is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Here, the intention is to clarify that the thoroughly imagined nature does not exist, while the dependent nature is not being discussed. Up to this point, Dharmapāla and others have interpreted the scriptural passage.

Bhāviveka, citing the scripture, raises this objection: "If the dependent nature exists, for what reason does the sūtra state that the nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-svabhāva*) [is non-existent]?"
There is nothing that is not empty. Furthermore, a sutra states: The Buddha told Subhūti, "The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena, such as form (*rūpa*), is entirely non-existent.
Again, another sutra says: The Buddha told Mahāmati, "The nature of all phenomena is devoid of any nature, because that which previously existed or previously did not exist cannot arise.
Dharmapāla explains in general that this contains an intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*). What is this intentional meaning? It is as follows:
These sūtras refute only the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); they do not mean that everything is non-existent.
If everything were non-existent, it would constitute a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). How is it known that there is this underlying intention (*abhiprāya*)?
Because it is made manifest in other sūtras as being expressible; that is to say, the Blessed One spoke these words: "I speak only with reference to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)."

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is entirely non-existent. If one gives rise to attachment based on the literal expression, claiming that the intrinsic nature of both defiled and pure phenomena is non-existent, that is a misapprehension of emptiness (*durgṛhīta-śūnyatā*) and is termed a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). This has been explained in detail therein.
For this reason, Master Vasubandhu states in the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*: "It is not that one understands all phenomena to be non-existent in every respect; rather..."

This is called "entering the selflessness of phenomena" (*dharmanairātmya*). Thus, realizing that the various phenomena—which are the conceptual constructs of the deluded—lack a self-nature (*svabhāva*) is what is meant by entering the selflessness of phenomena.

It is not because the ineffable reality (*dharmatā*), which is the domain of the Buddhas, is also entirely non-existent that it is called the selflessness of phenomena. Furthermore, the first volume of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Regarding..."

There is no such thing as a causeless [entity], yet to insistently establish it as existing is called "superimposition" (*samāropa*). To insistently deny that which exists as being non-existent due to its lack of a cause is called "depreciation" (*apavāda*).
Furthermore, he says: regarding the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the imagined nature), there is only superimposition and no depreciation, because it does not exist at all;
for depreciation can only arise with respect to that which exists. Regarding the *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature)...
There is superimposition (*samāropa*), because it exists as a substantial entity. Superimposition occurs only with respect to that which is non-existent; likewise, there is no denial (*apavāda*).
This is because [the imagined nature] exists only as a false appearance. With respect to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), there is no superimposition, because it is truly existent;
there is only denial. As explained extensively therein, and furthermore according to the thirty-sixth and seventy-fifth [chapters] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there is denial.
Those who claim that the dependent and the perfected natures are non-existent are all said to be those who have wrongly grasped emptiness (*ayoniśaḥ-śūnyatā-grāhin*), as analyzed previously.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 37, states: "Those with an excess of craving cling to the view of existence (*astidṛṣṭi*);
those with an excess of views cling to the view of non-existence (*nāstidṛṣṭi*). Such beings cling to these two views—existence and non-existence—which are both false and unreal."
[This] indeed subverts the Middle Way. It is like a person walking on a narrow path, with deep water on one side and a great fire on the other;
death results from both sides. Clinging to existence and clinging to non-existence—both are lost. This is explained at length. Question:
What is the difference between this general emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the seventeen types of emptiness? Answer: There are two interpretations. One says: "In essence, there is no difference."

There is a distinction between the general and the specific. One explanation states: this general emptiness negates the nature of what is grasped (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), whereas the preceding seventeen types of emptiness eliminate mental images;
thus, there is a difference between them.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how many kinds of superior samādhis are encompassed by this śamatha and vipaśyanā?"

The commentary states: The thirteenth [section] concerns the gateways for encompassing all stages of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bhūmi*) through calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). This consists of two parts:
first, the question; second, the answer. This is the inquiry.

The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: "Good son, as I have taught, there are immeasurable kinds of superior samādhis belonging to the immeasurable śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas; you should know that all of them are subsumed within this."
The commentary states: This is the second correct teaching of the Tathāgata.

It should be understood that all the immeasurable concentrations (*samādhi*) of the three vehicles are subsumed within this śamatha and vipaśyanā; there are no other distinct concentrations that are not included therein.
"Bhagavān, what is the cause of this śamatha and vipaśyanā? The commentary states:
This is the fourteenth section, the Gate of the Causes, Results, and Functions of Śamatha and Vipaśyanā. It contains three parts: first, the cause; second, the result;
and third, the function. This [passage] concerns the cause. First there is the question, followed by the answer; this is the question.
"Good son, pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the right view established through pure hearing and reflection serve as its cause.

Commentary: This is the second answer; it means that because this śamatha and vipaśyanā attain the state of stability, the Pratimokṣa precepts and the two types of wisdom—those of hearing and reflection—during the state of dispersion serve as its cause.
“World-Honored One, what is the fruit of this śamatha and vipaśyanā? The commentary states:
This is the second section, which distinguishes the fruits of śamatha and vipaśyanā. First there is the question, followed by the answer; this is the question.
"Good son, [there is] a well-purified mind; well-purified by means of wisdom is taken as its fruit. The commentary states:
From here below is the direct answer, which has two successive sections; this is the first. "Purified mind":
the term "mind" (citta) indicates meditative concentration (samādhi); it is the fruit of śamatha. "Well-purified wisdom" is the fruit of vipaśyanā. This...
This is explained in terms of the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). If one relies on the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*), all obtain both fruits. Furthermore, it says:
"A well-purified mind and well-purified wisdom" are called "wholesome" (*kuśala*) because they refer to the untainted (*anāsrava*). An alternative version states:
"Taking well-purified precepts, a well-purified mind, and well-purified wisdom as its fruits" is an error. And...
Upon examining the original manuscripts of the sutras and śāstras,
as well as the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, none of them mention the precepts. Furthermore, son of good family,
you should know that all mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas belonging to all śrāvakas and Tathāgatas alike are obtained through this śamatha and vipaśyanā.
"Result. The commentary states: This second section provides a further explanation of that result. However, there are differing interpretations regarding this passage.
One school asserts that this text mentions only Śrāvakas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas. If one follows this interpretation, the word "etc. (ādi) serves as an inclusive term.
This refers to all bodhisattvas. Therefore, Ghanavyūha states:

"Because they are neither the primary instructors nor the disciples to be converted by all śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, buddhas, and pratyekabuddhas, they are omitted and not mentioned. One interpretation says:
"The mention of 'śrāvakas' here also includes pratyekabuddhas; the rest is as previously stated. Another interpretation says: "The word 'etc. (ādi) applies generally to both pratyekabuddhas and..."
Regarding the various bodhisattvas, the rest is as previously explained. The general meaning is as follows:
all dharmas, whether mundane or supramundane, attained by those of the three vehicles are the fruits obtained through śamatha and vipaśyanā. Question:

Since all fruits attained by the Buddha are untainted (anāsrava), how can they be called mundane (laukika)? Answer: There are two kinds of the mundane: first, the mundane in its essential nature (svabhāva-laukika);...

Because they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are called "mundane" (*loka*). Second, although their essence is without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are called "mundane" because they take the mundane as their object;
this refers to the mind and other factors associated with subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Therefore, the World-Honored One possesses mundane dharmas.
"Bhagavān, what function do this śamatha and vipaśyanā perform? The commentary states:
From here downward is the third section, clarifying the functions of śamatha and vipaśyanā. First there is the question, followed by the answer; this is the question.
"Good son, this has as its function the liberation from two bonds, namely, the bond of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) and the bond of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*).
The commentary explains: The Tathāgata correctly teaches that its function is the liberation from these two bonds, namely, the bond of signs and the bond of coarse heaviness.

Regarding the "bond of signs," one interpretation states that it refers to the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*); by means of tainted signs, it causes the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) [to be bound].
Lacking mastery is called "bondage by signs" (*nimitta-bandhana*). This means that the signs themselves are the bondage; thus it is named "bondage by signs.

One interpretation states that the seventh *manas* consciousness constitutes the essence of bondage by signs. Because of the seventh consciousness, the other consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, lack mastery over their respective objective signs.
If one follows this explanation, it is called "bondage by signs" because they are bound by signs. This is termed "coarse."
The heavy fetter (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*) also has two types. First, the state of unserviceability (*akarmanyatā*) upon impure phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) is called the heavy fetter.

Because it is neither identical to nor different from impure phenomena—since it has no separate substance—it is said to be "not different. Because it differs in terms of being abandoned or not abandoned, it is said to be "not identical.
Second, the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) are collectively termed the heavy fetter. Although there are these two types, [they are both included].
The seeds grasped by the mind are called "coarse heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulya*). A detailed analysis is as already explained in the "Chapter on Ultimate Truth.
Bhagavān, according to what the Buddha has taught, among the five kinds of fetters, how many are obstacles to *śamatha*, how many are obstacles to *vipaśyanā*, and how many are obstacles to both?
The commentary states: From here below is the fifteenth section, the "Gate of the Distinctions among the Various Obstructions to Calm Abiding and Insight.

This section contains four parts: first, the gate of the five fetters that obstruct calm abiding and insight; second, the gate of the five hindrances that obstruct calm abiding and insight; third, the gate of the analysis of the five types of distraction;
and fourth, the treatment of the eleven obstructions through calm abiding and insight. This is the first part. Within this, there are two sub-sections.

First the question, then the answer; this is the question itself. Among the five fetters (*pañca-bandhanāni*), how many are obstacles to serenity (*śamatha*), how many are obstacles to insight (*vipaśyanā*), and how many are obstacles to both?
Regarding the "five fetters," according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, they are called the "five mental bonds" (*pañca-citta-bandhanāni*).

Because afflictions and unwholesome dharmas entangle the mind and are not relinquished, they are termed "mental bonds. The first is attachment to one's own body; the second is attachment to the five external sensual desires.
Third, associating with laypeople and monastics; fourth, having no delight in the noble speech;
and fifth, being content with only a small attainment of wholesome dharmas. According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the fourth chapter explains the three obstructions (*āvaraṇa*).
It states: "There are three obstructions, namely greed, hatred, and delusion. Because one relies upon these three, one is attached to the body and wealth and lacks clear comprehension."

Delighting in clamor and bustle, one becomes complacent upon attaining a small measure of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*). Because of this, one is unable to cultivate various wholesome qualities;

therefore, it is called "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*). The commentary explains: according to the sequence of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, "lack of clear comprehension" corresponds to what the sutra describes as being unable to follow one’s will regarding the various holy teachings (*ārya-śāsana*).
In the seventh [chapter] of the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*, the *Samuccaya* is first presented, followed by...
The meaning of "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) is explained by means of five kinds of obstructions. Thus, that treatise states:
"Furthermore, this attachment to the body and so forth is spoken of in reliance upon five kinds of mental obstructions. What are these five? They are: attachment to the body;

dwelling in association with those attached to various sensual desires; lacking compliance with instructions and exhortations; and regarding the categories of the wholesome, being satisfied with what one has attained."

It is complete. Because the mind is obstructed, it is called "mental obstruction" (*citta-vivāda*). The commentary explains that the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* and the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* differ;
specifically, what is the third [topic] in the former is treated as the fourth in the latter. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 8, cites these five names but does not provide an explanation.
Therefore, I shall now formulate the questions based on these five.
"Noble son, attachment to the body is an obstacle to śamatha; being unable to act according to one's will regarding the various holy teachings is an obstacle to vipaśyanā."
The commentary states: From here on, the Tathāgata explains correctly. That is to say, attachment to the body and attachment to wealth—these two kinds [of attachment] can obstruct *śamatha*.
Because one cannot follow one's will regarding the various holy teachings, one is unable to discern their intended meaning;
therefore, they unilaterally obstruct *vipaśyanā*.
One delights in living in company and is easily satisfied with little; it should be known that both of these act as obstacles: because of the first, one is unable to engage in cultivation;
because of the second, the applied effort of cultivation does not reach its ultimate consummation.
The commentary states: This clarifies the obstacles that hinder both [śamatha and vipaśyanā]. Within these dual obstacles, there are two types:

first, dwelling in fond association with others, by which one is unable to cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā; second, being content with little, by the power of which the śamatha and vipaśyanā one cultivates do not reach their ultimate consummation.
"Bhagavān, among the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), how many are obstacles to *śamatha*, how many are obstacles to *vipaśyanā*, and how many are obstacles to both?
The commentary states:

This is the second section [following the previous], concerning how the five hindrances can obstruct the gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Within this, there are two parts; first, the actual [explanation].

The preceding section clarifies that the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) are able to obstruct *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. The subsequent section, beginning with "Thereafter, the World-Honored One," clarifies the gate of the perfect transmission of the two paths of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Within the former [section], there are two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. This [passage] is the question.
Good son, restlessness and remorse are obstacles to śamatha; lethargy, sleep, and doubt are obstacles to vipaśyanā;
you should know that sensual desire and ill-will are obstacles to both.

The commentary states: This is the second part, the Tathāgata’s direct response. Among the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), restlessness and remorse are obstacles to calm abiding (*śamatha*) because they cause mental agitation.
Lethargy, drowsiness, and doubt are obstacles to insight (*vipaśyanā*) because they result in a lack of clarity and decisiveness.
Greed and hatred obstruct both, as the fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) possess a predominant obstructive function.

However, regarding these five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇāni*), their essential nature (*svabhāva*), the definition of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and the explanation of their names are as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 48.

It says: "There are five hindrances, namely: the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*), the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*), the hindrance of lethargy and drowsiness (*styāna-middha-nīvaraṇa*), the hindrance of restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*), and the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*).
Question: What constitutes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these five hindrances? Answer: They consist of thirty [factors] of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The entities constitute the intrinsic nature [of the hindrances]. That is to say, greed and ill-will each consist of five classes within the desire realm, making ten entities.

Dullness and agitation each consist of five classes across the three realms; these are both unwholesome and neutral, and it is only those that are unwholesome which are established as hindrances—thus making ten entities.
Sleep consists of only the five classes of the desire realm; it is wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral, and it is only those that are unwholesome which [are established as a hindrance].
The hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are established as five matters. *Regret* (*kaukṛtya*) belongs only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);

it is both wholesome and unwholesome. That which is exclusively unwholesome is established as one matter among the hindrances. *Doubt* (*vicikitsā*) pervades the three realms and the four categories (*prakāra*); it is both unwholesome and neutral (*avyākṛta*).
That which is exclusively unwholesome is established as four matters among the hindrances. For this reason, these five hindrances take the thirty matters of the desire realm as their basis.
Regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Question: What are its characteristics? The Venerable Vasumitra stated: "Intrinsic nature is itself the characteristic;
the characteristic is itself intrinsic nature, because the intrinsic nature and the characteristic of all phenomena are not separate.

Furthermore, the intense pursuit of various sensual desires is the characteristic of greed; the intensification of hostility toward sentient beings is the characteristic of hatred; and the sinking of body and mind [is the characteristic of delusion].

This is the characteristic of sloth (*styāna*). Physical and mental agitation is the characteristic of restlessness (*auddhatya*). That which causes the mind to become dull and withdrawn is the characteristic of sleep (*middha*).

That which causes the mind to experience regret is the characteristic of remorse (*kaukṛtya*). That which causes the mind’s mode of activity to be hesitant and indecisive is the characteristic of doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Having already explained the intrinsic nature and characteristics of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), I shall now explain why they are called "hindrances. Question: For what reason are they named hindrances? Hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*)...
What is the meaning of this? The answer is: the meaning of "obstructing" (*āvaraṇa*) is the meaning of "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*).

That is to say, because they obstruct the roots of goodness that constitute the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the Noble Path, they are called hindrances. A detailed explanation is as found in that [text].

According to the seventh fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, the meaning of "hindrance" is that which prevents the wholesome factors (*kuśalapakṣa*) from becoming manifest. (End of the main treatise. They shroud the mind and obstruct all wholesome factors, preventing them from proceeding.
