"Although one has attained mastery over phenomena at this stage, there remain residual obscurations, and thus it is not yet called 'ultimate. This refers to the presence of subtle, innate [afflictions]."

The cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), as well as the seeds of spontaneously arising afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), are all severed instantaneously when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) manifests.

One thereby enters the stage of the Tathāgata. For this reason, it is said that on the stage of Buddhahood, two types of delusion (*moha*) and their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) are severed:
first, the delusion of extremely subtle attachment toward all objects of knowledge, which is precisely what is referred to here as "subtle."
The obstacle of knowledge. Second is the ignorance of extremely subtle obstruction, which refers to all the seeds of afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*) that arise spontaneously within this context.

Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "Upon attaining enlightenment, one suddenly severs both the afflictive and cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), becoming an Arhat and a Tathāgata, and realizing Great Nirvāṇa and Great Enlightenment. This sūtra corresponds to these two [obstacles].
This is a type of delusion. However, the *Ghanavyūha* states that in the eleventh stage, one counteracts the "subtle, extremely subtle, and most subtle cognitive obscurations" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
This mentions only the cognitive obscuration; it is likely an omission by the translator, as no other treatises mention such an obscuration to the Buddha-stage.

Therefore, it is not [grammatically] subordinated. Regarding the explanation of the name: among the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaḍ-vibhakti*), this is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (locative determinative compound).
This is because, by being able to permanently destroy such hindrances, one ultimately realizes the omniscient vision that is unattached and unimpeded.
"Based on the object of focus that consists in the fulfillment of what is to be done, one establishes the most perfectly pure *dharmakāya*.

The commentary states: This clarifies the second benefit of abandoning obstacles. The text has two sections. The first clarifies the attainment of wisdom and vision through the abandonment of obstacles;
that is, because one is able to permanently abandon the two kinds of obstacles, one ultimately attains [the fruit] in their respective order.
The vision of omniscience is unattached because phenomena are empty; the vision of omniscience is unobstructed because persons are empty.

Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, fascicle nine, states: "Attachment is the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); obstruction is the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*). By this, it is proven and known.

The wisdom of the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is called "non-attachment" (*asaṅga*); the wisdom of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is called "unimpeded" (*apratigha*).

Both establish the *dharmakāya* with respect to their objects of focus (*ālambana*), because they rely upon the fourth type of object—the perfected accomplishment of what is to be done (*kāryapariniṣpatti*).
By severing the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), they establish the *dharmakāya* of pure *tathatā*. Alternatively, it may be said that they establish two kinds of *dharmakāya*.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva, by diligently practicing in reliance upon śamatha and vipaśyanā, realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
The commentary states: From here below is the sixteenth [section], the gate of realizing bodhi through śamatha and vipaśyanā. First there is a question, followed by an answer;
this is the question: "How is it that a bodhisattva, having already attained śamatha and vipaśyanā, diligently practices by relying upon śamatha and vipaśyanā?"
[They] realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Maitreya: "Noble son, if bodhisattvas have already attained śamatha and vipaśyanā, and based upon the seven kinds of suchness, regarding the dharmas as they have been heard and reflected upon, by means of a mind of supreme concentration, within..."
"Thoroughly examined, well-considered, and well-established; one inwardly contemplates with correct reflection within the nature of *tathatā*. The commentary states:
From this point downward is the second section, the Tathāgata’s formal exposition. This contains two parts: first, the explanation;

second, the conclusion beginning with "Good son, thus... The former part contains two sections: first, clarifying the diligent cultivation of various practices during the stage of the cause (*hetu-bhūmi*); second, [the subsequent...]

At the end, it clarifies the realization of bodhi at the stage of fruition. Within the preceding section, there are three parts: first, the teaching (dharma); second, the analogy; and third, the application.
Regarding the teaching, there are two interpretations. One states that it is divided into four based on the four types of paths.

First, the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) is clarified. Second, from "He, regarding the lower... onwards, the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*) is clarified. Third, from "The *saṃgha* is...

onwards, the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-avasthā*) is clarified. Fourth, from "Furthermore, regarding... onwards, the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-avasthā*) is clarified. This is the first [section], clarifying the stage of equipment; it consists of two parts.

The first clarifies that the practitioner, while in the stage of equipment, has already attained calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). The latter... based on the seven... [text continues].
Regarding the phrase "Based on suchness," there are three sections in the text. First, "based on the seven kinds of suchness" indicates the object of contemplation;
that is, during the stage of the equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), one relies on this mind to contemplate the seven kinds of suchness.

Second, "as for what has been heard as it is" and so forth, distinguishes the basis of the three types of wisdom. "As for what has been heard as it is" refers to the basis of the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*). "Hearing" means...

"Listening" refers to the arising of ear-consciousness through the faculty of the ear to hear verbal teachings. "Among the dharmas contemplated" refers to the basis for the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*);
"reflection" means deliberation, which is the mental factor of volition (*cetanā*) that gives rise to the wisdom of discerning dharmas.

"By means of a mind of superior concentration" refers to the basis for the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*); "cultivation" means repeated practice, which is the superior concentration that gives rise to [wisdom].
"Because one generates wisdom by cultivating the antidotes. Regarding the phrase "later, with respect to what is well-determined," this distinguishes the wisdom that has been generated;
this refers to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), which is able to well-determine [the object] based on the seven kinds of suchness (*tathatā*).

Regarding "well-reflecting," this is the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). Regarding "well-abiding" and so forth, this is the wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), because of internal contemplation within the seven kinds of suchness.

One version states: It is divided into three parts. First, the stage of application (*prayoga*) is explained; next, the stage of seeing (*darśana*) is explained; and finally, the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is revealed.
Within the stage of application, it is further divided into two: first, the contemplation of thorough investigation (*paryeṣaṇā*) as it truly is;
and second, the removal of all signs (*nimitta*) therein. This is the first [section]. The text has two divisions. The first explains reliance upon the seven kinds of true suchness (*tathatā*).

One performs the contemplation of thorough investigation (*paryeṣaṇā*). Subsequently, following the stage of excellent ascertainment, one performs the contemplation of reality as it is (*yathābhūtapratyavekṣā*).

That is to say, the Bodhisattvas, relying upon the seven kinds of true thusness (*saptavidhatathatā*) and according to what they have heard and reflected upon, by means of the power of superior concentration (*samādhi*), perform the four contemplations of thorough investigation during the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*).

They are able to excellently ascertain and excellently deliberate, retaining consciousness while dispelling signs (*nimitta*). During the stages of Patience (*kṣānti*) and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*agradharma*), they perform the four...
One contemplates according to reality. Within the well-established nature of suchness, one engages in correct internal reflection to eliminate the grasping consciousness.
A detailed explanation of its characteristics has already been provided previously. Although there are two interpretations, for now we shall rely on the latter.
Because he correctly contemplates suchness, his mind is even able to abandon the manifestation of all subtle signs, let alone coarse ones.
The commentary states: Second is the elimination of all signs; herein there are two parts. First, the clarification of elimination; subsequently, "once that... [and so forth].
He dwells extensively in lower-level clarity and skillfully cultivates the purification of the mind. This section has three parts: first, the designation of what is to be eliminated;

second, from "Good son" onwards, the manifestation of the characteristics of that which is to be eliminated; third, from "Regarding their active manifestation" onwards, the actual explanation of the elimination. This is the first part.
Because those Bodhisattvas in the stage of application rely upon the seven kinds of true suchness (*tathatā*) and engage in correct reflection, they are able to observe them.
The mind is able to abandon even the subtle manifestations of all that is grasped and appropriated; how much more so the coarse manifestations?

By "coarse manifestations" is meant all manifestations appearing during states of distraction, or perhaps all manifestations appearing under the influence of defilement, or perhaps the manifestations of the desire realm and lower stages. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle ten, states: [text follows].
One version says: What are the coarse characteristics? They refer to all the coarse characteristics of the lower stages that are being observed.

Good son, as for what are called the subtle characteristics: they refer to characteristics not grasped by the mind, or characteristics of experiencing, or characteristics of discerning, or characteristics of affliction and purification.
The commentary states: From here below is the second section, which clarifies the characteristics of that which is to be eliminated (*prahātavya*).
There are twenty-one types of such things to be eliminated, subsumed within eleven sections. This is the first, clarifying the four characteristics beginning with "appropriated" (*upātta*).

These correspond, in their respective order, to the objects of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): body, sensation, mind, and phenomena. Herein, the intended meaning is that they rely upon the appropriated and so forth.
It manifests as a reflected image; this is called the "subtle characteristic" (*sūkṣma-nimitta*). All subsequent instances are to be understood accordingly.
It may be an internal characteristic, an external characteristic, or both an internal and external characteristic.

The commentary states: Regarding the second set of three characteristics, beginning with the "internal," there are briefly three interpretations of these "internal" and "external" aspects. The first says: [self...]

One's own body is called "internal," while the bodies of others are called "external"; together they are termed "internal-external. One interpretation states that the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are called "internal" and the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are called "external";
together they are termed "internal-external. Another interpretation states that sentient beings (*sattva*) are called "internal" and non-sentient things (*asattva*) are called "external";

together they are termed "internal-external. Therefore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 138, states: "However, there are three distinctions regarding internal and external phenomena (*dharmas*)."

First, internal and external in terms of continuity: that which resides within one's own designated body is called internal; that which resides in another's body or in insentient matter is called external.
Second, internal and external in terms of locus: that which is the support for the mind and mental factors is called internal;

their objects of cognition are called external. Third, internal and external in terms of sentient and insentient: phenomena belonging to the category of sentient beings are called internal; phenomena belonging to the category of insentient things are called external.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and other texts agree with the second explanation. They state: "Internal emptiness refers to the six internal bases;
external emptiness refers to the six external bases; internal-and-external emptiness refers to the six internal-and-external bases."
Some say: "I shall practice all that accords with benefiting sentient beings.

The commentary states: The third [verse] reveals the characteristic of benefiting others. Benefiting others is precisely what is termed the "practice of benefiting sentient beings" in the *Vyākhyāyukti*.
This means benefiting all sentient beings by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). Furthermore, it is explained as self-benefit and benefit for others.
Among these practices, this is the practice for the benefit of others, as explained at length in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Chapter 35).
It is characterized either by correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) or by suchness (*tathatā*).

The commentary states: "The fourth [practice] has the characteristics of correct knowledge and suchness. Alternatively, one may distinguish five characteristics within this context; thus there are five characteristics.

This refers to the suchness (tathatā) of correct wisdom that discriminates names and signs; it is explained in this way by emphasizing the predominant factors. For now, only two aspects are mentioned.
If one were to provide a detailed analysis of the five aspects, including names and so forth, it would be as found in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 72, and elsewhere.

"Or the characteristics of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. The commentary explains: The fifth [section] distinguishes the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 77, states: "Question:

What are the respective characteristics of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path? Venerable Pārśva replied: Oppression is the characteristic of suffering; growth and proliferation are the characteristic of its origin."

Quiescence is the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*); renunciation is the characteristic of the path (*mārga-lakṣaṇa*). These are explained at length in that treatise through four successive expositions.
They may be conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) or unconditioned characteristics (*asaṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).

The commentary states: The sixth [section] distinguishes the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*). That which is associated with the four characteristics, such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth, is called a characteristic of the conditioned.

That which is contrary to these characteristics is called a characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*). This is explained in detail in the third fascicle of the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, the 128th fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, and other sources.
"Either having the characteristic of permanence, or having the characteristic of impermanence.
The commentary states: The seventh [category], the characteristic of permanence and impermanence, is in essence no different from the previously mentioned conditioned and unconditioned;
it is spoken of only because their meanings differ.
Either suffering has the characteristic of being subject to change, or suffering has the characteristic of not being subject to change.

The commentary explains: the eighth [type of] suffering, characterized by change and so forth, refers to the two feelings of pleasure and pain, which are called "suffering with the characteristic of being subject to change.

The feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is called "suffering with the characteristic of not being subject to change. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that it refers to the suffering of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

The suffering of other-nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is characterized by the nature of changeability. The suffering of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is characterized by the absence of changeability.

As extensively explained in the *Madhyāntavibhāga* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the four truths are all pervaded by the three natures (the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra’s* statement that "suffering and its origin are not different from their own nature" is a specific interpretation by the translators).
There are characteristics that are different from conditioned phenomena, and there are characteristics that are identical to conditioned phenomena.

The commentary states: "The ninth [category] consists of the characteristics that are both identical to and different from the conditioned. The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, chapter fifty-one, says:

"Specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) refer to the specific characteristics of all phenomena; for example, resistance (*bādhanā*) is the specific characteristic of form (*rūpa*), and experiencing (*anubhava*) is the specific characteristic of sensation (*vedanā*)."

Apprehending images is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of perception (*saṃjñā*). Volitional activity is the specific characteristic of formations (*saṃskāra*). Discernment is the specific characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
There are thus immeasurable such specific characteristics. That which is common to all phenomena is called their common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*);

for example, suffering is the common characteristic of all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), impermanence is the common characteristic of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), and emptiness and selflessness are the common characteristics of all phenomena.
Characteristics. There are such immeasurable common characteristics (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*).
Alternatively, having known that "all is all," there is the characteristic of all. The commentary states:
the tenth is the knowledge of all characteristics (*sarva-lakṣaṇa-jñāna*). Regarding the phrase "having known that all is all": as mentioned above...

The former specifically reveals various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), whereas this [latter] reveals them collectively. By citing the knowing wisdom (*jñāna*), it reveals the characteristics of that which is known;

this is to reveal the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena. The phrase "possessing all characteristics" reveals the differentiated characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), meaning that each and every one possesses all characteristics such as being visible or invisible.
Alternatively, the former may be understood as the characteristic of the full extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*).

The "all" mentioned subsequently refers to the nature of things as they are (*yathāvad-bhāvikatā*), or the characteristic of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), or the characteristic of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
The commentary states: the eleventh [section] distinguishes the two characteristics of selflessness. *Pudgala* is here translated as "one who undergoes repeated existence" (*saṃsārin*).
This refers to repeatedly coming and going to take various realms of existence (*gati*). The old translation "human" (*ren*) is erroneous. *Manuṣya* means "human.
If one adheres to the old translation, there are two faults: first, the fault of failing to encompass all realms of existence; second, the fault of contradicting the Sanskrit sound.
For this reason, it is known that the current translation is correct. These two [aggregates] are without self-characteristics, as in the *Yogācāra*...
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, fascicle 93, states: "Regarding the non-existence of a person (*pudgala-nairātmya*):
it means that apart from all dependently originated formations (*saṃskāra*), no separate, substantial self can be found. Regarding the non-existence of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*):
it means that these very dependently originated formations are not a real self by nature, because they are impermanent."
"He is able to abandon those manifesting [phenomena]. The commentary states:

This third section clearly explains the removal [of obstructions]. That is to say, regarding those aforementioned manifesting signs, the mind that contemplates *tathatā* (suchness) is able to correctly remove them.
Question: These signs are of the nature of *paratantra* (dependent origination); how is this so?
It is said that this is called "removal" (*vibhāvanā*). The explanation states: as previously mentioned, it is called "removal" because [the object] does not manifest before one;

it is not called "removal" by way of a principle that dispels the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) through its causes and conditions. Furthermore, another explanation holds that it is called "removal" because the defiled dependent nature is severed.
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 36, states: "Because it can sever and can relinquish, it is called 'removal'."
He dispatches [them].
Because he dwells frequently in such practice, from time to time he thoroughly cultivates his mind so that it is freed from all fetters, hindrances, and distractions.
The commentary states: The second is the thorough cultivation of the mind, which refers to the ability to contemplate the characteristics of *tathatā* (suchness) as described above.
By means of this, one is able to cultivate the minds that serve as antidotes to the five fetters, the five hindrances, and the five types of distraction.
From this point onward, with respect to the seven kinds of suchness, there arise seven distinct types of internal, personally realized wisdom of thorough penetration;
this is called the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Commentary: From here below, the second section clarifies the stage of the path of seeing. This contains two parts: first, the actual clarification of the path of seeing.

The following section, beginning with "Because one subsequently attains this," clarifies the superior benefits (*viśeṣa*) of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). This constitutes the first formal explanation of the path of seeing;
it is called the "path of seeing" because one sees the principle for the first time. Thus, the sixth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* by Asvabhāva states:

"It is called the path of seeing because one sees the previously unseen, supreme dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Furthermore, the ninth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "The [path of] application..."
Immediately following the practice of uninterrupted application, when this wisdom arises, one realizes and experiences suchness; this is called the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*).
Because it is the first illumination of the principle, it is also called the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). However, this path of seeing itself is of two kinds:

first, the true path of seeing (*tattva-darśana-mārga*), which arises immediately after the supreme mundane dharma (*laukika-agra-dharma*) and simultaneously realizes the suchness of the emptiness of both persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā-tathatā*), while suddenly severing all afflictions of the path of seeing.

The severance of delusions is called the true path of vision (*darśana-mārga*). However, this present explanation of "individually and internally realizing the seven true suchnesses" (*saptatathatā*) is stated from the perspective of verbal designation (*vyañjana*).
If one realizes the aspect of the actual nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena in their state of flux (*pravṛtti*), it is called the individual internal realization of the true suchness of flux.
In this manner, up to the point where if one realizes the aspect of the actual nature of the four noble truths (*catur-āryasatya*), it is termed "individual realization."

The true suchness of the four truths is not [perceived] in this stage of the path of seeing characterized by signlessness (*animitta-darśanamārga*). Prior to and following it, there are seven distinct moments of internal realization.

Second, the path of seeing characterized by signs (*sanimitta-darśanamārga*) consists of either three moments of mind: namely, the wisdom that takes the designation of sentient beings as its object, and the wisdom that takes the designation of phenomena as its object.

The wisdom that universally discerns phenomena as mere designations conditioned by sentient beings consists of either sixteen moments of mind, namely the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) and so forth.

These two types of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are explained at length in the ninth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the fifty-eighth [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, as well as in other specialized treatises.

By virtue of attaining this, one is said to have entered the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-nyāma*), been born into the family of the Tathāgatas, realized the first stage (*bhūmi*),
and is further able to enjoy the sublime qualities of this stage.
The commentary states: From here below is the second section, which explains its benefits (*anuśaṃsa*). This consists of two parts: first, the clarification of the four kinds of benefits;
second, the clarification of the benefits regarding the object-condition (*ālambana*) of the limit of phenomena (*vastuparyanta*), which follows later. This is the first part.
Furthermore, these benefits are based on the eight kinds of benefits of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) found in the ninth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. Therefore:

That treatise states: When a bodhisattva attains these two paths of vision (*darśanamārga*), they are born into the family of the Tathāgata, abide in the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), and thoroughly penetrate the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
They attain all forms of equality and are constantly born within the great assemblies of all Buddhas.

Having attained mastery over many hundreds of gateways, they know for themselves that they will soon realize great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) and be able to bring benefit and happiness to beings until the end of the future.
All [of these] are based on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. There are six benefits; thus, the *Saṃgraha* states:

"Upon entering the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), one thoroughly penetrates the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), is born into the family of the Tathāgatas, attains the mind-nature that is equal toward all sentient beings, attains the mind-nature that is equal toward all bodhisattvas, and attains the mind-nature that is equal toward all Buddhas. These are the six kinds of benefits. If...
The detailed analysis is as found in the sixth fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Vyākhyāyukti* (Exegesis on Non-nature).

The eight kinds of benefits are as found in the eighth fascicle of the Liang translation. The ten kinds of benefits are as found in the tenth fascicle of the Liang translation. Now, based on this sūtra, there are four kinds of benefits.
1. Entering the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-nyāma*). 2. Being born into the family of the Tathāgatas. 3. Realizing the first stage (*bhūmi*). 4.

Furthermore, being able to enjoy the superior virtues of this stage. Regarding the term "rightness and departure from birth": "rightness" refers to the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-ārya-mārga*). Regarding "departure from birth":
it refers to the conceptual afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), which are capable of producing rebirth within the six realms.
The four types of birth and so forth are like raw food that can give rise to various diseases; the name "birth" (jāti) is established based on this analogy.
When the Path of Seeing arises, one becomes free from those afflictions that are like "birth," and thus it is called "leaving birth" (vairāgya).
According to the twenty-third fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa*, the "patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) has two names; as that treatise states:
This very state is called "entry into the state of correctness" (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and is also called "certainty in correctness.

This is because one has for the first time entered the state of correctness free from corruption (*niyāma*), and has also for the first time entered certainty in correctness. The Sūtra speaks of "correctness," which refers to Nirvāṇa;

alternatively, the term "correctness" denotes the various Noble Paths. "Birth" (*jāti*) refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), or to those whose faculties (*indriya*) have not yet matured. The Noble Ones...

The Path is able to transcend; therefore, it is called "born of detachment" (*vairāgyaja*). It is able to definitively grasp *nirvāṇa*, or to definitively comprehend the characteristics of the Truths;
thus, the various Noble Paths receive the name "definitive. Reaching this stage is what is termed "entry. The commentary explains:

according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, there are two kinds of "right nature" (*samyaktva*): *nirvāṇa* and the Noble Path. Regarding "birth," there are two meanings: first, the birth of afflictions is like raw food.
Second, when the Noble Path has not yet matured, it is termed "birth" (*jāti*).
This is stated in the *Nyāyānusāra* (63) and the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā* (7), which largely agree with the *Abhidharmakośa*. According to the *Vibhāṣā*, there are also two meanings.

First, the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) are like raw food. Thus, the third fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "Furthermore, the afflictions abandoned through seeing cause all..."

Sentient beings fall into the various evil destinies and undergo intense suffering. This is like raw food remaining in the body for a long time, which can cause all manner of extremely painful afflictions.
For this reason, these afflictions are called "birth" (*jāti*); they are extinguished by the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Therefore, it is called "freedom from birth" (*niḥsaraṇa*). Furthermore, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and other such views are stubborn and difficult to subdue, like a wild beast in a cage;

thus they are called "birth. Since the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) can extinguish them, it is called "freedom from birth. Alternatively, when the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) have not yet matured, this is called "birth."

Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states: "Furthermore, all afflictions, or various forms of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), which prevent the roots of goodness from reaching fulfillment and cause the moisture of existence (*bhava*) to arise with faults, are all termed 'birth' (*jāti*). Once the Path of Seeing has arisen..."
It crushes their power so that they no longer produce the faults of superior birth (*abhyudaya*). For this reason, the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) alone is called "leaving birth" (*vairāgya*);
the detailed explanation is as found in that [text]. Regarding the Mahāyāna teaching on the "place," it is explained in the commentary and notes of the eighth fascicle.

As for the expression "born into the family of the Tathāgata," the *Nirabhilāpyadharmatā-vibhāga* (or *Asvabhāva*) explains: "The Buddha-dharmadhātu is called the family of the Tathāgata; one realizes this..."
[This] is a meeting; therefore, it is called "birth. Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "To be born into the family of the Tathāgata" means that by this, the lineage of all Buddhas is rendered unbroken.
According to the first fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*: "The family of these Buddhas is called the family of the Tathāgata.
Now, because this Bodhisattva practices the path of the Tathāgata in continuous succession, [it is so called]."

[The practitioner] comes to the stage [of the Bodhisattva]. This is explained at length through many successive methods in that treatise. As for the realization of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), it shall be explained below.
Furthermore, regarding the ability to enjoy the superior virtues of this stage, this subsumes the six remaining benefits of *vijñaptimātratā*.
Because he had previously attained śamatha and vipaśyanā, he had already acquired two kinds of objects of focus:
namely, the object of focus consisting of the conceptual image and the object of focus consisting of the non-conceptual image. At this present time, he...
"Because one attains the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga), one further realizes the object-condition (ālambana) that is the limit of phenomena.
The commentary explains: This second section clarifies the excellence of the object-condition.

That is to say, because one has already attained two types of object-conditions prior to this stage, at this present Path of Seeing, one further attains the third, the object-condition that is the limit. Thus, there are three types of object-conditions.
The characteristics of the distinctions among these objects have already been explained as before.
Furthermore, as one progresses and cultivates the path of meditation within each successive stage, one does so precisely with respect to these three kinds of objects of focus.
"Reflecting with mental attention. The commentary states:
From here below is the third section, explaining the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). The text consists of two parts. The first clarifies progressive cultivation;

"cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) has the meaning of increasing clarity. This refers to the period after the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), wherein within the subsequent nine stages, contemplative wisdom gradually increases. Furthermore, it is explained as follows: the latter...
The latter [text] explains the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) in detail. Since these ten stages are not one, it uses the term "successive" (*uttarottara*) repeatedly.
Regarding the phrase "subsequently, within such as these," it distinguishes the possession of three conditions:

namely, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) internally and correctly contemplating the ultimate limit of all phenomena—the true object that is *tathatā*—without projecting mental images; and subsequently, through post-attainment wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), forming mental attention.
There are only two kinds of objects: those with conceptual differentiation and those without conceptual differentiation.
By this very passage, it is proven that all ten stages (bhūmis) possess these three types of objects.
It is like a person who uses a fine wedge to extract a coarse wedge.
The commentary states: The second analogy is as follows. Just as when people in the world wish to split wood, they first use a coarse wedge and subsequently use a fine wedge;
by means of the fine wedge, they drive out the coarse wedge.

In this way, by relying on this skillful means of "using a wedge to extract a wedge" to eliminate internal signs, the Bodhisattva eliminates all signs that accord with the category of affliction (*saṃkleśapakṣa*).
Because these signs are eliminated, the heavy burdens (*dausthulya*) are also eliminated.
The commentary states: The third [section] presents the dharma as being analogous to the example (also termed "application"). Within this, there are two parts:

first, it clarifies how the Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) emerges from two kinds of bonds; second, it reveals how the mind is refined in the subsequent stages. This is the first part.

That is to say, the Bodhisattva of the first stage relies on this—using a wedge to extract a wedge—to eliminate the internal signs of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) through the Noble Path (*āryamārga*). Because these signs are eliminated, all...
All bonds of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) are completely eliminated. Because the bonds of signs are eliminated, the bonds of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*) are also eliminated.

Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (64) states: "If one practices with regard to the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*) and does not practice with regard to signs, because one does not practice with regard to signs, one attains liberation from all bonds of signs.
Because one attains liberation from all bonds of signs, regarding coarse..."
Even those who are bound by heavy fetters can attain liberation. The distinct characteristics of these two fetters have already been explained as before.
Question: How is it known that from the first bhūmi upward, one is able to sever the two fetters? Answer: As stated in the ninth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:

"In this stage of preparatory application (*prayoga-avasthā*), the fetter of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) has not yet been dispelled, nor has the fetter of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*) been severed. Furthermore, in the second fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* translated during the Liang dynasty...
The fourth fascicle states: "If one attains non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), one immediately understands the fetters of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*).

Since the fetters of signs do not arise, the fetters of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*) are accordingly extinguished. Thus, we know that prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*), these two fetters are not severed.

However, this teaching employs the analogy of "using a wedge to extract a wedge"; the various teachings differ. According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the reflected image (*pratibimba*) is likened to a fine wedge, while the original object (*bimba*) is likened to a coarse wedge.
Physical pliancy is the subtle wedge; physical heaviness is the coarse wedge. One uses the subtle wedge to eliminate the coarse wedge.

Thus, the *Ṣaṭsaptati* (Treatise on the Sixty-seven) states: "The cultivation of elimination refers to a certain person who, by means of mental engagement with the signs of the images traversed in samādhi, eliminates them through the skillful means of using a wedge to extract a wedge, thereby casting them aside."
Regarding the characteristics of intrinsic nature: it is like using a fine wedge to drive out a coarse wedge;
likewise, when a practitioner uses physical pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) to eliminate physical heaviness (*dausthulya*), this is called the cultivation of elimination (*vibhāvanā-bhāvanā*).
Furthermore, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Xianyang lun), fascicle 16, states: "The cultivation of elimination refers to when someone contemplates the images that are the objects of samādhi."
By means of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), one eliminates the fundamental nature and characteristics of all phenomena so that they no longer appear. The remainder is the same as in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
According to the Liang commentary, using a coarse wedge to drive out a fine wedge is a metaphor for using superior wisdom to eliminate inferior wisdom within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Therefore, the *Ekādaśa* states: "Just as those in the world who wish to split wood first use a fine wedge and subsequently use a coarse wedge, so too is it for the practitioner who destroys the afflictions (*kleśa*):
first they employ the inferior path, next the middling path, and finally the superior path."
According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the Noble Path is likened to a fine wedge, while the seeds of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) are likened to a coarse wedge.

Thus, the eighth fascicle of Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "The treatise says: Regarding the distinction of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), it refers to the wisdom that takes all general characteristics as its object."
By means of the principle of "using a wedge to extract a wedge," all obstructions and heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) within the *ālayavijñāna* are eliminated. The commentary explains:
"The wisdom that takes general phenomena as its object abides by counteracting and destroying all obstructions; it is like using a fine wedge to remove a coarse wedge.
Those various defiled dharmas and their perfumed seeds residing within the fundamental consciousness are called "coarse. All...
The path of remedy (*pratipakṣa-mārga*) is able to eliminate those [seeds], and thus it has the sense of being "subtle. Furthermore, the eighth fascicle of the *Anabhāvavāda-śāstra* states:
"Because the Noble Path is subtle, it is like a fine wedge; because the seeds of that which is to be remedied are coarse and heavy by nature, they are like a coarse wedge.
The rest is the same as Vasubandhu’s [explanation]. Based on these scriptural teachings, various interpretations of this sūtra passage differ. One school says:

The intent of this sutra is the same as that of the Liang commentary: using the wedge of superior wisdom to extract the wedge of inferior wisdom. One interpretation states that the intent of the sutra is the same as that of Vasubandhu and others:
using the wedge of noble wisdom to extract the wedge of afflictions. Another interpretation states that this sutra explains by way of manifesting the characteristics [of the phenomena].

This is consistent with Vasubandhu and others when speaking in terms of general characteristics; there is no contradiction between them. That is to say, when Bodhisattvas are in the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrvaka*), they attain the fundamental meditative concentrations (*mauladhyāna*).

Through the pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) of the body, they eliminate the heaviness and rigidity (*dausthulya*) of the body; subsequently, by means of the subtle images (*pratibimba*) within concentration, [they eliminate the heaviness of the mind].

One eliminates external coarse characteristics, or uses subtle characteristics of reflected images to eliminate the original coarse characteristics. Bodhisattvas on the stages (bhūmi) employ true contemplation (*bhūtadṛṣṭi*) to eliminate the characteristics of reflected images;
even the process of eliminating delusions through wisdom can be understood by following this logic.
Alternatively, one may interpret this as a combined teaching of the Dharma and its analogies based on the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Because they have forever eliminated all coarse habitual tendencies (*dauṣṭhulya*) regarding signs, they gradually refine their minds within each successive stage, just as one refines gold.
The commentary states:
the second refinement of the mind refers to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), because at that time one has forever eliminated the power of the two fetters.
Regarding the subsequent stages: one refines the mind like refining raw gold. This method of refining gold is as explained in the thirteenth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
It states: "One should refine the mind according to the method for refining raw gold.
There are, in brief, three ways to refine raw gold: first, refinement by removing impurities; that is, [gradually] from within the nature of the gold..."
First, removing coarse, medium, and subtle impurities. Second, refining through intensive processing, which means repeatedly melting and boiling that very [metal].
Third, refining through tempering, which means that after the melting and boiling, one further polishes and treats it to remove defects such as flaws and blemishes.
Furthermore, the thirty-first [chapter] states: "For example, it is like a wise smith of gold or silver, or his disciple, from time to time..."
Just as gold and silver are smelted and refined so that all impurities are discarded, becoming pliant, malleable, and compliant,
and their seeds are transformed according to what is desired; likewise, the practitioner who diligently cultivates yoga causes the mind to turn away from all impurities such as greed,
and establishes it wherever one wishes— whether in the category of *śamatha* or otherwise.
Or, regarding the category of vipaśyanā, one is able to skillfully harmonize each respective [object] therein, remaining unshakable and unwavering;
according to one's inclination, among various meanings, one is able to accomplish everything exactly as it has been resolved through faith and understanding.
"Up until the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, one attains the objective support of the fulfillment of what was to be done.
The commentary states: The second [point] clarifies its state of fruition, which is the attainment of *bodhi* (within the five stages, this is the fifth, the ultimate stage). That is to say:

Not only does one refine the mind through each successive stage (*bhūmi*), but even upon attaining unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*) within the ultimate state, one further attains the fourth type of object of focus—namely, the object of focus consisting of the fulfillment of what is to be done—by relying on that state.
Within the state of Buddhahood, all four types of objects are fully present. Furthermore, it is explained that these are attained prior to the stages.
Regarding the two kinds of objects: within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they are termed "partial realization," while within the stage of Buddhahood, they are termed "perfected fulfillment.
Although there are these two interpretations, the former explanation is superior.
Good son, because such a bodhisattva correctly practices internal śamatha and vipaśyanā,
they realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The commentary states: This is the second concluding statement. It means that because Bodhisattvas, both prior to and upon the stages (*bhūmi*), diligently practice the two paths of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how does one practice so as to bring forth the vast majesty and virtue of a bodhisattva?
Commentary: From here below is the seventeenth section, the Gate of Bringing Forth Vast Majestic Virtue. Within this, there are two parts; first—
Question: [The following] is the answer to the question.
"Good son, if bodhisattvas thoroughly understand the six sense bases, they are able to bring forth all the vast majesty and virtue of a bodhisattva."
The commentary states: From this point downward is the second section, the Tathāgata’s direct response. This contains two parts: first, the formal explanation based on the questions;
second, the conclusion beginning with "Good son. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, a brief answer indicating the number;

second, listing the names according to that number; third, a detailed explanation of each in sequence. This is the first: the brief answer indicating the number, which states: "The various Bodhisattvas are skilled..."
Knowing the six sense bases brings forth great majestic power.
First, skillfully knowing the arising of the mind; second, skillfully knowing its abiding; third, skillfully knowing its emergence;
fourth, skillfully knowing its increase; fifth, skillfully knowing its decrease; sixth, skillfully knowing the skillful means.
The commentary states: The second [section] enumerates the names according to their number.
How does one thoroughly know the arising of the mind? The commentary states:
From here below, the third section provides a sequential and detailed explanation. The detailed explanation of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) is divided into six parts. This...

This refers to the first explanation, which concerns the thorough knowledge of the arising of the mind. Within this, there are two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. This is the question.
"Thorough knowledge" refers to the knowing wisdom; "the arising of the mind" refers to the mind that is known. The subsequent passages should all be understood accordingly.
This refers to knowing, as it truly is, the distinctions in the arising of the mind through its sixteen modes of activity; this is called "skillfully knowing the arising of the mind.

The commentary states: From here on is the second part, the formal response. This consists of two sections: first, the general response; second, the detailed explanation. This is the general response.
Regarding the distinctions in the arising of the sixteen modes of mind (*ṣoḍaśākāracittotpāda-viśeṣa*), the commentary states:
the second section provides a detailed explanation of the sixteen modes of mind. This consists of two parts: first, the restatement of the subject; second, the explanation.
This [sentence] is the general restatement.
First is the arising of the stable receptacle-consciousness that cannot be cognized, namely the *ādāna-vijñāna*.
The commentary states: From this point downward, the sixteen types of mind are explained in sequence, one by one;

this constitutes the first of the sixteen. This explanation of the initial mind has two sections: first, the designation of the mind’s name; second, the presentation of its essential nature (*svabhāva*). Now, to explain this passage:

There are two interpretations. The first states: "That which cannot be cognized" refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), whose mode of perceiving (*ālambana-ākāra*) cannot be cognized because it is constantly continuous and bound.
It is called "firmly abiding" because it maintains and upholds the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
It is called the "vessel-consciousness. As for the *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness), this refers to its essential nature.

In the Sanskrit language, *ādāna* means "to grasp" or "to maintain. It has three meanings: first, it grasps and maintains the sense organs as well as their bases; second, it grasps and maintains the seeds.
Third is the bond of grasping that links birth and continuity. Regarding the first point, "that which cannot be cognized" refers to the external receptacle world, which is a common-result fruit;
it is that which cannot be cognized as having the distinct characteristics of being either one's own transformation or the transformation of another.
"Second, consciousness arises with various modes of activity (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*).

The commentary explains: this clarifies the arising of the second type of mind. First, its name is indicated; subsequently, its essential nature (*svabhāva*) is set forth. This is the indication of the name:

"consciousness arises with various modes of activity" means that because the modes of activity that take an object are not uniform, they are called "various modes of activity. It is "consciousness" that arises with these as its objects.
This is named after its object. Because it takes the perceived object as its objective support (*ālambana*), it is called "the consciousness that arises with an objective support.

This refers to the conceptualizing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that simultaneously apprehends all objects such as form, as well as the sensations that simultaneously apprehend internal and external objects.

The commentary states: The second [section] clarifies the essential nature [of consciousness]. This consists of two parts: first, the explanation of the contaminated mental consciousness (*sāsrava-manovijñāna*);

second, the explanation of the uncontaminated mental consciousness (*anāsrava-manovijñāna*). This is the first part. That is to say, at one time, it simultaneously apprehends all six objects, such as form and so forth.

"Discriminating mental consciousness" refers to the discriminating mental consciousness that arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses, or the discriminating mental consciousness that arises subsequent to them;
it perceives and experiences the objects of the twelve internal and external bases (āyatana) all at once.
The discriminating consciousness may,
either suddenly or in a single thought-moment, an instant, or a brief duration, manifest entry into many meditative concentrations, see many Buddha-lands, and see many Tathāgatas;
this is the discriminating consciousness.
The commentary states: The second [type of consciousness], the untainted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), is a *kṣaṇa* in the Sanskrit language;

here it is called "the shortest duration," which is equivalent to one thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*). Thus, the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* says: "In the time it takes a strong man to snap his fingers, sixty *kṣaṇas* elapse; one *kṣaṇa* constitutes one thought-moment.
The Sanskrit term *lava* is here translated as "a brief interval" (a moment); the Sanskrit term *muhūrta*...
*Muhūrta*. This is translated as "a brief moment. According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, fascicle 12:
one hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute one *tatkṣaṇa*; sixty *tatkṣaṇas* constitute one *lava*; and thirty *lavas* constitute one *muhūrta*.
The meaning of this is that, by virtue of the power of mastery over the untainted (*anāsrava*) state attained subsequently, or at a certain time...
In a single moment of thought, one manifests entry into many meditative absorptions, sees many Buddha-fields, or sees many Buddhas. This is the conceptualizing consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*).

However, this subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), when contrasted with the mind associated with outflows (*sāsrava-citta*), is called "non-conceptual"; yet, when contrasted with the wisdom of the fundamental essence (*mūla-jñāna*), it is also called "conceptual.
Question: It may be acceptable that one sees many Tathāgatas in a single moment; however, how can one [do so] in a single moment?
Question: They enter many meditative absorptions (*samādhi*). Answer: The supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is inconceivable;
they are able to enter various meditative absorptions in every moment of thought. Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, chapter fourteen, states:
"Only the World-Honored Buddha and Bodhisattvas who have attained great supernormal powers can, according to their wish, enter into the distinctions of immeasurable *samādhis* from moment to moment."

Therefore, another explanation is that one may enter various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) as appropriate; it is not the case that one actually enters all absorptions in a single moment of thought.

If this were not so, how could one enter many Buddha-fields in a single moment? Since no sentient being possesses multiple bodies, one manifests transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) to enter many Buddha-fields.
Third, consciousness arises with a limited object-condition (*ālambana*), namely, consciousness bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The commentary states: this reveals the third mind. The five characteristics [discussed] below are all explained in reference to the eighth *ālayavijñāna*.
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 51, says: "The *ālayavijñāna*, within the desire realm, takes a narrow and limited [object] as its objective support."
The object of sensation. Because it discerns a limited objective support (*ālambana*), the *Miśraka-śāstra* states: "Small" refers to the inferiority of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Fourth, the consciousness that arises with great characteristics as its objective support refers to the consciousnesses associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The commentary states: To distinguish the fourth consciousness, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says:

"In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the ālayavijñāna takes as its object a vast domain of appropriation (*upādāna*), because it discerns a vast object of appropriation. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states:
"'Vast' refers to the predominance of the form realm."
Fifth, consciousness arises with an immeasurable aspect as its object; that is, consciousness associated with the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness.
The commentary explains: to distinguish this fifth consciousness, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"The ālayavijñāna, in the formless realm, in the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness, takes as its object immeasurable appropriated realms and discerns immeasurable appropriated [realms]."
Regarding the object of focus (*ālambana*), the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "The immeasurable" refers to the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness, because they are boundless.
Sixth is the consciousness that arises in relation to the subtle characteristic; this refers to the consciousness associated with the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The commentary states: This explains the sixth characteristic. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says:
"The ālayavijñāna, in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), takes as its object a subtle appropriation; it is because it discerns the subtle object of appropriation."

Seventh is the arising of consciousness with the aspect of the limit (*paryanta*) as its object; this refers to consciousness bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The commentary explains: it clarifies that the seventh mind is the ultimate limit within the three realms, and is therefore called the "limit.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The ālayavijñāna, in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, takes extremely subtle grasping as its object."
It is the object of sensation (*vedanā*). This is because it discerns the objective support (*ālambana*) consisting of the appropriated atoms (*paramāṇu*).

The *Exposition of the Dharma* (Dharmasaṃgīti), chapter seventeen, explains these five characteristics in the same manner as the *Yogācārabhūmi*. Alternatively, these five characteristics may apply to all six consciousnesses as appropriate.

Eighth is the arising of the signless consciousness (*animitta-vijñāna*), which refers to supramundane consciousness (*lokottara-vijñāna*) and the consciousness that takes cessation (*nirodha*) as its object.
The commentary states: this clarifies the eighth mind. Supramundane consciousness is the consciousness associated with the untainted Truth of the Path (*anāsrava-mārga-satya*);

because it is far removed from the signs of all tainted conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), it is called "signless. This encompasses the eight kinds of untainted pure consciousnesses (*anāsrava-śuddha-vijñāna*) and—

"Consciousness conditioned by cessation" refers to consciousness conditioned by the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). This includes both the eight untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses and the tainted (*sāsrava*) mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Ninth is "consciousness accompanied by suffering," which refers to the consciousness of those in the hells.

The commentary states: This clarifies the ninth consciousness, namely that which exists in its entirety within the hells (*naraka*), and in those portions of the hungry ghosts (*preta*) and animals (*tiryagyoni*) where suffering is experienced exclusively.
As the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* says: "Consciousness associated with suffering is like the consciousness of the miserable realms."
Tenth is the arising of consciousness accompanied by mixed feelings; this refers to consciousness operating within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The commentary explains that this clarifies the tenth mind: among human beings, the gods of the desire realm, and a portion of the hungry ghosts (*preta*) and animals (*tiryagyoni*), the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) is associated with feelings that arise in conjunction and intermingle—namely, painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*), pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*), and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanā*). This is profound.
The *Guhyasūtra* states: "Consciousness associated with various sensations is like the consciousness of the desire realm;
eleven types of consciousness accompanied by joy arise, namely, the consciousnesses of the first and second dhyānas."

The commentary states: This clarifies the eleventh mind, namely, its association with the sensation of joy (*saumanasya*) in the first two dhyānas, which is accepted by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools alike.
However, according to the Mahāyāna tradition, although they share the same substance, there are distinctions in their meanings; thus, there is also the sensation of pleasure (*sukha*).

Because this sūtra aims to distinguish between the five sensations, it speaks here specifically of the sensation of joy. The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "Consciousness associated with joy is like the consciousness of the first and second dhyānas."
The twelfth consciousness arises accompanied by pleasure; that is, the consciousness of the third dhyāna.

The commentary states: regarding the twelfth mind, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says that in the three lower dhyānas, [consciousness] invariably functions in conjunction with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "Consciousness associated with pleasure is like the consciousness of the third dhyāna."
Thirteenth: consciousness arises accompanied by neither-pain-nor-pleasure. This refers to the consciousness of the fourth dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The commentary explains that this clarifies the thirteenth mind, namely all stages from the fourth dhyāna upward, which are exclusively [of this nature].

It is associated with neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*). This extends to the sixth consciousness, as well as the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, whether they are contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "Consciousness associated with neutral feeling is like that of the fourth dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)."
The fourteenth is the defiled consciousness that arises in conjunction [with afflictions].
This refers to the consciousness associated with the various primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). The commentary explains: this clarifies the fourteenth mind;
as appropriate, it refers to the seven contaminated (*sāsrava*) consciousnesses that are associated with the six root afflictions and the twenty secondary afflictions.
Fifteen types of consciousness arise in association with the wholesome; that is, consciousness associated with faith and the other [wholesome factors].

The commentary explains: this clarifies the fifteenth mind, namely, the six contaminated (*sāsrava*) consciousnesses and the eight uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses that are associated with the eleven wholesome dharmas, such as faith.
Sixteen types of consciousness arise in association with the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); that is to say, those consciousnesses that are dissociated from it.
The commentary explains: this clarifies the sixteenth mind, namely, the six contaminated (*sāsrava*) consciousnesses that are neither associated with the wholesome nor with the defiled.
And as for the eighth consciousness:
how does one thoroughly know the abiding of the mind?
The commentary states: regarding the second [point], "thoroughly knowing the abiding of the mind," first there is the question and then the answer. This is the question. "Thoroughly knowing" means...
The wisdom that is capable of knowing. Regarding "the mind in which the mind abides," this is what is known; the subsequent sections are explained according to this principle.
That is to say, it refers to knowing the *tathatā* (suchness) of discernment as it truly is.
The commentary states: this explains the two answers. That is to say, it refers to knowing, as it truly is, the mind associated with non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). To discern...

The distinct *tathatā* (separate suchness). One dwells in reliance upon suchness; alternatively, that which is termed "discerning *tathatā*" refers to the *vijñapti-mātra-tathatā* (suchness of representation-only) among the seven types of *tathatā*.
This is the wisdom of contemplation itself, which is named discerning *tathatā*, rather than the *tathatā* of actual nature.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states: "The *tathatā* of representation-only refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). The meaning of this is as follows: [it is] like...
Truly knowing the mind associated with the contemplation of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) as it abides in dependence upon its objects is called "skillfully knowing the abiding of the mind.
What is meant by "skillfully knowing the emergence of the mind"?
The commentary states: regarding the third [point], skillfully knowing the emergence of the mind, there is first a question and then an answer; this is the question.
That is to say, knowing as it truly is the emergence from two kinds of bonds— namely, the bond of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) and the bond of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*)—
and being able to skillfully know how to cause the mind to emerge from these.
The commentary states: This is the second answer. It means that one knows, as it truly is, the mind associated with non-conceptual wisdom, which emerges from two kinds of bonds.
Once this knowing mind has thoroughly understood [the situation], it should cause the mind associated with non-conceptual wisdom to emerge from those two bonds.
"What is meant by 'skillfully knowing the increase of the mind'?
The commentary explains: the fourth [point] is skillfully knowing the increase of the mind. First there is the question, followed by the answer; this is the question.

It means knowing, as it truly is, the mind that counteracts the fetters of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) and the fetters of latencies (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*), when that [mind] is increasing and when it is accumulating.
"They also increase and they also accumulate; this is called 'knowing increase well.

The commentary states: This is the second answer. It means that when one knows as it truly is the mind that counteracts the two bonds, at the time of its increase and at the time of its accumulation, the wisdom and other factors associated with that mind which counteracts the bonds also increase and also accumulate.

It is called "skillful knowledge of increase. Regarding the distinction between "increase" (*vṛddhi*) and "accumulation" (*upacaya*): when [the defilements] manifest and further intensify, it is termed "increase";
when they perfume and form seeds, it is termed "accumulation. Alternatively, the initial stage of increase may itself be termed "increase."
To arise repeatedly and again is called "accumulation.
What is meant by "knowing well the decrease"?
The commentary states: the fifth [point] is knowing well the decrease. First the question is posed, then the answer follows; this, then, is the question.

This means knowing as it truly is that when the mind—which is defiled by the signs of those opposites and by coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*)—declines or diminishes, this [mind] also declines and this [mind] also diminishes; this is called "knowing decrease well."

The commentary states: This is the second answer. It means that when the mind, which is defiled by the two types of bonds to be abandoned, undergoes decline and diminution, the views and other factors associated with that defiled mind likewise diminish. This is called "knowing well the diminution.
One should understand that the distinction between "decline" (*parihāṇi*) and "diminution" (*apacaya*) is that the latter is the opposite of the former, involving growth and accumulation.
"What is meant by 'skillfully knowing the means'?
The commentary states: Regarding the sixth [topic], "skillfully knowing the means," there is first a question and then an answer; this is the question.

It refers to knowing, as it truly is, liberation, the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), whether for the purpose of cultivation or for their relinquishment.

The commentary states: This is the second answer. It means that one knows, as they truly are, the cultivation of the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhvāyatana*), and the ten totalities (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*).
These are the merits of these three categories [of meditative objects], which are capable of dispelling the obscurations associated with those three categories.

By means of this skillful method (*upāya*), one gives rise to various merits such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the state of being without conflict (*araṇā*). Therefore, it is called "skillful method. However...
This skillful means draws forth various merits; the various teachings differ on this point.

According to the explanation in the fourth fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, among the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), it is the fifth liberation that draws forth these merits. Thus, that treatise states:

"In order to give rise to various noble qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the absence of strife (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhi-jñāna*), and the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), one further practices..."

Regarding the skillful means for the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*anantya-vijñānāyatana-vimokṣa*), there are three different textual traditions according to the twelfth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

First, one text states only that within the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), the first liberation induces the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the various noble supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhi-jñāna*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisamvid*), and so forth. Furthermore, that same text says: "Among the ten spheres of totality..."

Through the eight spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), one brings forth the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the noble ones. Through the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānakṛtsnāyatana*), one can bring forth the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and so forth.
Through the sphere of space (*ākāśakṛtsnāyatana*), everything is transformed into space according to one's wish. Furthermore, it says:

"The liberations (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are called the paths that lead [to these results]. This is also stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 72.

"Regarding the statement that 'the three categories are able to induce [attainment],' the commentary explains: A practitioner at the initial stage of contemplation must necessarily take liberation as the starting point.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* provisionally refers to liberation; subsequently, one gradually cultivates the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) which are capable of inducing [attainment].

However, speaking according to the ultimate reality, all three categories are capable of inducing various meritorious qualities. Thus, in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and in this scriptural passage, all three are capable [of induction]."
They induce qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). However, regarding the distinctions between these three categories, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 85, states: Question:
What is the difference between liberation (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*)? Answer: Their very names constitute the distinction;
that is to say, this is called "liberation," this is called "sphere of mastery," and this is called "sphere of totality. Furthermore, roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) of inferior grade are called...
Liberation (*vimokṣa*). Middling roots of goodness are called "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*); superior roots of goodness are called "totalities" (*kṛtsnāyatana*).

Furthermore, minor roots of goodness are called liberation; great roots of goodness are called totalities. Furthermore, that which is solely the cause is called liberation; that which is solely the fruit is called totality;
that which encompasses both cause and fruit is called a base of mastery. Furthermore, that which is capable of renunciation and turning away is called liberation.
That which is able to overcome and subdue objects is called a "sphere of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*). That which is able to expand the object of focus is called a "universal base" (*kṛtsnāyatana*).

Furthermore, that which consists solely of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) is called a "liberation" (*vimokṣa*); that which is able to subdue the afflictions is called a "sphere of mastery"; and that which is non-dual and immeasurable with respect to its object of focus is called a "universal base.
Furthermore, one who has attained liberation has not necessarily already attained the spheres of mastery and universal bases; if one attains [the latter]...
Regarding the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*): one who has attained them has necessarily attained liberation, though they have not necessarily attained the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).

If one has attained the spheres of totality, one has necessarily attained both liberation and the spheres of mastery. Why is this? Because one enters the spheres of mastery from liberation, and one enters the spheres of totality from the spheres of mastery.
This is called the distinction between liberation, the spheres of mastery, and the spheres of totality. If explained in detail, [it is as follows]... [complete].
As explained in another chapter:
"O son of noble family, regarding the vast majesty and power of all bodhisattvas— whether already manifested, yet to be manifested,
or currently being manifested."

The commentary states: This is the second summary. It means that because a bodhisattva who thus well understands the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) knows these six bases, they have already been able to manifest vast powers such as the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) in past lives, will be able to manifest them in future lives, and are currently able to manifest them in the present life.

The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught that within the realm of nirvana without remainder, all sensations (*vedanā*) are extinguished without remainder and forever; which sensations are those that are extinguished therein?"

The commentary states: This is the eighteenth section from here on. Regarding the gate of the cessation of sensation within the state of nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), there are two parts:

first the question, and second the answer. This constitutes the interrogation. The text has three sections: first, the presentation of the teaching that is the subject of the inquiry; second, the actual phrasing of the question;
and third, [the conclusion], as should be understood according to the sūtra.
"Good son, to speak in brief, there are two kinds of feeling that are extinguished forever without remainder.
[Commentary]: From here below is the second section, the Tathāgata’s formal exposition. Within this, there are two parts; first is the formal exposition based on the question.

This is followed by the concluding summary at the end. The explanation consists of two parts: first, the brief answer indicating the number; second, the detailed explanation through question and answer.
This is the brief answer.
What are these two?
The commentary states: From here below is the second section, a detailed explanation through question and answer. First the question, then the answer. This is the question:
first, the experience of the heavy burden (*dausthulya*) that serves as the basis; second, the experience of the objective sphere which is its fruit.
The commentary states: From here below follows the detailed explanation. This consists of two parts: first, the formal explanation of the various feelings;

second, the explanation of their permanent cessation, beginning with the phrase "as for the remainder. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, a brief response regarding the two types of feeling; second, a sequential and specific explanation.
This is the first [point]. Second is the specific characteristic of sensation (*vedanā*). Various explanations differ. One says:

"Sensation of the heavy burden of the basis" refers to contaminated sensation (*sāsrava-vedanā*) that arises in dependence upon the six sense-faculties; it is named after its faculties and is thus called the "basis.

Because it is accompanied by the heavy burden of the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), it is termed the "sensation of the heavy burden of the basis. As for "sensation of the objective sphere which is its fruit":
This refers to the six external objects. Because they are produced by the force drawn forth from the six internal faculties, the six objective spheres are called their "fruits.
Since this experience of the objective spheres arises conditioned by those [faculties], it is called "experience of the fruit-spheres of those. In reality, there are two [types].
The essence of sensation (*vedanā*) is without differentiation; it is only according to the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) that two types of sensation are explained figuratively.

One interpretation states: "Sensation as the heavy burden (*dausthulya*) of the basis" refers to sensation as seeds (*bīja-vedanā*); "sensation as the object which is its fruit" refers to sensation as manifest activity (*samudācāra-vedanā*).

This means that contaminated seeds (*sāsrava-bīja*) serve as the basis for manifest fruits, or that they are accompanied by the heavy burden of the seeds of the two obstacles (*dvi-āvaraṇa*). Therefore, it is so called.

The "basis" refers to coarse sensation (*audārika-vedanā*). If it refers to manifest sensation (*samudācāra-vedanā*), because it is produced by the sensation of seeds (*bīja-vedanā*), it is called "the sensation of its resultant object. One interpretation states:

the "basis of coarse dysfunction (*dausthulya*)" refers to all tainted sensations (*sāsrava-vedanā*) that depend upon the six internal sense bases (*ādhyātmika-ṣaḍāyatana*), taking as their objects the six sense bases and their respective domains within the internal body;
