these are established based on the supporting sense organs (*indriya*) and the associated mental factors (*dharma*).
Regarding its name: because it relies upon the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), or because it is accompanied by the seeds of the two hindrances and their coarse latencies (*dauṣṭhulya*).

As for that which experiences the objects resulting from those [faculties], this refers to the six external objects; they serve as the dominant results (*adhipati-phala*) for the six sense faculties. Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"Due to the power of the experience of the six faculties, such as the eye, the six objects arise. This second type of feeling relies upon the six internal sense faculties.

Because it takes the six external objects as its conditions and derives its name from those objects, it is called "the feeling of the objective sphere" (*viṣaya-vedanā*), which refers to the feeling of the objective sphere among the twelve links of dependent origination, alongside the feeling of self-nature (*svabhāva-vedanā*). Although there are three such explanations, for now we shall rely on the third.
It should be known that there are four kinds of the experience of the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the basis (*āśraya*).

The commentary states: This is the second section in sequence, providing a detailed explanation. Within this, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the experience of the heaviness of the basis;
second, the explanation of the experience of the objective sphere (*viṣaya*), which is its fruit. Regarding the former, there are three sections: first, the heading indicating the number; next...
The names are listed according to their numerical order, and they will subsequently be explained again in response to difficulties; this is the first [section].

First, the sensation that is the support for the material (rūpa); second, the sensation that is the support for the immaterial (arūpa); third, the sensation of the heavy burden (dausthulya) when the fruit has already been fully realized;
fourth, the sensation of the heavy burden when the fruit has not yet been fully realized.

The commentary states: Second, the names are listed according to their numerical order. However, regarding these four types of sensation (*vedanā*), there are differing explanations, of which there are three traditions.
The first master’s explanation is largely the same as that of the third master; therefore, it will not be recounted separately. The second master previously stated:
"Sensation with a material basis refers to the seeds of sensation in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); sensation without a material basis refers to..."

This refers to the seeds of feeling belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). "Coarse and heavy feeling" (*dauṣṭhulya-vedanā*) whose fruit has already matured refers to the seeds that are currently yielding their fruit.
"Coarse and heavy feeling" whose fruit has not yet matured refers to the seeds of feeling that have not yet yielded their fruit. According to one interpretation:

Feeling that has a material basis refers to feeling associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness. Feeling that lacks a material basis refers to feeling associated with the mental consciousness.
These constitute the two types of feeling: bodily and mental. Feeling whose fruit is already fully matured...
This refers to the present resultant feeling produced by past ignorance, formations, and so forth.

Regarding "feeling whose result is not yet fully realized," this refers to the causal feeling associated with karma and afflictions that is capable of inducing future results. Although there are various explanations, the third is correct, as it accords with the literal meaning of the text.
"Experiencing when the fruit has already matured" refers to present experiencing. "Experiencing when the fruit has not yet matured" refers to future causal experiencing.
The commentary states: this third point is a re-explanation following a further objection; it means that the first [type] is the experiencing of the present fruit obtained from past karma.
The latter refers to the feeling associated with the karma and afflictions that can induce future maturation (*vipāka*);
as it is the cause for future results, it is called "feeling as the cause for the future.
Briefly stated, there are four types of feeling regarding those resultant objects.
The commentary states: From here below is the second section, which explains the experience of those resultant objects. This section consists of two parts:
first, the presentation of the headings and the enumeration; second, the listing of the names according to that enumeration. This is the first part.
First, the appropriation of the basis; second, the appropriation of requisites; third, the appropriation of enjoyment; and fourth, the appropriation of attachment. The commentary states:
the second [section] enumerates the names according to their number. Regarding these four types of appropriation, various explanations differ.
One school asserts that all four of these appropriations are active manifestations (*samudācāra*); as for their distinctions, there are four kinds. The first is the appropriation of the basis.
These are: first, the experience conditioned by the receptacle world; second, the experience of requisites, which refers to the experience conditioned by the tools of livelihood;

third, the experience of enjoyment, which refers to the direct experience of enjoying clothing, food, and so forth—these three being experiences conditioned by present objects; and fourth, the experience of longing attachment.

This refers to the feelings (*vedanā*) produced by taking as objects the three preceding realms of the past. One interpretation states: first, the feeling based on support (*āśraya-vedanā*), which is the feeling that takes the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) as its object;
second, the feeling of requisites (*pariṣkāra-vedanā*), which refers to the feeling that takes clothing, medicine, and so forth as its objects;

third, the feeling of enjoyment (*upabhoga-vedanā*), which is the combined description of both the feelings of support and requisites; fourth, the feeling of attachment (*anurāga-vedanā*), which refers to looking back with longing toward wealth and possessions.
It is "reception. One explanation states that they follow this sequence: first, one takes the vessel-world as the object; next, clothing, medicine, and so forth;
next, the present; and finally, the past.
Within the realm of nirvana with remainder, all fruitional sensations that have not yet reached fulfillment are extinguished;
one experiences the sensation born of contact through clear wisdom (*vidyā-saṃsparśaja-vedanā*), which is the antidote to those [fruitional sensations], and this experience is shared [with others].

Alternatively, when those fruitions have already reached fulfillment, both types of sensation are entirely extinguished, and one experiences only the sensation born of contact through clear wisdom in the present.

The commentary states: From here below is the second section, which explains its permanent cessation (*parinirvāṇa*). This contains two parts: first, the explanation of the permanent cessation with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-parinirvāṇa*);
second, the explanation of the permanent cessation without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-parinirvāṇa*). This is the first part. It explains this passage through two successive methods.
Various explanations differ on this point. One school says: "Regarding the experience when the fruit has not yet been fully realized, all [previous] experiences have already ceased.
This means that at the moment of the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*), one has already severed and extinguished future karmic fruits, afflictions (*kleśa*), and their associated experiences.

As for the experience arising from the contact of clear wisdom (*vidyā-sparśa*) which serves as the antidote to those [afflictions], it refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) experience associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), which serve as the antidotes to those karmas and afflictions.

It is "appropriation" (*upādāna*). Regarding "appropriation as shared": this refers to the appropriation of the shared vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), which is what the Sūtra describes as "appropriation as support" (*āśraya-upādāna*).
It is stated briefly without mentioning the two other types of appropriation—appropriation of resources (*pariṣkāra-upādāna*) and appropriation of utilization (*paribhoga-upādāna*).

This is because appropriation characterized by longing (*anunaya-upādāna*) is excluded, as it is associated with craving (*rāga*). Alternatively, regarding "appropriation whose fruit has already been fully realized": this is due to...

Within the experience that has already been fully perfected, there is both that which is accompanied by heaviness (*dausthulya*) and that which is free from heaviness. Within the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there is only experience free from heaviness;

therefore, the word "or" is used. [The text] briefly omits mention of the experience that takes the form-aggregate as its basis and the experience that takes the formless-aggregate as its basis, because such experiences still arise in one beyond training.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "both types of experience have all ceased," this refers to the basis (*āśraya*).

The sensations of heaviness and rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*), as well as the sensations of their resultant objects, have all been severed. Only the sensation born of contact with clarity (*vidyā-saṃsparśaja-vedanā*) is currently experienced.
According to this, all sensations belonging to one whose outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya*) are termed "sensations born of contact with clarity. One [teacher] says: [end of quote].

"Regarding 'when the fruit is not yet fully accomplished, all sensations have already been extinguished': this refers to the time when one possesses the remainder of the basis (*sopadhiśeṣa*), at which point one is able to extinguish the seeds of future sensations, such that they are all severed.
Regarding 'experiencing the sensation born from contact with the light that is its antidote':

this refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) sensation of the path that serves as the antidote. Regarding 'experiencing that which is co-existent': this refers to the sensation regarding the objective sphere (*viṣaya*) of that fruit. Or..."
Furthermore, regarding those who have already attained the fulfillment of that fruit, this refers to the experience of receiving [results] currently manifesting and presently being given.
This is based on those who are still far from entering the remainderless [nirvāṇa]. Within the state of having a remainder (sopadhiśeṣa), these three types of feeling are fully present.

As for the statement that "the two kinds of feeling have all been extinguished, and one only experiences the feeling born of contact with clarity," this is based on those who are about to enter [the remainderless state].
At the time of the nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*), one employs only uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mind, because it takes as its object that which is without remainder.

Subsequently, when cessation occurs, one experiences the shared feeling (*sahabhū-vedanā*) and the fully matured feeling that is its fruit; thus, only uncontaminated feeling remains. Therefore, it is said:

"Furthermore, when both kinds of feeling have entirely ceased, there is only feeling born of contact with clarity (*vidyā-saṃsparśaja-vedanā*). This refers to contact with clarity being exclusively uncontaminated.
It is explained in this way. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that this passage represents two masters’ distinct explanations.
The former school states that within the state of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder), only the causes for future feeling are extinguished, while three types of feeling remain;

this is because they maintain that only untainted (*anāsrava*) feeling is considered "feeling born of clear contact" (*vidyā-saṃsparśaja-vedanā*), and thus it is said that "three feelings exist. The intention of the second master’s explanation is that [in the state] of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)...

All sensations present within the human body—comprising both those associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those free from outflows (*anāsrava*)—are collectively termed "sensations born of contact through clarity" (*vidyā-saṃsparśaja-vedanā*).
It is based on this meaning that it is said: "In the state of having a remainder of support (*sa-upadhiśeṣa*), two kinds of sensation have all been extinguished.

These are: first, the sensation of the coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the aforementioned basis; and second, the sensation of the objects which are its fruit. When these two types of sensation have all been extinguished, there remains only...

The feeling produced by contact with clear knowledge (*vidyā-saṃsparśaja-vedanā*) exists in one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). One explanation states that there are two successive stages. Regarding the intent of the first stage:

among the eight types of feeling, at the time of *nirvāṇa-with-remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), one experiences only the cessation of those feelings whose fruit has not yet been fully realized, because they are associated with karma;

alternatively, one experiences them as the feeling produced by contact with clear knowledge which serves as their antidote, thereby further attaining untainted (*anāsrava*) feeling. Thus, one experiences [feeling].

"Common to all" means that among the eight types of feeling, excluding those that are not yet fulfilled and those whose fruits are already fulfilled, the remaining six feelings are common to both ordinary persons and noble ones;
therefore, they are called "common. Question: How can one beyond training (aśaikṣa) possess feelings of attachment?

Answer: There are two kinds of attachment: first, craving, which an Arhat has already eliminated; second, that which is non-defiled (akliṣṭa). It is this latter kind that exists for one beyond training.
The association with desire also exists in Arhats; therefore, it is said to be "shared.

Alternatively, one might say that only the five feelings are shared, because those associated with attachment and longing are excluded due to their association with greed and because they are easily understood; thus, they are omitted from the explanation.
Alternatively, it may be that the recipient has already fully realized that fruit. This clarifies that within the body of an Arhat, there is the experience of seeing the present fruit.
Question: Why is this experience not called "shared"? Explanation: In reality, it is indeed shared.
In order to contrast it with the previously unfulfilled feelings, there is a difference regarding their existence or non-existence; therefore, they are explained separately.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "both types of feeling have all ceased, and one only experiences present feeling born of clear contact," the Commentary provides two interpretations.
The first says: because all feelings within the body of an Arhat are free from latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), they are called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). This was stated previously.

Regarding the eight feelings (*vedanā*), because they are exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*), how can it be said that all are without-outflows (*anāsrava*)? As for the statement regarding "two kinds," this refers to the two fundamental feelings previously mentioned, which subsume the eight feelings.
One explanation states: when entering the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), the eight feelings are extinguished;

yet, it is said that there are feelings without-outflows because, upon entering the mindless attainments, one retreats from the preparatory stages (*prayoga*), and thus [the presence of] non-extinction is spoken of as a metaphorical designation (*prajñapti*). Based on this...
It is indeed extinguished.
At the time of parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu), this too is eternally extinguished.

The commentary states: the second [point] clarifies eternal extinction without remainder; that is to say, within the state of nirvana without remainder, this clarifies that contact gives rise to sensation.
They are also extinguished. Alternatively, as stated above, the co-existent sensations and so forth are also extinguished.
Therefore, it is said that within the realm of nirvana without remainder, all sensations are extinguished without remainder and forever.
The commentary states: The second summary should be understood as follows.
At that time, after the Blessed One had spoken these words, he again addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family, you have now skillfully inquired, relying upon the perfectly complete and most utterly pure path of sublime yoga."
“Tathāgata, you have already attained certainty and supreme skill in yoga.
The commentary states: Within the extensive prose exposition, there are two major divisions. First, the detailed analysis of the characteristics of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;

second, the concluding praise and exhortation to study. The preceding section has already explained the characteristics of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. From here on is the second part: the conclusion, praise, and exhortation.

Regarding "learning," there are three parts within it: first, praising the benefit of the inquiry; second, from "I have already [taught] for you" onwards, revealing that the Buddha speaks in common with them;
and third, from "O sons of good family" onwards, exhorting beings to practice and learn. These correspond to the first two [sections], as can be understood from the sutra.
I have already proclaimed for you the complete and most perfectly pure path of sublime yoga.
All those who were, will be, or are currently the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the past, future, and present have taught, or will teach, it in exactly this same way.
The commentary states: This reveals that the Buddha teaches in common with others. That is to say, the sublime path of śamatha and vipaśyanā which I have taught was not taught by me alone;
all Buddhas of the three periods of time teach this same meaning.
"O sons of good family, whether they be sons or daughters of good family, all should rely upon this courageous diligence and practice it correctly.
The commentary states: The fourth [section] encourages beings to practice and study, as can be understood from the sutra.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
[The] commentary says: Within this chapter, there are two main divisions: first, the explanation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; second, the practice and upholding according to the teaching.
Within the formal exposition, there are two main divisions: first, the prose; second, the reiterative verses. Alternatively, this single chapter may be divided into three parts:
first, the extensive explanation in prose; second, the reiterative explanation in verse; and third, the practice in accordance with the teaching.
This present section is the second, the reiterative explanation in verse. Within it, there are two parts: first, the introductory verses; second, the [reiterative] verses...
This is repeated; this is the first [section].
Within the provisional establishment of yoga regarding phenomena, if one acts with negligence, one loses the great purpose.
By relying upon these phenomena and yoga, if one practices correctly, one attains great awakening.
The commentary states: From this point forward, the verses are cited for formal explanation. There are five lines of verse, which are divided into five sections.

The first section consists of one verse, which clarifies the gains and losses regarding the conformity and opposition of the yoga of phenomena (*dharmayoga*). The second section consists of one line of verse, which clarifies that there are gains and losses to be had.

Next, there is one verse that reveals the virtue of being free from defilement through miraculous birth (*upapāduka*). Next, there is one verse concerning the loss incurred when wishing to preach the Dharma.

Next, there is one verse on abandoning attachment to gain while benefiting sentient beings. This is the first [section], which clarifies the gains and losses regarding compliance and opposition based on the yoga of relying upon the Dharma;
that is to say, the provisional establishment of dharmas as taught within the twelvefold division of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).
In the yoga of the path of śamatha and vipaśyanā, if one acts with negligence, one loses the great benefit and the fruit of great nirvāṇa.
If one relies upon this teaching and practices correctly by relying on śamatha and vipaśyanā, one attains great bodhi.
Seeing something to be attained and seeking to escape from difficulty— if one considers such a view to be the attainment of the Dharma, Maitreya,
that person is as far from yoga as the great earth is from space.

The commentary states: The second [point] clarifies the faults of what is apprehended. That is to say, when relying on meditation and contemplation to investigate, one perceives something that is apprehended.
If one clings to this perception as the dharma that is apprehended, believing it will liberate one from the perils of birth and death, one is far removed from yoga.
It is like the relationship between the great earth and space. Thus, the *Saṃghāṭasūtra* says: "If one discriminates all dharmas with the mind, they are all erroneous."
One does not use the mind to discriminate that all phenomena are correct. According to the twenty-fifth fascicle of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there is a verse which says:
"The distance between space and the great earth is vast; The distance between this shore and the other shore of the ocean is likewise vast."
The places where the sun rises and sets are far apart; between the True Dharma and the false Dharma, the distance is even further.
In this sutra, only the first metaphor is cited.

To benefit sentient beings with steadfast resolve yet fail to act, while having already awakened and diligently practicing for the sake of beings—only a wise person would do such a thing until the end of the kalpa.
[He] attains the supreme joy of detachment.
The commentary states: This is the third quality of detachment through transformational birth (*nirmāṇa*).

It means that while Bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings with firm great compassion, they do not form such thoughts as "I am the one who benefits" or "those are the ones being benefited. There is neither subject nor object.
Having realized this principle, one is able to diligently cultivate deeds that benefit sentient beings until the end of the kalpas, thereby attaining the supreme joy and bliss free from defilement.
Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "The contemplative practice of a bodhisattva involves grasping things according to their phenomena and grasping them according to their suchness (tathatā).
One does not form the thought: 'This suchness is of such a kind,' for these categories cannot be fully described."
If a person preaches the Dharma out of desire, they are said to have abandoned desire only to take it up again.
Having obtained the priceless jewel of the Dharma, the fool instead wanders about begging.
The commentary states: The fourth [point] explains the fault of preaching the Dharma out of desire.

If a person preaches the Dharma for others in order to seek fame and gain, this is called "discarding desire only to take up desire again. Speaking of the Dharma with the mouth is called "discarding desire," yet craving fame and profit in the mind is called "taking up desire again.
As stated in the *Śata-śāstra*, the verse censuring impure observance of the precepts says:
Like two rams butting heads, advancing only to retreat again—so too is the matter of your upholding the precepts for the sake of desire.
Though the body may uphold the precepts, the mind is dragged away by desire;
such an action is impure, so what is the use of these precepts?
In this way, such foolish people obtain such priceless jewels of the Dharma, yet they do not seek unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, but instead seek worldly fame and profit.
It is like a foolish person of the world who obtains a priceless jewel but instead goes about begging.
Furthermore, it is explained that if a person, out of desire, preaches the Dharma while seeking emptiness, they are said to abandon existence and return [to the mundane].

Furthermore, they are attached to emptiness. These foolish people, having obtained such priceless jewels of the Dharma, fail to understand the intent of the teaching and instead give rise to an attachment to emptiness.
They remain attached to contention, clamor, and frivolous proliferation; they ought to abandon these and exert supreme diligence in order to deliver all devas and the world.
"In this yoga, you should train. The commentary states:
This is the fifth virtue, which consists of abandoning attachment while benefiting sentient beings. One should relinquish contentious debate, worldly clamor, and frivolous proliferation;
instead, one should arouse supreme, courageous diligence and diligently cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* in order to deliver the world.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, within this Dharma-gate of the Profound Secrets, what should this teaching be named? How should I uphold it?"

The commentary states: From this point downward is the third section, "Receiving and Upholding According to the Teaching. This section has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. Here, Maitreya requests the Tathāgata to speak.
There are two intentions behind his questions: first, to ask for the name of the teaching; second, to ask about its reception and upholding.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: "Good son, this is called the teaching of the definitive meaning of yoga.
You should uphold this teaching of the definitive meaning of yoga."

The commentary states: From this point downward is the second section, which provides the formal answers to the questions. This section contains two parts: first, the formal answers to the two questions;
second, following the phrase "this yoga," a praise of the benefits of the teaching. This is the first part.
When this definitive teaching on yoga was being expounded, within that great assembly, six hundred thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Three hundred thousand śrāvakas became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
One hundred and fifty thousand śrāvakas attained the exhaustion of all outflows, and their minds were liberated.
Seventy-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the vast yoga of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
The commentary states: This is the second praise of the excellence of the teaching, which has four aspects; the first is the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Second, one attains the purity of the Dharma-eye by distancing oneself from dust and leaving behind defilement. Third, with all outflows (*āsrava*) forever exhausted, the mind attains liberation.
These three benefits have already been explained as before. Fourth, one obtains the vast *yogamanasikāra*. The emptiness of both persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*) is termed "vast.
As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the two paths of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are termed "yoga. As in the *Ṣaḍdharmasūtra*...

The *Dharmasthāna-sūtra* states that when a bodhisattva attains the mental engagement (*manasikāra*) of calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) focused on the two types of emptiness, it is therefore called the "mental engagement of vast yoga.

According to the forty-sixth [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, one should know that there are five great fruits and benefits when Buddhas and bodhisattvas preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings: first, a certain class of sentient beings becomes distant from the dust [of afflictions].
First, they were freed from defilement and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Second, a class of sentient beings attained the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
Third, a class of sentient beings gave rise to the mind of right aspiration for unsurpassed enlightenment.

Fourth, a class of sentient beings realized the most supreme Dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*) of a bodhisattva. Fifth, a class of sentient beings received, upheld, recited, and practiced the correct conduct.
Through successive skillful means, he causes the eye of the True Dharma to abide for a long time without perishing.

According to the *Vyūha* (The Ornament), chapter twelve, when a bodhisattva preaches the Dharma, they are able to obtain eight fruits. First, among those who listen to the Dharma, some may resolve to attain bodhicitta.

Second, some attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Third, some, regarding all phenomena, become free from dust and free from defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye;
this is said to be subsumed under the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). Fourth, some attain the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*).

Fifth, they cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time, because through this correct teaching, it is received and upheld in succession. Sixth, they cause those who have not yet studied the meaning to study the meaning. Seventh...

Those who have not yet severed their doubts are caused to sever them; those who have already severed their doubts are caused to experience the great flavor of the excellent Dharma without obstruction.
In this sutra, there are four benefits for the purpose of yoga practice: they serve as the meaning of the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Commentary on the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra, Scroll Eight (Sūtra Text Four).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Yuance of Ximing Monastery.
The Seventh Chapter: The Perfection of the Grounds (Bhūmi-pāramitā).

Alternatively, because śamatha and vipaśyanā are concise, they were explained first; because the perfections arising from the grounds are extensive, they are explained later. The purpose for their inclusion has already been stated;
now, the explanation shall follow.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, there are ten stages of the bodhisattva, namely:

the Stage of Utmost Joy, the Stage of Freedom from Defilement, the Stage of Radiant Light, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom, the Stage of Supreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Stage of Manifestation, the Stage of Far-Reaching Travel, the Stage of Immovability, the Stage of Excellent Wisdom, and the Stage of the Dharma Cloud.
Furthermore, it is said that the Stage of the Buddha constitutes the tenth."
1. Regarding these stages (*bhūmi*), by how many types of meanings of purification are they subsumed?

The commentary states: the third [section] provides the formal explanation according to the text. Within this chapter, there are two major divisions: first, the section of the formal exposition through question and answer;
second, from "At that time, Avalokiteśvara... onwards, the section on receiving and upholding the teaching. Within the former, there are two [subdivisions].
First, there is an extensive explanation in prose; subsequently, there is a concise statement in verse. Alternatively, this chapter may be divided into three parts:

first, an extensive explanation in prose; second, a concise statement in verse; and third, the practice in accordance with the teaching. Although there are these two views, we shall follow the former explanation for now.
Within the preceding prose section, it is further divided into four parts: first, an extensive clarification of the various stages (*bhūmi*); second, the contemplation of oneself...
The Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha again, saying: "World-Honored One, how many kinds of matters are there that these bodhisattvas should study?
Below this, the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) are explained in detail. Then, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha again, saying:

"World-Honored One, regarding the latent tendencies of afflictions (*kleśānuśaya*) within these stages (*bhūmi*)," below which he specifically explains the obstacles to be remedied by the perfections arising in dependence upon each stage.
Fourth, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said, 'If one follows the Śrāvaka vehicle...
This clarifies the Buddha’s intention in teaching the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

The reason for explaining it in four sections is that one relies upon the stages (*bhūmi*) to give rise to the perfections (*pāramitā*), and by relying upon the perfections, one eliminates obstacles; thus, one attains the fruit of the One Vehicle. Therefore, four sections are taught. Regarding the explanation of the stages:
The middle section is further divided into six parts: first, the classification of the stages (*bhūmi*) according to the four kinds of purity and the eleven factors;
second, the explanation of the etymological meanings of the stage names; third, the classification of the stages according to the twenty-two types of ignorance (*moha*);

fourth, the classification of the stages according to the eight kinds of excellence; fifth, the classification of the stages according to superior rebirths; and sixth, the classification of the stages according to the three vows.
Regarding the first section: first there is the request, and then the teaching. This constitutes the first inquiry by the Bodhisattva.
The text has three parts: first, the clarification of the interlocutors; second, from "As the Buddha... onwards, the presentation of the teaching requested; and third, from "In this way... onwards...
This is the formal introduction of the inquiry. The term "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva" is the name of the bodhisattva who poses the question.

It means that this bodhisattva internally possesses wisdom and compassion, and externally observes the three karmas; without exerting effort, he acts with spontaneous mastery. He is called Avalokiteśvara because he observes with sovereignty.
Alternatively, the name is established based on his wisdom and its object. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara dwells in the Great [Compassion]..."
The Gate of Compassion (*karuṇā-mukha*). The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The subtle power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom can rescue the world from suffering.

The *Anantamukhasādhaka-sūtra* calls him Avalokitasvara. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* calls him Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. The *Samantabhadraprabhāsa-sūtra* calls him Samantaprasādika-prabhāsa-svara Bodhisattva. The *Ānanda-mukha-dhāraṇī-sūtra* calls him Sarvadarśin-viśvāśvāsaka Bodhisattva.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* calls him Avalokita-svara Bodhisattva. The *Niyata-dhāraṇī-sūtra* calls him Prabhāsa-svara Tathāgata. The *Buddhadūṣaka-sūtra* calls him Avalokiteśvara Tathāgata. The *Avalokiteśvara-samādhi-sūtra* states: "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva has already attained Buddhahood in the past; his name is Dharmodgata."
The *Tathāgata-avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* states: "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva shall succeed Maitreya Buddha, receiving the name *Samantaprabhā-guṇa-parvatarāja-buddha*.

Next, regarding the phrase "as taught by the Buddha" and so forth, this refers to the teachings posed for inquiry, namely the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and others, which fully explain the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as well as the stage of the Tathāgata (*tathāgatabhūmi*).
Regarding the phrase "these stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth," this is the formal statement of the inquiry. There are two intentions in the question:
first, to ask how many types among the four purities are subsumed within these ten stages; second, to ask how many of the eleven divisions are subsumed therein.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "Good son, you should know that the four kinds of purity of the stages are subsumed within eleven divisions.
Commentary: From this point downward is the second section, the Tathāgata’s formal exposition. Within this, there are two parts. First is the statement of the thesis and the brief response.
The subsequent questions and answers provide a detailed explanation; this is the first [section].
As for the question, "What are the four kinds of purity that encompass all the stages (*bhūmi*)?
the commentary states: from here below is the second section, consisting of questions and answers with a detailed explanation. This contains two parts; the first explains the four kinds of purity.
Purity can encompass all the stages (*bhūmi*). How is it that they are called "lower"? This clarifies that the eleven divisions can encompass all the stages.
First, the question is posed; subsequently, the answer follows. This, then, is the question.
That is to say, the purity of superior intention (*adhyāśaya-viśuddhi*) subsumes the first stage; the purity of superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-viśuddhi*) subsumes the second stage;

the purity of superior mind (*adhicitta-viśuddhi*) subsumes the third stage; and the purity of superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā-viśuddhi*), because it becomes increasingly sublime in each successive stage, should be understood to subsume everything from the fourth stage up to the Buddha-stage.
The commentary says: From here below is the second part, the formal response. This consists of two sections: first, the explanation; second, the conclusion. This is the explanation.

It means that there are four kinds of purity, as taught in the sūtra. According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 79, these are called the "four abodes," which correspond exactly to the four kinds of purity in this sūtra. As for the term "superior intention" (*adhyāśaya*):
Regarding "purity being subsumed within the first stage": *āśaya* in the Sanskrit term *brahma-āśaya* is translated here as "intention" (*yìlè*).

There are differing views among various teachings concerning the essential nature of this intention. According to the Liang Dynasty commentary, its essence is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). Thus, the ninth [chapter] states:

Joyful faith (*śraddhā*) is none other than non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). Furthermore, the eleventh [chapter] states that non-conceptual wisdom is the pure mental activity (*manas-karma*).
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Chapter Forty-seven, its nature is resolute conviction (*adhimukti*). Therefore, the "Chapter on Aspiration" (*Adhimukti-paṭala*) says:

"With pure faith as the precursor and the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) as the precursor, one possesses resolute conviction regarding all the Buddha-dharmas; this is the seal of understanding."

This is definitive; it is called the bodhisattva’s *adhyāśaya* (resolute intention). According to the seventh chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, its essence consists of faith (*śraddhā*) and aspiration (*chanda*).
Thus, that treatise states: "The essence of *adhyāśaya* consists of faith and aspiration. Vasubandhu’s commentary on the seventh chapter likewise agrees with Asvabhāva; thus, that treatise states:
"The intrinsic nature of *adhyāśaya* refers to aspiration (*chanda*) and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*). "Aspiration" (*chanda*) means seeking (*prārthanā*).

"Faith" (*śraddhā*) is defined as "resolute conviction" (*adhimukti*). The *Mahāvyutpatti* is likewise. Furthermore, the ninth fascicle of the *Liang* translation of the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya* states:

"Within the authentic teaching, the mind is resolved and free from doubt; therefore, it is called 'faith. Regarding the dharmas thus believed, one seeks and desires to practice them; therefore, it is called 'delight' (*ruci*).
However, regarding the specific categories and numbers of these types of mental delight, they are as set forth in the forty-eighth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, where there are ten."

Regarding the *āśaya* (intentional disposition), that treatise states: "If Bodhisattvas, having previously attained purity of intentional disposition through ten kinds of mental dispositions while in the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*), what are these ten?
First, they maintain a disposition free from deception toward all teachers, those worthy of respect, and fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Second, they possess patience and gentleness toward fellow Bodhisattvas who practice the same Dharma..."

1. The intentionality of being gentle and easy to dwell with; 2. The intentionality of subduing all afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the activities of Māra, such that the mind operates with mastery; 3.

The intentionality of perceiving the profound faults of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*); 4. The intentionality of perceiving the profound benefits of great parinirvāṇa; 5. Regarding all [phenomena]...
7) The intention of constantly and diligently practicing the excellent and sublime Dharma of Bodhi; 8) The intention of delighting in seclusion for the sake of being compliant with that practice;
9) The intention of having no attachment or longing for worldly positions of influence, gain, or honor associated with defilement;
10) The intention of distancing oneself from the Lesser Vehicle and proceeding toward the realization of the Great Vehicle.
Joy. Tenth is the intention to bring about all benefit and welfare for all sentient beings.
Thus, by relying upon these ten kinds of non-erroneous intentions (*āśaya*), one proceeds; therefore, it is called "purity of intention.
If analyzed in detail, there are fifteen types of intention, as found in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 47. If based on [the perspective of] the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)...
According to the root treatise, the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) has eight characteristics: 1. By way of the provisions (*sambhāra*):
this refers to the thorough cultivation of the two provisions of merit and wisdom on the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryā-bhūmi*). 2. By way of endurance (*kṣānti*):

this refers to attaining the supreme patience in discerning the Dharma (*dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*), which is either the "superior patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) or the "highest mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*). 3. By way of the object (*ālambana*): this refers to taking as one's object the profound and extensive sublime teachings of the Mahāyāna. 4. By way of activity... [text continues]

1. By way of mental attention (*manasikāra*): that is to say, the realization that all phenomena are merely conceptual constructions; this is called mental attention. 2. By way of the five antidotes (*pratipakṣa*):

that is to say, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). 3. By way of its essential nature (*svabhāva*): that is to say, this aspiration has faith (*śraddhā*) and desire (*chanda*) as its essential nature.
4. By way of auspicious signs (*nimitta*): that is to say, those on the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*) and those on the grounds themselves who see the Buddhas within the womb.
This is a portentous sign. Because there are eight benefits, it means that one realizes awakening is near, as it can be attained without difficulty.
A detailed analysis is provided in three verses with their prose commentary, as fully explained therein.

If one follows the root text relied upon by Vasubandhu—which contains the phrase "because of the removal of the lower [obstacles] through their antidotes"—the statement that "superior morality subsumes two stages" means:
The second stage is the distancing from all subtle stains of transgression. Abiding in this stage, one is fully endowed with natural morality (*prakṛti-śīla*);
even the most minute unwholesome karma shall no longer manifest. Through this purity of morality, the second stage is subsumed.
For a detailed analysis, see the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 48. It is said that the purity of the superior mind (*adhi-citta-viśuddhi*) subsumes the third stage.
This refers to what is stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (48):

"In this stage, one is able to attain the four mundane dhyānas, the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and dwells fully established therein.
Having remained there for a long time, one again relinquishes those dhyānas and other attainments, and returns to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) for the sake of sentient beings."
It is capable of performing beneficial purposes, as explained in detail therein. It continues until it says: "Because the internal mind is pure, it can emit radiance;
therefore, it is called the 'Abiding in the Higher Mind' (*adhicitta-vihāra*). For this reason, the purity of the higher mind subsumes the third stage (*bhūmi*).
This is explained extensively in the forty-eighth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi*. As for the phrase "the purity of the higher wisdom," it begins from the fourth [stage].
"From the stage of the [Bodhisattva] grounds up to the Buddha ground" refers to the higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) that encompasses the final eight stages.

This is because, from the fourth stage onward, the various gateways of wisdom become increasingly superior and sublime in each successive stage. Specifically, the fourth stage is the dwelling of higher wisdom associated with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*);

the fifth stage is the dwelling of higher wisdom associated with the truths (*satya*); and the sixth stage is the dwelling of higher wisdom associated with dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

One should abide in the stage of superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā-vihāra*). The seventh is the stage of signlessness with application (*sābhoga-nirnimitta-vihāra*). The eighth is the stage of signlessness without application (*anābhoga-nirnimitta-vihāra*).
The ninth is the stage of the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*). The tenth is the stage of the most supreme and perfected bodhisattva (*parama-samudāgata-bodhisattva-vihāra*).
The eleventh is the stage of the Tathāgata (*tathāgata-vihāra*). These are explained in detail in the forty-eighth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi*. Question: How is it known that the...

The four stages above are all [characterized by] wisdom (*prajñā*). Answer: As listed previously in the seventy-ninth [section], among the four types of abodes, the fourth is called the Abode of Higher Wisdom (*adhiprajñā-vihāra*).
Therefore, it is known that from this point upward, the stages are distinguished in terms of wisdom.
"Good son, you should know that these four kinds of purity universally encompass all the stages (*bhūmi*).
The commentary states: This is the second summary of the connections. That is to say, the four purities are actual virtues, whereas the "stages" are provisional designations.
Thus, this is a case of the real encompassing the provisional.
"What is called the eleventh type of division that encompasses all the stages?
The commentary states: From here on, the second section clarifies how the eleven divisions encompass the eleven stages. This section has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer.
This is the first part, posing the question in accordance with the teaching. Although there are eleven divisions and eleven stages...
The stages (*avasthā*) are not distinct in their divisions, yet they differ in meaning. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"Because it can sustain the meaning of a bodhisattva, it is called a 'ground' (*bhūmi*); because it serves as the sense of a dwelling place for enjoyment, it is called a 'station' (*vihāra*).

The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states: "Delighting in abiding is called 'abiding' (*vihāra*)," as explained at length therein. The commentary explains: "The term 'division' (*bhāga*) signifies the sense of [the ten]... (text fragment). Specifically, the ten...
The first stage (*vihāra*) consists of distinct segments; these are explained as "parts" (*bhāga*) in a figurative sense. As stated in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Chapter on Similes:
"Regarding the 'part' of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*): all dharmas that combine to constitute the first stage are called the 'part' of the first stage.

This refers to the allowance within the thirteen stages (*trayodaśa-vihāra*) that the first three stages constitute the [first] eleven stages. These eleven stages are as described in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Forty-seven states: namely, the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-vihāra*), the stage of practice through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*),

the stage of extreme joy (*pramudita-vihāra*), the stage of superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-vihāra*), the stage of superior mind (*adhicitta-vihāra*), the stage of superior wisdom associated with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya-saṃprayukta-adhiprajñā-vihāra*),

the stage of superior wisdom associated with the truths (*satya-saṃprayukta-adhiprajñā-vihāra*), the stage of superior wisdom associated with dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-saṃprayukta-adhiprajñā-vihāra*), and the signless stage involving application and effort (*sābhisaṃskāra-sābhoga-nirnimitta-vihāra*).

The dwelling of signlessness without application or effort, the dwelling of unimpeded analytical knowledge, the supreme and perfected bodhisattva dwelling, and the Tathāgata dwelling are explained extensively as they appear in those [other] texts.
In this sutra, with the exception of the first two dwellings, it is categorized by name based on eleven dwellings;
therefore, in this context, the stages (*bhūmi*) are subsumed under these categories.

This refers to how Bodhisattvas, having previously on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), have thoroughly cultivated the patience of resolute belief (*adhimukti-kṣānti*) by relying upon the ten types of Dharma-practice.
The commentary states:
From this point downward is the second section, the Tathāgata’s formal exposition. This contains two parts; first, the formal answer based on the inquiry.
The section beginning with "Afterward, the good son" concludes the preceding explanation by way of summary. Within the formal response, eleven sections are explained, constituting eleven parts.
This explanation of the first section subsumes the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). It contains two parts: first, clarifying the stage prior to the ground before entering the first bhūmi;
second, "surpassing the lower," which refers to transcending that pre-ground stage to attain entry into the first bhūmi. This is the first [of those two].

However, regarding the explanation of the two stages, there are two interpretations based on eleven divisions. The first follows the tenth fascicle of the *She dasheng lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) translated during the Liang dynasty;
it explains the eleven stages by way of abandoning the three obstacles and attaining superior merits within each individual stage. As for the distinction:
in the first stage, one abandons three types of obstacles and attains ten merits; subsequently, there are nine stages, each [abandoning obstacles and attaining merits].
One abandons the three obstructions and attains the eight merits.

In the final stage, one abandons three kinds of obstructions and attains seven merits, which serve as the causes and conditions for the perfection of the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), as will be explained in detail below.

One interpretation states that within each stage, the various practices cultivated according to their respective requirements serve as the causes and conditions; for example, in the Stage of Great Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), one cultivates the ten dharma-practices.
And with superior resolve and patience as their causal conditions. Regarding what is called "stages" (*bhūmi*), it refers to the distinct divisions of eleven stages, which are termed "stages.
Concerning the explanation of the first stage, the text is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the causes for practicing subsequent conduct prior to the stage;
second, clarifying the perfection of one's own stage. This is the first part. The phrase "all bodhisattvas" introduces the contemplation.

The "practitioner" (yogācāra) refers to a person (pudgala) who possesses both the innate and acquired dispositions (*gotra*). For one who previously resided in the stage of resolute belief (*adhimukti-bhūmi*), this is the stage of the basis for practice;

that is, within the five stages previously described—namely, the stages of equipment (*sambhāra*), application (*prayoga*), seeing (*darśana*), meditation (*bhāvanā*), and culmination (*niṣṭhā*)—one relies on the first two stages to give rise to profound faith and understanding.
This is called the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*). Therefore, it is included in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
The seventh fascicle states: "Those who have attained profound faith and understanding regarding the various stages (bhūmi) definitively confirm the teachings on those stages as being truly thus.
Regarding 'relying on the ten dharma-practices' and so forth, this means initiating practice according to the stages;

that is, relying on the stage of superior practice (viśeṣa-carī-bhūmi), one initiates the ten right practices. As for these ten right practices, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 74, states: Furthermore..."
Within the Mahāyāna, there are ten dharma-practices that enable bodhisattvas to bring sentient beings to maturity.

What are these ten? They are: writing down, upholding, and making offerings to the teachings of the sūtras and so forth, which are included within the Bodhisattvapiṭaka and are consistent with the Mahāyāna.
Bestowing it as a gift upon others; listening with reverence when others correctly explain it; reciting it oneself for one's own enjoyment; receiving and internalizing it;
having received it, chanting it aloud with a broad voice; explaining and revealing it extensively to others;
dwelling alone in seclusion to contemplate, examine, and enter into the signs of cultivation. Question: Among these ten kinds of Dharma-practice, how many are...?
It can produce the path of vast merit and virtue. Question: How many are the paths of application (*prayoga-mārga*)? Answer: One; namely, the ninth. Question:

How many are the paths that purify obstacles (*āvaraṇa-viśodhana-mārga*)? Answer: One; namely, the tenth. These ten correct practices are explained in detail as previously stated in the fourth fascicle of the record.
Regarding the phrase "because of having excellently cultivated the patience of resolute conviction" (*adhimukti-kṣānti*), this refers to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* translated during the Liang dynasty.

The ten fascicles state: "When a bodhisattva first dwells in the stage of vows and practices (*praṇidhāna-caryā-bhūmi*), they achieve the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) that accords with the ten kinds of dharma-practices.

By virtue of achieving this patient acceptance of vows, they transcend the stage of vows and practices and enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). As for 'vows,' these are the ten great vows."

"Kṣānti" (patience/endurance) refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). The *Zhendi ji* (Record of the True Meaning) states: "In the first stage (*bhūmi*), one attains the patience of the vow for non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and accomplishes the ten great vows.
According to this *Liang-lun* (Treatise of the Liang Dynasty), "superior practice" (*viśeṣa-caryā*) is precisely the non-conceptual wisdom of the first stage.

Now, to explain the intent of the sutra: the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*) are collectively termed "kṣānti"; alternatively, it may refer to the "supreme patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) and the "worldly-first dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

First, the patience of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-kṣānti*). (The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "In the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryā-bhūmi*), one cultivates ten kinds of faith. The *Anupūrvasamudgata-parivarta* states: "Bodhisattvas in the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryā-bhūmi*) possess ten dharma-practices, which are the well-cultivated patiences of bodhisattva liberation.")

Having transcended that stage, they enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from error (*samyaktva-niyāma*). By this cause and condition, those bodhisattvas bring this portion to fulfillment.

The commentary states: This second section, following the preceding one, clarifies the fulfillment of one's own portion (*svabhāga-paripūri*), namely the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), by means of the aforementioned stages of preparatory skillful means (*pūrvopāya-bhūmi*).

By the power of causes and conditions such as the ten dharma-practices (*dharmaparyāya*), one transcends that stage of skillful means (*upāyabhūmi*) and realizes entry into the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), the state of correctness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
For this reason, this portion is perfected. The commentary explains: "Correctness" (*samyaktva*) is precisely the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*);
it is called "correctness" because it is the opposite of "falsehood" (*mithyātva*). [It] severs afflictions (*kleśa*) and harms sentient beings... [as before].

Just as "arising" refers to digested food, so too is it called "arising" [in the sense of being produced]. Because the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*) is able to abandon the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), it is termed "right nature and departure from arising" (*samyaktva-niyāma-avakrānti*).
If one were to analyze this in detail, it has already been explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states:

"Having transcended that stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), one enters the fixed group (*niyāma-gotra*). The *Saṃtati-sūtra* states: "Transcending and ascending, one departs from arising. Although the phrasing differs, the meaning is the same.
The meaning is not contradictory. Regarding the "entry into the state of rightness and departure from birth" (*samyaktva-nyāma*) based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, there are two interpretations.

One states that "birth" refers to having something to be attained, while "the state of rightness and departure from birth" refers to the wisdom of non-attainment. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Sutra 468) says:
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, [one] realizes and enters the Bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth."
"By what is a bodhisattva born? By what is he free from birth? The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All that bodhisattvas apprehend is birth; all that they do not apprehend is freedom from birth. It is explained in detail as therein.
One interpretation states that what is called "birth" (jāti) refers to attachment to the Dharma (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).

Just as undigested food (*pūrvāhāra*) gives rise to affliction, the wisdom that realizes emptiness can extinguish that birth; therefore, it is called "the state of correctness beyond birth" (*samyaktva-nyāma*).
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicle 484, states: "If a bodhisattva practices the six perfections without skillful means, they fall into duality."
While abiding on the stages and not yet having entered the bodhisattva’s state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What dharma is called 'arising'? Subhūti replied: "Arising refers to a bodhisattva’s attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) that accords with them; it is this very attachment to dharmas."
This is called "arising. Just as the arising of undigested food can cause affliction, the removal of this is called "separation from arising.
The full explanation is as stated there. Furthermore, see the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, fascicle 36 (408), and the fourth chapter of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*.

This is also the same as the subsequent explanation. A detailed exposition of that sūtra is found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 31. According to the Liang dynasty commentary (*Dazhidu lun*), in explaining this sūtra:
because of the power of the causes and conditions for severing the three kinds of hindrances and attaining ten kinds of meritorious qualities, the first stage (*bhūmi*) is perfected.
Therefore, the tenth [fascicle] states: "Each stage is able to extinguish three hindrances and each attains superior merit."
Regarding the ability to extinguish the three obstacles on the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*): first is the ignorance of conceptualizing a self in phenomena (*dharmātman-vikalpa-avidyā*);

second is the ignorance of karma leading to the evil realms (*durgati-karma-avidyā*). These two types of ignorance induce the *saṃvṛti-saṃsāra* (conventional saṃsāra) and are termed "heavy burdens" (*dausthulya-vipāka*).

To extinguish these three obstacles, one practices right effort (*samyak-vīrya*). By practicing right effort, once the three obstacles have been extinguished, one attains tenfold perfection. First, one enters into bodhi...
1. The stage of the certainty of the bodhisattva’s right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*). 2. Birth into the family of the Buddhas. 3. A lineage that is beyond reproach or suspicion. 4.
Having already turned away from all worldly conduct, because one is determined never to commit the wrong action of killing. 5.

Having already reached supramundane conduct, because the various stages attained are necessarily untainted (*anāsrava*). 6. Having already attained the suchness of the bodhisattva-dharma, by virtue of attaining [the realization of] self-...
7. Because he has already well established himself in the station of a bodhisattva, due to his realization of the true dharma of a bodhisattva.
8. Because he has already reached equality with the three times, due to his awakening to the suchness (*tathatā*) of the selflessness of all phenomena.
9. Because he is definitively situated within the lineage of the Tathāgatas, as he will certainly attain buddhahood in the future. 10. Because he has already departed from the destruction of the egg.

As for the matter: because the Buddha’s path shatters the husk of ignorance and attains parinirvāṇa externally, the Bodhisattva, upon the first stage (bhūmi), realizes these ten parts by virtue of perceiving the meaning of the all-pervading nature of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). By means of these parts, the first stage is brought to completion.

The commentary states: "The eleven stages each eliminate three obstacles" refers to the twenty-two types of ignorance and the eleven types of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) mentioned in the sutra, as will be explained in detail later.
Yet, regarding subtle transgressions, he has not yet attained correct awareness while they manifest through error;
for this reason, he is still not perfected in this respect.
The commentary states: From here below is the second section, which distinguishes the second division, the Vimalā-bhūmi (Stainless Ground). This contains two parts:

first, it clarifies that the preceding divisions and subsequent practices are not yet fulfilled; second, for the present [division] below, it clarifies that its own division is perfected through cultivation.

This is the first stage. Because at this initial stage there still exists a subtle delusion regarding transgressions committed through error, one has not yet been able to eliminate the fault of such erroneous transgressions.
Due to these causes and conditions, it is not yet perfected.
In order to bring this factor to fulfillment, they practice with diligent effort and are thus able to realize it;
by these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas bring this factor to completion.
The commentary states: The second [point] clarifies the perfection of one's own cultivation of diligence. As it is said in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, in the section on "Abiding":

"Precisely because these ten types of intention have become superior and are utterly perfected, these bodhisattvas enter and realize the second stage, the 'Abiding in Higher Ethics' (*adhiśīla-vihāra*).
Within this abiding, they are fully endowed with natural ethics (*prakṛti-śīla*). It continues: "Utterly..."
Even minor evil courses of action that involve transgressions of the precepts do not manifest, let alone those of medium or superior degree;
this is explained at length as in that [text]. By these causes and conditions, this factor is perfected. The *Cheng weishi lun shuji* (Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*) states:
"In the first stage (*bhūmi*), the bodhisattva does not yet possess superior capacity and has not yet fully realized the subtle transgressions within the bodhisattva precepts."
Because of [their] practice. The reason they have not yet succeeded is due to three obstacles: first, ignorance regarding subtle transgressions;
second, ignorance regarding the various aspects of karmic activity. These two types of ignorance induce the saṃsāra of expedient means, and are therefore termed "coarse and heavy retribution.

To extinguish these three obstacles, one cultivates right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*). By virtue of cultivating right effort, once the three obstacles have been extinguished, one enters [the state of non-conceptualization].
In the second bhūmi, one attains eight kinds of pure merits: first, purity of faith and aspiration; second, purity of mind; third, purity of compassion;
fourth, purity of the pāramitās; fifth, purity of seeing and serving the Buddhas;
sixth, purity of maturing sentient beings; seventh, purity of birth; and eighth, purity of majestic power. Regarding the higher and higher stages...
It is distinct from the stage of the Tathāgata. These eight qualities become increasingly superior and more excellent; by virtue of these factors, the second stage is perfected.
The commentary states: the eight kinds of purity will be explained in detail later.
Yet, they have not yet attained mundane meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) and attainments (*samāpatti*), nor the perfection of the *dhāraṇī* for hearing and retaining [the teachings].
For this reason, in this respect, they are still not fully perfected.
The commentary states: From here below is the third section, which distinguishes the Radiant Stage (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*) as included within the third part.

This contains two sections: first, clarifying that the practices of the second stage are not yet fulfilled; second, clarifying the cultivation of one's own stage to bring it to fulfillment. This is the first [section].

This means that although that bodhisattva has already perfected the portion of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*), they have not yet attained the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) subsumed under the superior concentration of the third stage, nor the *dhāraṇī* of perfect hearing and retention.

Regarding "meditative concentration" (*samādhi*), in the Sanskrit language it is *samādhi*; here it is translated as "equal holding" (*samādhi*), so called because it is free from both dullness and agitation. It is named...
"Samādhi" (等持) means to hold the mind so that it abides in a single object; thus it is called "samādhi. In the Sanskrit language, it is *samāpatti*, which here is translated as "equipoise" (等至).

The meaning of "equal" (*sama*) is as explained previously. "Equipoise" (*āpatti*) refers to reaching the ultimate limit; because one reaches the state of ultimate tranquility, it is called "equipoise.
Since both of these types [of concentration] are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) and are subject to destruction, they are termed "mundane" (*laukika*).
However, regarding the name of this meditative absorption (*samādhi*), according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it has three names: *samāhita*, *samādhi*, and *samāpatti*.
Thus, that treatise states: "That which is called the stage of *samāhita* refers to the stage of superior concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*).
It is free from dullness and agitation; it is that which can equally induce [the mind], or that which induces equality, or that which is the object of equality."
Because it induces [equanimity], it is called the "ground of meditative equipoise" (*samāhita-bhūmi*).

According to one interpretation, this name applies exclusively to all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) that possess mind, as these are all capable of equally inducing meritorious qualities; it does not extend to those without mind.

This is because the preceding verse states that it is "concomitant with *samādhi*," and *samādhi* is a mental factor (*caitta*) belonging to the category of "object-specific" factors. The two absorptions without mind...
Because it cannot produce all the qualities of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*), it is not a stage of equipoise (*samāhitabhūmi*).

If that is so, why is this stage of equipoise taught? Briefly, there are four kinds of stages of equipoise: namely, the dhyānas, the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the concentrations (*samādhi*), and the attainments (*samāpatti*).
Regarding "dhyāna," it refers to the four dhyānas. Regarding "liberation," it refers to the eight liberations. Regarding "concentration" (*samādhi*), it refers to...
These are the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*), and the concentration of signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*).

Regarding "attainment" (*samāpatti*), it refers to the five attainments of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-samāpatti*). (The five attainments are: first, contemplating the various impurities within one's own body; second, contemplating white bones with consciousness moving among them; third, contemplating white bones with consciousness moving among them, abiding in both this life and future lives;

fourth, contemplating white bones with consciousness moving among them, not abiding in this life but abiding only in future lives; fifth, contemplating white bones with consciousness moving among them, not abiding in either this life or future lives. These are explained in detail in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 40. Yoga...

[This is] the twelfth [chapter]. There is no fault in [the inclusion of] the eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) attainments, the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) attainments, the four formless (*ārūpya*) attainments, the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
These two mindless attainments are the fruits of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-phala*).

Therefore, it is given that name. In reality, however, it is not meditative equipoise (*samāhita*). According to one interpretation, this name applies to the essential substance of all meditative states, whether in a state with consciousness or without consciousness.

If it is a meditative state with consciousness, it is because it can equally draw forth various meritorious qualities, and because it also draws forth the equal faculties, the great elements, and so forth;
furthermore, it is drawn forth by the equal means of practice, such as the absence of laxity and excitement, and the lack of remorse due to ethical discipline.
Because it brings forth [these qualities], it is called "equipoise" (samāhita).

Even though a mindless absorption cannot bring forth sublime virtues, it is nonetheless called "equipoise" because it brings forth the equilibrium of the faculties, the primary elements, and so forth, and because it is induced by that state of equipoise.
If that is so, why does the preceding verse state that it is "accompanied by samādhi"? There is no fault here;

the verse is abbreviated and merely says it is "accompanied by that. In reality, however, it is not actually accompanied [by samādhi], because it was stated later that "equipoise" (samāhita) applies to both states with and without mind.
According to the true meaning, the name "ground of equipoise" has both general and specific applications; it refers to both states with mind and without mind.

Because they encompass both [the desire and form realms], they are called "universal" (*sāmānya*). As for the subsequent mention of the non-conceptual attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), since these are also the essence of the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*), they exist only within the contaminated (*sāsrava*).

Because the superior uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) concentrations are not present in all distracted states of mind (*vikṣipta-citta*) such as those of the desire realm, they are called "restricted" (*prādeśika*).
This is because the subsequent statement specifies that only the dhyānas and so forth are termed the stage of meditative equipoise, and not those in the desire realm.
One-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*). This is induced by meditative equipoise (*samāhita*), which is further induced by freedom from regret, joy, and bliss;

the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is not so. By extension, this applies to the higher realms as well: if one is in a state of distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), it is likewise not meditative equipoise, as it is identical to the desire realm.

Based on these contrasts, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) can be established: there may be that which is associated with concentration (*samādhi*) but does not belong to a state of meditative equipoise, namely, the distracted mind of the desire realm and so forth.
The mind and mental factors associated with samādhi within the state [of meditative concentration], or those belonging to the stage of equipoise (samāhita-bhūmi) that are not associated with samādhi;

that is to say, the essence of samādhi within the state of concentration, as well as all dharmas present in the states of the non-conceptual attainment (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
Alternatively, there are states that are both concentration (*samādhi*) and meditative absorption (*samāhita*).

These refer to the mind and mental factors within the stages of the dhyānas and the formless realms (*ārūpya*) during states of conscious absorption, excluding the factor of concentration itself. Or, there are states that are neither;

this refers to all dharmas other than those in the aforementioned superior stages. Furthermore, the terms *samādhi*, *samāpatti*, and *samāhita* differ in their breadth and scope. III. [End of Section]
The term *samādhi* refers to the mental factor (*caitasika*) of one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) among the various mental concomitants.

It universally encompasses all states of consciousness characterized by the presence of mind, whether in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*) or distraction (*vikṣipta*). Nevertheless, in various sūtras and śāstras, it is spoken of as "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*), "wishlessness" (*apraṇihita*), and so forth, based on its preeminent aspects;
these are termed *samādhi*. The term *samāpatti*, however, universally designates all meditative attainments, both those with and without mind.

Regarding the essential nature of all states within this stage, the various sūtras and śāstras—speaking from the perspective of what is preeminent—designate only those meditative concentrations associated with the five types such as "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) as "attainments" (*samāpatti*).
The term "equipoise" (*samāhita*) refers generally to the meritorious qualities of all states, whether with or without mental activity.
Therefore, within this stage, it encompasses all meritorious qualities of the states of meditative concentration; thus, it is comprehensive in total.

Therefore, it is a partial designation for the stage of the ground (*bhūmi*). However, within this present context, two names are briefly distinguished, because those two names are able to encompass both concentration and distraction, as well as states with and without mind.
As for *dhāraṇī*, this is translated as "total retention" (*saṃgraha*); its essence consists of mindfulness and wisdom.
However, this dhāraṇī briefly consists of four types, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 45.
Thus, that treatise says: "What is the bodhisattva’s sublime dhāraṇī? It should be known that such a sublime dhāraṇī briefly consists of four types:
first, the dhāraṇī of phenomena (*dharma-dhāraṇī*); second, the dhāraṇī of meaning (*artha-dhāraṇī*); third, the dhāraṇī of mantras (*vidyā-mantra-dhāraṇī*)."
Noble Lady, fourth is the Bodhisattva’s *dhāraṇī* for attaining patience. What is the Bodhisattva’s *dhāraṇī* of the Dharma?
It refers to the Bodhisattvas who have attained such sustaining power of mindfulness and wisdom;

by virtue of this sustaining power, they hear what has never been heard before—those collections of names, phrases, and syllables that have not yet been rehearsed or mastered—and [retain] them in their proper sequence.
Interweaving and combining them, he sequentially compiles immeasurable sūtras and is able to maintain them without forgetting for immeasurable periods;
this is called the bodhisattva’s dharma-dhāraṇī. What is the bodhisattva’s meaning-dhāraṇī? It is as previously described.

As for this distinction: it refers to the ability to maintain, without forgetting, the immeasurable meanings and purports of those teachings over an immeasurable period of time, even though one’s mind has not yet become warmed by them nor has one yet mastered them thoroughly.
This is called the bodhisattva’s *artha-dhāraṇī*. What is the bodhisattva’s *mantra-dhāraṇī*?
It refers to when bodhisattvas have attained such mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that, by means of...

This mastery consists of empowered mantra-syllables capable of removing the calamities and afflictions of sentient beings, causing those syllables to be entirely efficacious and never in vain, and able to eliminate various kinds of disasters and afflictions;
this is called the bodhisattva’s dhāraṇī of mantras. What is the bodhisattva’s ability to attain the bodhisattva’s dhāraṇī of patience? It refers to all...
The bodhisattva accomplishes the practice of natural and firm causes;

he is endowed with sublime wisdom, dwells alone in seclusion, remains silent and without speech, and perceives that there is never any substantial entity. He travels along the path and eats with moderation, avoiding impure food.
Eating in moderation, they constantly engage in profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*). During the night, they sleep little and remain awake much.

They are able to contemplate with precision the mantra verses for attaining the bodhisattva-patience (*bodhisattva-kṣānti*) as taught by the Buddha. As explained extensively therein, this is detailed in a separate chapter.
The meaning here is that meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and attainment (*samāpatti*) are the causes of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), while *dhāraṇī* is...
