These are the causes for the wisdoms arising from hearing and reflection. However, because that bodhisattva has not yet attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), which are the causes for the arising of the three types of wisdom, for this reason, they have not yet perfected this portion of the higher mind (*adhicitta*).
In order to bring this factor to fulfillment, they practice with diligent effort and are thus able to realize it;
by these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas bring this factor to perfection.
The commentary states: The second [point] clarifies the perfection of one's own diligent cultivation.

This means that through the power of the causes and conditions for attaining meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and dhāraṇīs in the third stage, this division is perfected. The *Liang* commentary explains:
The Bodhisattva, while in the second stage, has not yet attained superior capability;

he has not yet acquired the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), or the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining, nor is he fully endowed with the power of mindfulness. The reason he has not yet attained these is due to three obstacles.
First, the ignorance of desire-attachment; second, the ignorance regarding the dhāraṇī of complete hearing and retention.

The *saṃskāra-bhava* (birth through effort) induced by these two types of ignorance is called the "coarse and heavy retribution" (*dausthulya-vipāka*). To extinguish the three obstacles, one practices right exertion (*samyak-prahāṇa*).
By practicing right exertion, once the three obstacles have been extinguished, one enters the third stage (*bhūmi*) and attains eight kinds of increasingly superior purity.
The four dhyānas and so forth, up to the thorough penetration of the ultimate reality of the dharmadhātu—by means of these factors, the third bhūmi is perfected.
However, one is not yet able to dwell in the frequent cultivation of the bodhipakṣa-dharmas as they have been attained;
the mind has not yet abandoned attachment to the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and attachment to the dharmas. For this reason, within these factors, it is not yet fully perfected.
The commentary states: From here below is the fourth section, which distinguishes the *Arciṣmatī-bhūmi* (the Blazing Wisdom Stage) as included within the fourth part. This section has two parts:

first, it clarifies that the practices of the [preceding] three stages are not yet fulfilled; second, it clarifies the diligent cultivation for fulfillment on this stage itself. This is the first part.
It is said that for two reasons, that bodhisattva has not yet attained the perfection of the fourth limb of enlightenment:

first, they have not been able to dwell extensively within the various factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) as they have acquired them; second, they have not yet been able to relinquish their attachment to meditative concentration (samādhi-rāga) and their attachment to the Dharma (dharma-rāga).
Due to these two reasons, they have not yet reached perfection in this particular limb.
In order to bring this factor to fulfillment, they practice with diligent effort and are thus able to realize it;
by these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas bring this factor to completion.

The commentary states: The second [point] clarifies the cultivation of its own stage to bring it to fulfillment. This refers to the attainment of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) in the fourth stage;
subsequently, through the power of abandoning the causal conditions for craving toward both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and dharmas, this division is brought to fulfillment.

The Liang dynasty treatise says: "In the third stage, the Bodhisattva has not yet attained superior capacity and is unable to follow the aids to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya*) as they have been realized."

Within the dharmas of this stage, one dwells for as long as desired; however, one has not yet been able to relinquish attachment to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and attachment to dharmas, nor does one dwell with a completely pure mind.
The reason one has not yet succeeded is due to three obstacles: first, ignorance regarding attachment to meditative absorption (*samāpatti*); second, ignorance regarding attachment to dharmas.
The coarse and heavy retribution (*dausthulya-vipāka*) resulting from these two types of ignorance is the *saṃskāra-bhava* (birth through volitional effort). In order to extinguish it—

Because of these obscurations, one cultivates right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*). By cultivating right effort, once the three obscurations have been extinguished, one enters the fourth stage (*caturthī bhūmi*).

Therein, one attains eight kinds of increasingly superior purity, as well as dwelling at will within the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), and so forth, up to the thorough penetration of the non-appropriated meaning of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Through these factors, the fourth stage is perfected.
Yet they have not yet been able to observe the principles of the truths as they truly are;

nor have they yet been able to cultivate the mental attention that abandons the one-sided orientation of either rejecting saṃsāra or pursuing nirvāṇa; nor have they yet been able to cultivate the factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣadharma) subsumed under skillful means.
For this reason, within this section, [the stage] is not yet complete. The commentary states:
From here below, the fifth part distinguishes the fifth section, which subsumes the Extremely Difficult to Conquer Stage (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*). Within this, there are two [parts].
The first section clarifies that the practice of the fourth stage (*bhūmi*) is not yet complete; the latter section clarifies how one cultivates this stage to bring it to fulfillment.
This is the former: although one has already attained the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) in the fourth stage, for three reasons, one does not attain the fifth stage.
First, although one has attained the thirty-seven factors, one is as yet unable to observe the principles of the truths (*satya*) as they truly are.
Regarding the various truths (*satya*), they are as explained in detail in such works as the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* concerning the four noble truths and the two truths, etc.

Second, there are two types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) involving the abandonment of what has not yet been attained and the total turning away from saṃsāra while exclusively grasping for nirvāṇa;
these are as described in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, because one has not yet attained the path that makes no distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. Third, being unable to...
The factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) subsumed under skillful means (*upāya*). Question:

Since the factors for the path (*mārga-pakṣa*) have already been attained in the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), why has one not yet cultivated the factors conducive to enlightenment? Explanation: There are two kinds of factors conducive to enlightenment.
First, the thirty-seven [limbs], as previously explained. Second, the three kinds of factors for the path subsumed under skillful means, as described in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
The fifth stage (*bhūmi*) of the *Sūtra* states: First is the aid to the path of insatiability, because one skillfully accumulates the practice of merit as an aid to the path.
Second is the aid to the path of tireless diligence, because one constantly seeks the practice of wisdom as an aid to the path.

Third is the aid to the path of indefatigability, because one gathers the practice of great compassion as an aid to the path. Therefore, these are explained sequentially, yet they do not contradict one another.
It is contrary [to perfection]. Due to these three conditions, this stage remains incomplete.
In order to bring this stage to completion, those bodhisattvas practice with diligent effort and are thus able to realize it.
"For this reason, this factor is fulfilled.
The commentary explains: the second [section] clarifies the cultivation of the dharmas of one's own stage to fulfillment.

That is to say, for a Bodhisattva of the fifth stage, by virtue of the power of the three conditions mentioned above, this factor is fulfilled. The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty states: "The Bodhisattva, in the fourth stage..."

One has not yet attained superior capability. While practicing the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, one is unable to abandon the mind that either exclusively rejects or exclusively accepts saṃsāra and nirvāṇa;
nor is one able to attain the factors of the path to enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma) subsumed under the four kinds of skillful means.
The reason for this inability is due to three obstacles: first, the conceptualization of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as being exclusively rejectable or acceptable.
Illumination. Second, the ignorance regarding the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) as subsumed under skillful means.

The birth-and-death (saṃsāra) caused by these two types of ignorance is termed "heavy burden" (dausthulya) retribution. To extinguish these three obstacles, one practices right effort (samyag-vyāyāma).
By practicing right effort and having extinguished the three obstacles, one enters the fifth stage (bhūmi), attains eight kinds of increasingly superior purity, and attains equanimity (upekṣā).
From the turning away from and abandoning of the mind that grasps [at objects], up to the penetration of the meaning that the continuum of the *dharmadhātu* is non-different—
by virtue of this factor, the fifth stage is perfected. However,
one is as yet unable to observe the flow of saṃsāra as it truly is, and because one still gives rise to much weariness toward it.

One has not yet been able to dwell extensively in the mental attention (*manasikāra*) that is signless (*animitta*). For this reason, within this section, regarding what is "not yet fulfilled," the commentary states:
From here below, the sixth section is explained, which subsumes the *Abhimukhī* (Manifest) Bhūmi. This section contains two parts:

first, clarifying that the subsequent practice in the five [preceding] bhūmis is not yet fulfilled; second, clarifying the cultivation of one's own bhūmi so as to bring it to fulfillment. This is the first part.
This means that although one attains the contemplation of the truths in the fifth stage, there are two causes and conditions for not yet attaining the sixth stage:
first, one is unable to observe, in accordance with reality, the principle of dependent origination within the flow of saṃsāra;

second, because one gives rise to much aversion toward that suffering, its origin, and defilement, one is unable to dwell extensively in signless mental attention (*animitta-manasikāra*). Due to these two conditions, [one does not attain the sixth stage].
Regarding the sixth stage, it has not yet been perfected;
in order to bring this stage to completion, those bodhisattvas practice with diligent application and are thus able to realize it.
"For this reason, this factor is fulfilled.
The commentary explains: the second [point] clarifies how the cultivation of the dharmas of one's own stage is brought to fulfillment;

that is to say, because Bodhisattvas in the sixth stage realize the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), this factor is fulfilled. The *She lun* (Treatise on the Compendium) of the Liang dynasty states: "In the fifth stage, the Bodhisattva has not yet..."
It is a superior capacity because one has realized, in accordance with reality, the arising and continuity of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).

This is due to having extensively practiced the cultivation of revulsion toward the characteristics of conditioned phenomena. However, one is unable to dwell for a long duration in signless contemplation as desired;
the reason for this inability is due to three obstacles: first, ignorance regarding the arising and continuity of all conditioned phenomena.

The two types of conceptualization repeatedly give rise to ignorance (*avidyā*). These two forms of ignorance induce the causes and conditions for birth and death (*saṃsāra*), which is termed "coarse heaviness" (*dausthulya*) as its retribution.
To extinguish these three obstacles, one practices right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*).

By practicing right effort, once the three obstacles have been extinguished, one enters the sixth stage (*bhūmi*), attaining eight kinds of increasingly superior purity and no longer realizing the characteristics of the continuous arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
...and so forth, until one penetrates the meaning that the dharma-realm is neither defiled nor pure. By virtue of this factor, the sixth stage is perfected;
yet, one is still unable to dwell in the cultivation of signless mental attention (animitta-manasikāra) without deficiency or interruption. For this reason, [the seventh stage is entered].
Within this section, [the practice] is not yet perfected. The commentary states:
From here below, the seventh section clarifies the inclusion of the Far-Reaching Ground (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*) within the seventh division. This consists of two parts:
first, clarifying that the practice in the six preceding grounds is not yet complete; second, clarifying the cultivation of one's own ground to bring it to perfection. This is the first part.

This means that while one attains the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in the sixth stage, one has not yet attained the purely signless contemplation (*animitta-bhāvanā*) within the seventh stage.

Because there is no deficiency during the time of signless contemplation, it is said to be "without deficiency" (*anūna*). Because it is not interrupted by signs, it is called "uninterrupted" (*nirantara*).

Thus, the *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only), fascicle nine, states: "In the first five stages, contemplation with signs (*sanimitta-bhāvanā*) predominates; [contemplation without signs does not]."
In the sixth stage, signless contemplation (*animitta-vipaśyanā*) is predominant and contemplation with signs (*sanimitta-vipaśyanā*) is minor;
in the seventh stage, there is exclusively signless contemplation. For this reason, within this section, [the practice] is not yet perfected.
In order to bring this factor to fulfillment, they practice with diligent effort and are thus able to realize it.
By means of these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas bring this factor to completion.
The commentary states: The second [section] clarifies the cultivation of the dharmas of one’s own stage to bring them to fulfillment.

This refers to the Bodhisattva of the seventh stage, who is able to realize the signless mental attention (*animitta-manasikāra*) that is flawless and uninterrupted. By virtue of this cause and condition, this portion is fulfilled.

The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) translated during the Liang dynasty states: "The Bodhisattva, in the sixth stage, has not yet attained superior capacity; he is still unable to abandon the subtle [defilements] of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)."
Subtle mental activities regarding signs arise, such that one is unable to dwell for a long duration, continuously and without interruption, within the contemplation of signlessness as desired.
The reason for this inability is due to three obstacles: first, ignorance regarding the arising of subtle mental activities regarding signs.
Second is the ignorance regarding the skillful means of mental cultivation that is consistently associated with signs.

The birth-and-death resulting from the causal conditions of these two types of ignorance is called the "retribution of heaviness" (*dausthulya*). One practices right effort in order to extinguish the three obstacles.

By practicing right effort, once the three obstacles have been extinguished, one enters the seventh stage and attains eight kinds of supreme purity, as well as the departure from the subtle [defilements] of conditioned phenomena.
Subtle conduct gives rise to all dharmas, up to and including the realization of the non-differentiation of the various meanings within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
By virtue of this stage, the seventh bhūmi is perfected.
Yet, one has not yet been able to relinquish effort within the dwelling in the signless, nor has one attained mastery over signs;
for these reasons, this stage remains as yet incomplete.
The commentary states: From here below, the eighth section clarifies the inclusion of the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*) within the eighth part. This section contains two parts:

first, it clarifies that the preceding part and subsequent practice are not yet fulfilled; second, it clarifies the fulfillment through diligent cultivation of one's own stage. This is the first part.

This means that bodhisattvas on the seventh stage have not yet been able to relinquish effort within the dwelling in the signless (*animitta*), nor have they yet attained mastery over signs (*nimitta*).
For these reasons, they are still not fully perfected in the eighth stage.
In order to bring this factor to fulfillment, they practice with diligent application and are thus able to realize it.
By means of these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas bring this factor to perfection.
The commentary states: The second [section] clarifies the perfection of diligent cultivation regarding the dharmas of one’s own stage.

This refers to the Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage, who are able to relinquish effort within that dwelling in the signless (*animitta-vihāra*) and further attain mastery over signs (*nimitta-vaśitā*).

By virtue of these causes and conditions, this portion is perfected. The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) translated during the Liang dynasty states: "In the seventh stage, the Bodhisattva has not yet attained supremacy..."
Yes. One has not yet been able to dwell in the practice of signlessness with a mind free from effortful application, nor has one attained mastery over the signs of benefiting oneself and others.
The reason for this inability is due to three obstacles: first, ignorance regarding the exertion of effort in the contemplation of signlessness;
second, ignorance regarding mastery over the practice of signs. These are the two types of ignorance.

The existence of birth and death that is experienced is called "coarse and heavy retribution" (*dausthulya-vipāka*). One practices right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*) in order to extinguish the three obstacles.

Having extinguished the three obstacles through the practice of right effort, one enters the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*), attains the eight kinds of increasingly superior purity and the state free from effortful application (*anābhoga*), and dwells in the cultivation of the signless (*animitta*) and so forth, until one penetrates the dharmadhātu as being without increase.
Regarding the meaning of "diminution":

because of this factor, although the eighth stage is fulfilled, one has not yet attained great mastery in teaching the Dharma through all its categories, including synonyms, various characteristics, etymologies, and distinctions.
For this reason, within this factor, [the stage] is not yet fully perfected.
The commentary states: From here below, the ninth section clarifies the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*). This section contains two parts:

first, it clarifies that the preceding stages and subsequent practices were not yet fulfilled; second, it clarifies the fulfillment through diligent cultivation within one's own stage. This is the first part.

"Different names" refers to the object of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*). "Various characteristics" refers to the object of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).

"Distinctions in etymological interpretation" refers to the analytical knowledge of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*). "Attaining great mastery in proclaiming the Dharma through all categories" refers to the object of the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*).
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 43, states: "First, the knowledge of the various gateways of the Dharma, namely—"

1. The Bodhisattva’s unimpeded wisdom regarding phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*). 2. The wisdom regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇajñāna*), namely the Bodhisattva’s unimpeded wisdom regarding meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*). 3.
The wisdom regarding the etymological explanations of phenomena (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), namely the Bodhisattva’s unimpeded wisdom regarding linguistic expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*). 4.

The wisdom regarding the distinctions between categories and phrases (*padaprabhedajñāna*), namely the Bodhisattva’s unimpeded wisdom regarding eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*). These pertain to the Bodhisattva of the eighth stage.
Because they have not yet attained the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of the ninth stage, they are said to be "not yet capable. For this reason,
regarding the ninth division,
in order to bring that division to completion where it was previously incomplete, those bodhisattvas practice with diligent effort and are thus able to realize it.
"By reason of these causes and conditions, this stage is fulfilled. The commentary explains:
the second [stage] clarifies the fulfillment of diligent cultivation within one's own stage. That is to say, in the ninth stage, one attains the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*);
therefore, it is called "attainment. By reason of these causes and conditions, this stage is fulfilled. The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty states: "The Bodhisattva..."
In the eighth stage, one has not yet attained superior capability; one has not yet attained mastery over the characteristics, distinctions, names, and categories within the perfect teaching;
and one has not yet attained the *dhāraṇī* of skillful exposition. The reason for this inability is as follows:

Due to three obstacles: first, ignorance regarding the mastery of eloquent speech and the *dhāraṇī* of immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables for the purpose of teaching the Dharma through immeasurable correct explanations;
second, ignorance regarding the arising of understanding by resolving doubts through the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

The existence-in-existence (*bhava-bhava*) brought about by these two types of ignorance is called the "heavy burden" (*dausthulya*) retribution. In order to extinguish these three, [one should practice].
Because of these hindrances, one cultivates right effort; because of right effort, the three hindrances are extinguished.

Having entered the ninth stage, one attains eight kinds of increasingly superior purity, as well as mastery over the characteristics of the perfect teaching of the Dharma, up to the meaning of the basis for mastery over the knowledge that penetrates the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). By virtue of these factors, the ninth stage is perfected.
The commentary states: According to the Liang translation of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, two types of ignorance obstruct the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

Specifically, the first type of ignorance obstructs three of the analytical knowledges, while the second type of ignorance obstructs the fourth analytical knowledge. This citation from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the text of this sutra was established by Paramārtha himself;
it does not appear at all in the Sanskrit version of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*. Furthermore, regarding the third [point] of the cited text...

Ignorance (avidyā) merely obstructs eloquence (pratibhāna). Therefore, one should know that the claim that [the practitioner] relies upon the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence is an error of the translators.
Furthermore, because they have not yet attained the full realization and experience of the manifest Dharmakāya, for these reasons, within this section:
"Still not yet perfected. The commentary states:
From here below, the tenth section clarifies the *dharmameghā-bhūmi* (Cloud of Dharma) as subsumed within the tenth stage. This section contains two parts:

first, it clarifies that the preceding stages and subsequent practices are not yet fulfilled; second, it clarifies the fulfillment through diligent cultivation of one's own stage. This is the first part.
This means that because the causes for the ninth stage are not yet fulfilled, one has not yet been able to realize the perfectly complete Dharmakāya.
The *Tattvārthā* commentary states: "Because the causes for the ninth stage are not yet perfected, one has not yet attained the perfectly complete three bodies (trikāya).
For this reason, within this portion [of the path], it is still not yet complete."
In order to bring this factor to fulfillment, they practice with diligent effort and are thus able to realize it.
By means of these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas bring this factor to completion.
The commentary states: The second [section] clarifies the perfection of one's own cultivation (*svabhāga-pratipatti*).

This means that because the causes are perfected in the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*), one is able to realize the perfected *dharmakāya*. For this reason, this portion is perfected. The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) translated during the Liang dynasty states:
"In the nine stages, the bodhisattva does not yet possess superior capacity; he has not yet been able to attain the perfect teaching of the Dharma."
Regarding the body: one has not yet attained the unattached, unimpeded, and perfected six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). The reason for this failure is due to three obstructions:
first, ignorance regarding the six supernormal powers; second, ignorance regarding entry into the subtle and secret Buddha-dharmas.
The existence and birth-and-death produced by these two types of ignorance are called the retribution of heavy defilement (*dausthulya*).

In order to extinguish these three obstacles, one practices right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*). By practicing right effort, once the three obstacles have been extinguished, one enters the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), attains the eight kinds of increasingly superior purity, and is able to attain the perfectly expounded *dharmakāya*, and so forth, until reaching full penetration of the Dharma.
The meaning of the basis for mastery over realms and karma. Through these divisions, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are perfected. Paramārtha’s commentary states:
"The three bodies obtained through the perfection of the ten stages are called the 'perfected dharma-body' (*pariniṣpanna-dharmakāya*);

this refers correctly to the dharma-body. From the dharma-body emerge the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Wisdom is itself the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). By attaining mastery over karma, the transformation body is accomplished."
Yet, they have not yet attained the unattached and unimpeded sublime wisdom and sublime vision that pervades all objects of knowledge.
For this reason, within this particular stage, they are still not fully perfected.
The commentary states: From here below, the tenth section is specifically explained as being subsumed within the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*). This section contains two parts:

first, explaining that the preceding sections and subsequent practices have not yet reached fulfillment; second, explaining the fulfillment through diligent cultivation within one's own stage. This is the first part.
That is to say, in the tenth stage, one has not yet attained the wondrous knowledge and wondrous vision of non-attachment to the emptiness of all objective phenomena through universal cognition,
nor the unimpeded wondrous knowledge and wondrous vision regarding the emptiness of persons; for these reasons, within this particular stage, one is as yet not fully perfected.
In order to bring this factor to fulfillment, one practices with diligent application and is thus able to realize it.
By this cause and condition, this factor becomes fulfilled; because this factor is fulfilled, all factors are brought to fulfillment.

The commentary states: The second [point] clarifies the perfection of diligent cultivation within one's own stage (*svabhūmi*). This means that upon attaining this Buddha-stage, one realizes the all-encompassing knowledge and vision (*sarvajñajñānadarśana*).
By virtue of these causes and conditions, the Buddha-stage is perfected. Because the Buddha-stage is perfected, all eleven types of divisions (*aṅga*) attain perfection.
The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) translated during the Liang dynasty states: "The Bodhisattva’s ten stages have not yet attained superior capability."
One has not yet attained the pure and perfect *dharmakāya*, nor has one been able to attain unattached and unimpeded vision and knowledge regarding all objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
The reason one has not yet attained this is due to three obstacles: first, the subtle attachment-ignorance (*sūkṣma-saṅga-avidyā*) regarding all objects of knowledge;
second, the subtle obstruction-ignorance (*sūkṣma-āvaraṇa-avidyā*) regarding all objects of knowledge.
The birth-and-death resulting from these two types of ignorance is called the retribution of heavy impediments (*dausthulya*).
To extinguish these three obstacles, one practices right effort. By practicing right effort, once the three obstacles have been extinguished, one enters the eleventh stage, the Tathāgata-bhūmi.
One attains the seven kinds of supreme purity and the purity of transcendence from birth (*niḥsaraṇa-viśuddhi*).

Furthermore, one attains the pure and perfect *dharmakāya*, as well as unattached and unimpeded vision and knowledge (*darśana-jñāna*). Through these factors, the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*) is perfected.

One interpretation states that the eleven stages are subsumed within the eleven divisions; there are three such patterns. Within the first division, the text consists of two sections. The first clarifies...
In the preceding stage, cultivation has not yet been perfected. In the subsequent [verse], it clarifies that one has already transcended that lower ground and that one’s own ground is now fulfilled.
Following that, for each of the nine sections concerning those bodhisattvas, there are three parts by analogy: first, concluding the fulfillment of the preceding stage;

second, clarifying that the subsequent stage is not yet fulfilled with the words "but has not yet... and so forth; and third, clarifying the practice required to bring it to completion with the words "in order to... and so forth. After that, regarding those bodhisattvas...

The eleventh section, "The Manifestation of the Power of Samādhi," consists of four parts: first, concluding the completion of the preceding stage; second, indicating that the subsequent stage is not yet complete with the words "yet not" (*wei er*);

third, explaining how to cultivate it so that it becomes perfect with the words "in order to cause" (*wei ling*); and fourth, re-concluding the completion of this section with the words "this section being fulfilled" (*ci fen man*).
Although there are two interpretations regarding the first part, the former is considered correct.
"Good son, you should know that these eleven divisions universally encompass all the stages (*bhūmi*).
The commentary states: this second summary should be understood.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, for what reason is the first named the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*)?"
"Up to what point is it called the Buddha-ground?

The commentary states: This is the second section, explaining the meaning of the names of the grounds. First the question is posed, then the answer follows. This constitutes the general inquiry regarding the meaning of the names of all the grounds.

The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "Good son, because one accomplishes the great purpose and attains an unprecedented supramundane mind, giving rise to great joy, it is therefore called the first stage, the Stage of Utmost Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi)."
The commentary states: From this point downward is the second section, the Tathāgata’s formal exposition, which explains the eleven stages (*bhūmi*).

This constitutes eleven parts. This [first part] explains the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). There are two meanings to this explanation: first, the attainment of the benefit of oneself and others;

second, the attainment of the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*). Therefore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle one, says: "Accomplishing unsurpassed self-benefit and benefit for others, it is the initial realization of the state of the noble ones (*ārya*)."
Therefore, it is named "Joyful" (*pramuditā*). The commentary explains that the "sacred state" (*ārya-bhūmi*) refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
There are extremely many explanations for the name of this stage across various teachings, which cannot be recounted in full. To summarize the essentials:

sometimes a single meaning is used to explain the name "Extremely Joyful," as in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, where the Bodhisattva Good Awakening and the Four Heavenly Kings simultaneously illuminate the principle of the equality of the two truths; or as in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
It is said: Because, by means of this, one first attains the supreme merit capable of accomplishing the welfare of oneself and others, it is so called.
Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* (Commentary on the Compendium of the Great Vehicle) agrees with the *Saṃgraha*.

Furthermore, the third chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that because one correctly realizes the unsurpassed clear observation (*abhisamaya*) and dwells in superior joy, it is named "Joyful" (*pramuditā*). The first fascicle of the *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra* says:

One first attains the flavor of the wholesome dharmas because the mind is filled with great joy. Thus, the term "Supreme Joy" (*pramuditā*) may be explained through two meanings, as in this very *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra* and other texts;
or it may be explained through three meanings, as stated in the first fascicle of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*:

One attains the supramundane mind; having not previously attained it, one now attains it for the first time. Because this great matter and great function are fulfilled according to one's aspirations, it is called "Joy" (*pramuditā*).
(The "great matter" refers to self-benefit; the "great function" refers to benefiting others. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle nine, states:

"Because one has initially acquired the noble nature, fully realized the two kinds of emptiness, and is able to benefit oneself and others, great joy arises. If one were to analyze this extensively, there would be many factors such as faith, reverence, and so forth.
The nine kinds of mindfulness of the Buddha and so forth, the ten kinds of transcendence from worldly realms, and the ten kinds of joy are as described in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Because one is far removed from all subtle transgressions of the precepts, the second stage is named the "Stainless Ground" (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
The commentary states: The second [stage], the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*), is also described in this sutra as having a profound and secret continuity.

The *Benevolent Kings Sutra* (*Renyōkyō*) calls it "Freedom from Distance," for its verse says: "The Bodhisattva King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, free from distance, manifests his form throughout the six realms and a thousand lands.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* (*Kongōkōmyōkyō*) states that all subtle errors, violations of the precepts, and transgressions are...

Because it is pure, it is called the Ground Free from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*). The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "Being far removed from the defiled mind of stinginess, envy, and broken precepts, it is named the Ground Free from Defilement.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "It is free from the defilements of afflictions that give rise to erroneous thoughts, violations of the precepts, and so forth."

Because it is fully endowed with pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), it is called the "Stainless Ground" (*vimalā-bhūmi*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Because one is utterly remote from the stains of violating ethical discipline.

Vasubandhu’s commentary explains: "It is the accomplishment of natural ethical discipline (*prakṛti-śīla*); it is not like the first ground, where natural ethical discipline is accomplished through deliberate selection and guarding.
Because all stains of violating ethical discipline have already been removed," the intention of Asvabhāva is the same as Vasubandhu’s; this is what is revealed.

The *Yanglun* (Treatise on Elevation) states: "Transcending the stages of the two vehicles, one realizes pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), which serves as the antidote to all stains of transgressing the precepts.

The *Shizhulun* (Treatise on the Ten Abodes) states: "Because one practices the ten paths of wholesome action and is free from all stains, it is called the Ground of Freedom from Stains (*vimalā-bhūmi*). The *Cheng weishi lun* (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra) states:
"Possessing pure ethical discipline and being far removed from the stains of afflictions that give rise to even subtle transgressions, it is named the Ground of Freedom from Stains."
Because the samādhis and the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining that he has attained serve as the basis for immeasurable light of wisdom,
the third stage is therefore named the Radiant Stage (Prabhākārī-bhūmi).

The commentary states: The third [stage] clarifies the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*). This means that because one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the third ground, the light of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) is emitted;

and because one attains the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retention, the light of wisdom derived from hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā-mayī-prajñā*) is emitted. Therefore, the third is named the Ground of Radiance.
Alternatively, it may be that the provisional ground serves as the basis for the emission of light, and is thus called the Ground of Radiance.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* calls it the "Ground of Clarity" (*Prabhākarī-bhūmi*), while the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* calls it the "Ground of Radiance.

The reason it is not referred to as the "Ground of Emitting Light" (*Prabhākari-bhūmi*) is due to differences in the translators. The *Ratnaketuparipṛcchā-sūtra* names it the "Ground of Clear Wisdom" (*Vidyāmati-bhūmi*).

Thus, its verse states: "Clear wisdom shines with emptiness like a blazing celestial king; manifesting forms throughout the myriad lands, he guides all living beings. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* refers to it as "Immeasurable... [and so forth].
The Samādhi of the Radiance of Wisdom is unshakable and cannot be overcome, for it takes the Dhāraṇī of Hearing and Retaining as its foundation;

therefore, it is called the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*). The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "Because the three roots of goodness—non-attachment, non-hatred, and so forth—further increase and become luminously pure, it is named the Ground of Radiance.
This is largely the same in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*’s *Daśabhūmika* chapter and the *Śīla-samvara-sūtra*.

Regarding the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Because it is the basis for non-retrogressive meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and attainments (*samāpatti*), and because it is the basis for the great light of the Dharma, it is called the Stage of Emitting Light (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*). Vasubandhu’s commentary explains:
"In this stage, one is never separated from *samādhi* and *samāpatti*; because there is no retrogression, [it is so named] regarding the Mahāyāna."
Because the Dharma can produce radiance, it is called the Ground of Radiant Emission (*Prabhākarī-bhūmi*). If explained in detail, it is as Vasubandhu (Wuxing) interprets in his commentary.
The *Śrāvakabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states: "Attaining the extremely pure aggregate of samādhi and serving as the basis for the radiance of great wisdom is called the Ground of Radiant Emission.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Having accomplished supreme concentration and the great dhāraṇīs of the Dharma, one is able to emit boundless [light]."

Because of the light of sublime wisdom (*prajñā-prabhā*), it is called the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*). In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 49, it is called the Ground of Having Light.
Because the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) attained therein burn away all afflictions (*kleśa*), and because this wisdom is like a flame, the fourth [ground] is so named.
It is named the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).

The commentary explains: the fourth is the Ground of Blazing Wisdom. This means that the flames of wisdom regarding the various factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) burn away the fuel of the afflictions (*kleśa*); therefore, it is called "Blazing Wisdom.
The profound underlying intent (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) of the continuity [of the teachings] is the same as this sūtra. According to the *Ratnarājasūtra*, it is also named...
Arciṣmatī. Therefore, that verse says: "Arciṣmatī, Subhāprabhā, Tejo-vīrya; the King of Tuṣita roams through the land of faith.

The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* states: "Because it can burn away afflictions with the fire of wisdom, and because it increases radiance as the locus for practicing the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), it is called the 'Blazing Ground' (Arciṣmatī).
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "Day and night, it constantly emits the light of wisdom."
Because of the brilliance of its flames. Just as the light of a *maṇi* jewel is not extinguished by other lights, it is therefore called the "Flame Stage" (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).

The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*’s "Ten Abodes" is largely identical to the "Ten Stages. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Because the fire of wisdom can burn the fuel of the afflictions without forgetting them, it is named the 'Flame Stage. (Regarding 'without forgetting':

since innate afflictions continue spontaneously and one’s wisdom arises the very moment they are about to manifest, it is said that one does not forget them). The *Vyavahāra-śāstra* says: "By means of..."
The wisdom of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) constitutes its nature as flame, while the two obstacles—of afflictions and of knowledge—constitute its nature as fuel.

Because a bodhisattva on this stage can give rise to the flames of wisdom to burn the fuel of these two obstacles, it is named the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*:
Because all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas) incinerate all obscurations, it is called the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi). Vasubandhu’s commentary states:

Because one dwells in the most excellent factors of enlightenment within this stage, and by dwelling therein, one is able to burn all root afflictions (kleśa) and secondary afflictions (upakleśa) until they are reduced to ashes;
therefore, it is named the Stage of Blazing Wisdom. There is no [further text].

The nature and the intention are the same. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Because it dwells securely in the most excellent factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and increases the flames of wisdom that burn the fuel of the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called the 'Flame Wisdom' stage (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* calls it the "Increasing Radiance" stage.

The commentary explains that according to the *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra* and other texts, it is called the "Flame" stage because it burns the fuel of the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*). Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "It is able to burn all fundamental [afflictions]."
That "the afflictions and secondary afflictions are all reduced to ashes" refers to the permanent severance of what is to be known.

The subduing and severance of afflictions is termed "being reduced to ashes. Otherwise, it would contradict the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, which speaks of "retaining the afflictions until the afflictions are exhausted," and so forth.
Because one attains mastery over those very factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) only through extremely arduous skillful cultivation,
the fifth stage is therefore named "The Extremely Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjayā).
The commentary states: The fifth stage clarifies the "Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjaya). It is called Difficult to Conquer because one attains mastery amidst that which is difficult to cultivate.

Its characteristics are consistent with this. The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* says: "Because the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are practiced through skillful means, and victory is attained amidst what is difficult to conquer, it is named the Difficult to Conquer Stage.
The *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* names it the "Stage of Supreme Wisdom" (*Jñānavati*). Thus, its verse says:

The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "Because the three truths are clearly illuminated from afar by supreme wisdom, and because the celestial king of the Nirmāṇarati heaven rules over ten billion lands, it is called the 'Difficult to Conquer' stage (*Durjayā-bhūmi*).
This is because the mastery of superior wisdom through the skillful means of practice is difficult to attain, and because the afflictions of views and thoughts cannot be subdued.
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "The roots of goodness of that stage [are purified] by means of skillful means..."

Because the power of wisdom and contemplation increases, becoming ever more superior, luminous, and pure—such that it cannot be matched by the roots of goodness of the lower stages, nor by the roots of goodness of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), nor by worldly roots of goodness—it is called the "Difficult to Conquer" stage (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*).
The intent of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* (Ten Stages Chapter) and the *Bhadraśīla-sūtra* is the same as that of the *Daśabhūmika*.
The *Śāstra* states: "Because one attains worldly wisdom and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and is thus able to deliver those who are difficult to deliver, it is named [the Difficult to Conquer]."

Regarding the *Sudurjayā-bhūmi* (The Ground Difficult to Conquer): The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that on this ground, the bodhisattva’s definitive and sublime wisdom regarding the noble truths (*āryasatya*) is so extremely difficult to surpass that it is named the "Difficult to Conquer" ground.

The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states that within the fifth ground, there are two kinds of detachment: first, the absence of affliction while diligently transforming sentient beings; second, the absence of a mind that refuses to transform [sentient beings].

Regarding "the absence of affliction and difficulty": the Bodhisattvas of this stage are able to transcend two difficulties and achieve victory over them; thus, it is named the "Difficult-to-Conquer" (Sudurjayā) stage. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:

"Because conventional wisdom and ultimate wisdom are mutually contradictory, the ability to unify these difficult-to-unify [wisdoms] and bring them into correspondence is why it is called the Difficult-to-Conquer stage.
Asaṅga’s and Vasubandhu’s interpretations are consistent with the *Saṃgraha*. The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* [also agrees].
The *Śāstra* says: "To realize the extremely pure wisdom-aggregate (*prajñā-skandha*) that knows all phenomena as objects of knowledge through the truths is exceedingly difficult;
because it abides neither in saṃsāra nor in quiescent nirvāṇa, it is called 'Extremely Difficult to Conquer' (*Sudurjayā*). The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* says:

"In the fifth stage, the power of merit is so flourishing that none of the Māras can destroy it; therefore, it is named the 'Difficult to Conquer' Stage (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*). This is established in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
The intent of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* is the same as that of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

One observes the flow and transformation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) before one's eyes; furthermore, it manifests only after extensive cultivation of mental attention (*manasikāra*) regarding the signless (*animitta*).
For this reason, the sixth stage is called the "Manifest" (*Abhimukhī*) Stage.

The commentary states: The sixth [stage] is the analysis of the Ground of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*). This means that within this stage, one directly observes the flow and turning of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).

first the question, and later the answer. This is the general question: "In the eleven stages, how many types of delusion and heavy burdens (*dauṣṭhulya*) are there?"
These serve as the objects to be countered (*vipakṣa*). However, regarding these eleven types of coarseness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the ignorant, various teachings differ.

Specifically, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, "Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī" on the seventh stage, the *Sugatamatavibhaṅga*, and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, "Anupamabhūmi-parivarta," all share the same original text as this scripture but represent different translations.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* lists the names of these various ignorances but does not provide an explanation. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* of the Liang dynasty...

In the tenth fascicle of Vasubandhu’s Commentary (*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*), it is stated that twenty-two types of delusion (*moha*) bring about eleven kinds of coarse retributions (*dausthulya-vipāka*).
The first eight delusions can bring about the four types of "preparatory" (*upapatti-prayoga*) birth-and-death; the next six can bring about "causal" (*hetu-pratyaya*) birth-and-death;

the next six can bring about "existence-within-existence" (*bhava-bhava*) birth-and-death; and the final two can bring about "non-existence" (*abhava*) birth-and-death. These are precisely what is brought about by them.

The retributive fruit of transformation (*pariṇāma-vipāka*) is considered a coarse and heavy retribution (*dausthulya-vipāka*). Now, upon careful examination, the *Liang* commentary contains three errors:

first, the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* does not contain the term "non-discrimination" (*avikalpa*); second, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* cited therein does not distinguish four types of birth-and-death;

and third, it asserts that the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) does not induce the two types of birth-and-death—segmented (*bheda*) and transformative (*pariṇāma*)—as is established in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
In the ninth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the meaning of the sūtra is explained in detail; therefore, I shall now rely upon that work to explain the text of this sūtra.
Regarding the points of agreement and difference therein, I shall provide a correct interpretation according to the text.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "Good son, within these stages (bhūmi), there are twenty-two kinds..."
Ignorance (*moha*). It is countered by eleven types of grossness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
The commentary states: the second part is the Tathāgata’s correct exposition. This consists of three sections: first, a general heading; second, a detailed explanation;
and third, from "Good son" onwards, the explicit explanation of the meaning of ignorance. This [present section] is the general heading. There are twenty-two [factors] across the eleven stages.
Folly and the eleven types of gross dysfunction (*dauṣṭhulya*) constitute the obstacles to be overcome.
Specifically, regarding the first stage (*bhūmi*), there are two types of folly: first, the folly of clinging to a person (*pudgala*) and to phenomena (*dharma*).
"The two delusions regarding the afflictions of the two evil destinies, as well as their respective coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*), are the objects to be countered.
Commentary: From here on, the second section provides a detailed explanation according to the sequence of the eleven stages (*bhūmi*).

Within each stage, there are two delusions and one coarse heaviness, forming eleven sections. This refers to the two delusions and the coarse heaviness of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). These two delusions... [are able to... these two delusions.
Regarding the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there are two interpretations. One states that "ignorance" (*moha*) and its "category" (*pakṣa*) are collectively termed "ignorance.

This refers to the first two types of ignorance on the first stage (*bhūmi*). First, the attachment to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-abhiniveśa*), which is the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*) in this context.

Second, the ignorance regarding the defilements of the miserable realms (*durgati-saṃkleśa-moha*), which refers to the various karmas and their fruits within those miserable realms. It should be understood that these categories of ignorance are collectively termed [the obstacle].
"Foolishness. Hereafter, the explanation follows this principle. One interpretation states: "In this context, only delusion (*moha*) is mentioned. Therefore, it further says:

"Alternatively, it refers only to the two types of delusion that arise together with the categories of sharp and dull hindrances. The commentary explains: "The five [delusions] associated with the sharp [hindrances] are called 'the delusion of attachment to self and phenomena' (*ātmadharma-abhiniveśa-moha*);
the five associated with the dull [hindrances] are called 'the delusion of defilement in the miserable destinies' (*durgati-saṃkleśa-moha*). Question: If that is so, regarding the sharp...

Regarding the statement that the two dull [faculties] are both deluded by afflictions (*kleśa*), by which delusion are they subsumed? The explanation says: it is stated according to whichever is predominant;

alternatively, from the perspective of simultaneous occurrence, one may speak of them as two delusions. Question: In the school of Dharmapāla, what serves as the essence of the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*)?

The explanation says: Dharmapāla himself has two interpretations. First, according to the actual comprehensive discussion, among the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), those that arise through discrimination (*parikalpita*)—the second...
When the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) manifests, one severs only one type [of affliction] and is said to attain the nature of an Arya.
When the Bodhisattva’s Path of Seeing manifests, both types are severed in full, and he is said to attain the nature of an Arya.

When the two true Paths of Seeing manifest, the seeds of those two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) are necessarily no longer present; just as light and darkness cannot coexist, they are like the two pans of a scale.

When the head is raised or lowered, it is likewise; for all things that are mutually contradictory, this principle must necessarily hold. Therefore, there is no fault of both natures being established simultaneously.

At the time of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), the seeds of the afflictions have already ceased to exist; why, then, is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) further produced? This is because the mental orientation (*citta-abhiprāya*) differs:

[the former] aims at the abandonment of the afflictions, while [the latter] aims at the realization of cessation (*nirodha*). It is for the sake of abandoning the heavy impediments (*dauṣṭhulya*) of that category [of afflictions] that the path of liberation arises at the time of the path of uninterrupted transition.
Although the seeds of delusion are absent, the capacity for such susceptibility has not yet been relinquished.
To relinquish this, one gives rise to the path of liberation and realizes the unconditioned state (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) belonging to this category.

One view holds that while in reality it encompasses both obstacles, the intended meaning of the sūtras and śāstras refers only to the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), because it obstructs the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and is abandoned solely by Bodhisattvas; thus it is called "coarse."
Regarding "the heavy": various teachings differ. The *Saṃtati-sūtra* speaks of eleven faults to be remedied; the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* speaks of eleven pairs;
the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* speaks of relying on the two types of coarse and heavy minds. Although these various teachings differ in their terminology, their meanings do not contradict one another.

This is because, when speaking in terms of seeds, they all agree that the afflictions lack functional capacity (*akarmanya*). Thus, the *She-lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty [states]: [omitted].
Regarding the Mahāyāna, the term "coarse heaviness" (*dausthulya*) as a karmic retribution is self-evident in the True Dharma (the *Tattva*), yet it is not found in the original Sanskrit manuscript.

In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun), there are two interpretations; therefore, the text further states: "The mention of 'coarse heaviness' reveals those two kinds of proclivities (*anuśaya*) or the state of unserviceability (*akarmanyatā*) arising from them.

It is like the statement that the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is abandoned upon entering the two meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*); although the faculty of suffering thus abandoned is not manifest..."
It is called "coarse heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulya*). This case should be understood in the same way. The subsequent mention of "coarse heaviness" should be explained by analogy with this.
In the second bhūmi, there are two types of ignorance: first, the ignorance of subtle transgressions;
second, the ignorance regarding the various courses of action (*karmagati*), along with their corresponding coarse heavinesses, which constitute the objects to be remedied.
The commentary states: Regarding the second [stage], the discernment of the obstacles to the *Vimalā-bhūmi* (the Stainless Stage), there are two interpretations based on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

One says: "The delusion regarding subtle transgressions" refers to a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) [afflictions]; "the delusion regarding various karmic destinies" refers to the three types of action resulting from those aforementioned transgressions.
Another says: "Alternatively, it is simply the delusion regarding the initiation of karma and the lack of understanding regarding karma. To explain: the former...

Both ignorance regarding meaning (*arthamoha*) and the category of ignorance (*mohapakṣa*) are collectively termed "ignorance. Furthermore, according to the subsequent intent, there are two types in their respective order:

first, the ignorance that initiates karma; second, the ignorance that fails to comprehend karma. These two aforementioned ignorances constitute the obstacle of wrong practice (*mithyāpratipatti-āvaraṇa*) among the ten obstacles.
The explanation of the term "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) has already been stated above.
In the third stage, there are two types of delusion: first, the delusion of desire and greed; second, the delusion regarding the perfection of the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining.
Along with their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*), these constitute the objects to be remedied.
The commentary states: Regarding the obstacle to the third stage, the Radiant (*prabhākārī*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "First is the delusion of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-moha*).

This refers to that which obstructs superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*) within this stage. Because it was previously frequently associated with sensual desire, it is called the 'delusion of sensual desire'.

(The explanation notes: In reality, this is an obstacle to the knowable (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*); however, it is termed 'desire' because it is of the same substance as sensual desire. Now, having attained superior concentration and cultivation...
Once that which is to be accomplished has been permanently severed, desire and greed are accordingly subdued, because from beginningless time they have functioned in dependence upon it.
Second is the delusion regarding the perfection of *dhāraṇī*, which is that which obstructs the wisdom of hearing and reflection within this context.
Taken together, these two delusions constitute the obstacle of dullness and rigidity.
In the fourth stage, there are two types of delusion: first, the delusion of attachment to meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and second, the delusion of attachment to phenomena (*dharma*).
These, along with their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*), are the factors to be remedied.
The commentary states: Regarding the obstacle to the fourth stage, the *Jñānālokālaṃkāra* (*Yanhuì dì*) says:

"First, the delusion of attachment to meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), which corresponds here to that which is associated with attachment to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Second, the delusion of attachment to phenomena (*dharma*), which corresponds here to that which is associated with attachment to the Dharma.

These are subsumed under the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Because these two delusions are abandoned, the two attachments of the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*) no longer manifest. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* further states:
This is the fourth among the ten obstacles, the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle afflictions (*sūkṣmakleśa-samudācāra-āvaraṇa*).

It refers to a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) aspect within the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), comprised of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, which co-arises with the sixth consciousness.

It is called "subtle" because it is of the lowest grade, because it does not function as a deliberate object-condition (*amanasikāra-ālambana*), and because it follows along with present activity for a long time. (The commentary explains that the meaning of "subtle" is analyzed through these three points. This explains the fourth [obstacle].
The factors conducive to enlightenment pertaining to the stages are permanently severed upon entering the fourth stage.

This is because they previously arose with the same substance as the innate view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and other afflictions that spontaneously arise within the sixth consciousness; for this reason, they were designated by the name "afflictions.

Now, in the fourth stage, having attained the untainted factors conducive to enlightenment, those [afflictions] are forever extinguished, and these views of self and so forth are likewise [extinguished].

It is never practiced. On the first, second, and third stages, the practice of giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation is similar to that of worldly beings. Only upon the fourth stage, through the cultivation and attainment of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), is it termed "supramundane.
Therefore, it can permanently destroy the two types of view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth. How do we know this [supramundane path] is associated with the sixth consciousness?
For the view of self and other afflictions associated with the seventh consciousness are of a nature and character that are incompatible with the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*).

Because it is contrary [to the path], it does not arise from the eighth bhūmi onward; however, from the seventh bhūmi downward, it can still manifest, as it serves as a basis and support for other afflictions (*kleśa*).
This [affliction] is coarse while those others are subtle; thus, there is a sequence in their suppression. For this reason, it is associated only with the sixth [consciousness].

The mention of "view of a self" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth also includes the beginningless cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), namely attachment to meditative concentration (*samādhi-tṛṣṇā*) and attachment to the Dharma (*dharma-tṛṣṇā*).

That is the craving for the dharma of meditative concentration (*samādhi-dharma-tṛṣṇā*), which still increases even in the third stage; it can only be permanently severed upon entering the fourth stage, because the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) are particularly antithetical to it.
In the fifth stage, there are two types of delusion: first, the delusion of exclusively directing one's attention toward the rejection and turning away from *saṃsāra*.
Second is the delusion of exclusively directing one’s mental attention toward *nirvāṇa*, along with its corresponding *dauṣṭhulya* (coarse heaviness), which serves as the object to be remedied.
The commentary states: "This is the obstacle to the fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*).

As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it refers respectively to those who are weary of *saṃsāra* and delight in *nirvāṇa*. That is to say, among the ten obstacles, this is the fifth: the obstacle regarding *nirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle."

A portion of the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) causes one to loathe birth-and-death and aspire to nirvana, similar to the two lower vehicles’ loathing of suffering and longing for cessation.
These obstruct the path of non-differentiation in the fifth stage; upon entering the fifth stage, they can be permanently severed.

(The commentary explains: The fifth stage takes the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths as its skillful means, entering that path of non-differentiation regarding the defiled and pure causes and effects within the Four Truths. Therefore, it is able to sever both types of delusion that lead toward the two [vehicles].)
In the sixth stage, there are two types of delusion: first, the delusion of directly observing the flow and circulation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
second, the delusion of the frequent manifestation of signs (*nimitta*). These, along with their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*), are the factors to be counteracted.

The commentary states: Regarding the obstacle to the sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "First, the delusion regarding the flow and transformation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as they manifest;
this refers to the grasping at a defiled agent here, because the flow and transformation of conditioned phenomena are subsumed under the defiled portion.

Second, the delusion regarding the frequent manifestation of signs; this refers to the grasping at a pure agent here, because one apprehends pure signs. [This occurs] because the observation of signs is frequent."

[The practitioner] practices, yet is unable to abide for a long time in the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-vipaśyanā*). (The commentary explains: the former delusion clings to the gate of the flow of suffering and its origin; the latter delusion clings to the gate of the pure signs of cessation and the path.

This is precisely the sixth of the ten obstacles, the obstacle of the active manifestation of coarse signs (*sthūla-nimitta-pravṛtti-āvaraṇa*), which refers to a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) aspect within the cognitive obscuration (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).
The active manifestation of coarse signs of defilement and purity constitutes an obstruction to the path of non-defilement and non-purity in the sixth stage;
upon entering the sixth stage, these are permanently extinguished.
In the seventh stage, there are two types of delusion: first, the delusion of the active manifestation of subtle signs; second, the [delusion of... one...

[This refers to] the delusion regarding the skillful means of mental attention (*manasikāra*) directed toward the signless (*animitta*), as well as its corresponding heavy residues (*dausthulya*), which are the objects to be countered.
The commentary states: "The obstacle of the seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (*dūraṃgamā*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "First, the delusion regarding the manifestation of subtle signs;

this is precisely what is meant here by 'clinging to the existence of arising,' because there still exists a subtle sign of arising within the process of saṃsāra. (The explanation states: "Clinging to the existence of the arising of conditions, [which is] arising and ceasing...")

Regarding the phrase "flowing and turning" (*saṃsāra*): in reality, this applies to both [birth and] cessation; however, for the sake of brevity, only the former is mentioned here. Second is the delusion of purely applying mental attention (*manasikāra*) to seek the signless (*animitta*).

This refers to those who cling to the existence of cessation, as they still grasp at the subtle signs of cessation and return (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). (The commentary explains: this means they cling to the signs of the cessation and return of dependent origination.

They apply themselves diligently to the mental attention of the signless alone, yet are unable to give rise to superior practice regarding emptiness (*śūnyatā*). This is the seventh among the ten obstacles.

The obstacle of the manifestation of subtle characteristics refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that involves the manifestation of subtle characteristics, such as grasping at arising and ceasing.
This obstructs the sublime path of signlessness in the seventh stage; upon entering the seventh stage, it can be permanently severed.
In the eighth stage, there are two types of delusion: first, the delusion of applying effort toward the signless;
second, the delusion regarding mastery over signs. These, along with their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*), constitute the objects to be remedied.

The commentary states: Regarding the obstacle to the eighth stage, the Immovable (*acalā-bhūmi*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "First, the delusion regarding the application of effort toward the signless;
second, the delusion regarding mastery over signs, which prevents one from attaining mastery over signs. This also includes [the obstacle to] the Buddha-fields.

Because it is a portion of the [noble] marks, from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, the purely untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) arises spontaneously; therefore, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms never manifest again.

However, subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the seventh consciousness may still arise, as the fruit of the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna-phala*) does not contradict them.

(The commentary explains that "the fruit of the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons" refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) induced by the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons, as well as the meditative absorption of cessation [*nirodha-samāpatti*]). This is the tenth [stage].
The eighth among the hindrances is the obstacle to applying effort toward the signless (*animitta*).

This refers to a portion of the innate aspect (*sahaja*) of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which prevents the signless contemplation from arising spontaneously. In the first five stages (*bhūmi*), contemplations with signs (*nimitta*) are frequent while those without signs are rare;
in the sixth stage, contemplations with signs are rare while those without signs are frequent; and in the seventh stage, it is purely [signless].
Although the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-bhāvanā*) is constantly continuous, it still involves applied effort (*prayoga*).

Because there is applied effort within signlessness, one is not yet able to manifest signs and lands spontaneously (*svarasena*). Such applied effort obstructs the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*) in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*);
therefore, upon entering the eighth stage, one is able to sever it forever. Because it is severed forever, one attains two [mastery].

Mastery. In the ninth stage, there are two types of delusion: first, the delusion regarding mastery over the dhāraṇīs of subsequent wisdom and eloquence concerning immeasurable teachings and immeasurable phrases and syllables;
second, the delusion regarding mastery over eloquence (*pratibhāna*). And...
"That which is coarse and heavy (*dauṣṭhulya*) is the object to be countered.
The commentary states: "This is the obstacle to the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says:

"First, there is the delusion regarding the mastery of the *dhāraṇīs* of wisdom and eloquence concerning the immeasurable teachings, the immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables, and their successive [elaborations]. Regarding the immeasurable...
Mastery over the dhāraṇī of teaching the Dharma refers to the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*);
it is mastery over the retention of that which is expressed, because within a single meaning, all meanings are manifested.

Mastery over the dhāraṇī of immeasurable phrases, names, and syllables refers to the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*); it is mastery over the retention of that which expresses, because within a single [phrase]...

Because all names, phrases, and syllables manifest within every name, phrase, and syllable, one who possesses mastery over the dhāraṇī of subsequent wisdom and discrimination is said to have the unimpeded analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).

This refers to mastery over the retention (*dhāraṇī*) of the successive explanations and definitions of vocal sounds, because within a single sound all sounds are manifested. Second is the delusion regarding mastery over eloquence (*pratibhāna-vaśitā*). Eloquence...
Mastery of eloquence refers to the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), because one skillfully understands the appropriate capacities [of beings] and is adept at teaching them.
Ignorance can obstruct these four kinds of mastery; all such obstacles are subsumed within the ninth obstacle herein. That is, among the ten obstacles, it is the ninth:
the obstacle of lack of desire to engage in the benefit of others. This refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which causes—

Not desiring to apply oneself diligently to the work of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings, but instead delighting in cultivating one's own benefit—this obstructs the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of the ninth stage.
Upon entering the ninth stage, one is able to sever it forever.
In the tenth stage, there are two types of ignorance: first, ignorance regarding great supernormal powers; second, ignorance regarding the realization of subtle secrets.
Along with their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*), these are the factors to be remedied.
The commentary states: Regarding the obstacle of the tenth stage, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "First, the delusion regarding the great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);
this refers to the activities arising from the obstacles within this [stage]. Second, the delusion regarding the realization of subtle secrets;
this refers to the obstacle here to the great cloud of Dharma-knowledge and that which it contains. Thus, among the ten obstacles, the tenth pertains to all...
The obstacle regarding the lack of mastery over phenomena refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that prevents one from attaining mastery over all phenomena.
This obstacle obstructs the great cloud of Dharma-knowledge and the activities arising from its contained treasury belonging to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Upon entering the tenth stage, it can be permanently severed.
In the stage of the Tathāgata, there are two types of ignorance: first, the ignorance of extremely subtle attachment toward the entire sphere of all that is knowable;
second, the ignorance of extremely subtle obstructions and their corresponding coarse residues (*dauṣṭhulya*), which are the objects to be counteracted.
The commentary states: "The eleventh is the obstacle to the stage of a Tathāgata. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says:

"First, there is the delusion of extremely subtle attachment toward all objects of knowledge; this is the 'subtle cognitive obstacle' (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) mentioned here. Second, there is the delusion of extremely subtle obstruction;
this refers to all seeds of spontaneous afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that one attains bodhi..."

At the time of awakening, one suddenly severs the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), thereby becoming an Arhat and attaining the state of a Tathāgata, as one realizes Great Nirvāṇa and Great Bodhi.
Consequently, among the ten obstructions, a single obstruction is separately distinguished within the tenth.

Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* further states this: although one has attained mastery over phenomena in this stage, there remain residual obstacles that prevent it from being called "ultimate.
Specifically, there are innate subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as well as seeds of spontaneously arising afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) manifests, these are all severed instantaneously, and one enters the stage of a Tathāgata. Extensively...
The citations from various scriptures are fully presented in a separate chapter.
Noble son, it is on account of these twenty-two kinds of delusion and eleven kinds of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) that the stages (*bhūmi*) are established.
The commentary states: From here below is the third section, which explains the intent behind [the mention of] ignorance and so forth. This section contains two parts:
first, clarifying the intent behind explaining ignorance and so forth; second, praising bodhi as being free from all fetters. This is the first part.
That is to say, because one wishes to establish the eleven stages (*bhūmi*), the various ignorances and their eleven corresponding heavy obstructions (*dausthulya*) are explained.
"And *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is free from those bonds. The commentary states:
The second [verse] praises supreme awakening as being free from all bonds. This consists of two parts: first, the Buddha’s own statement; [and second, the subsequent explanation].

This was subsequently praised by the Bodhisattva; it is the teaching of the Buddha, referring to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), which is far removed from all delusions and their corresponding heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*).

Again, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is most marvelous and rare, even unto the accomplishment of great benefit and great fruit."
The commentary states: From here below is the second section, the praise of the bodhisattvas. Within this, there are two parts: first, the general, and later, the specific.
