therefore, he now lies down according to their arrangement. Some say it was to demonstrate his distancing from the auspicious customs falsely clung to by the world;
for in that country, when someone dies, they are made to lie upon a bed with their head toward the north.
The Buddha, in order to shatter their false attachment to auspiciousness, therefore commanded that even before his parinirvāṇa, he be laid out lying with his head to the north.
Some say this was intended to manifest the Buddha’s reverence for the True Dharma;

that is to say, because he already knew that after his parinirvāṇa, the unsurpassed torch of the Dharma would blaze fiercely in the northern direction and not be extinguished for a long time, he [lay] upon the bed facing north.
"lay down with his head toward the north. This is explained at length. He further said: "As it is taught:

At that time, the Blessed One approached the prepared bed, lay down on his right side with his right cheek downward, placing one foot upon the other, facing west, with his head toward the north. He remained in the posture of radiance, possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One lie down on his right side? Answer: It was to manifest the Buddha’s... [intention].
Because he lies down like a lion. As stated in the Sūtra, there are four ways of lying down:
namely, the lion king’s way, the way of gods and ghosts, and the way of those addicted to desire. The lion king lies on his right side; the god lies face upward; the ghost lies face downward;
and those addicted to desire lie on their left side with their bodies touching the ground. The Buddha is the unsurpassed lion among men.
Therefore, he lay on his right side. Question: For what reason did the World-Honored One lie down to enter parinirvāṇa rather than sitting?
Answer: It was to demonstrate that the Tathāgata is free from deception. If the Buddha had entered nirvāṇa while sitting, those who lack faith would have said, "This is a mere pretense and madness;
how can a dead person remain sitting upright? Some say it was to prevent future [misconceptions].

Because they slander the noble ones, if those who were to attain parinirvāṇa while sitting were instead to enter nirvāṇa while lying down in this present age, the world would then slander them, saying, "They are not arhats."
If this is so, why did they not enter parinirvāṇa while sitting together? Question: For what reason did the World-Honored One enter parinirvāṇa during the middle watch of the night?
Answer: Because this time is most tranquil. That is to say, that land is hot;
during the day it is unfit for work, and most people perform their various activities during the early and late watches of the night, whereas only the middle watch [is suitable].
[The Buddha] divided [the night]. All was tranquil. Because the Tathāgata always delights in and praises tranquility, he entered parinirvāṇa during the middle watch of the night.
Some say it is because he always delights in practicing the Middle Way.
That is to say, when the Buddha was formerly a bodhisattva, in his final birth among the gods, he dwelt in Tuṣita Heaven, which is situated in the middle [of the celestial realms]. At that time...
In his later life, he resided in the city of Kapilavastu in Central India. During the middle watch of the night, he eluded the city walls to renounce the household life.

He practiced the Middle Way and realized unexcelled enlightenment. For the benefit of sentient beings, he taught the sublime Dharma of the Middle Way, which is free from the extremes of existence and non-existence.
He entered *parinirvāṇa* at the middle watch of the night, and so forth, as explained in detail.

According to the forty-third fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there are ten meanings that manifest *nirvāṇa*: namely, to clarify that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely impermanent;
that all conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) are not secure; to clarify that *parinirvāṇa* is peace and tranquility; and to remain far removed from all... [text truncated]

Because of all fears, and because gods and humans delight in the physical body, [the Buddha] clarifies that the physical body is impermanent and subject to decay, in order to cause them to seek the eternally abiding, pure dwelling-body; he clarifies that the power of impermanence is absolute and irreversible;
he clarifies that conditioned phenomena do not follow one's desires and lack autonomy; and he clarifies that all phenomena within the three realms are like unbaked earthenware vessels.
Because it is not solid; because it is clear that parinirvāṇa is the most real and indestructible;
because it is far removed from saṃsāra and is neither arising nor ceasing. Nirvāṇa is demonstrated by these ten matters. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle three, states:
For what reason does he manifest entry into *nirvāṇa*? It is to cause sentient beings who are indolent to cultivate the path with a diligent mind.

As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, fascicle 568: "Furthermore, there are devas and humans who delight in hearing about perfect quiescence (*parinirvāṇa*); for their sake, the Bodhisattva manifests *parinirvāṇa*.
Thus far has been a brief description of the Tathāgata’s manifestations of transformation; if one were to analyze them extensively, it would be as [described] by the Buddha.
The *Lalitavistara Sūtra*, the *Saṃdarśana Sūtra*, the *Hetupratyaya Sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the *Mahāvyūha Sūtra*, and others—
these are called the Tathāgata’s skillful means in manifesting transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).
